17c36bf15ca9.title: Purpose
17c36bf15ca9.content: Ensure every entry in the bibliography (content/schema/references.ts) is well-formed, reachable, accurately cited, and backed by evidence. The skill operates at two levels: . | Automated pipeline — bun run pipeline/bib-qa.ts evaluates the machine-checkable tags per reference. | Agent-assisted review — when invoked by a collaborator or during QC, the agent performs deeper checks that require network access or content understanding. | . The per-reference QA tag vocabulary, the verification status model and the intake tooling are in bib-qa/qa-tags.md; consult a row when tagging.

512e8b964a3a.title: When to Invoke
512e8b964a3a.content: . | User says “validate bibliography”, “check references”, “bib QA” | During QC review of a chapter or the full paper | When authoring: adding a new ref() entry to references.ts | Before submission / publication readiness checks | .

191910b03060.title: Workflow
191910b03060.content: 1. Generate the QA report . cd content && bun run pipeline/bib-qa.ts # → writes content/bib-qa.json # With URL checking (slower, needs network): cd content && bun run pipeline/bib-qa.ts --check-urls . 2. Review the dashboard . Open ui/bib-qa.html in a browser (served at /folio/bib-qa.html when the folio server is running). The page loads bib-qa.json and displays: . | Summary cards (total, clean, warning, failing) | Filterable/searchable reference list | Per-reference detail panel with QA tags, metadata, citations, and images | Lightbox for screenshot viewing | . 3. Fix issues (agent workflow) . For each failing reference, the agent should: . | Missing URL: Search for the article DOI or URL. Use WebFetch to verify the URL loads. Update references.ts with the URL/DOI. | URL does not resolve: Check if the DOI has changed. Try https://doi.org/<DOI> and common publisher patterns. Update if the canonical URL has moved. | Incomplete metadata: Fill in missing fields (authors, year, journal, publisher) from the article page or CrossRef API: https://api.crossref.org/works/<DOI> . | Uncited reference: Determine if the reference is used somewhere not yet scanned (e.g., a comment, a proof sketch). If genuinely orphaned, flag for author review — do NOT delete without consent. | Missing screenshot: For references where the cited result (theorem, figure, table) is critical to the project’s argument, capture a screenshot of the relevant page/result and save it to content/bib-qa-images/<refid>.png (or .jpg, .pdf). Multiple images: <refid>-1.png, <refid>-2.png. | . 4. Re-run and verify . cd content && bun run pipeline/bib-qa.ts --check-urls . Screenshots are optional for non-critical references.

111e4e91099e.title: File Layout
111e4e91099e.content: content/ schema/references.ts ← Bibliography source of truth (CSL-JSON) pipeline/bib-qa.ts ← QA pipeline script (pass/fail per tag) pipeline/validate-bib.ts ← Comprehensive correctness audit (--doi / --cross-check / --crossref / --arxiv / --pandoc) pipeline/validate-references.ts ← Key-resolution + citation cross-check bib-qa.json ← Generated QA report (gitignored) bib-qa-images/ ← Screenshot evidence <refid>.png ← Named by reference id <refid>-1.png ← Multiple images per reference uploads/ ← Full-paper PDFs / data tables for offline citation verification. <id>.pdf ← One file per cited paper (where publicly downloadable) scripts/ gen-bib-papers-list.py ← Scan references.ts → bib-papers-list.txt bib-papers-list.txt ← Generated batch-intake list upload-bib-papers.sh ← Batch download → commit-per-paper → SSH push → optional gh pr create upload-to-uploads.sh ← Single-file intake (ad-hoc additions) ui/bib-qa.html ← Standalone QA dashboard .

51e8b9f50017.title: Integration with Other Skills
51e8b9f50017.content: | Skill | Integration | . | editor | When adding \cite{} to content, verify the reference exists and passes QA | . | content-validation | The uses-resolve constraint validates \cite{} keys; bib-qa adds deeper checks | . | todo-review | Low-scoring references can generate TodoItems for the author | . | bib-human-review | Human-validated review status drives the verification model | .

077c6774f5f7.title: Adding a New Reference (checklist)
077c6774f5f7.content: When authoring adds a ref() entry: . | Required fields: id, type, title, author, issued | DOI: Include if available (validates format automatically; validate-bib --doi confirms it resolves) | URL: Include direct link to article page (prefer arxiv, numdam, archive.org, or faculty pages — these are the patterns gen-bib-papers-list.py can auto-extract for intake) | Run QA: cd content && bun run pipeline/bib-qa.ts | Cross-check description: When adding -- Ref: [<id>] <desc> to a formal-proof file, include the author surname or a significant title word in <desc> so validate-bib --cross-check confirms the description anchors the entry. Bare theorem/section refs (“Theorem 3.2”) will warn; ideally write “Smith, Theorem 3.2 — uniqueness of …”. | Run validate-bib: cd content && bun run validate-bib --cross-check to confirm no anchor mismatch; pair with --strict in CI. | Local PDF intake (optional but recommended for theorem-citing references): add the paper to scripts/bib-papers-list.txt or place the PDF in uploads/<id>.pdf directly via bash scripts/upload-to-uploads.sh <url-or-local-path>. | Screenshot (Optional): For theorem/result citations, capture the relevant page to content/bib-qa-images/<id>.png. | Cross-check citation site: Ensure \cite{<id>} appears in the relevant .md file or -- Ref: [<id>] in the relevant formal-proof file. | .

b30bfe9a83df.title: Investigating wrong-work resolutions
b30bfe9a83df.content: When validate-bib --cross-check or a code reviewer flags an entry’s metadata as not matching the citation comment, the canonical workflow is: . | Confirm by inspecting uploads/<id>.pdf if present: file uploads/<id>.pdf → real PDFs report “PDF document, version X.X”; landing pages report “HTML document”. HTML files are likely intake failures (numdam landing pages, NIST CGI lookups etc.). | For HTML landing pages: update the URL-pattern logic in scripts/gen-bib-papers-list.py (e.g. numdam.org/item// → /item/.pdf), regenerate `bib-papers-list.txt`, delete the broken `uploads/.pdf`, re-run `upload-bib-papers.sh`. | For wrong-work resolution (entry metadata names a different paper than the citation comment intends): two options — a. Update the entry’s title / author / DOI / issued to match the cited work (the citation comment is canonical), or b. Split the key into <id>a and <id>b and update each citation site to use the right variant. This is an author-judgement call; the bib QA agent should propose a resolution but defer the choice via AskUserQuestion. | .

31425059196f.title: Output Format
31425059196f.content: The bib-qa.json schema: . { "generated": "2026-04-07T...", "totalRefs": 101, "summary": { "pass": 380, "warn": 45, "fail": 12, "unchecked": 68 }, "entries": [ { "id": "einstein1905", "type": "article-journal", "title": "...", "authors": "Albert Einstein", "year": "1905", "url": "https://doi.org/...", "doi": "10.1002/...", "journal": "Annalen der Physik", "tags": [ { "key": "has_url", "label": "Has URL", "status": "pass", "detail": "..." } ], "citedIn": ["content/.../relativity.md"], "images": ["bib-qa-images/einstein1905.png"], "score": 5 } ] } .

0386dd912669.title: Verification status rendered in PDF/HTML
0386dd912669.content: The bib-qa-verifications.json status surfaces in the rendered bibliography (PDF + HTML) via the annotation field in references.bib: . @book{boyd-vandenberghe-2004, author = {…}, title = {{Convex Optimization}}, annotation = {[Verified+Fixed] 18 fixes by 2026-05-19}, } . pipeline/export-bibtex.ts reads content/bib-qa-verifications.json at export time and injects a short status marker per entry. Format: . [] [] [by ] [] . Status symbols: [Verified] — verified-clean (every site checked, no fix) [Verified+Fixed] — fixed (misattributions resolved) [Partial] — partial (some sites verified + fixed) [Pending] — pending (not yet examined) [Uncited] — bib orphan (no citations) [Paper-Mismatch] — local PDF ≠ bib metadata [Unfetchable] — not in uploads/ . Rendering targets: . | LaTeX/biblatex: the annotation field renders via \printfield[brackets]{annotation} in custom styles, or \bibliographystyle{plainnat-annote} for natbib. | Pandoc HTML: CSL templates that include the annote field display it inline; some styles render it as a separate paragraph. | bib-qa.html dashboard: already surfaces the full verification object from bib-qa.json (typed sidecar). | . When adding new entries or updating verification status, regen both: . cd content bun run export-bibtex # → references.bib with annotations bun run pipeline/bib-qa.ts # → bib-qa.json for dashboard .

154fb77a6c81.title: Always cross-check arxiv for mirror preprints
154fb77a6c81.content: When verifying a published-journal paper, check arxiv.org for a free preprint mirror and use it as the uploads/ intake target: it is stable and unpaywalled, its content usually matches the published version (section numbering may differ), and gen-bib-papers-list.py converts arxiv.org/abs/<id> → arxiv.org/pdf/<id>. Workflow when adding/auditing an entry whose primary URL is a publisher landing page (doi.org, journal site, etc.): . | Search the paper title on https://arxiv.org for an arXiv:<id> preprint by the same authors. | If found, add URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/<id> to the references.ts entry (alongside, not instead of, the DOI). | The batch intake picks up the arxiv URL on the next regen. | .

3f2cbb1d6ca6.title: Paper-mismatch class: PDF resolves to wrong content
3f2cbb1d6ca6.content: The gen-bib-papers-list.py URL converter can yield a valid PDF with the WRONG content. Two common cases: . | numdam volume prelims: numdam.org/item/AST_YYYY__VOL__R1_0/ resolves to the volume’s PRELIMINARY PAGES (front matter), NOT a specific chapter. The per-chapter URL pattern is /item/AST_YYYY__VOL__<startpage>_0/ — different starting page per chapter. | archive.org filename guess: archive.org/download/<id>/<id>.pdf works only when the PDF filename inside the item matches the item id. For re-digitised scans where the upload was named differently (<id>_bw.pdf, <id>_text.pdf, an arbitrary stem), the guess fails with 401/503/404. The reliable fix is to consult archive.org/metadata/<id> JSON to discover the actual PDF filename. | . Detection workflow: . | pdftotext -layout -f 1 -l 1 uploads/<id>.pdf and inspect the title page. | Compare the title page to the references.ts entry’s title field. | If they disagree, mark the entry as paper-mismatch in content/bib-qa-verifications.json with a note explaining the downloaded content vs the expected content. | The references.ts URL itself usually needs the fix (not the entry’s bib metadata); update the URL and re-run upload-bib-papers.sh to fetch the correct file. | .

0b95d20f2ec8.title: Cross-citation-content verification workflow
0b95d20f2ec8.content: When verifying a paper against its citation sites, the canonical procedure: . | Extract the PDF from the upload branch: git show origin/claude/upload-bib-papers-<date>:uploads/<file> > /tmp/<id>.pdf. | Read the title page (pdftotext -layout -f 1 -l 1) — confirm the local PDF matches the references.ts entry’s title. | Read the section list (pdftotext -layout + grep for ^[0-9]+\.\s+[A-Z] or ^Section) — identify the chapters / subsections cited. | For each citation site (-- Ref: [<id>] line in a formal-proof file or \cite{<id>} in .md): read the surrounding code/prose to find the specific claim being attributed, then verify the paper covers that claim. Common types: . | Title/scope match: paper title or §N heading verbatim matches the citation text → verified-clean. | §N misattribution: paper has §N but it covers a different topic than the citation says → fix the § number in the citation. | Wrong work: paper covers a different topic entirely → flag as partial / paper-mismatch; defer to author judgement. | . | Update both: content/bib-qa-verifications.json status + docs/coordination/<date>-bib-verification-ledger.md log row. | Commit per-paper (granular history); the bib-qa skill picks up the new status on next bib-qa.ts run. | . Skill outputs: . | bib-qa.json (gitignored, regenerated via cd content && bun run pipeline/bib-qa.ts) carries the verification field on each entry, including status, verified_at, verified_by, fixes_applied, fix_commit, note. | The verification_status QA tag (see bib-qa/qa-tags.md). | .

76e4ccb37ee8.title: bib-qa — the QA tag vocabulary
76e4ccb37ee8.content: Every tag a reference can carry, with what it means and when to apply it.

a2060c080110.title: QA Tags (per reference)
a2060c080110.content: | # | Tag | Auto? | Description | . | 1 | has_url | ✓ | Entry has a URL or DOI-derived URL | . | 2 | url_resolves | ✓* | URL responds with HTTP 2xx AND page contains expected title/author (--check-urls flag) | . | 3 | metadata_ok | ✓ | Title, author(s), year present; type-specific fields complete | . | 4 | cited_in_paper | ✓ | Referenced by \cite{} in .md/.tex or a -- Ref: comment in a formal-proof file | . | 5 | has_screenshot | ✓ | Screenshot exists in content/bib-qa-images/<id>.* | . | 6 | has_local_pdf | ✓ | Full paper PDF / data file present at uploads/<id>*.{pdf,txt} for offline verification | . | 7 | verification_status | ✓ | Per-paper verification record exists in content/bib-qa-verifications.json with status ∈ {verified-clean, partial, fixed}. Pending/uncited/unfetchable/paper-mismatch all warn. | . * ✓* = automated but requires --check-urls flag (makes network requests). Each tag resolves to pass, fail, warn, or unchecked. The score is the count of passing tags. Verification status model (bib-qa-verifications.json) . content/bib-qa-verifications.json is the hand-curated per-paper verification sidecar. bib-qa.ts loads it and surfaces it as the verification_status QA tag and in each entry’s .verification field of bib-qa.json (shown by the bib-qa.html dashboard). “Verified” is separate from bibliographic correctness: it means someone has read the PDF and confirmed the citation sites’ descriptions match the cited paper’s content: . { "entries": [ { "id": "boyd-vandenberghe-2004", "status": "partial", "local_pdf": "uploads/boyd-vandenberghe-2004-convex-optimization.pdf", "verified_at": "2026-05-19T05:50:00Z", "verified_by": "<reviewer>", "fixes_applied": 4, "fix_commit": "66b3caf7f", "note": "§5.5.3→§5.5.2, ..." } ] } . Status values: pending (not yet examined), verified-clean (every citation site checked, no fix needed), partial (some sites verified + fixed, others remain), fixed (misattributions resolved), pending-placement (author wants to keep the reference but hasn’t decided where to cite it yet; tag passes the verification_status QA check), uncited (bib entry has zero consumers AND author hasn’t claimed it; decision pending), paper-mismatch (local PDF ≠ references.ts metadata; escalate), unfetchable (not in uploads/). Author triage moves an uncited entry to pending-placement (or verified-clean if a citation is added in the same triage). The verification_status tag passes for verified-clean / partial / fixed, warns for pending / uncited / unfetchable, and fails for paper-mismatch. When verifying a paper: . | Update the entry’s status, verified_at, verified_by, fixes_applied, fix_commit in content/bib-qa-verifications.json. | Append a row to the “Verification log” table of docs/coordination/<date>-bib-verification-ledger.md. | Commit both with any -- Ref: fixes, one commit per paper. | Re-run cd content && bun run pipeline/bib-qa.ts to regenerate bib-qa.json. | . Intake & local evidence (uploads/ workflow) . The uploads/ directory holds full-paper PDFs and data tables for offline verification of citation correctness. Once a paper is in uploads/, the has_local_pdf tag passes, and reviewers can verify: . | That the -- Ref: [<id>] comment’s free-text description (e.g. “Theorem 3.2 (Pieri rule for SYT)”) actually matches the cited paper’s content, | That the entry’s title, author, issued.year resolve to the same work the citation comments describe (catches wrong-work mismatches where the metadata names a different paper than the citation intends). | . Batch intake pipeline . | Tool | Purpose | . | scripts/gen-bib-papers-list.py | Scan content/schema/references.ts for entries with publicly-downloadable URLs (arxiv, numdam, archive.org, OEIS, faculty pages); emit scripts/bib-papers-list.txt | . | scripts/bib-papers-list.txt | Generated list, one entry per line: <url>\|<target>\|<description> | . | scripts/upload-bib-papers.sh | Read the list, download each file (idempotent by file existence), commit per-paper to a fresh claude/upload-bib-papers-<utc-ymd> branch via SSH; optional --pr to auto-open PR | . | scripts/upload-to-uploads.sh | Single-file intake for ad-hoc additions (manual sources, scans, guidelines etc.) | . Run from any clone with network access: . python3 scripts/gen-bib-papers-list.py # regenerate the list bash scripts/upload-bib-papers.sh --dry-run # preview bash scripts/upload-bib-papers.sh --pr # download + commit + push + open PR . The script pushes with git push --force-with-lease, so a re-run replaces the prior branch tip. MCP services for intake + reaudit . If .mcp.json ships paper/scholar MCP servers and the session’s network policy allows arxiv.org / api.openalex.org, use them. Where the allowlist blocks those hosts they fail soft: use the offline pipeline above (gen-bib-papers-list.py + upload-bib-papers.sh) and run the download on a normal-network machine. The servers are an accelerator, not a replacement. | Server (.mcp.json key) | Tools (most useful) | Use for | . | paper-search-mcp | search_arxiv, search_pubmed, search_biorxiv, search_medrxiv, search_google_scholar, download_arxiv, read_arxiv_paper | Find arxiv preprints by title for URL-missing entries; bulk-download to uploads/; pull parsed paper text for validate-bib --cross-check cross-references | . | openalex-paper-search | OpenAlex get_work, search_works, get_work_citations, get_work_references, author disambiguation | Fill metadata gaps for DOI-only refs (canonical title/author/year/venue); resolve wrong-work mismatches via author IDs; citation-network mapping | . Workflows that gain leverage from these servers . | URL backfill for no-URL entries (offline-prep, network-only step is the actual fetch): . # Pseudo-code; run from a session with arxiv.org allowed. for entry in references.ts where entry.url is None and entry.type in {"article-journal","article"}: hits = paper_search_mcp.search_arxiv(query=entry.title, max_results=3) if best_match(hits, entry).confidence > 0.8: propose entry.url = hits[0].url # human reviewer accepts . | Verification cross-check — for any entry in bib-qa-verifications.json whose status is partial or pending, read_arxiv_paper(arxiv_id) returns the parsed body. Grep the cited -- Ref: [<id>] <description> keywords against that body to confirm the description anchors a real passage. | Author-ID-based wrong-work resolution — when a single bib key citation-splits across two unrelated works, OpenAlex author IDs cleanly disambiguate them. | Metadata enrichment for paywalled entries — for doi.org URLs we can’t fetch, OpenAlex get_work(doi=…) returns canonical title/author/year/venue without paywall, filling references.ts gaps without downloading the PDF. | . Local CLI wrapper for both paths: a CLI such as cat-harness-tools/adapters/bib-mcp-cli.py can drive the same paper-search-mcp / pyalex libraries without an MCP server, from a normal-network machine: . # Prereqs (one-time): pip install paper-search-mcp pyalex pip install playwright && playwright install chromium # for scholar-snapshot # Status — probes network, lists what's possible: cat-harness-tools/adapters/bib-mcp-cli.py status # Backfill URLs for no-URL entries (dry-run by default): cat-harness-tools/adapters/bib-mcp-cli.py backfill-urls # propose cat-harness-tools/adapters/bib-mcp-cli.py backfill-urls --apply # write to references.ts # Download missing arxiv PDFs: cat-harness-tools/adapters/bib-mcp-cli.py download --apply # Enrich DOI-only entries with OpenAlex canonical metadata: cat-harness-tools/adapters/bib-mcp-cli.py enrich-doi --apply # Capture HTTP 'as-viewed-on' evidence pages (HTML/PDF + SHA-256): cat-harness-tools/adapters/bib-mcp-cli.py snapshot --apply # Capture Google Scholar / Books preview PDFs via headless Chromium: cat-harness-tools/adapters/bib-mcp-cli.py scholar-snapshot --apply # Run all of the above in dry-run mode: cat-harness-tools/adapters/bib-mcp-cli.py audit . Each subcommand is idempotent (re-running skips entries already done), and fails fast when the required host is denied. The snapshot / scholar-snapshot outputs land in content/bib-qa-evidence/<refid>/ as <utc>-<source>.{html,pdf} + <utc>-<source>.meta.json (the “as-viewed-on” provenance record), which a reviewer can check without re-fetching. validate-bib — comprehensive correctness audit . pipeline/validate-bib.ts is the umbrella correctness audit (complement to validate-refs which is just key-resolution). Five selectable modes: . | Flag | Mode | Network? | . | --doi | HEAD/GET each DOI via doi.org with proper User-Agent; expect 301/302 (success redirect) or 200; warn on 4xx/5xx | ✓ doi.org | . | --cross-check | Parse -- Ref: [<id>] <desc> comments in formal-proof files; warn when neither the entry’s author surname nor any significant title word appears in the description | ✗ | . | --crossref | Fetch api.crossref.org/works/<DOI> per entry; compare canonical title/author/year against the entry | ✓ api.crossref.org | . | --arxiv | Resolve arxiv.org URLs for entries whose URL field is on arxiv.org | ✓ arxiv.org | . | --pandoc | Pipe a sample LaTeX citation through pandoc-citeproc; verify the rendered output is well-formed (catches missing CSL fields) | ✗ (needs pandoc binary) | . | --all | Run all five | ✓ | . | --strict | Exit non-zero on any failure (default: warn-only) | n/a | . Network requirement: --doi / --crossref / --arxiv modes need outbound HTTPS to doi.org / api.crossref.org / arxiv.org respectively. Behind an allowlist-only proxy they report uniform 403s and validate nothing; run them from a normal-network machine. The --cross-check heuristic uses a small set of tunable parameters (prose word threshold, title-word length threshold, stopword list) documented inline in validate-bib.ts.

e3d54aa38f0c.doc: Block actions: [edit] and [feedback] on every block
e3d54aa38f0c.title: Block actions: [edit] and [feedback] on every block
e3d54aa38f0c.content: A reader who finds something wrong in a block is one click from proposing the fix or saying what is wrong, and the click lands on the block, not on the repository. The links are per block, because a block is what a comment, a change-set and an edit are about. The code is folio-assistant-core/scripts/block-actions.ts; the Tool is block-actions; the document build (build-document-site.ts) draws the links on every labelled block, and the public-comment overlay adds the issues that already discuss the block.

e9fa7b7173bc.doc: Block actions: [edit] and [feedback] on every block
e9fa7b7173bc.title: What each link does
e9fa7b7173bc.content: | link | opens | what the person does next | . | ✎ edit | the block’s source (folio/<doc>/<chapter>/<root>.md, or its .ts if it has no .md) in GitHub’s editor, on main | edits and proposes the change; GitHub makes the branch and the pull request, which is reviewed like any content change (content-change-review.bpmn) | . | 📣 feedback | a new issue about the block | describes the problem; the issue is intake, and a public-comment folio triages it like any other comment (public-comment skill) | . | discussed in #n | the issue of each change-set the block’s comments are in | joins the existing discussion instead of opening a duplicate | .

478a429b8510.doc: Block actions: [edit] and [feedback] on every block
478a429b8510.title: Every issue is coded with its content
478a429b8510.content: [feedback] codes the issue with the slug of the document it came from: the title reads Feedback [dpi-h-ra]: <section> — <block> and the body opens with **Content:** \dpi-h-ra``. A folio with several documents, or a repository that takes issues about more than one thing, can then sort feedback by what it is about without opening it. The code is in the title rather than only a label because GitHub silently drops a prefilled label when the reporter has no triage rights, and most public reviewers do not.

6b4343064309.doc: Block actions: [edit] and [feedback] on every block
6b4343064309.title: The issue form is the folio’s, and optional
6b4343064309.content: With no form, [feedback] opens a blank issue whose body already says which block, which section, the source link and the block’s address on the site. It works on day one. A folio that wants structured feedback adds a GitHub issue form at .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/block-feedback.yml (start from the shared templates/issue-forms/block-feedback.yml, whose answers the drafting review sheet imports: skill review-sheet-script) (another name with --issue-template). The link then names the form and prefills only the fields the form declares, matched by id: . | field id | filled with | . | block | the block’s label (its anchor) | . | section | the heading the block is under | . | source | the block’s source path in the repository | . | page | the page it renders on | . | url | the block’s address on the published site (needs --site-url) | . | content | the document’s slug, the code the issue is triaged by | . A form may declare any subset, and fields it does not declare are not sent. Add the questions you want answered (what is wrong, a suggested wording, the reviewer’s organisation) as further fields; they are left for the person.

04ee68dc1049.doc: Block actions: [edit] and [feedback] on every block
04ee68dc1049.title: Where the repository comes from
04ee68dc1049.content: GITHUB_REPOSITORY in CI, else the checkout’s origin when it is on GitHub, else --github <owner/repo>. No repository, no links: a page with no links is honest, a page with broken ones is not. --no-block-actions turns them off for a build that should have none.

10a5a088ade4.doc: Block actions: [edit] and [feedback] on every block
10a5a088ade4.title: Two forms of the same links
10a5a088ade4.content: . | Full (blockActionsHtml): every href written into the page. Used on a one-page document and on index.hydrated.html, so the links work without JavaScript. | Compact (compactActionsHtml + compactActionsScript): the block’s facts as data attributes, and the hrefs built in the browser when a pointer or focus reaches them. Used on a lazy page’s shell, where a prefilled URL per block would bloat the page. The browser builder, BLOCK_URLS_JS, is held equal to editUrl and feedbackUrl by block-actions.test.ts; change both together or the test fails. | . The recipe lives in the harness, cat-harness-tools/src/core/edit-links.ts, so every layer can use it; this package re-exports it. It is published once as assets/js/edit-links.js (held equal to the code by a test). On a page, mark a link data-fa-link="edit|source|feedback" and either give its host the facts (data-src, optional data-repo, data-line, data-block, data-sec) or leave a GitHub blob/edit href, which the runtime reads the facts from. Generators that write Markdown use markdownEditLink. Three places keep their own link on purpose: the public-comment dashboard’s Discuss (it opens a change-set discussion, not feedback on a block), the bootstrap site’s Improve this page (bootstrap-tools may import nothing outside itself), and an IG page’s per-section ✎ / 📣 (SOURCE_LINKS_JS in build-ig-site.ts): a section’s heading can live in an included file, and its issue is titled after the section with the page apart. The IG page’s own Edit this page link does use the recipe. Any page that shows edit or feedback links uses these, not a URL of its own: one recipe, so a change to the issue form or the branch reaches every page at once.

c422b1faec0b.doc: Block actions: [edit] and [feedback] on every block
c422b1faec0b.title: In the library: edit opens the folio, never the source
c422b1faec0b.content: A library entry is a frozen source: the version published for public comment stays in library/ exactly as circulated, and the changes the review asks for are made in folio/. So the library’s Document view (cat-harness-tools/scripts/lib/library-document.ts, drawn by the platform viewer and by build-library-site.ts on a folio’s site) shows: . | link | on | opens | . | source | the document, each section | the library’s own file on GitHub, read-only | . | 📣 feedback | the document, each section | an issue coded with the entry: Feedback [<entry>]: <section> | . | ✎ edit | each section, and its contents row | the FIRST folio block of the folio section MATERIALISED from it | . A section is matched to the folio by its number, else its title, through the folio-review-anchors/v1 file whose library names the entry. A section the folio has no counterpart for (a PDF’s front matter) gets no ✎ edit, because a guessed link would open the wrong block. The platform’s own library has no materialisation, so it shows source and feedback only. bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/build-library-site.ts --repo <folio> --out _site publishes a folio’s library at <out>/folio-assistant-core/<library dir>/<entry>/, the same <base>/<handler>/<kind>/<subject> route every viewer follows.

11c3fd001b23.doc: Block actions: [edit] and [feedback] on every block
11c3fd001b23.title: Using it as an agent
11c3fd001b23.content: # one block's links, to hand a reader bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/block-actions.ts --repo <folio> --block prose:1-1-4-a8e0b3 # every block's, as JSON bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/block-actions.ts --repo <folio> . When someone in a chat says “this paragraph is wrong”, give them the block’s feedback link, not the repository’s issue page, and the edit link if they can propose the wording themselves.

01b6a6070ef8.doc: Block actions: [edit] and [feedback] on every block
01b6a6070ef8.title: What not to do
01b6a6070ef8.content: . | Do not point [edit] at the frozen review version under library/. Comments cite it, so it is never edited; the folio’s blocks are. | Do not point [edit] at the staging branch. An edit is a proposal to the published text, so it starts from main; a different branch is an explicit --edit-branch. | Do not hand-write issue URLs in a folio’s pages. They drift when a block is renamed; the build recomputes them from the manifests every time. | .

4f09f6998b92.title: Block Change Summary
4f09f6998b92.content: Skill id: block-change-summary · Package: content-lifecycle-ext · Refines delivery-summary for content folios. When delivering changes in a content folio (alongside the server restart command, commit/diff links, and staging links from delivery-summary), list every content block that changed, with a clickable link and a short explanation of what changed.

e0d8fe263fce.title: 1. How to find changed blocks
e0d8fe263fce.content: Extract labels from changed content blocks: the .ts manifest, the .md content and whatever sibling file the content type adds (a .md-only edit is still a block change). Add the content type’s sibling extensions to the pathspec; a paper folio, for example, adds 'content/**/*.lean': . # Collect changed content files (any sibling triggers the block) changed=$(git diff origin/main..HEAD --name-only -- \ 'content/**/*.ts' 'content/**/*.md' \ | grep -v '/rendered/' | grep -v 'schema/' | grep -v 'pipeline/') # For each, resolve to the sibling .ts and pull the label for f in $changed; do ts="${f%.*}.ts" [ -f "$ts" ] || continue label=$(grep -oP "label:\s*['\"]\\K[^'\"]+" "$ts" 2>/dev/null || echo "") [ -n "$label" ] && echo "$ts|$label" done | sort -u .

ad395a1d52ad.title: 2. Link format
ad395a1d52ad.content: The viewer runs on localhost:<viewer_port> (from the instance’s viewer configuration). Each block links via its label anchor: . http://localhost:8080/assistant/#<label> .

7a2496048a5c.title: 3. Presentation format
7a2496048a5c.content: Group by chapter. Use a markdown table with columns: Block (a GitHub blob link to the block’s .md file, always), Siblings changed (blob links to the .ts or the content type’s other siblings, only those that also changed), What changed (1-line description). Never make a sibling the primary link: readers want narrative first. | Block | Siblings changed | What changed | . | def:central-object | ts | Updated notation | . | sec:scope | — | Added first SVG render | . Viewer anchor links (http://localhost:8080/assistant/#<label>) may be added as a row-end column when the folio-assistant is running locally; the .md blob URL is the canonical reference.

d6d80e3c99e5.title: 4. GitHub blob links — ALWAYS PROVIDE
d6d80e3c99e5.content: Every created or modified file (.md, .ts, siblings, config files) gets a blob URL on the pushed branch: . https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/blob/<branch>/<relative-path> . Never report “created/edited foo.md” without it. If the branch is not yet pushed, say so; do not give a URL that will 404.

f90cddc33b08.title: 5. Categorize changes
f90cddc33b08.content: Explain the nature of changes — don’t just list files. Common categories: . | Narrative edit: .md content was modified | Re-rendered SVG: notation/style change caused SVG hash update | New SVG render: block got its first rendered SVG | Structural change: label, uses[], a sibling reference, or kind changed | New block: entirely new content block added | .

9de1d8bbcb96.title: Example block table in a delivery summary
9de1d8bbcb96.content: Combined with delivery-summary and staging-review: . Changed content blocks . Chapter 1: . | Block | Siblings changed | What changed | . | def:central-object | ts | Rewrote point 3 for clarity | . | rule:main-criterion | — | Re-rendered SVG (notation update) | . | sec:scope | — | Added first SVG render | .

055037d9f921.title: Block Density — Topic Coherence and Table Extraction Skill

6a561f2cb37c.title: Purpose
6a561f2cb37c.content: Every content block should be atomic: one topic, one concept, one result. This skill detects blocks that violate atomicity and proposes concrete splits.

ed911fab72cf.title: When to Use
ed911fab72cf.content: . | “block density” / “block audit” / “topic coherence” | “split blocks” / “oversized blocks” / “long blocks” | “extract tables” / “large tables” / “table audit” | Before a release or after bulk content creation | When reviewing new or significantly changed content | .

604c6cf4e236.title: Rules
604c6cf4e236.content: A content type supplies its own block-kind rules. The layer that ships a content type specifies which statement kinds forbid inlined large tables and which long-form block kinds admit length exceptions, and links down to this skill from its side. R1 — Single-topic blocks . A block should address one logical unit: . | A definition defines one thing. | A formal claim or rule block states one result or requirement. | A remark interprets one statement. | . If a block’s .md content addresses multiple distinct topics (detectable by keyword analysis showing stronger affinity to a different chapter than its home chapter), it should be split. The child blocks may belong in different chapters. Example: A block in chapter-a/ that spends 3 paragraphs on topic A and 5 paragraphs on an unrelated topic B should be split: the topic-A material stays in chapter-a, the topic-B material moves to the chapter and section where topic B is the primary subject. R2 — Block length limit . Blocks exceeding 40 non-blank lines (~2/3 of a printed page) are candidates for splitting. This is a soft limit — some blocks (such as worked examples or extended derivations permitted by the content type) legitimately need more space. But any block over 40 lines should be reviewed. R3 — Table extraction (STRICT) . Tables with more than 5 data rows (excluding header and separator) must not be inlined in a remark, definition, example, or any of the content type’s formal statement block kinds. Instead: . | Extract the table to a new table block with kind: "table". | Give it a label like tbl:<parent-block>-data. | Add an .md file containing the table content. | Reference the table from the parent block via uses: ["tbl:..."]. | Add the new table block to the same section in the chapter manifest. | . Rationale: Large tables break the reading flow of formal statements. They should be independently labelled and cross-referenceable. Exceptions: . | Index and appendix tables that are inherently tabular — those may remain as-is or be converted to table blocks. | Blocks whose kind is already "table" are exempt. | . R4 — Placement of split children . When splitting a block, each child block should be placed in the chapter and section where its content topically belongs, not necessarily where the parent lived. Use the content-graph skill’s forward-reference analysis to find the optimal placement.

6939ca3ca096.title: Analysis Script
6939ca3ca096.content: cd content && python3 pipeline/block-density-audit.py [folio-dir] . The script reports three categories: . | Large tables (HIGH) — tables >5 rows inside non-table blocks | Oversized blocks (MEDIUM) — blocks >40 non-blank lines | Multi-topic blocks (LOW) — blocks with stronger keyword affinity to a different chapter than their home | .

e210aa2f600a.title: Workflow
e210aa2f600a.content: . | Run the audit script. | Triage findings by severity (HIGH → MEDIUM → LOW). | For each HIGH finding (large table), propose a table block extraction. | For each MEDIUM finding (oversized), review content and propose split if multiple topics are present. | For each LOW finding (multi-topic), check whether the block should move or split. | Get user approval before making changes. | After changes, re-run the audit to confirm improvement. | .

8e81259b9547.title: Integration
8e81259b9547.content: A content type’s own skills are named by the layer that ships the type, which links down to this one; this table names only what every folio has. | After this skill | Use next | . | Before creating a block | content-graph PR1–PR7 — placement checklist | . | Feature branch ready to merge | /prepare-merge (slash command) — upstream check + density audit + one-voice | . | Split a block | the content type’s validation skill (check the new blocks validate) | . | Move a child block | content-graph (check forward refs improved) | . | Extract a table | the content type’s validation and rendering-audit skills | .

7fc74217e50d.title: Blocked build dependencies — read the refusal before you work around it
7fc74217e50d.content: Outbound HTTPS from an agent container goes through a proxy. A failed download looks the same from a build log whatever caused it, and the three causes have nothing in common: . | what you see | what it is | what to do | . | CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403, curl 000 | policy: the environment’s network settings deny the host | nothing in the container fixes it. Say which host, point the person at the environment’s network settings, or hand the step to an agent that has the access (below) | . | HTTP 429 Too Many Requests | the upstream is rate-limiting the shared egress address | use a mirror of the same content (below). Retrying the same host usually fails again | . | timeouts, 5xx | the host, or the route to it | retry with backoff, then try a mirror | . Ask the proxy, not the log. curl -sS "$HTTPS_PROXY/__agentproxy/status" lists recentRelayFailures with the host and the kind of refusal; a connect_rejected there is policy, full stop. Never disable TLS verification or unset the proxy to get past any of these.

e2e508a67d58.title: Maven Central through a 429
e2e508a67d58.content: Measured 2026-10-06, building Grobid from source: . | host | result | . | repo.maven.apache.org | 429 — Gradle’s default mavenCentral(); the build failed in 28 s | . | repo1.maven.org | 200 (intermittently 429 earlier the same hour) | . | maven-central.storage-download.googleapis.com | 200 — Google’s mirror of Maven Central | . | plugins.gradle.org, services.gradle.org | 200 | . Gradle: pass the init script, which repoints every repository and plugin lookup at the mirror without touching the project’s build files: ./gradlew build --init-script cat-harness-tools/scripts/gradle-maven-mirror.init.gradle . With it the same Grobid build succeeded in 3 min 45 s. -Dmaven.mirror=<url> picks another mirror. Maven: the equivalent is a <mirror> in ~/.m2/settings.xml with <mirrorOf>central</mirrorOf> and the same URL. Do not commit the mirror into a project’s build files. The 429 is a property of this egress path, not of the project; CI runners reach Maven Central directly.

d75aa81d85b4.title: Hosts that are policy, not load
d75aa81d85b4.content: Measured from the same container on the same day — re-check before relying on it, because the policy is the environment’s and can change: . | huggingface.co: denied (403 on CONNECT). Model weights live there (Nougat, most transformer checkpoints). The code installs from PyPI; the weights do not. | codeload.github.com archives: denied. github.com release assets were denied on 2026-10-06 and answered 200 on 2026-10-09 — re-check, and prefer finding-software’s pinned, checksummed release rung when it is open. git clone over HTTPS works either way. | PyPI and npm: open. | . A change to the environment’s network settings may not reach a container that is already running. When it does not, hand the step to an agent that has the access rather than stall: open a work item whose steps run end to end without this session (install, run, the exact scoring command, where the result goes), and give the person a one-line instruction of the form “do bean X on branch Y of repo Z” (agent-handoff). Code the step needs, such as a reader for the tool’s saved output, lands first, in this session, so the other agent only runs the tool.

0d3811b6d2be.title: Running code from outside the repository
0d3811b6d2be.content: Cloning and building a third-party project is running code nobody here wrote. Do it only when the person has asked for that tool by name, keep it under the scratch directory rather than the repository, and commit only what reads its OUTPUT. A session’s permission check may refuse the clone until the person says to go ahead.

fc454f4fa01b.title: Relationship first, visualisation later
fc454f4fa01b.content: Treat a board like the OMG specifications treat BPMN layout: relationship first, visualisation later. BPMN separates the semantic model — bpmn:process, its tasks and its flows — from Diagram Interchange: BPMNDiagram, BPMNShape, BPMNEdge, which say where each of those was drawn. They are two documents about one subject, and the layout one points at the semantic one, never the other way. A folio board is the same shape: . semantic model notes, anchors, content nodes what is true diagram interchange board-positions.json where it was drawn .

95060a98dd3e.title: What follows
95060a98dd3e.content: A folio is complete with no board. Deleting every board loses layout and no content. That is the test to apply when you are unsure whether something belongs on the board or in the folio: if losing it would lose a fact, it is not layout. A note carries no x, no y, no board, no position — for the same reason a BPMN task carries no coordinates: layout lives on top of notes, not as data within them. One note may sit on several boards, at different places, without the note arbitrating between them. A coordinate on the note could not express that; a layer above it does so for free. An orphan is swept from the LAYER, which is the easy direction: one file, one pass, and nothing edited out of a note a person owns.

3fb3e09eb559.title: The arrow, and how it is kept
3fb3e09eb559.content: folio ──▶ board ──▶ position ──▶ note allowed note ──▶ position / board / folio REFUSED . This is a property a future edit can break silently, so it is checked rather than described. schemas/board-positions.test.ts asserts two things against the SOURCE: . | no field named x, y, board or position appears in todo.ts, carried-note.ts, landing-sticky.ts or note-anchor.ts; | board-positions.ts imports zod and nothing else — it names notes by id, and an id needs no type from the layer below. | . The first guards the failure that actually happens: somebody adding coordinates to a note “for convenience”, which makes a content node carry state and gives one note two answers on two boards.

dea311c6d1c1.title: Two graph typologies, because they are two things
dea311c6d1c1.content: | kind | holds | what it is | . | boards | content | what a board is and what it shows | . | board-positions | state | where each note was drawn | . content-context-and-state-graphs refuses a content node that carries state, which is the same rule one level up. And check:graph-typology-work asks a sharper question of the second: it is state, written by a running process every time somebody moves a note — but state that records a position in a PROCESS is work, and state that records a position on a CANVAS is not. Both kinds declare recordsWork: false.

84fb3d04ef2a.title: A board declares what it SHOWS, and absent means everything
84fb3d04ef2a.content: schemas/ui/board.ts: an optional filter over pages and kinds, OR within an axis and AND across them. Absent is the default and it means the whole folio — a query rather than a stored list, because a list of content nodes needs something to notice that a listed node was renamed and that a new one was never added, and a query has nothing to fall behind. Every harness above the floor has a board filled with all contents, which is the absent filter — so the minimal board and the total board are the same document.

ca28d1e8b5dc.title: Mergeability is the reason for the shape, and its limit is stated
ca28d1e8b5dc.content: Positions are the most concurrently-edited state a folio has: two sessions moving two notes is the ordinary case. So the document is sorted and indented, one note per line-block, and the sort is idempotent — a writer that reshuffled on save would conflict with every other save. It is a partial fix. Two notes that sort adjacent still conflict, because the inserted lines overlap. This removes the guaranteed conflict, not every conflict, and it should not be trusted further than that.

ad40fd89522e.title: What this skill is NOT
ad40fd89522e.content: Not the rendering. How a board draws, when a card becomes its avatar and what an open window does are board-windows. Not the tiles. Which boards and viewers a reader can reach is harness-tiles.

32018a1bff2b.title: Processes that run this skill
32018a1bff2b.content: | process | step(s) that name it | . | Board: place a note | Write the note into the folio — with no coordinate; Record x,y for this note on THIS board; Sweep positions whose note is gone | . | Board: relocate content to the trashcan | Relocate the content to the trashcan; Drop its positions and sweep orphans | .

49d374d4140a.doc: Start in the avatar, open into a window
49d374d4140a.title: Start in the avatar, open into a window
49d374d4140a.content: Everything starts as its avatar, and [x] closes a window back to it. Opening projects a window onto the board; selecting any part of a window raises it. Each content kind controls its own avatar and rendering, and opens into a full-screen panel with fixed controls such as [x], [linksrc] or [edit].

515bfc3e7fe8.doc: Start in the avatar, open into a window
515bfc3e7fe8.title: TWO mechanisms, and conflating them is the defect
515bfc3e7fe8.content: |   | trigger | who | . | semantic zoom | the card’s rendered width crosses a declared threshold | automatic | . | open / close | [x], or opening a card | a person | . An open window is not a zoom state: it is projected onto the board rather than being the card grown large, so it survives zooming out. Only [x] closes it. Collapsing the two gives a board where a card can close itself with no action taken, and where [x] and a zoom-out are indistinguishable. Semantic zoom is the GLASS’s, not the board’s . Every board slot — a landing sticky and a todo sticky alike — is one component: the same closed square tile (--fa-sticky-tile-size) with the theme’s faded art, and the same compact icon row underneath it. A slot is its closed tile at every width, so semantic zoom does not run on the board. It decides what a card shows on the folio glass, where a card is resized freely. Do not add a width observer to the board grid: it would be a zoom with nothing to change, and the next agent would read it as the card’s state.

fc3431314d23.doc: Start in the avatar, open into a window
fc3431314d23.title: One sticky, one icon row, in one order
fc3431314d23.content: Under every sticky, on every panel: view, edit, pin, send to fsh-guts, as icon buttons. An icon-only control carries aria-label (what a screen reader announces) AND title (the same words on hover); they are not interchangeable. No control sits inside the card body. The open window’s bar uses the same icons for the same acts. A link the sticky cannot serve is absent, never dead.

ba1e9ee92106.doc: Start in the avatar, open into a window
ba1e9ee92106.title: Pin is a toggle onto the FOLIO glass
ba1e9ee92106.content: There is one store answering “what is on my glass”: the folio. A second store holding a page-level copy of the card gets no glass tools, no folio geometry and no shelve, and has to be special-cased by the glass filter and count. | Pin makes the sticky a folio asset — todo/<id> (the key the glass’s own Todos panel pulls a todo out under, so the two ways onto the glass agree) or landing/<slot> — with shown: true, drawn by the glass’s own card path and placed by placeOnGlass. A landing sticky’s theme, picture URL and text travel in the entry as data, never as stored markup. | Unpin is shelveFromGlass — the middle of the three states below. The entry stays; the same pin puts it back, where the reader left it. | The pressed state is the store’s answer (folioStateOf(key) === "glass"), never the button’s memory. The glass’s own × shelves too, and the row’s pin follows it. | .

b6fd93fef22d.doc: Start in the avatar, open into a window
b6fd93fef22d.title: Send to fsh-guts asks first
b6fd93fef22d.content: A control a reader has to ask about has not said what it does, so discard is named for where it goes (Send to fsh-guts, the trashcan that is kept) and opens a confirmation that names the sticky, says it is restorable and per-browser, and says where it is restored from — the fish in the navbar’s icon row. Focus starts on Cancel; Cancel and Escape do nothing but close it. A dialog whose dismissal performs the act did not ask. The window bar’s send is the same act and takes the same confirmation. The inverse is Restore in fsh-guts.

5823143b6575.doc: Start in the avatar, open into a window
5823143b6575.title: The threshold is declared, inherited, and traceable
5823143b6575.content: schemas/kg/semantic-zoom.ts (instance data: semantic-zoom.json): a folio default (belowPx) with a per-kind override (byKind) — the repository’s inheritance rule (inherit everything, override anything; a variant states only what it CHANGES). So: . | the folio always has a number, and every kind resolves to one; | a kind that states nothing is complete, not invalid — requiredness is checked after resolution, never on the declaration; | an override carries a required because, and the resolver returns the source alongside the value, so a reviewer can tell a deliberate override from a folio default that does not fit. | . The boundary is stated once. Strictly below the number, so the declared width is the last one that still shows words. A boundary written one way in a comment and the other way in the renderer makes a card flicker.

2f14e73fefb5.doc: Start in the avatar, open into a window
2f14e73fefb5.title: Z-order: selecting any part raises
2f14e73fefb5.content: Windows stack, and selecting any part of one raises it — not a title bar, any part, because a reader who clicks into a window’s content has already said which one they mean. Z-order is session-only. The DI layer carries no z: a committed stacking order would make every raise a file write and every two sessions a conflict, on the most concurrently-edited state a folio has. If that proves wrong, z is one optional field in the positions document.

17ccb54c3ef5.doc: Start in the avatar, open into a window
17ccb54c3ef5.title: The chrome is fixed; the kind fills it in
17ccb54c3ef5.content: A content kind declares which controls it offers, and the platform fixes the frame: . | [x] is always present and always in the same place, so a reader learns the frame once; | a declared control that names nothing known is a finding, not a missing button; | a control the environment cannot perform is hidden, and the reason reported — a dead [edit] 404s for exactly the reader who cannot edit, which reads as “this page is broken” rather than “you cannot do this”. | .

6a9d03c58eff.doc: Start in the avatar, open into a window
6a9d03c58eff.title: Closing must have a reachable inverse
6a9d03c58eff.content: An action whose inverse is not reachable is not a toggle. On an overlay, close may set hidden, because the launcher tile re-opens it. On a board that IS page content, hidden removes a section of the page, so the inline board collapses to a control in its own position, and focus follows it — left alone, focus lands on <body> and the keyboard position is gone. A control two clicks deep inside a collapsed launcher does not count as reachable. A default of “hidden” is allowed only with the inverse on screen. The glass’s tile strip starts slid away; its “Show tiles (N)” tab stays in view, in the strip’s own position, and the same tab hides the tiles again. See harness-tiles §”The glass strip”.

085b640f5436.doc: Start in the avatar, open into a window
085b640f5436.title: The floor, which is not negotiable
085b640f5436.content: This instance’s declared interaction profile is low-dexterity. Every board action is keyboard-operable; drag is an accelerator and never the only way in. Targets are at least the tile size. And the board is ALWAYS collapsible to a linear, tile-based listing — a board that cannot be read linearly cannot be read by a screen reader, printed, or translated. The listing is the ARTEFACT and the board is the overlay . The board is an extra laid over a simple tile-based listing. So the floor must be correct with no JavaScript at all, not merely when the board is toggled off: notes built only by docs-ui.js from a fetch of assets/todos/index.json give a reader with JavaScript off no note, no count, and no hint that notes exist. Three checks follow: . Document order, never the board’s order. The board may stack by BPMN subprocess depth; the floor does not, because document order is what a screen reader and a printout depend on, and a floor that reordered would be a second answer to “what comes next”. Collapsed, never removed. When the board mounts it moves the listing into a disclosure so the page does not show the same notes twice. It does not delete it, hide it from assistive technology, or display: none it: a listing the board removed would have no way back while the board is open. Assert against the SERVED HTML. A test that reads the DOM passes because the board built that DOM. The assertion is on bytes the server sent — a browser context with javaScriptEnabled: false over the same renderer the generator writes with.

e2a40c944875.doc: Start in the avatar, open into a window
e2a40c944875.title: The folio belongs to the HARNESS, not to the library
e2a40c944875.content: A content library is something a reader browses — a replica, a published instance, any folio published as a site. A folio is the reader’s own surface: their notes, the assets they have materialised, the documents they created or linked. So the folio visualisation is cat-harness’s, available by convention on any harness, and a library never implements its own. A library may have its own landing page and its own harness; neither is licence to build a second folio. Consistency is the requirement: a reader moving between libraries must find the same folio, because the point of carrying a folio is that it does not change underneath them. A note or a todo MAY reference nodes in another KG library. The folio is not scoped to the library it is pulled down over, so a renderer must not assume local resolution.

b999e2c44180.doc: Start in the avatar, open into a window
b999e2c44180.title: A tile, or an avatar?
b999e2c44180.content: A tile is what the HARNESS declares, an avatar is what the FOLIO holds, and a theme is how either one looks rather than a third kind. The test is in harness-tiles §”A tile, or an avatar?”, and only there, because one rule with two homes is free to drift.

5507f3b26ab1.doc: Start in the avatar, open into a window
5507f3b26ab1.title: An asset has THREE states, not two
5507f3b26ab1.content: Pulling the folio down gives a glass — a surface over whatever is being browsed, carrying sticky notes and the avatars of materialised assets, including materialised KG like cat-bootstrap or cat-harness themselves. | state | where the asset is | how it got there | . | in the library | not the reader’s at all | the default | . | in the folio, not displayed | materialised into the folio’s own reproduce directories — library/ for the bytes, uploads/ for a source — off the glass | the reader closed it, “back in library” | . | on the glass | displayed in the pulled-down folio | the reader pulled it out of the library | . “In the folio” is not folio/. The folio is the reader’s REPOSITORY, of which library/ and uploads/ are declared parts — both carry dependents: "reproduce". folio/ is a different graph typology: renderable authored content. corpus-grep searches library/ only, so a node materialised anywhere else reads as ABSENT to every consumer. Closing returns an asset to the middle state and NEVER to the first. Only its display goes. Putting it back on the glass is a separate act performed from the library, not from the glass it just left. A two-state model would make closing a sticky and un-materialising an asset the same gesture, and a reader tidying their glass would silently discard work; the middle state is what makes closing cheap enough to do freely. When you implement close, check that the library offers the way back — not that the glass does. Close says where the way back is, at the moment of closing. The glass’s [x] opens a confirm that names the instance’s library and links it; Escape and Cancel leave the card where it is, and only the confirm shelves it — after which the glass says, with the same link, where the asset went. Naming the library matters because a reader holding assets from several libraries would otherwise have to remember which one each came from. The place is the card’s own, so there are three. A library card goes back to its instance’s library, a todo to the Todos board, and a landing sticky pinned to the glass to the page it was pinned from; calling a sticky “your Todos” would send the reader to a list it was never on. One function answers “where does this card go back to”, and the confirm, the status after it and the [x] button’s own label all read it, so the three cannot disagree. The confirm is the page’s one confirm dialog, shared with sending a sticky to fsh-guts, so focus-on-Cancel and Escape-cancels are stated once. Opening a library card goes to the asset’s visualizer when its index entry declares one, else to its entry page; resizing is a corner drag, with +/− in move mode and the move bar’s buttons as the non-drag path.

7751a2808c90.doc: Start in the avatar, open into a window
7751a2808c90.title: Two settings panels, two names, each points to the other
7751a2808c90.content: The glass has its own settings (theme, avatars, opacity, blur), and the page has its own under ▦ Actions (scheme, reading preferences, the Discarded fish, Declared kinds). They are named “Glass settings” and “Page settings”, so a screen reader does not read two controls identically, and each panel opens with a link to the other, as its first control, because a reader who opens the wrong panel needs a pointer to the right one. Site chrome and board state are unrelated settings but they are neighbouring places, and a reader moves between places. | The names are declared once (SETTINGS_NAMES in docs-ui.js), because each panel’s link prints the OTHER panel’s name; a panel renamed in one place only would leave the other panel’s link naming something that no longer exists. | The link must OPEN its target, not toggle it, and not open it underneath. The glass’s openPanel closes a panel that is already open, and the open glass covers the sidebar where Page settings lives. So the glass-to-page link shuts the glass first, and the page-to-glass link shuts the launcher first. In both cases focus lands on the target panel’s heading. | No link to nothing. A page with a glass and no sidebar has no launcher. Each panel registers an opener, and the link is drawn only when its target registered one. | . The same holds for any future pair of panels that share a word: name each one for what it acts on, and point each one at the other. scripts/tests/settings-labels-distinct.test.ts checks the source; test/settings-crosslinks.e2e.ts checks the rendered page at 1280×800 and 390×844, by mouse and keyboard.

8d4b64ddacd5.doc: Start in the avatar, open into a window
8d4b64ddacd5.title: Lazy window content fetch and render safety
8d4b64ddacd5.content: Rendering the board with N cards makes 0 per-card detail fetches up front: each board slot (todoSlot / renderBoardTiles) renders only its summary tile/avatar. When a card carries a per-card detail or artifact URL (detailHref, bodyHref, artifactHref, or a non-inlined jsonldHref), opening its window (openCard / createLazyWindowLoader.openWindow) fetches that card’s content lazily on open, caches the result by card id (so re-opening uses the cached result and never pre-fetches the other N - 1 cards), and renders any body or tool/skill output through the declared renderToolOutput (RENDER_AS: text, url, markdown, json) and safeHref boundary (schemas/ui/render-output.ts, site-chrome/assets/js/docs-ui.js). A refused URL scheme (such as javascript:) is never fetched and is shown as escaped text.

9314607b1b0a.title: Not this skill
9314607b1b0a.content: The layout layer and why a note carries no coordinates: board-diagram-interchange. Relocating content out of a folio is deletion-requires-confirmation, applied by the content core’s processes/ui/board-relocate.bpmn.

df29ac5e5cc4.title: bpmn-authoring
df29ac5e5cc4.content: Skill id: bpmn-authoring · Package: workflow · Named by l2-dak-authoring.bpmn (Business processes · BPMN 2.0, Business analyst lane) and crdm-requirements.bpmn (Phase 2: Map current workflow (BPA), Agent lane). Author BPMN 2.0 business process diagrams — both a DAK’s L2 business processes and this repository’s own processes/**/*.bpmn.

ad89ec90d732.title: Inputs and outputs
ad89ec90d732.content: schemas/skills/bpmn-authoring/: . | in — processName (required), sourceWorkflow, existingBpmn, participants | out — bpmnFile, diagramFile, taskCount, gatewayCount, participantCount | . graphviz is a declared capability with degradation: skip — layout help degrades, authoring does not stop.

1ae9546adb30.title: Diagram Interchange is not optional
1ae9546adb30.content: A .bpmn with no DI section — no explicit x/y on its shapes — parses and renders blank, although the XML looks complete. bun run cat render:bpmn renders every diagram to docs/assets/img/workflows/ with bpmn-js in headless Chromium; bun run cat render:bpmn:check fails when an SVG is stale. Run the renderer and look at the SVG before you call a diagram done.

9b8cdc428244.title: Readable at 100%: check it before and after (author check)
9b8cdc428244.content: Every diagram you write or touch must, when you are done: . | fit 1400 × 900 in diagram units, so its 16px text reads at about 14px in a 1200px band without zooming; every task a fixed 120 × 120 square: boxes never grow to fit their names, and a name that does not fit is shortened (TASK_SIZE in the tools layer); | have no label on another label, on a flow (its own included), on a box or across a lane line: a gateway’s question above the diamond, its answers beside their flows, every label inside one lane; | have right-angled flows and every name inside its box, pool and lane names inside their strips; | have no crossing flows, and the lane order that keeps flows between lanes shortest. | . bun run cat bpmn:detangle <file> reports all of it, and --write fixes what it can (lane order, right angles, box and lane sizes, label places). Run it before and after, and put both counts in the PR. The same findings are in render:bpmn’s warnings and the process’s QA report, so a reviewer sees what the author left. The procedure, and why the budget is 1400 × 900, is bpmn-detangle.

ac89370659c4.title: In this repository, a diagram is executable
ac89370659c4.content: processes/**/*.bpmn are not pictures. workflow_start / workflow_next / workflow_complete run them, and workflow_complete refuses a step that is not enabled. That has consequences for how you author: . | Every activity carries <bootstrap.processes:skill ref="…"/> naming the skill that implements it, and <cat-harness.processes:bean store="beans/"/> where it touches the work plan. bun run cat check:workflow-refs fails on a ref that resolves to nothing, and bun run cat kg:audit additionally fails when the named skill exists but no package can serve it. | Every lane names a role. Declare the role once as a top-level <bpmn:resource id="<role id>" name="<title>"/> (before the collaboration and the process), and set partitionElementRef="<role id>" on the lane; the id is the role’s in scenarios/roles.json, verbatim. Lane names are free text; an explicit ref is the join that does not depend on spelling. <bootstrap.processes:role ref> is the deprecated form. A diagram using any bootstrap.processes: element declares the namespace as the first child of <bpmn:definitions>: <bpmn:import namespace="https://litlfred.github.io/bootstrap/v0/processes/ns/" location="https://litlfred.github.io/bootstrap/v0/processes/ns.jsonld" importType="http://www.w3.org/ns/json-ld"/>. | A store is not a lane. Lanes are for people and agents, the roles that act. A place where things are kept, such as the work plan (work items), a corpus, a session record, an activity log or a published bucket, is a <bpmn:dataStoreReference>. The tasks that read or write it point at it with data associations, and each task sits in the lane of whoever does it. A “Work plan — beans” lane holding “Open the bean” says the store does the work, when the agent does. | The process’s own bpmn:documentation opens with what it is for. Its first sentence is the diagram’s row on the publication-workflow page. kg-export carries it on the Process node as summary (the whole text as description), the page reads it from the published named-subgraph JSON-LD (bun run cat subgraph:jsonld) rather than from anything written by hand, and check:process-index fails when a declared diagram’s node has none. So that sentence says what the process does or answers — not who asked for it, which work item or issue it came from, or where the work got to. Those belong later in the documentation, or in the work item. | A gateway may be computed rather than chosen — see dmn-authoring. | Policy is declared on the process. <cat-harness.processes:policy enforcement="strict"/> means workflow_gate refuses a step that is not enabled; absent policy means strict. Steps marked relaxable="false" may never be relaxed by any package. | .

58ac59410885.title: Readable diagrams: what the research supports
58ac59410885.content: These rules are what holds up from the BPMN comprehension research, checked mechanically. kg:audit reports each rule below per process (src/workflow/diagram-quality.ts in the tools layer). The sources, and how strong each rule’s evidence is, are in the process-model-quality methodology. | Separate routing from work. A task never has two outgoing flows: put an exclusive or parallel gateway after it, or a reader must guess fork vs choice (activity-implicit-split, major). A loop-back INTO a task is fine. A gateway either joins or splits, not both (gateway-mixed). A question is a gateway, never a task: a box named “Should it leave now?” or “Separate this graph?” is a decision drawn as work. If someone must judge first, draw that as a task (“Judge whether it should leave”) or a call to Process_AskThePerson, then the question on the gateway after it. | Keep it small. Split by phase into call activities past 20 flow nodes (process-size). That 20 is house style. The only threshold with evidence is 7PMG’s 50 (process-decompose, major), and it predicts modelling errors such as deadlocks, not reading speed. | One start event per process level (process-single-start). Several named end events are fine, and the work item CLOSE pattern needs them. | A decision is a question, its branches are the answers (decision-label-question). | Label activities verb-object: imperative verb, then its object (Review the draft, not Draft review) (activity-label-verb-first). The evidence is one study of how ambiguous labels felt (29 students), so this is reported, never gated. | A name says the step, nothing else. No trailing [skill] slug: the skill is in <bootstrap.processes:skill ref>, and the page links it from there. No step numbers (“1 ·”, “Phase 2:”, “P1.1”): the flows already give the order, and a number in front breaks verb-first. A number that cites a section of a source document goes in the task’s documentation. A list of numbered steps is a sign the diagram copies a document’s outline; group the steps into phases instead. | . Split by phase: how . A diagram can be right in every step and still unreadable on its page. When process-size fires, or a diagram has a start event per lane, split it like this: . | The top-level process shows the phases. Each phase is a <bpmn:callActivity calledElement="…"> to its own process. Keep at the top only what moves the work between phases: who hands off to whom, and the decisions that send it back (rejected → revise). A loop that crosses phases is drawn at the top; a loop inside a phase stays in that phase. | A phase lives in its own file, <parent>-<phase>.bpmn, next to the parent, with its own process id (Process_<Parent><Phase>) and a first documentation sentence that says what the phase does. It becomes the phase’s row on the publication-workflow page like any other diagram’s. | A phase that ends two ways ends in two named end events, and the caller’s gateway right after the call reads which one it reached, as GW_BeanYours reads Process_BeanOpen’s. | Keep the node ids when you move nodes into a phase. A test, a schema or a skill that points at Task_X then changes only its file and process, not its id. | Open and close the work item at the top, once. A process that is only ever called runs on its caller’s work item, so a phase calls neither Process_BeanOpen nor Process_BeanClose (check:bean-calls). “Once” holds for the top as well: a process with several outcomes routes them all into one Process_BeanClose call, which decides itself whether the work item is completed, scrapped or blocked, and only then branches to its named end events. One close per outcome repeats the same box and makes the diagram wide. | A caller’s adjudication accepts looks one level down. If the judgement moves into a phase, put accepts on the call to that phase, and take it off any caller further up. | Name a call activity for the phase, verb-object like any activity (“Review the change”), not for its file. | . A phase that only one parent calls is still worth its own file: the point is the page a reader opens, not reuse. Untangle every diagram you touch . The same discipline as ArchiMate views (archimate-models §”Untangle every view you touch”), and the same geometry: a change never adds a tangle. Run bun run cat kg:audit before and after, and compare edge-crossing, edge-through-node and edge-rectilinear for the diagram. Say both counts in the PR. Route loop-backs in the channel below the lane (bpmn-processes §”Edge routing”), then look at the rendered SVG. What the evidence does NOT support . Do not import these from style guides or model output; each was checked: . | Mandatory left-to-right flow. Figl & Strembeck 2015 (44 people) found no significant difference in accuracy or time across four directions. Lay out left-to-right for consistency, not because it reads faster. | A word cap on labels, a gateway fan-out cap of 4, and a fixed colour palette. No study behind them. Colouring matching split and join gateways made novices more accurate and experts faster, not more accurate (Reijers et al. 2011). | OR-gateways need no rule: the process model refuses inclusive gateways at load. | .

0bda878ee29b.title: If it has actors, activities and a control flow, it is BPMN
0bda878ee29b.content: Not a Mermaid fence. Mermaid stays for the things that are not processes — component maps, lattices, navigation graphs. The audit of which is which is on the publication workflow page, which the content core authors.

067ad43cd68b.title: Why this skill is in a platform package
067ad43cd68b.content: It covers both a DAK’s L2 business processes and this repository’s own processes/**/*.bpmn, and platform processes such as crdm-requirements.bpmn name it, so it cannot live in a content-type package: a platform process depending on a content-type package crosses the boundary the platform-boundary-guard subagent keeps. Its DAK material stays here rather than in a second skill, because a generic skill naming a domain worked example is ordinary, and two skills that must be read together to author one diagram are not.

79969e522a36.title: When a layer above transforms it
79969e522a36.content: A layer built on this one may transform an authored business process into another artefact — FHIR Shorthand, for instance — and then the BPMN is a source artefact rather than documentation of one. Author it knowing it will be transformed: names and ids you choose here appear in what is generated. That layer’s own tooling skill has the mechanics; this one names no layer above it.
