b510a0ef3e4b.title: Corpus-Grep Skill
b510a0ef3e4b.content: Disambiguation. This skill formalizes the backward check (“has this already been resolved somewhere in the corpus?”). Its forward complement is the formalize-first discipline (“can a structural claim prune the hypothesis class before I run a wide search?”). Run corpus-grep before declaring an item open; run formalize-first before launching an expensive numerical scan. The two are duals — backward against known results, forward against the hypothesis class.

abd369646587.title: Role
abd369646587.content: Gate every “this is open / unresolved / a gap” declaration behind a mechanical four-path search of the corpus. The originating source file’s status note (## Status, Open question, Phase 3 open, a TODO in a code or formal-source file, a PR-description “still open”) is not authoritative — prior agents routinely land a resolution as an audit doc, an adjacent chapter’s block, an implemented witness script, or a coordination ledger entry weeks before the source file’s note is updated. This skill catches that lag.

4a69c8ed405d.title: When to run this skill (STRICT)
4a69c8ed405d.content: Run the checklist before any of the following land in a durable artifact (audit doc, content block .md/.ts, code or formal-source comment, PR description, coordination ledger) or are asserted as fact in chat: . | “X is open” / “Open X” / “open problem” / “open question” | “TODO: derive X” / “pending derivation” / “still missing” | “this is a gap” / “no proof exists” / “not yet implemented” | “X is not wired into compute” / “nothing computes X” | . If you are about to type any of those about a corpus topic, stop and run the four paths first.

2d5ccc90005f.title: When NOT to run it (scope boundary)
2d5ccc90005f.content: The checklist gates factual corpus-status claims only. It does not gate, and must never be used to suppress: . | Skeptical assessments — “this looks fitted”, “this is numerology”, “hidden degrees of freedom here”. | Outside-view critique of a derivation’s rigor. | Reception / publishability / referee forecasts. | . Those are critical-distance judgments (see the repo’s Critical-distance license), not open-item declarations, and are never gated by this skill. Voicing them in chat does not require running corpus-grep first.

34b94aead16c.title: The four-path checklist (run all four)
34b94aead16c.content: | # | Path | What it catches | . | 1 | grep -rln <topic> docs/audits/ | Owner-authorised resolutions land as audit docs ahead of the source file’s status note being updated. | . | 2 | grep -rln <topic> content/ (full tree) | Related conjectures / propositions cross-cut chapters: a block in one chapter may answer a question raised in another. | . | 3 | grep -rln <topic> folio-assistant/computations/ | Implemented code may already discharge the content. | . | 4 | docs/coordination/<theme>.md | The coordination ledger — a prior agent may have already closed the item. | . Search the full content/ tree, not just the chapter you started in. The whole point of path 2 is that the resolution lives somewhere you did not expect.

4c7af4aa18aa.title: Mechanical recipe
4c7af4aa18aa.content: Pick a TOPIC that is the keyword / regex of the claim (an identifier, a label fragment, a phrase — e.g. delta_lambda, bring_color, c_3.*Taylor, kashaev.*density). Then run all four paths in one sweep: . TOPIC='delta_lambda' # ← keyword or regex for the claim under test for d in docs/audits content folio-assistant/computations docs/coordination; do if [ -d "$d" ]; then echo "=== $d ===" grep -rln -e "$TOPIC" "$d" 2>/dev/null fi done . Prefer the harness Grep tool (output_mode: "files_with_matches", one call per path or a single call with path set to the repo root and a glob) over shell grep when running inside an agent — results integrate with the permission UI and file links. The shell snippet above is the portable fallback. Widen the topic if the first pass is empty: try a synonym, the formal declaration name, the block label, the function name, and the witness-JSON key. A single spelling is not a clearing.

fee556d1e016.title: Decision procedure
fee556d1e016.content: . | Any non-trivial hit in (1)–(4) ⇒ the item is NOT open. Read the hit, then document the existing resolution instead of declaring a gap. Cite the file (audit doc / block .md / witness / ledger entry) that resolves it. | All four empty, modulo the originating file itself ⇒ you may declare the item open. “Modulo the originating file” means: a hit that is only the source file you are auditing does not count as a clearing — it is the very note you already mistrust. | Unsure whether a hit is the resolution ⇒ open the file and read it. A filename match is a lead, not a verdict. Treat a hit as resolving only if it actually discharges the claim (an audit verdict, a proved block, a passing witness, a ledger “CLOSED”). | .

ed373e43b59d.title: Where this discipline is codified (cross-references)
ed373e43b59d.content: This skill is the canonical, self-contained statement. It is invoked by, and consistent with, these codified instances: . | The folio’s own AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, where it states the rule for its corpus. | A content type’s own audits, which apply the checklist to their declarations. For a paper folio these are the science layer’s proof-gap-audit §K (proof-gap declarations), compute-author and compute-audit (before declaring a statement “not wired into compute”) and lean-environment-setup (before declaring a capability unavailable). | .

571283cdd8e0.title: Covered is not reachable — and check:tools cannot tell you which
571283cdd8e0.content: A skill can be satisfied by the neighbours of its mechanism while the mechanism itself is reachable from nothing. check:tools reports the skill as covered and is right to: coverage is a relation between a Tool and a skill, never between a Tool and a command. For example, kg-export can be satisfied by a publishing node, a serving node and schema carriers while no node runs an export; translation-manager by extract, inject, status, signoff and validate nodes while none reaches the round-trip QA.

98c1afd93a6d.title: The two questions, kept apart
98c1afd93a6d.content: “Does this skill have a Tool?” — bun run cat check:tools, and bun run cat tools:coverage for which of the uncovered ones warrant one. “Is this command reachable by asking the graph?” — no instrument answers this yet; it has to be measured by hand. A skill showing as covered is not evidence that its code is reachable. Do not use the first question to answer the second: the cause of an invisible mechanism is structural, because nobody asks the second question.

6f95a574b54f.title: What to do when you meet one
6f95a574b54f.content: Add the node for the mechanism. Then two things not to do: . | Do not widen an existing node’s satisfies to make the gap look closed. That makes the graph assert a node does something it does not. | Do not give the new node the same I/O as an existing one unless it really is a substitute. Alternatives are derived from a shared skill plus an identical I/O signature (deriveAlternatives), and export-then-publish-then- serve are complementary steps, not competing arms. | .

18324bf66e8a.title: Two reasons NOT to write maintains
18324bf66e8a.content: maintains.artefact is a single path. A generator that writes one file per subject — gen-skill-docs, gen-schema-docs, gen-block-jsonld — has no single artefact to name. A declaration naming one file out of tens is worse than absent: it looks like a complete provenance record. A maintains claim asserts the artefact is published. Verify that by reading the build, not by assuming: cat-harness/ns.jsonld is a real claim because .github/workflows/docs-site.yml writes it. Remove a claim in the same change that retires its artefact: a claim outliving its artefact is the same 404 from the other side. An artefact nobody publishes is exactly the 404 the drift check exists to prevent. And the drift check only covers its own producer . kg:schema:check reconciles maintains both ways, but its unproduced direction runs only over artefacts whose declaring Tool invokes bun run cat kg:schema, because a maintained artefact is not necessarily produced by the schema exporter. So a maintains claim on any other producer’s artefact is unchecked: it can rot to a 404 and nothing notices. The fix — not yet built — is to assert every declared artefact is present after _site/ is assembled, with could-not-determine kept distinct from present.

d914076930f2.title: Adding a Tool type is fail-closed, and that is deliberate
d914076930f2.content: check:tools refuses a command-line input whose type could express a shell payload, against the membership list in schemas/tools/tool-types.ts. A newly added type is absent from that list and therefore unsafe by default. Adding it is a deliberate step, not an oversight to route around — and the fix for an enumerable input is the enum, never a looser type that happens to pass. Where the enum duplicates a union declared elsewhere, guard it in both directions: satisfies catches a member that stops being valid, and a conditional type catches a member added to the union and not here. An unavoidable duplicate is fine; an unchecked one is not — see directory-conventions.

510a8bac08c4.title: Five cases, most invisible to the instruments
510a8bac08c4.content: | case | what exists | what is missing | what sees it | . | 1 | a skill | a Tool | check:tools, tools:coverage | . | 2 | a skill and Tools for its neighbours | a Tool for the mechanism | nothing — this skill | . | 3 | a mechanism | any skill stating the capability | nothing | . | 4 | a skill, a mechanism, a Tool | a command — it runs in-process only | nothing | . | 5 | a skill, a mechanism, a command | anything that invokes it | nothing | . Case 5 is case 4’s inverse — the entry point is present and the callers are absent — and it is discussed under §Reachability is PLURAL below, because the useful question there is how many dispatch points this should have. A script whose only references are its own usage string and a line of skill prose telling a human what to type is case 5: its mechanism is inlined in prose.

bac5f4b6f751.title: The third case: a mechanism with no skill at all
bac5f4b6f751.content: A generator that renders theme and avatar nodes into the site’s stylesheets is a textbook maintains pair, and yet no generic skill need state the capability. tools:coverage cannot see this: it enumerates skills and asks which lack Tools, so a capability nobody has stated is absent from the list it walks. (site-presentation-assets is the skill that now states that one.) . satisfies requires at least one skill, so a node cannot be written without one: . | Do not stretch a neighbouring skill to make the node validate. The resulting satisfies edge is simply false. | Do not write the skill as a wrapper for the command. A skill states a capability generically and names no script; one that exists to give a script somewhere to point is a Tool with front matter. | . Authoring the skill is a design act — a claim about the platform’s capability vocabulary, inherited by every dependent instance — so it goes to the owner rather than being decided in passing. Write the skill before the nodes. Once the gap is closed, remove any note announcing it: an agent that believes a stale gap either avoids the capability or rebuilds it.

af5fba1b839a.title: The fourth case: a mechanism with no command, reachable in-process only
af5fba1b839a.content: Cases 1–3 are about a missing node or a missing skill. This one has both, and is still unaskable: the mechanism has no command, so no CI job and no person can run it. For example, checkFolioProfile in pipeline/profile-check.ts catches what schema validation structurally cannot — a block valid against its own schema but wrong for the folio’s content profile, because adapters partition disjointly while profiles nest. Its only caller is the MCP tool registration, so it is reachable by an MCP-connected agent and by nothing else: not a gate, not a sweep, not a person at a shell. Every instrument that asks “can this be reached” answers yes. Ask which callers, not whether. “Reachable from MCP” and “reachable from CI” are different claims, and a durable verdict needs the second. Giving a library function its first command . Prefer a qa-sweep axis to a one-off check script: a sweep verdict is durable where a printed one is not — a printed verdict cannot distinguish “wrong since it was written” from “broken in the commit under review”. Watch the library’s defaults. checkFolioProfile resolves through readFolioProfile, which turns an undeclared profile into "paper" — correct for a validator, which validates against the wider vocabulary, and wrong for a reporter, which must use readDeclaredFolioProfile or report pass on a folio that declares no content type at all. A library’s defaulting is usually what erases the third state. When you give a library function its first entry point, the value it resolves for its own use is not the value a verdict may report. Check which of the two you are reading — by running it, not by reading it.

bed03b36d727.title: Reachability is PLURAL — “which caller should this have?” presumes one
bed03b36d727.content: One mechanism can have several dispatch points, so the question to ask is not which caller should this have but: . What should be able to start this — and is each of those a trigger or a Tool? . The two are different objects, and which one a dispatch point is follows from who initiates: . | dispatch point | it is a | because | . | a named command | Tool | a caller invokes it; that is what a Tool node IS | . | a BPMN activity | trigger | the process fires it when the step is reached | . | a QA sweep axis | trigger | the sweep fires it per subject | . | a schedule or a watcher | trigger | time or an event fires it | . None of them is an alternative to another, by the same argument deriveAlternatives makes about sharing a skill: they are different ways the same work gets started. Enumerating the dispatch points also finds the ones already built. For each candidate, check whether it exists (an activity may already carry the skill, so workflow_next already hands it to an agent), whether it is possible (a sweep cannot run a check whose verdict originates outside it), and only then what is missing. Presented as a choice, the options waste proposals; enumerated as dispatch points, they are a short audit with one action. Read the mechanism’s entry point before proposing dispatch points. A name and a position in a diagram say what something is for; an argument list says what it does — for example, whether it performs a check or only records a verdict somebody else produced.

72c178bf0edb.title: The same failure one level out: a KIND, not a mechanism
72c178bf0edb.content: Ask what is missing of a kind of node and the same mistake appears: counting kg-qa sidecars over the work item store, finding zero, and calling work items unaudited when several gates audit them. Coverage is a relation between an instrument and the question it was built for — see audit-coverage, with bun run cat audit:coverage as the second question.

42dd26ba89b4.title: CRDM — the data-modelling phase
42dd26ba89b4.content: This skill says WHEN and WITH WHOM. It does not say how to model. That is data-modelling, and it is deliberately free of CRDM so a folio modelling data outside a requirements process can read it without inheriting a methodology it is not running. Where the two disagree, the technique wins and this page is wrong.

75d57bfd84b7.title: Where it sits, and why there
75d57bfd84b7.content: Between requirements (phases 2–4) and sign-off (phase 5). Requirements are statements about things; the model says what the things ARE. The entities come from the business-process analysis (phase 2), and phase 5 must not sign off requirements whose nouns were never pinned. Drafted too early, the model is invented from nothing; drafted too late, two stakeholders approve the same sentence meaning different things. Call_DataModel in crdm-requirements.bpmn is the callActivity after Call_Requirements and before Call_Signoff.

fa7f252c675e.title: What it consumes
fa7f252c675e.content: | from | what | . | phase 1, needs | the domain vocabulary the BA actually used | . | phase 2, BPA | the activities — every verb whose object is a candidate entity | . | phases 3–4, requirements | each requirement’s nouns, which the model must be able to express | . A requirement the model cannot express is a finding, not a modelling failure. It means the requirement is about something nobody has named, and the remedy is to name it. That is why this phase sits after requirements rather than before.

33cb8dc5c9f2.title: The sign-off, and who gives it
33cb8dc5c9f2.content: The agent drafts; the BA confirms the entities are the ones they meant; the stakeholders confirm the cardinalities. Those are two different questions and are asked of two different lanes on purpose: . | Are these the things? — a naming question, and the BA owns the domain vocabulary. | Is it really one per? — an operational question, and the people who run the process know where the exceptions are. | . The agent asks both and decides neither: the BA knows the domain, the agent does not guess, because a wrong cardinality is invisible until the data arrives.

27cfa6f85752.title: What it hands on
27cfa6f85752.content: A declared model, readable by a tool, per step 6 of the technique. Phase 5 signs off requirements against it: whether each requirement is expressible, not only whether it is wanted.

0d672f2dfeba.title: The loop, and when to leave it
0d672f2dfeba.content: Like every other CRDM phase this one loops until confirmed, and the gateway is the phase. Leave when the BA recognises the entities and the stakeholders have answered every cardinality — not when the model looks complete, because an unanswered cardinality is a hole exactly where the exceptions live.

e8c62d3d33ee.title: Not decided by this skill
e8c62d3d33ee.content: Whether the model is expressed as Zod, JSON Schema, a class diagram or prose is placement’s question and the folio’s choice. This phase requires only that the artefact is declared, so the next phase can read it rather than be told about it.

3ad153812b3e.title: Feature-request detection (CRDM trigger)
3ad153812b3e.content: Detect when a user request is a feature request (platform capability change) rather than a content request (writing, editing, reviewing folio content). When a feature request is detected, the agent works through requirements rather than implementing directly.

cebb4a50a6a8.title: Applies when
cebb4a50a6a8.content: Requirements that come from stakeholders who must sign them off, on work tied to a folio’s domain — WHO SMART Guidelines, an IG, a programme’s content. The requester is a content developer working through a BA, and the answer depends on what the folio says. Not for a platform capability change raised by somebody building the tooling with a content-agnostic answer — that is spec-kit.

f4c056fa43a4.title: Which requirements methodology — the fork this detection now carries
f4c056fa43a4.content: Detecting a feature request does not select CRDM by itself. There are two parallel requirements methodologies, and methodology-adoption forbids blending them. The signals below tell you a request needs requirements; this fork tells you whose. |   | governs | requester | the answer depends on | . | crdm — this methodology | stakeholder-facing WHO/IG work: needs assessment, BPA, stakeholder sign-off | content developers, via a BA | a folio’s subject matter | . | spec-kit | folio-assistant feature development; software-development best practice, closer to a scrum process | tool developers | nothing a folio says — content-agnostic | . Most of the signals listed below are spec-kit’s, not CRDM’s — the “Platform-level change requests” and “Direct capability requests” categories especially, since both describe somebody building the tooling. Read the categories as this needs requirements, then apply the fork. Two things bind under either methodology and are not a reason to pick one: the issue-association rules at the end of this file, and the spec-before-code gate.

28783cbc940e.title: Detection signals
28783cbc940e.content: Scan every user request for these categories of phrasing. A single match is enough to flag; two or more from different categories is high confidence. Direct capability requests . Phrases where the user explicitly asks for new functionality: . | “I need a way to …”, “can you add …”, “we need a tool that …” | “there should be a skill for …”, “add a QA check for …” | “the renderer should support …”, “make the pipeline do …” | “can we add a new block kind for …”, “we need a content type for …” | “it would be great if the agent could …” | “the agent should …”, “the agent needs to …”, “we will need to …” | “build me …”, “create a tool …”, “develop a feature …” | . Workflow gap descriptions . Phrases where the user describes a process that does not work today: . | “right now I have to manually …”, “there is no way to …” | “the current process for … is broken”, “this workflow doesn’t handle …” | “we can’t do … yet”, “it’s missing …”, “it doesn’t support …” | “every time I need to …, I have to …” (manual workaround pattern) | “other people need to be able to …” | . Platform-level change requests . Phrases that imply changes to folio-assistant itself (not folio content): . | “change the schema to …”, “modify the pipeline …” | “add a new adapter …”, “the constraint should …” | “update the CI to …”, “the workflow should fire when …” | “the MCP tool needs to …”, “register a new tool for …” | “the upstream change requests to …”, “upstream asks” — a change asked of a tool this platform DEPENDS ON is still a platform change; the folio is not where it lands either way | References to files under schemas/, pipeline/, adapters/, src/, scripts/, .github/workflows/ | . Cross-cutting concerns . Phrases that affect multiple folios or content types: . | “for all papers …”, “every folio should …”, “across all content types …” | “when any user …”, “the platform should …” | “this needs to work for both document and paper folios” | . Review-surfaced needs . Phrases that emerge during content review: . | “this review process would be easier if …” | “we need a way to triage these comments …” | “the feedback workflow should …” | “stakeholders need to be able to see …” | “can we make the review process more …” | . A request for a plan . A request for a plan ALWAYS produces a requirements document and a work plan for review before implementation. | “plan”, “make a plan”, “plan the …” | “approach”, “what approach would you take” | “proposal”, “propose …” | “how would you …” | “come up with …” | . A plan request needs requirements under either methodology, and content requests are not exempt: “plan the edits to chapter 3” triggers it as surely as “plan the new validator”. The fork above still decides WHOSE requirements — this signal never selects a methodology and never blends them. The operation is the same for both and lives in the content layer, in the plan-request-gate skill (skill_fetch plan-request-gate): produce a requirements document and a work plan, put them where this methodology says (CRDM: committed under docs/proposals/), hand both over as absolute GitHub permalinks, and stop until sign-off is recorded on the issue. The definition of a requirement both methodologies share is the requirement-definition skill (skill_fetch requirement-definition). Self-declared genre . The mirror of "Migration record: …" below. Some documents say what they are in their own first line, and a proposal or a design document argues for a change that does not exist yet — which is a feature request whichever category its sentences fall into. | “Proposal: …” as a document’s OPENING line | “design document for …” | . Anchored to the opening line. On the adjudicated corpus an unanchored proposal adds no false alarm and catches one more item (a change register for pipeline changes not yet built). The anchor stays until an owner decides, because changing a detector to fit its own 27-item eval set is tuning to the test.

102e8febbf5f.title: What is NOT a feature request
102e8febbf5f.content: Do not trigger CRDM for: . | “Write the next section of chapter 3” — content authoring (but “plan the next section” is a plan request — see §”A request for a plan”) | “Fix the typo in the overview” — content editing | “Run content_validate” — tool invocation | “What does this block kind mean?” — information request | “Review chapter 5” — content review within existing workflow | “Create a bean for …” — work-plan management | “Migration record: …” — a record of work already DONE, not a request for work; the tense is the signal | Bug reports about existing features (unless they imply a redesign) | .

aa17fccf45a1.title: On detection — what to do
aa17fccf45a1.content: Do NOT use the term “CRDM” with the user. It is internal methodology jargon. If new session and the first request is a feature: . | Acknowledge the request as a feature/capability change | Explain that you will help them work through the requirements before building | Start Phase 1 (needs assessment) | . If existing session and the user is already in a CRDM cycle: . | Incorporate the new request into the current requirements document | Continue with the current phase | . If existing session and the user is doing content work (not in CRDM): . | Synthesise what you have heard as a feature need | Ask the user: . | “This sounds like a platform change rather than content work. Would you like to pause and work through the requirements now, or should I note it for later?” | If pause: enter CRDM Phase 1, return to content work when done | If later: create a work item with as much context as possible, linking to any relevant GitHub issue | . | .

4aa29ded8e81.title: Issue association
4aa29ded8e81.content: Feature work should be linked to a GitHub issue: . | Scan open issues for a match — search by title/body keywords | If match found — ask user: “This looks related to #NNN — should I add your requirements there?” | If no match in open issues — scan recently closed issues | If no match at all — ask the user to create an issue (do NOT create without permission) | Do not proceed without an issue link — the issue is where stakeholders do feature sign-off; without it, there is no review surface | . Requirements may span multiple issues. The agent should link to all relevant ones and note the relationship.

f38dffc95222.title: After implementation
f38dffc95222.content: When a PR is merged that addresses a feature from this process: . | Post a summary comment on the linked GitHub issue describing what the PR accomplished | PRs are for code review (agent and human coders, code reviewers) | Issues are for CRDM stakeholders — the requestor, the BA, and updates from the coding team for feature sign-off | Many work items per issue — they are not synonymous | .

d77978e46d9d.title: A feature is a COLLABORATION you are joining, not a fix you are making
d77978e46d9d.content: When a feature comes up in conversation, it starts or joins a collaborative design between this user, other users and authors, and other agents. It is not a one-off fix: put it into epics and stories, create or update the artefacts it needs, and link them from the owning harness’s docs/ page. The default that is wrong . A feature surfaces mid-conversation, the agent understands it, and the agent builds it, with the conversation standing in for requirements. Everything needed to review the decision — the alternatives, the reason, who else it affects — stays in a chat log nobody else will read. What to do instead . 1. Assume the conversation is not the first. Before treating a feature as new, look for the collaboration it belongs to: an open issue, an epic, a work item, a sibling session’s branch, a spec. This repository has many of each and they are cheap to search. A feature that arrives without a home usually has one. 2. There are OTHER PARTICIPANTS, and they are not all present. Other authors, other users, other agents working other branches. Two consequences: . | the record has to be legible to somebody who was not in the conversation — which is what the issue is FOR, as against the PR (code review) and the work item (work plan); | a sibling session may already be solving it. Check before you build, and if their answer differs from yours, that is a design discussion to have on the issue rather than a merge conflict to win. | . 3. Structure it: epics and stories, not a task. A feature that is worth doing is worth a place in the roadmap. This store’s hierarchy is milestone → epic → feature → task, and check-bean-parents enforces that every open work item has a home. A feature filed as a bare task with no parent lands in the roadmap’s Miscellaneous section, where it stops being planned. An epic cannot parent an epic here. When the subject already has an epic, the new work is a FEATURE under it — a second epic beside it splits one subject across two roots, which is how a roadmap becomes unreadable. 4. Write the artefacts, and LINK them from docs/, because an artefact nobody can navigate to is one nobody reads. The harness that owns the capability owns the link — so a change to cat-harness’s pipeline is linked from cat-harness’s docs/, not from wherever the agent happened to be working. Which harness owns it is usually answered by which instance declares the directory the change lands in. The test . If this session ended now, could somebody who was not in it pick the feature up — find what was decided, what is still open, and who else is affected — without reading the chat? . If the answer is no, the collaboration has not been joined yet, whatever has been built. What this does NOT mean . It does not mean every small change becomes an epic. The trigger is the same one opening-brief uses: irreversibility and surprise, not size. A one-line fix to a typo in a generated file is a fix. A one-line change to a schema that three instances resolve against is a feature, because other people have to live with it. Nor does it mean stopping work to do paperwork first. continual-progress still holds — branch, commit, push, open the PR from commit #1. The point is that the record is collaborative, not that the work pauses.

77ac1c4b9085.title: Related work first
77ac1c4b9085.content: When a requirement is initiated or updated in chat, find the related work before anything else. That means work items, issues and open PRs, each categorized and summarized, followed by one question to the user about whether and how to coordinate. The procedure is related-work-coordination, and crdm-issue-linking.bpmn calls it as Process_RelatedWork.

0af09c80bcdd.title: Phase 1 — Needs assessment (detail)
0af09c80bcdd.content: This skill expands the Phase 1 summary in crdm-requirements-workflow.md. The agent facilitates; the BA provides domain knowledge.

4370208a6908.title: Identifying the requester
4370208a6908.content: Determine who is asking and their role: . | Role | What they bring | . | BA / Feature Requestor | Domain knowledge, stakeholder access, sign-off authority | . | Content Author | First-hand experience with the gap | . | Managing Editor | Cross-folio perspective | . | Technical Reviewer / SME | Deep subject-matter expertise | . | Programme Lead | Strategic priority, resourcing | . The requester is the BA for this CRDM cycle. They interact with the agent; stakeholders interact with the BA.

cd81a60946d8.title: Identifying stakeholders (systematic 4-step approach)
cd81a60946d8.content: . | Check each active folio’s <name>.config.json roles — authors, editors, reviewers, contributors, affiliations | Check .github/CODEOWNERS — subsystem ownership | Check recent activity — gh issue list --search "...", gh pr list --search "..." for who’s been working in the area | Ask the BA directly: “Who else is affected by this change?” | . Categorise stakeholders: . | Approvers/Governance — must sign off (e.g. review committee) | Direct Operators — will use the feature daily | Downstream Consumers — affected indirectly (e.g. country adaptation teams) | .

0d1c977a0bae.title: Gathering source material
0d1c977a0bae.content: The request may arrive through any of these channels: . | Source | How to access | . | Chat messages in the current session | Current context | . | GitHub issue body or comment | gh issue view <number> | . | Uploaded document (Word, PDF) | uploads/ directory | . | Referenced document in library | library/ directory | . | Issue comment attachment | Download via gh | . | Pasted Teams/email discussion | Current context (motivation, not spec) | . Probing discipline: begin with the end in mind. Distinguish: . | Symptoms vs root causes | Workarounds vs missing capability | One user’s need vs shared need | .

bbc59351e0c6.title: Synthesising a needs statement
bbc59351e0c6.content: Every needs statement follows this structure: . | Current state — what exists today (specific, not vague) | Gap — what is missing or broken (the actual problem) | Desired outcome — what should happen after the feature | Who benefits and how — named roles, concrete improvements | Workflow rationale — how this fits the broader process | . No jargon (STRICT) . Write for business stakeholders and domain experts, not developers: . | ❌ Avoid | ✅ Use instead | . | Zod schema validation | “the system checks the structure” | . | AST traversal | “scanning the document” | . | TypeScript types | “the data format” | . | Pipeline stage | “processing step” | . | CLI flags | “options” | . | MCP tool | “assistant capability” | .

9db80870914b.title: Posting to the issue
9db80870914b.content: . | Scan for existing issue first — gh issue list --search "..." | Never create an issue without BA permission | Post the needs statement as a comment: gh issue comment <number> --body-file /tmp/needs-statement.md . | .

2729c79108a7.title: Requesting feedback
2729c79108a7.content: After posting, ask the BA: . | “Does this capture what you need?” | “Are any stakeholders missing?” | “Is the desired outcome specific enough to test?” | . The BA coordinates with stakeholders. The agent does not contact stakeholders directly.

09a2abcf9444.title: Exit gate
09a2abcf9444.content: BA confirms the needs statement before proceeding to Phase 2.

0336d93b6b32.title: Requirements from a recorded walkthrough
0336d93b6b32.content: A walkthrough recording is the best source a CRDM round can have: the stakeholder reacting to a working thing, in their own words. It is also easy to over-trust, because a transcript reads like a record and is not one. The tool is cat-harness-tools/scripts/meeting-recording.py (stdlib + ffmpeg; --help per subcommand).

3ceb28bdb9cb.title: 1. Inventory what was actually uploaded
3ceb28bdb9cb.content: List the files before promising anything, because a request can promise a video that was not uploaded. A Teams .docx transcript never contains the shared screen; its images are speaker avatars. Say what is missing, do what can be done, and list what waits for the missing file.

76aa649e13ca.title: 2. Two exports of one recognition are one transcript
76aa649e13ca.content: meeting-recording.py compare A B gives word similarity and where they differ. | pair | similarity | what the differences were | . | Teams .docx against its .vtt | 0.980 | interjections in another cue; words joined at a .docx line break | . | Vosk small-en (independent) against Teams | 0.802 | mostly Vosk’s errors, but also Teams’ (“Lightner” → Leitner, “philtres” → filters) | . The first number is not confirmation: both files carry every word Teams misheard. Only an independent recognition can disagree with it. A lower similarity from a weaker model is expected and still useful, because what you read is where they disagree, filtered with --keys to names and domain terms. Record the names the recogniser mangled (“Tini”, “Jiun” for Chinni; “Saroop” / “Swarupu” unresolved) in the requirements document, and ask rather than guess any name neither transcript settles.

1e9bfe6497e2.title: 3. An independent transcript, offline
1e9bfe6497e2.content: meeting-recording.py transcribe VIDEO --model DIR --out vosk.json needs the vosk package (PyPI) and a model directory. It downloads nothing. In a sandbox whose proxy refuses Hugging Face and the Vosk model host, find a model already packaged somewhere the network allows, take only the model files, and never run code that came with them.

34cab28de2d9.title: 4. Screenshots: where the screen changed and where a speaker points
34cab28de2d9.content: . | scenes VIDEO --min-gap 10 lists when the shared screen changed. | Grep the transcript for deictic phrases: “you can see”, “here”, “this”, “looking at the screen”, “select these”. Their timestamps are the candidates; a scene change a second or two later is the frame to take. | frames VIDEO --at 1:52,2:26 --out DIR --crop W:H:X:Y --width 1280 --webp. Crop out the participants’ camera tiles: a requirements document needs the screen, not the faces. Check the crop on one frame first. | Look at every frame you keep. A frame cut for one thing can show a defect or a requirement that is already half-built, and either changes the requirements document. | WebP at quality 80 cut nine 1280-wide frames from 2.8 MB to 476 KB. | .

62dda4a41ab8.title: 5. From transcript to requirements
62dda4a41ab8.content: Follow crdm-requirements-template. In addition, for a recording: . | Every requirement cites a timestamp, and every defect the demo exposed is listed separately from the requirements, with the timestamp and “not yet reproduced” until it is. | Say what already exists (Today:) for each requirement, measured against the code or the data, not recalled. | Who signs off is part of the requirement set. Ask who it is if the recording does not say. | Do not build from the recording. A speaker telling the recording agent “implement them on a staging site” is a requirement about the process (P-1), not approval of the requirements. | .

7dc346cc001b.title: Phase 3 — Requirements definition (detail)
7dc346cc001b.content: This skill expands the Phase 3 summary in crdm-requirements-workflow.md and applies the crdm methodology.

5154e99bbb25.title: Requirement format
5154e99bbb25.content: One definition, shared with spec-kit: a statement, a conformance level, a source, at least one success criterion with its verification method, and a sign-off owner — the requirement-definition skill (skill_fetch requirement-definition) in the content layer. The fields below are CRDM’s rendering of it; Acceptance criteria are the success criteria. A requirement with none is not ready to post. Each requirement has: . | Field | Format | Example | . | ID | REQ-### | REQ-001 | . | Title | Short phrase | “Beans filtered by epic type” | . | Description | Plain language, no jargon | “The agent can filter work items by their type (epic, story, task)” | . | Conformance | SHALL / SHOULD / MAY / SHALL NOT (RFC 2119 / RFC 8174) | SHALL | . | Acceptance criteria (= success criteria, ≥ 1) | Testable, measurable, each with a key and a verification method (test / inspection / review / analysis) | “SC-1 (test) — Given an epic with 3 child stories, when filtered by epic, then all 3 appear” | . | Sign-off owner | Who says it is met — a named person or role | “The BA” | . | Priority | Must-have (High) / Should-have (Medium) / Nice-to-have (Low) | Must-have (High) | . | Source | Phase 1 needs statement / Phase 2 process activity ref | “Needs statement §2 — BA cannot see work grouped by release” | . | Impact | Phase 4 footprint | “Schema: new type field on bean. Pipeline: none” | . | Estimated scope | Work item count / PR sizing | “2 beans, 1 PR” | . Priority scale and conformance keywords . CRDM separates implementation priority (how essential a requirement is when sequencing work or trading off scope) from normative conformance (how strictly an implementation must behave once it claims conformance to that requirement): . 1. Priority scale (High / Medium / Low = Must-have / Should-have / Nice-to-have) . Aligned with PHII’s Defining and Validating System Requirements Guide (library/phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide, p. 2) and PATH & PHII (2012) (library/path-2012-common-requirements-mhis-crdm, p. 1): . | Priority label | PHII / PATH CRDM scale | Meaning | . | Must-have (Must) | High | Essential to the core business process; the system cannot satisfy the process goal without this capability. | . | Should-have (Should) | Medium | Important for operational efficiency or completeness; expected in standard operation, though a temporary workaround may exist. | . | Nice-to-have (Nice-to-have) | Low | Desirable enhancement that improves convenience or secondary workflows when resources permit. | . 2. Normative conformance keywords (SHALL / SHOULD / MAY / SHALL NOT) . While PHII’s informal prose grammar phrases requirement statements as “The system must or should…” (phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide, p. 1), the separate Conformance field uses uppercase normative keywords governed by IETF BCP 14 — library/rfc2119-key-words-requirement-levels (RFC 2119) and library/rfc8174-uppercase-vs-lowercase-2119-key-words (RFC 8174, specifying that only UPPERCASE words carry RFC 2119 normative meaning): . | SHALL (MUST) — mandatory requirement of the specification | SHOULD (RECOMMENDED) — recommended; valid reasons may exist in particular circumstances to ignore, but full implications must be understood and weighed | MAY (OPTIONAL) — truly optional capability | SHALL NOT (MUST NOT) — absolute prohibition | .

e73afddcafd3.title: Generating from conversation
e73afddcafd3.content: 4-step elicitation . | Listen and deconstruct — identify the nouns (entities), verbs (capabilities), and adjectives (qualities) in the BA’s description | Disentangle what from how — “I need to see beans grouped by release” is a requirement; “use a Jekyll page” is an implementation choice | Formulate testable criteria — every requirement must have a Given/When/Then or a checkable statement | Validate with the BA — read it back. “Does this capture what you need? Anything missing?” | .

2dc0011469cd.title: The document is a requirement set
2dc0011469cd.content: The requirements document as a whole is a RequirementSet (bootstrap-tools/schemas/requirement-set.ts, published as bootstrap/schemas/requirement-set.schema.json): reqset:<slug>, the methodology, the issue, a stage — draft → proposed → approved → planned → in-progress → delivered → accepted, or rejected, cancelled, superseded — its members (req: references, each with its own decision), its work plan (work item ids) and its sign-offs. Commit it beside the proposal as <slug>.requirement-set.json, or as a requirementSet: key in the proposal’s front matter; check:requirements judges it. The set’s stage and each member’s status are independent — a requirement outlives the document that proposed it — with one link enforced: a set is accepted only when every member it approved is in-force. The stage moves only through a sign-off (Phase 5’s BA_Signoff, close-out’s BA_Confirm), and check:requirements refuses approved/accepted without a human sign-off, planned without work items, and cancelled without a reason.

a564fee8aae5.title: Grouping requirements
a564fee8aae5.content: By workflow area . | Area | Examples | . | Ingestion | Document upload, structure extraction | . | Authoring | Block editing, chapter management | . | Validation | Schema checks, QA criteria | . | Rendering | PDF, HTML, Markdown output | . | Review | Staging, before/after comparison | . | Translation | PO extraction, machine + human translation | . | Release | Versioning, changelog, release gating | . By architectural layer . | Layer | Examples | . | Schemas | Type definitions, constraints, builders | . | Pipeline | Validators, renderers, extractors | . | Adapters/Tools | Block-kind routing, MCP tools | . | Skills | Agent guidance, workflow definitions | .

4407a919bbdd.title: Posting to the issue
4407a919bbdd.content: Format as a markdown checklist: . ## Requirements — [Feature name] ### Must-have - [ ] **REQ-001** (SHALL) — Beans filtered by epic type - _Source:_ needs statement §2 - _Acceptance:_ `SC-1` (test) — Given an epic, when `beans list --type epic`, then only epics appear - _Sign-off owner:_ the BA - _Scope:_ 1 bean, 1 PR - [ ] **REQ-002** (SHALL) — Release lifecycle skill - _Source:_ needs statement §3 - _Acceptance:_ `SC-1` (inspection) — Skill exists at `cat-harness/sdlc/skills/sdlc-core/release-lifecycle.md` - _Sign-off owner:_ the BA - _Scope:_ 1 bean, 1 PR ### Should-have - [ ] **REQ-003** — ... ### Deliverables summary | ID | Title | Priority | Beans | Status |---|---|---|---|---| REQ-001 | Beans filtered by epic type | Must | 1 | ⬜ | REQ-002 | Release lifecycle skill | Must | 1 | ⬜ | . UI / wireframe . Every requirement set carries this section, filled or marked not applicable. When a requirement changes a rendered surface (a page, a visualiser, the navbar, a form, an app screen), the wireframe is designed and chosen before implementation, by wireframe-design-review in Design use; its output (schemas/skills/wireframe-design-review/output.schema.json) supplies every row: . ### UI / wireframe - _Surface:_ the review page's heat map (REQ-004, REQ-005) - _Candidates:_ `docs/proposals/<slug>/wireframes/` — assets of this proposal - `a.html` — [staging](…) · web ![](…/checks/a-web.png) · mobile ![](…/checks/a-mobile.png) - `b.html` — [staging](…) · web ![](…/checks/b-web.png) · mobile ![](…/checks/b-mobile.png) - _Chosen:_ `b` by @requester ([where they chose](…): the conversation, the issue or the PR), because …; `a` rejected because … . Or, when no requirement changes a rendered surface: . ### UI / wireframe N/A — no rendered surface.

fedae7a7003c.title: Traceability
fedae7a7003c.content: Every requirement traces in both directions: . Needs statement (Phase 1) ↓ "Source" field Requirement (Phase 3) ↓ "Impact" field Impact assessment (Phase 4) ↓ bean reference Bean (Phase 5) — names its REQ / req: statements; `## Done when` copied from their acceptance criteria ↓ PR link PR (Phase 6) .

71fb99c4adfd.title: CRDM requirements workflow
71fb99c4adfd.content: Once a feature request is detected (see crdm-detect.md), the agent follows this workflow to gather, validate, and implement requirements collaboratively.

23037946f6f2.title: Method origin and how this workflow adapts it
23037946f6f2.content: This workflow adapts the Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) developed by the Public Health Informatics Institute (PHII) and applied to health information systems by PATH & PHII (2012) — see the crdm methodology node and the canonical SKOS glossary concept https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/glossary/platform/collaborative-requirements-development-methodology: . | PHII (2021/2023), Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM): A Collaborative Approach to Public Health Systems (library/phii-2023-crdm) | PHII (2016/2021), 5. Analyzing Technical Options: Defining and Validating System Requirements Guide (library/phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide) | PATH & PHII (2012), Common Requirements for Maternal Health Information Systems: Produced with the Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (library/path-2012-common-requirements-mhis-crdm) | . The relation to PHII and PATH CRDM is adapts: . | Phases that follow PHII & PATH CRDM: . | Phase 1 (Needs assessment) and Phase 2 (Business process analysis & redesign) follow PHII’s first two concentration areas (1. Business Process Analysis — think: How do we do our work now? and 2. Business Process Redesign — rethink: How should we do our work?), using swimlane task-flow diagrams across pools and actor lanes and a business process / gap matrix. | Phase 3 (Requirements definition) follows PHII’s third concentration area (3. Requirements Definition — describe: How can an information system support our work?) and PATH (2012)’s separation of activity-linked functional user requirements from cross-cutting non-functional / general system requirements, together with PHII’s priority scale (High / Medium / Low = Must-have / Should-have / Nice-to-have) and validation walkthroughs (Desk checking, Walkthrough, Peer review). | . | Phases and mechanisms that are the platform’s own extensions: . | Agentic BA-only facilitation channel: An LLM agent facilitates the process with the human BA (Role_BusinessAnalyst) over issues and pull requests rather than a multi-day in-person workshop. | Phase 4 (Codebase impact analysis): 7-dimension impact analysis across the repository’s schemas, skills, BPMN/DMN models, UI components, pipelines, tests, and downstream consumers (crdm-impact-analysis.md). | Phase 4b (Capability area dependency ordering & formalize-first rule): Grouping requirements into capability areas (CA-1, CA-2, …) ordered by a dependency DAG and formalizing existing implicit behavior before adding net-new features. | Phase 5 (Work-plan decomposition & specification filing): Creating agent work items (beans/) and human todos (todos/), and filing proposals from docs/proposals/<slug>.md to docs/requirements/<slug>.md. | Phase 6 (Implementation, branches/ preview & merge sign-off): Feature-branch delivery, automated verification gates, branches/<branch-slug>/ review, and explicit human owner confirmation before merging (merge-to-main.md). | . | .

7f171c8ae881.title: Actors
7f171c8ae881.content: | Actor | Role | Swim lane | . | BA / Feature Requestor | The person who identified the need and coordinates the CRDM process. Acts as Business Analyst: interacts with the agent, reviews increments, translates stakeholder feedback into agent-actionable direction. May be an author, editor, programme lead, or reviewer. | BA / Feature Requestor | . | Agent | The LLM agent running in the folio-assistant harness. Facilitates the process, synthesises inputs, implements on feature branches, posts summaries to the issue. Interacts with the BA only, not with stakeholders directly. | Agent | . | Stakeholders | The people affected by the feature who must review and approve it. They participate at defined checkpoints (needs confirmation, requirements approval, MVP testing, feature sign-off) — not in the day-to-day development loop. Examples: review committee, country programme managers, IT teams, end users. | Stakeholders | .

ff9fee4f6899.title: BPMN reference
ff9fee4f6899.content: processes/process/crdm-requirements.bpmn is the outer process — detection, the Feature? decision, then six phases, each a real subprocess in its own file: . | phase | file | what happens | . | Link the work to an issue | crdm-issue-linking.bpmn | scan, then link or ask; never create without permission | . | Phase 1 — needs | crdm-needs.bpmn | stakeholders, needs statement, loop until recognised | . | Phases 2–4 — BPA + requirements | crdm-requirements-definition.bpmn | current workflow, requirements, impact, loop until approved | . | Phase 4b — prioritization | (inline in Phase 4 exit) | dependency-order capability areas, formalize-first rule, BA confirms | . | Phase 5 — work items + sign-off | crdm-signoff.bpmn | requirements become work items, BA signs off, branch announced | . | Phase 6 — implement + acceptance | crdm-deliver.bpmn | implement, review increment, share MVP, take findings | . | Close-out | crdm-close.bpmn | stakeholder sign-off, BA confirmation (an adjudication, recorded as a requirement-signoff attestation that moves the set to accepted), then the close | . workflow_complete takes step ids such as A_Implement, A_Close and BA_Signoff by name; the interpreter enters a phase by itself and workflow_next tells you which one you are in (inside: Phase 6 Implement + acceptance). You cannot complete a phase — a phase is done when its steps are. Phase 6 is one subprocess, because a rejected increment, an MVP that is not ready, and stakeholder findings all route back into implementation, and a subprocess has one exit and cannot be re-entered once finished.

881faf5ed805.title: Every question you put to the BA carries its context first (STRICT)
881faf5ed805.content: Every phase of this process hands the BA a decision they were not inside the analysis for. The ordering rule in interaction-modality.md §4.1 governs this whole workflow, not just its explicit checkpoints: context → options → recommendation → question. Its test applies unchanged: . Can the BA answer without opening anything? . Terms the agent coined during its analysis feel defined to it and are new to everybody else. Three traps: . | An option name you invented. “Prefix-at-rest or prefix-at-install?” names two things that exist nowhere outside your own head and your own issue. Describe what each one does instead, and put the coined name in parentheses if it earns its place at all. | A question that resolves to “go read the issue”. The issue is where the BA goes for depth. It is never where the question’s terms are defined, and a question that needs it read turns a quick decision into a long one. | Options without their costs. “A or B” is not a choice; “A, which changes nothing here, or B, which rewrites every bootstrap.processes:skill ref in the diagrams” is. The BA is deciding on the consequences, so the consequences are the question. | . This applies to every surface this workflow uses: the chat, the summary comment posted to the issue after each round, the PR body, and a work item’s ## Done when.

6611eccc471d.title: Phase 1 — Needs assessment
6611eccc471d.content: Input: the feature request (from chat, issue, discussion, or upload) . | Identify the requester — who is asking? | Identify stakeholders — who else is affected? Check: . | <name>.config.json roles across active folios | GitHub CODEOWNERS | Recent activity on related issues | . | Gather source material — the request may come from: . | Chat messages in the current session | A GitHub issue body or comment | An uploaded document (Word, PDF) in uploads/ | A referenced document in library/ | An attachment to a GitHub issue comment | . | Synthesise a needs statement — write a clear, jargon-free statement of what is needed and why, with rationale linking to a concrete workflow | Post to the issue — the synthesised needs statement goes on the GitHub issue as a comment, not in chat | Request feedback — ask the requestor and stakeholders to review | . Loop: iterate until the needs statement is approved.

b9e809109586.title: Phase 2 — Business process analysis
b9e809109586.content: Input: approved needs statement . | Find the current workflow — check processes/**/*.bpmn for existing process diagrams that cover the affected area | Map the gap — where in the current workflow does the need appear? Identify the specific activity or decision point | Document current state — if no BPMN exists, document the as-is workflow in prose or create a new BPMN fragment | Identify bottlenecks — probe for the real pain point behind the stated request | . Post to the issue: current-state workflow description with gap identified.

c03f7046e2a4.title: Phase 3 — Requirements definition
c03f7046e2a4.content: Input: current-state analysis with identified gap . For each requirement: . | Functional requirement — stated as “SHALL” / “SHOULD” / “MAY” | Proposed implementation: . | Skill file (name, location, description) | MCP tool registration (if applicable) | Schema changes (Zod types, block kinds, constraints) | Pipeline changes (validators, renderers, scripts) | . | Acceptance criteria — testable conditions | Consumer burden — see below. A requirement that shifts work onto the consumer is not done. | Cross-references — link to related documentation pages under docs/source/, existing skills, existing workflows | Wireframe candidates, when a requirement changes a rendered surface — a page, a visualiser, the navbar, a form, an app screen. Before anything is built, run wireframe-design-review in Design use (Call_Wireframe in crdm-requirements-definition.bpmn): at least two candidates, each with a web and a mobile layout, committed as assets of the proposal under docs/proposals/<slug>/wireframes/ on the feature branch, and shown where the requester will look, chosen from context — the conversation, the issue the request came from, the PR, or several — each place carrying the same branches/ deep links and screenshots (staging-review, the deep-link rule, point 5). The candidates are the options Phase 4’s comparison lays out; the requester or BA chooses one at the review. Record “N/A — no rendered surface” in the template otherwise. The wireframe is part of the design process for adjudication (wiregen). | . Consumer burden is a requirement, not a nicety (STRICT) . Every requirement states what a downstream consumer must do to use the result — and the target is nothing. The standing rule: a downstream consumer must never have to string-manipulate, re-derive, or assume a rule in order to use what we publish. If an artefact makes a consumer parse a name, strip a prefix, substitute a base URL, or know a convention that is written down only in prose, the requirement is not met. Ask it in this form, because the failure is always phrased as a saving: . “We don’t need to emit X — it can be derived from Y.” . That sentence is the smell. A rule a consumer has to know is a rule a consumer can get wrong, and the cost is paid by someone who cannot see the code that made the assumption reasonable. Emitting the derivable field costs bytes in a regenerated artefact; the derivation rule costs correctness in every consumer. So emit the derivable field. For example, a preview knowledge graph’s nodes each carry an explicit prov:alternateOf link to their canonical counterpart, rather than relying on a documented base-URL substitution: a consumer should follow a link, not implement a substitution. Three checks that catch most of it: . | Would a consumer in another language need our source to understand this? If yes, emit the field. | Is the convention stated anywhere a machine can read? Prose in a skill is not machine-readable. A typed term in a @context is. | Does the artefact answer “what am I?” from itself? A preview that needs an external convention to be told apart from the canonical version fails this. Put it in the type, not in a filename or a path segment. | . This is also why the declaration file keeps a fixed name while artefacts are stub-named: a consumer must be able to open a repository it has never seen without first deriving a filename. See directory-conventions §Naming. Post to the issue: structured requirements with acceptance criteria.

8bae1a3e1ab9.title: Phase 4 — Impact analysis
8bae1a3e1ab9.content: Input: defined requirements . | Schema impact — which types, constraints, builders change? | Pipeline impact — which scripts under pipeline/ are affected? | Adapter impact — paper, document, dak? Does it ripple? | QA impact — new criteria? Modified criteria? Registry changes? | Folio impact — which active folios need migration? | Consumer impact — what must every downstream consumer change, and what must it now know? An impact analysis that lists only our own files has measured half the change. Enumerate: fields added or removed from published artefacts, IRIs or filenames that move, conventions a consumer would have to learn. A convention added is an impact, even when no file changed shape. | Test plan — what tests to add or update? Include at least one that asserts the consumer-facing contract, not only the internal one — a test over the emitted artefact, not over the function that built it. | Migration plan — steps, rollback, what breaks without it | . Post to the issue: impact assessment and migration plan. When the analysis yields more than one viable approach . Phase 4 often ends with a choice rather than a plan, and that is the moment the BA is handed a decision. Not a list of approach names with the analysis linked: a comparison, per decision-comparison — per option its pro, its con, what it changes downstream and how reversible it is, laid out where the rows can be read against each other, then one recommendation and a stated default. Items 1–6 above enumerate the downstream question for the change as a whole; the comparison asks it once per option, so an empty downstream column discards work already done.

d2cc9edab832.title: Phase 4b — Prioritization and dependency ordering
d2cc9edab832.content: Input: impact analysis complete, possibly multiple capability areas identified . When a feature request decomposes into more than one capability area (as most non-trivial requests do), the agent must explicitly order them before creating work items. This is not optional: a flat work item list has no implementation sequence, so the next session either guesses the order or asks the BA a question the analysis already answered. The prioritization protocol . | Identify capability areas — each is a coherent cluster of requirements that can be implemented and reviewed independently. Name them. | Map dependencies — draw the dependency graph: . | Does area A define concepts that area B assumes? | Does area A produce artefacts that area B consumes? | Does area A change structure that area B builds on? If yes, A must precede B. | . | Apply the formalize-first rule — within the dependency order: . | Structural/organizational work first (taxonomies, indexes, schemas) | Process/policy formalization second (skills, workflows, conventions) | Implementation third (code, pipelines, tools) | Visualization/UI last (dashboards, pages, views) | . Only the UI’s build comes last. Its wireframe is designed and approved in Phases 3–4 (step 6 of Phase 3), so the order fixes when it is implemented, not when it is decided. This is not arbitrary — a visualization built before the process is formalized will be rebuilt; a process formalized before the structure is organized will reference the wrong paths. | Present the order to the BA — as a dependency chain, not a list: Area 5 (structure) → Area 2 (process) → Area 3 (review) → Area 4 (planning) → Area 1 (visualization) . With one sentence per arrow explaining why the dependency exists. | BA confirms or reorders — the agent proposes, the BA decides. The BA may override the dependency order (e.g. “I need the visualization first even if it’s throwaway”) — that’s a legitimate business decision, and the agent records it as such rather than arguing. | . What this step produces . | A numbered list of capability areas in implementation order | A dependency rationale for each ordering decision | An estimate of scope per area (work item count) | A recommendation for which areas constitute the MVP release | . Post to the issue alongside the impact analysis. This becomes the input to Phase 5’s work item creation — work items are created in dependency order, not in the order the BA mentioned them. Cross-domain applicability . This step applies identically to code features, paper milestones, and project deliverables. The formalize-first rule is domain-independent: a paper’s structure (chapter order, block kinds) must precede its content (prose), which must precede its presentation (PDF layout).

dce2b8ace356.title: Phase 5 — Sign-off and bean creation
dce2b8ace356.content: Input: requirements + impact analysis reviewed and approved by stakeholders . | Post sign-off summary on the issue — what was agreed, what was deferred — and record it. BA_Signoff is an adjudication: the BA answers approve, amend, reject, defer or cancel, and A_RecordSignoff appends a requirement-signoff attestation for the requirement set (who, when, scope, outcome, the stage it moves the set to, the reason, and the permalink to the issue comment). GW_SignoffRecorded reads it back, so the phase cannot continue on a sign-off nobody recorded. An agent records the BA’s decision; it never makes it. | Create work items for each implementation unit — each naming the req: statements it delivers, with ## Done when copied from their success criteria, and listed in the set’s workPlan (a set at planned with no work items is refused): . | Follow the check-before-create protocol (see todo-manager.md) | Scope to a single PR-sized unit | Reference the parent issue in each work item | . | Offer the knowledge-graph destinations for the agreed set — A_OfferKg, BA_ChooseKg, A_RecordKg in crdm-signoff.bpmn. This step is not optional and its default creates nothing. See below. | . The agreed set is an ASSET, and Phase 5 is where it gets a home . The agreed set is a design-memory asset, so it goes into docs/; when it relates to a harness, feature or tool, its detailed design and planning go into that harness’s docs/. Without this step requirements end as an issue and a conversation: requirements are produced while building, and they are not the thing built. Three rules, and the first is the one a run skips: . | Ask; never pick silently. The destinations are DERIVED from the owning instance’s declared graphs at the time of asking, none is a listed answer, and if nobody answers nothing is created and “asked, answered none” is recorded. kg-contribution-offer carries the option set and the question that identifies a design-memory asset. | It goes in the OWNING instance’s docs/ — a cat-harness feature’s reasoning in cat-harness/docs/, a folio’s subject matter not in the platform at all. placement decides where inside it: architecture/ for why it is shaped this way, guides/ for how a person does something with it, reference/ for generated material that is never hand-edited. | Not fsh-guts. That is the declared non-rendered trashcan and its content may be thrown away or lost. A design record’s whole value is that it survives the conversation that produced it. | . What separates the record from the skills the same phase produces: a skill carries what a competent practitioner needs in order to do the task; everything past that line — background, options not taken, how to reach a data source, an API’s full surface when the task touches three calls — is documentation. Both directions fail silently, so state which one you are writing before you write it. A harness feature’s documents: proposed in docs/proposals/, filed in docs/requirements/ (STRICT) . When the feature is the harness’s own, the documents this process produces (initial analysis, MVP, the options, the agreed requirements) live and are updated under docs/, in two declared sub-graphs of it. | stage | where | what it is | checked by | . | Phases 1–5, and while building | docs/proposals/<slug>.md | the argument: needs, options, MVP, what was agreed | — | . | the feature ships | docs/requirements/<slug>.md | the promise: its front matter is a Requirement | check:requirements | . The directory says what KIND of document it is; the stage is a field. The requirements document is a RequirementSet whose stage (draft … accepted, or rejected, cancelled, superseded) is recorded in the set and moved only by a recorded sign-off. The directory follows the stage — a set reaching accepted is when its proposal is filed — but does not stand in for it, because a file’s location records neither the decision nor who made it. Both kinds, proposals and requirements, declare within: "docs". Every list of kinds (the navbar’s Folders among them) therefore draws them inside the Docs row, folded shut until the reader opens it. That is general behaviour for any kind declaring within, not a special case for these two. One proposal per feature, updated in place, never forked. A later phase edits the same page rather than writing a second one, so the history of the argument is git log on one file. Filing on ship is a MOVE, never a copy. In Phase 6, once the owner has said to merge: . | git mv docs/proposals/<slug>.md docs/requirements/<slug>.md, so git log --follow walks the requirement back through its argument. | Add the Requirement fields to its front matter, from bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json: . | id: req:<slug>. The id IS the file name. | status: in-force | proposedIn: the old path. | actors, description. | statements: one per agreed requirement, each with a key, a conformance level (SHALL, SHOULD, MAY or SHALL NOT) and one requirement sentence a reviewer can say yes or no to. A functional statement may add activity, capability (“I want”) and benefit (“so that”). A non-functional one may add a category. Keep the body: the reasoning stays with the promise it produced. | . | Point the feature’s test runs at the statements they check, in folio-test-run/v1’s requirements array, as req:<slug>#<key>. The test points at the requirement, never the reverse. | bun run cat check:requirements. It refuses a slug that is in both sub-graphs (a copy, or a proposal landing on an existing requirement), an id that is not its file name, and front matter the schema rejects. | . The schema names no outside concept. It lives in bootstrap, so every harness has it, and check:bootstrap-concepts fails if any bootstrap schema names a derivative’s content model, layer names, organisation or interchange standard. A harness that follows a particular standard maps that standard’s fields onto these fields in its own layer, never in the base. How filed requirements are organised, traced, superseded, and retired: . | The assessment of open requirements standards is in methodologies/requirements-standards-assessment.md, and the literature search, adopted/rejected methodologies, and the BPMN filing workflow (Process_RequirementsFiling, sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn) are in methodologies/requirements-filing-and-organisation.md. | Physical files stay flat at docs/requirements/<slug>.md (id: req:<slug>, statement keys req:<slug>#<key>), organised in docs/requirements/index.md under the eight canonical concern groups (code-lists/concern-group.json), with three-axis traceability (proposedIn, derivedFrom, dependsOn, beans, skills, processes, test/attestations/) and an immutable lifecycle (proposed → in-force → superseded | retired, never git rm). | . A folio’s features are not filed here. This applies to the harness’s own feature work. A folio’s subject matter lives in the folio, as Phase 5 already says.

cc8ba1f66cdb.title: Phase 6 — Iterative development
cc8ba1f66cdb.content: Input: work items . For each work item: . | Create feature branch — always, no exceptions. Before the first edit, run the collision review in coordinate §”Starting new work”. | Implement — following the accepted requirements, and, where a requirement changes a rendered surface, against the wireframe candidate the requester or BA chose in Phases 3–4. The delivery summary links the chosen candidate beside the after-screenshot. | Open PR — link to the work item and the parent issue | Deploy staging preview — the feature-staging.yml workflow auto-deploys to branches/<branch-slug>/ on gh-pages. The magenta “FEATURE BRANCH” banner at the top of every page links to the source branch and provides a “compare with main” link. | Post before/after comparison to issue — use the staging-review skill. Every changed page gets a before (main) and after (staging) URL pair in a Markdown table. See schemas/staging-comparison.schema.json for the schema: | Page | Before (main) | After (staging) | What changed |---|---|---|---| Landing | [main](…) | [staging](…) | Added badge | . | Iterate on PR feedback — code review is on the PR; visual review uses the staging preview URLs. When the change touches a folio’s blocks, the page a reviewer opens is the preview’s review page, branches/<slug>/review/: every changed block before and after, with the heat map and outline. The review itself runs through content-change-review.bpmn. The review coordinator slices the change and assigns the slices, reviewers work them in review-task, disagreements go to adjudication, and the coverage gate must pass before sign-off. | Ask user for explicit confirmation before merging to main. This is the merge-to-main sub-process, called from crdm-close.bpmn (Call_MergeToMain) once the sign-off is recorded and before the issue is closed, and run the same way for any increment the owner asks to land earlier. A stakeholder sign-off or the BA’s confirmation is acceptance of the feature, not authorisation to merge it. | Update documentation — the OWNING instance’s docs/ pages and the workflow BPMNs. For the harness’s own feature, file its proposal as its requirements once the merge is agreed: see “A harness feature’s documents” above. If Phase 5’s offer chose a docs/ destination, this is where that page is written and kept true; if the implementation diverged from what was agreed, the divergence is recorded there rather than smoothed. | Staging cleanup — a merged PR’s preview goes away on its own: the merge is the confirmation, since the main site now shows the same thing. Everything else is retained by default. While a PR that will not be merged is open, the user adds the staging:cleanup label; once it is closed the label can no longer reach it, and removal is a feature-staging.yml dispatch the user runs with cleanup_slug and a matching cleanup_confirm (see staging-review). Never remove a staging preview any other way, and never on your own initiative. | . Theme and UI review is NOT a Phase 6 step — it happens at ingestion . theme-ui-review runs only at ingestion of graphical assets for a website or app design, from ingest-theme.bpmn. GW_StakeholderOK’s accepted branch in crdm-deliver.bpmn closes the phase directly. Accessibility, branding and locales for a UI are checked there, not here, because at ingestion a finding is a decision about what the assets will be rather than a defect in something that shipped. When a round of implementation is complete (one or more work items resolved): . | Post a round summary comment on the issue — addressed to the BA and stakeholders, containing: . | What was accomplished in this round | What remains to be accomplished (open work items) | Links to updated content for review (staging URLs, docs pages) | Before/after comparison table for changed pages | . | Never close the issue without explicit authorization — the BA or stakeholder closes it, or the agent closes it only when the BA explicitly says to. An agent must never assume completion. | .
