de411abddc77.title: Create a sticky note
de411abddc77.content: A sticky note is a carried note: something a person or agent sticks onto the knowledge graph. This skill turns a moment in a conversation into one — drafting the words, choosing the theme, deciding where it goes — and shows it before it is attached to anything.

7a3c020dd4e7.title: The one rule that makes this safe
7a3c020dd4e7.content: Preview, confirm, then attach — in that order, always. A sticky lands in committed state: todos/items/ is a graph a person reads, and folio/ is rendered to a website. Writing first and asking afterwards means the wrong note is already in somebody’s list. The preview costs one exchange and is never skipped, not for a short note and not for an obvious one. An unattached sticky is a legitimate outcome. Previewed, looked at, and left where it is. That is not a failed run — a note nobody needed is cheapest when it never reached the graph.

f27d203f45d3.title: The six steps
f27d203f45d3.content: 1. Read the context, and say what you took from it . Name the moment the sticky is about: a ruling, a measurement, a question that went unanswered, a thing somebody will need again. If you cannot name it, there is no sticky to make. 2. Draft the words — quote, or interpret, and SAY WHICH . Two modes, and the choice is reported rather than silent: . |   | when | how | . | direct quotation | the words carry information their paraphrase loses — a joke, a term of art, a ruling’s exact scope | verbatim, down to the spelling. | . | interpretation | the point is clear but scattered across several turns, or the original was a fragment | write it plainly, and keep any phrase that was doing work. | . Prefer quotation when in doubt. A joke or an odd phrase often carries the only part that tells a reader anything; sanding it into a product sentence loses that. A summary is derived from the body’s first line unless the note needs its own. Two fields the author must keep in step is one field that drifts. 3. Choose the theme — a judgement, not a lookup . There is no role-to-theme mapping, and none should be added: the theme is an authoring judgement. Choose from what the note is doing: the shipped themes are grumpy-cat, engineer, library, analyst, plus the palette-only pale-sage, dusty-carolina, their -fade variants, and the two high-contrast themes. schemas/ui/themes.ts is the list; state the reason for the one you picked, in a clause. Two mechanical facts: . | A theme whose art the instance does not declare resolves to palette only, not to a broken image — resolveThemeBackdrop reports that third state rather than serving art that is not there. | An incomplete backdrop is refused wholesale. Two of three layouts renders as no art, not two thirds. Check bun run cat check:theme-art if you are about to rely on a role you have not seen render. | . 4. Decide where it goes — todos/ is the default, not the only answer . | destination | when | what it becomes | . | todos/items/ — the default | somebody has an outstanding item | a todo/1.0.0 node: status, priority, origin, plus the tags below | . | todos/feedback/ | it is about a specific block, with the submitter’s identity | the content-review feedback workflow the todo-review skill reads | . | folio/ | it belongs on a rendered page | a landing sticky — but a page’s sticky is a layer’s contribution, so it is declared in that layer’s <name>.json, not written here. A landing sticky lives in the folio/ of the instance it describes, never in another instance’s, so a mounted instance’s sticky arrives with the mount | . | nowhere | it was worth showing and not worth keeping | previewed in the conversation and left there | . todos/ is not beans/. A todo is a person’s outstanding item; a work item is the agent work plan. AGENTS.md forbids standing a second work plan beside beans/, so a sticky that is really agent work is a work item — use todo-manager, not this. 5. Bind it to the graph . A CarriedNote carries its attachments, and each is optional: . | anchor — page-global ({kind: "page", page}), a block ({kind: "block", block}), or none. Absent is a fourth state and means not yet placed. | roles, processes, tasks — what it is about in the process model. | identities — who it is assigned to, as provider:id (github:litlfred). Assignment is a tag, not a transfer: it says who should see it, and the person has not agreed to anything by being named. | references — KG corpus nodes by {kind, id}: a work item, a block, a skill. | artefacts — files and external things. | . Leave out what you do not know. An empty identities is unassigned, which is a real answer; a guessed one is a false one. 6. Preview, on the surface the reader is on . In the conversation when that is where the decision is being made — render it as it will read, not as a JSON dump. Show the theme, the placement and the assignment as a header, then the body as a reader sees it. On the knowledge graph when the note is one of many, or when its look matters — build the page and screenshot it. A rendered artefact cannot be assessed from a description of it, and defects that a green test suite misses show the moment somebody looks. Then ask, and attach only on a yes.

863b6670af5f.title: Worked example — an unattached one
863b6670af5f.content: Asked for a sticky about reading the documentation, explicitly not in todos/: . | Context — orientation. Somebody arriving at this repository asks a question the guides answer. | Words — interpretation, with one quotation kept. No ruling to quote, so the body is written; but “the documentation you will never read” is kept verbatim, because the repository’s own landing sticky already says it and it is the honest expectation. | Theme — grumpy-cat. RTFM is a grumpy sentiment and the cat is the one that carries it. Judgement, stated; no table consulted. | Placement — none. Explicitly not todos/: nobody has an outstanding item here, and filing it would put a signpost in somebody’s task list. | Bindings — none. identities empty, so unassigned. One artefacts entry pointing at the docs site is what the note is for. | Preview in the conversation, and stop. There is nothing to confirm, because there is nothing to attach. | .

42fd240a35d3.title: What this skill does not do
42fd240a35d3.content: . | It does not write a landing-page sticky. Those are a layer’s contribution, declared in its declaration — see sticky-contribution.ts. | It does not create work items. Agent work is todo-manager’s. | It does not delete or overwrite a sticky it did not make. Editing somebody else’s note is the deletion-requires-confirmation case. | .

65e9717138d8.title: Which graph to trace
65e9717138d8.content: “What does the argument actually rest on?” is an impact question, so trace the union of both dependency relations — not uses[] alone: . | editorial edges (uses[]) — what a reader must have read first. Agent/human maintained. | formal edges (lean.ref → Lean dep graph) — what the proof actually invokes. Machine-derived. | . A critical path built from uses[] alone is missing every formal dependency the narrative never introduces, and will understate what breaks when a block changes. Build the union with cat-harness-tools/pipeline/content-graph.ts — its accessors (out, in, cone) default to the union and take an optional EdgeKind filter: . bun run cat-harness-tools/pipeline/content-graph.ts content/<paper> . Check hasFormal before trusting a union result. When the Lean Atlas cache is absent the formal edge set is empty because the data was unavailable, not because the corpus has no formal structure — report that limitation rather than a confident path. Do not “fix” divergence between the two by editing uses[]. See AGENTS.md and the uses-editorial-review skill.

77503cf2805a.title: Overview
77503cf2805a.content: This skill traces the logical dependency chain of the paper from axioms to final results, classifying every block on the critical path by its context assumptions: . | GENERAL: Statement and proof work at the most general level, under the weakest assumptions — only the project’s axioms / the general theory’s axioms. | SPECIALIZED STATEMENT: The statement itself requires a particular realisation, model, or extra structure that the general theory does not assume. | SPECIALIZED PROOF: The statement is general, but the proof uses tools only available under stronger assumptions (a concrete model, analytic or geometric machinery, a specific group/space, numerical or empirical data, etc.). | MIXED: Some parts general, some specialised. | .

2fa2441afb05.title: When to Use This Skill
2fa2441afb05.content: . | “What assumptions does this result actually need?” | “Is this proof general or does it rely on a specialisation?” | “Which results need rewriting for the general case?” | “Trace the critical path from X to Y” | “Audit specialisation dependencies” | “What’s the minimal assumption set for theorem Z?” | “Separate the general core from the specialisation” | .

532d2dd1411b.title: Workflow
532d2dd1411b.content: 1. Identify the critical path . Trace the dependency chain on the union graph (see “Which graph to trace”), from the target result back to the axioms. 2. Classify each block . For each block on the critical path, read both the .md (narrative) and .ts (manifest) files. Classify by: . | Signal | Likely classification | . | Uses only the abstract/foundational vocabulary of the general theory | GENERAL | . | Invokes a concrete model, realisation, or extra structure not assumed by the general theory | SPECIALIZED | . | Pulls in analytic/geometric machinery, a specific group or space, or numerical/empirical data | SPECIALIZED | . 3. Identify mismatches . Flag blocks where: . | Statement is general but proof is specialised → candidate for a general proof rewrite | Statement mixes general and specialised language → candidate for splitting into two blocks | Proof uses heavier machinery when the general argument suffices | . 4. Propose actions . For each flagged block, propose one of: . | Rewrite proof at the general level (when the general argument exists) | Split statement into a general theorem + specialised corollary | Move to specialisation section (keep content, reorganise placement) | Add dual proofs (general + specialised via proofs[] array) | Accept as specialised (when no general alternative exists) | . 5. Architectural conventions . The paper follows a general core + specialisation architecture: . | General results (GENERAL) live in the main sections of each chapter. | Specialisations live in a dedicated section. | A suffix on a block name denotes a specialisation variant (e.g. a -C suffix marking the specialised form of a general block). | Statements that have both a general and a specialised proof list both in the proofs[] array of the .ts manifest. | The general proof is listed first; the specialised proof second. | . 6. The specialisation boundary . A critical path typically flows from foundational definitions through intermediate results to a target theorem, crossing a specialisation boundary below which blocks require a concrete realisation: . def:foundation (the project's axioms) → def:core-structure (general construction) → thm:main (general statement + general proof) ──── SPECIALISATION BOUNDARY ──── → cor:specialized-X (applies the general result to a concrete model) → ... (machinery available only under the specialisation) . Everything above the boundary is general; everything below requires a particular realisation.

023c2ce0edf5.title: Audit checklist
023c2ce0edf5.content: When auditing a critical path, check every object for: . | Lean completeness: .lean file exists? sorry count? status accurate? | Worked-example pair: *-example.ts/.md pair exists? Listed in examples[]? | Logical consistency: uses[] matches actual .md cross-references? | Notational consistency: per the project’s conventions. | Context classification: GENERAL vs SPECIALIZED — flag mismatches | Cross-references: all (#label) links resolve to existing blocks? | .

ae5f88791174.title: Output format
ae5f88791174.content: Produce a table with columns: | Block | Classification | Specialisation signals | Action needed | . Follow with specific recommendations, using AskUserQuestion for mathematical strategy decisions (with structured options, not free-text questions).

3212cf2b5273.title: Harness skills that dispatch here
3212cf2b5273.content: . | one-voice-integration-watcher: as the dependency-trace skill, when domain-boundary-correct fires. | domain-fencing: the example of a rule that splits cleanly; the union-of-two-relations model is in edge-kinds-and-blast-radius. | .

be92d5be8358.title: dak-l1-library
be92d5be8358.content: Skill id: dak-l1-library · Package: authoring-who-smart-guidelines · Named by l2-dak-authoring.bpmn step Build the L1 library from Component 1, in the Business analyst lane. Every library built for a DAK starts from the DAK’s own Component 1, “Health interventions and recommendations”: §1.1 lists the interventions, and §1.2 names the WHO guidelines and guidance the DAK operationalises, each with a printed (n) into the DAK’s reference list. Those sources are the DAK’s L1. Without them the library cannot answer what an L1 graph is for: which recommendation does this decision rule implement? .

8e43524fca67.title: Input and output
8e43524fca67.content: The contract is input.schema.json and output.schema.json. | In: where to look: the useCase (stage 1 of smart-guideline-end-to-end, guideline-use-case’s output), a dak whose Component 1 cites the sources (l2-dak-authoring.bpmn), or both; and whether to ingest what is not in library/ yet. | Out: l1Sources: the candidates, Component 1 sources first, then WHO IRIS and the jurisdiction’s own, each in-library, in-kg or not-yet, included or not with a one-sentence reason. Stage 2 (recommendation-extraction) takes it as its l1Sources. | .

4e1df31bcd93.title: The layering rule
4e1df31bcd93.content: Every layer points only upstream: L3 → L2 → L1 → library. An L1 node may name the library node it was read from; nothing in the library names L1. So an L1 document’s publication, sections and elements are specialisations (prov:specializationOf) of its library entry, sections and blocks, and L1 inherits whatever sectioning the ingest produced: an outline, inferred contents, or pages. The schema is smart-base’s l1-library layer (smart-base/kg/src/l1-library.ts), which imports smart-kg L1 3.0 unchanged.

ad5bf2bae3db.title: L1 or not — three sources, one precedence
ad5bf2bae3db.content: A document is L1 when it is WHO guideline content: a guideline, implementation guidance, a summary table, a position paper, a classification. A DAK is not (it is L2); neither is a technical specification. The answer is a classifications[] entry on the document’s intake.json (scheme https://smart.who.int/kg/layer, code l1), from up to three sources: . | source | written by | smart-kg derivation | . | declared | a person, with by and at | decided | . | context | this step: §1.2 introduces every card as guidance the DAK draws on (--record-context) | — the publication stays inferred | . | inferred | l1-membership.ts from the IRIS Dublin Core record (series, title words) | inferred | . declared > context > inferred. A lower record that disagrees is reported on every run, never dropped: the immunizations DAK’s §1.2 cites DDCC (28), so context says L1, and a declaration says it is not. With no record at all the document is undetermined: the L1 step does nothing and says what to record.

c1b435b01feb.title: The pattern
c1b435b01feb.content: The DAK itself is library-only: it is L2, so it gets no L1 graph. Reading its Component 1 is how the L1 sources are found; each of those is ingested individually and gets its own L1 graph. | Fetch the DAK from WHO IRIS with bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/fetch-dspace-item.ts <handle URL> --out uploads. It writes the PDF, the item’s Dublin Core record (folio-dublin-core/v1) and an intake.json whose licence is the record’s dc.rights, stated only when the repository states it. | Ingest it: bun run cat ingest uploads/<doc_id>/<doc_id>.pdf --library <lib>. A WHO PDF with no outline goes to pdf-structure, which keeps its inferred contents only if they pass the trust tests, else falls back to pages. | Read Component 1: bun run smart-base/scripts/extract-dak-l1-references.ts --entry library/<doc_id> --context-only. It lists §1.2’s citations and the reference each printed number names, with its URL, and flags those that rest on the printed number alone. Those references are the fetch list. | Fetch every L1 source, one by one, by where it lives: . | an IRIS or PAHO IRIS handle → fetch-dspace-item.ts; | a who.int item page (/publications/m/item/…) → bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/fetch-who-publication.ts <URL> --out uploads, which reads the page’s title, date, type, overview, page count and copyright into the Dublin Core record and takes its one PDF; | a reference whose URL is a listing (the summary-tables page lists Tables 1–4, each cited by its own card) → fetch each listed item, and record on each intake how it was reached. | . A source that is not a publication (a data portal, a blank reporting form) is not fetched; say so. Then ingest each (step 2). | Record the context decision: run step 3 again with --record-context. Each held source’s intake gets §1.2’s context classification, matched by handle or by its record’s dc.identifier.uri. | For each held source that is L1, run the L1 step: bun run smart-base/scripts/l1-specialise.ts --entry library/<doc_id> --validate-zod <smart-base checkout>. It writes smart-kg-l1-library.jsonld beside the entry. A source that is not L1 gets no L1 graph; its library entry is its only representation. | Check the edition. A who.int page serves the CURRENT edition, which may be newer than the one the DAK cites (“updated in 2024” against a 1 December 2025 table). Note it on the intake; do not treat them as one. | Leave fidelity to a person. The run lists each citation whose words differ from its reference title. Someone opens the DAK page and the source and confirms it; nothing marks that check passed automatically. | .

1027f6f73c98.title: What an L1 graph holds
1027f6f73c98.content: smart-kg-l1-library.jsonld, beside each L1 source’s entry: publication, publication-section (one per library section, front matter excepted, with the ingest’s confidence in its note) and publication-element (each figure, table and box the ingest’s figure reader found), joined by contains, each specializationOf its library-node. Section IRIs use the number as the contents page prints it (Annex 1, Section 2), so an annex does not collide with a chapter of the same number; a heading printed many times (“Analysis” under every chapter) takes its position among its namesakes. A publication with no ISBN or handle is identified by its page URL. It is JSON-LD that survives as RDF. Its @context is http://smart.who.int/kg/l1-library.context.jsonld, the layer’s identity, never fetched at run time. smart-base/kg/ generates that context from the same Zod source as the FHIR models and serves it through src/loader.ts; expand a graph with jsonld.js and that documentLoader. smart-kg’s own L1 context would drop every node class and property name and any predicate it does not know; the library context keeps all three (@vocab, properties as @nest with Dublin Core terms, predicates by declared IRI). A citation resolves by its printed number into the numbered list that holds every cited number with the most title agreement; a DAK has several numbered lists. Title agreement is only corroboration: a card often describes its source rather than naming it, so low agreement is flagged for step 8, not treated as a miss. publicationType comes from a declaration or the title’s own words (summary tables, guidance, position paper, classification). A guideline’s subtype turns on its GRC history, which a title does not carry, and a data portal has no type at all; neither is forced into the nearest code.

946e4d49e2c4.title: Where the files go
946e4d49e2c4.content: Each L1 graph is written beside its entry; smart-kg-l1.json is the recommendation extractor’s (extract-smart-kg-l1.ts). The DAK repository holds the library: library/<doc_id>/ for each entry, and uploads/<doc_id>/intake.json plus the Dublin Core record for each fetched item. The PDFs are pinned by sha256 and not committed.

33f1ced28d8d.title: What it cannot do yet
33f1ced28d8d.content: . | Element types the library does not extract: table rows, footnotes, charts, images, flowcharts, lists. L1 3.0 defines nine; the L1 step emits the three the ingest finds and names the other six in the publication’s note. | Recommendations in an L1 source are extract-smart-kg-l1.ts’s, which writes L1 1.0 and finds only printed labels. For a source with none, and for each recommendation’s scenario (persona, process, user story), see recommendation-extraction. | The position papers behind a summary table. (29) in the immunizations DAK is the routine-immunization summary tables, which cite the WHO vaccine position papers; following them is a fetch per paper, not automated. | Sources neither fetcher reads. fetch-dspace-item.ts speaks DSpace 7 and fetch-who-publication.ts reads who.int item pages; a PAHO IRIS item behind a different network policy, or a spreadsheet, is recorded with its URL and reported, not fetched. | .

a8dc6d0d37cd.title: Schemas this rests on
a8dc6d0d37cd.content: . | L1 3.0 and the l1-library layer: smart-base/kg/ — Zod, from WHO smart-kg main 3f5e477, generating the KG* logical models, code systems and value sets; | IRIs: smart-base/scripts/l1-kgid.ts, smart-kg’s kgid.mjs as tested; | the Dublin Core record: folio-assistant-core/schemas/dublin-core.ts; | the intake, its licence and its classifications: cat-harness-tools/schemas/library/intake.ts, cat-harness-tools/schemas/library/source-licence.ts. | .

a9b232d7090c.title: dak-postprocessing
a9b232d7090c.content: Skill id: dak-postprocessing · Package: authoring-who-smart-guidelines · Layer: smart-base, DAK kind, except the two Library strippers, which are fhir-harness — see §”One step is not WHO’s”. Everything WHO’s build (.github/workflows/ghbuild.yml) runs between publisher.jar finishing and deployment, gated by do_dak and by the contentTypes.dak section of the root index.config.json (see dak-preprocessing, which also says where the scripts come from). Each step runs inside the Publisher’s Docker container (docker exec -w /work ig-run python3 …), against output/.

97e5a5fba2db.title: The steps, and what each accomplishes
97e5a5fba2db.content: | # | script | what it produces | . | 1 | strip_library_binaries.py | removes base64 content.data from Library resources | . | 2 | strip_library_content.py | replaces inline CQL/ELM with a URL reference | . | 3 | generate_logical_model_schemas.py | a JSON Schema per logical model | . | 4 | generate_valueset_schemas.py | a JSON Schema per ValueSet, plus the enumeration-response schemas | . | 5 | generate_jsonld_vocabularies.py | JSON-LD vocabularies from the ValueSet expansions | . | 6 | generate_dak_api_hub.py | dak-api.html — the hub page, and the .openapi.json / .displays.json sidecars | . | 7 | update_translated_image_refs.py | rewrites image references inside translated HTML pages | . | 8 | generate_smart_liquid.py + inject_smart_liquid.py | IG metadata → Liquid variables, and the include injected into every markdown page | . Steps 3 and 4 share one workflow step. Steps 1–5 belong to fhir-harness, not to this overlay: they only transform what the Publisher emitted and add no constraint or profile. They stay in this table because ghbuild.yml still runs them in this phase. check:fhir-harness-exclusions reads the script names from this table and dak-preprocessing’s and refuses them in fhir-harness, except these five. Steps 6–8 are the WHO surface.

01518adec49f.title: Step 8 is the seam
01518adec49f.content: generate_smart_liquid.py reads the Publisher’s output/. It scans it for {ResourceType}-{id}.json and, for each, emits Liquid assignments named . smart__<ResourceType>__<id_normalized>__<category>__<key> . with categories url__canonical, url__page, url__json, text__display, link__html, and elements__<key> for scalars (name, title, description, status, version, …). Ids are normalised by replacing every non-alphanumeric character with _. This already turns IG Publisher metadata into variables Jekyll processes, aimed at the Publisher’s own Jekyll. Moving to just-the-docs re-points this bridge rather than building a new one. It is one build behind . The script writes input/pagecontent/smart.liquid.md, which the Publisher only processes on the next build, and also writes output/smart.liquid.html directly so the page exists in this one. A surface that needs two builds to converge cannot drive an incremental staging loop; under just-the-docs the variables are computed and consumed in one pass.

d5109e74690d.title: One step is not WHO’s
d5109e74690d.content: Steps 1 and 2 strip base64 binaries and inline CQL/ELM out of Library resources. Nothing in either is DAK-shaped: any FHIR IG that embeds CQL (any IG using hl7.fhir.uv.cql) produces oversized Library resources. By the smart-stack-layering test — would a non-WHO FHIR IG need this? — they belong in fhir-harness. The deploy phase’s “Delete files >100MB before deployment” step is the same concern one layer down.

eddbfbcb97fd.title: Steps 3–6 are the DAK API
eddbfbcb97fd.content: The schema, vocabulary and hub steps produce the surface the artefact index binds (ig-artifact-ingestion): .schema.json, .displays.json and .openapi.json per artefact, .jsonld vocabularies, and the enumeration schemas (ValueSets.schema.json, LogicalModels.schema.json). No IG publishes an artefact-index instance: an enumeration schema is a schema of a response, whose example happens to hold the list. On an IG repository’s own site: ig-site:sidecars . An IG repository whose index.config.json names smart-base as its site’s landing declares no steps of its own. The site route (cat-harness-tools stage-local.ts) runs the landing layer’s ig-site:sidecars, which is ig-site-sidecars.ts: . | It runs fhir-harness’s ig-api-gen.ts, the generic port of steps 3–6’s generators, over the cached AST. This layer passes only the label and its data types’ JSON-LD prefix. | The per-artefact sidecars, including <stem>.openapi.json, go to $SITE_WORK/ig-api/sidecars/. The enumeration schemas and the Swagger UI page openapi/index.html go to $SITE_WORK/ig-api/site/, which fhir-harness serves at the site root without replacing a path the site already holds. | $SITE_WORK/ig-api/ig-api.json says {"label": "DAK API"} when the IG declares a DAK (index.config.json contentTypes.dak, or a legacy dak.json; scripts/ig-dak-metadata.ts). Otherwise fhir-harness’s default label, “IG API”, stands. | . fhir-harness binds and serves the sidecars (ig-repo-site.ts, fhir-harness ig-build-pipeline §”The IG repository’s site route”) and never learns the DAK name. ig-index:build runs the same step when it builds an IG’s artefact index. The hub page is fhir-harness’s: ig-api-hub.ts draws it from the artefact index’s bound sidecars, with one loader, on the docs site, an IG site and an IG repository’s own site. This layer names only what WHO calls it: ig-api.json gives the label and the marker an IG’s own dak-api.md holds (<!-- DAK_API_CONTENT -->), and fhir-harness puts the hub at that page.

556205ae52c7.title: Step 5 depends on expansion, which depends on a terminology server
556205ae52c7.content: generate_jsonld_vocabularies.py reads ValueSet expansions, which exist only if the Publisher expanded them, which depends on tx, the optional terminology server input. With a dead or restricted tx the step produces fewer vocabularies, warns and fails nothing. A thin vocabulary output is not evidence of a thin ValueSet: check the expansion first.

8e8a2cc419bd.title: Step 7 renders nothing and is not translation
8e8a2cc419bd.content: update_translated_image_refs.py rewrites <img> references inside translated HTML that has already been built. Where the locale layer is part of rendering there is no built HTML to patch, and the step has nothing to do.

08f4b42137f8.title: What the QA reports say, and where they go
08f4b42137f8.content: Every script here uses the same QAReporter as the pre-processing scripts and emits a phase report: successes, warnings, errors, files_processed, files_expected, files_missing, and a summary with counts and a completion timestamp. qa.json from the Publisher run is uploaded as a workflow artifact. The qa-report graph typology (cat-harness-tools schemas/sdlc/qa-report.ts) takes the shape these scripts emit. Its schema enforces three rules: a summary may not disagree with the details it counts; files_missing must be a subset of files_expected, so an empty result stays distinguishable from a not-found; and running is never a pass — qaReportVerdict returns unknown for a script that died before finishing, not ok.

d03d942b1e3d.title: Binary artefacts on deploy and on release
d03d942b1e3d.content: The generic rule and the measuring Tool are ig-binary-artefacts and ig-binary-audit. What the WHO workflows do: . | ghbuild.yml deploys output/ with its binaries. The only binary step is “Delete files >100MB before deployment”, and no Publisher binary is that large. Each branch build deploys to branches/<branch>/, so each preview carries another full copy, full-ig.zip included. | On a GitHub release, release.yml hands off to smart-html. It runs only if publication-request.json exists, then calls WorldHealthOrganization/smart-html/.github/workflows/release.yml (pinned by commit). That runs smart-html’s scripts/ig_publisher.py, which builds and publishes into the smart-html webroot, leaves ig-build-zips/ out of the sitepreview copy, moves only files over 100 MB plus a copy of output/package.tgz into release-assets/, and uploads that to the release tagged GITHUB_REF_NAME. So a release gets package.tgz and, in practice, nothing else; every other binary goes to the webroot. | create_package_release.py is called by no workflow. It would cut a release and move the 19 named binaries out of output/. | downloads.md lists 19 release assets that no release carries, and leaves out full-ig.zip, the largest. fix_release_links.py correctly rewrites its WorldHealthOrganization/smart-base release links to the building repository; the list itself is what is wrong. | . These workflows belong to the WHO repositories and are not changed here.

bd5b8bd08199.title: Where the counterparts are
bd5b8bd08199.content: dak-preprocessing — the steps before the Publisher, most of which only populate sushi-config.yaml’s pages: and menu:. ig-publication — the Publisher run and the authority to release. ig-artifact-ingestion — the artefact index that binds what steps 3–6 produce.

563dfc147b70.title: dak-preprocessing
563dfc147b70.content: Skill id: dak-preprocessing · Package: authoring-who-smart-guidelines · Layer: smart-base, DAK kind (smart-stack-layering), with two steps that are not pre-processing at all — see §”Two of these are authoring, not pre-processing”. DAK Preprocessing is everything WHO’s build (.github/workflows/ghbuild.yml) runs between checkout and publisher.jar, gated by the do_dak input and by the contentTypes.dak section of the root index.config.json. Every script reads and writes that section through input/scripts/dak_index.py. An IG that still carries a legacy dak.json keeps building: dak_index.py --adopt-legacy reads it into the index for that build only, with a warning. Nothing is committed back. ghbuild.yml runs the copy in the IG’s own input/scripts/ when there is one, and otherwise downloads the script from litlfred/smart-base at a commit pinned in the workflow (SCRIPTS_BASE_COMMIT). Step names and script names are the stable handles; re-read the workflow before relying on a detail.

94b52d575aac.title: The steps, and what each one accomplishes
94b52d575aac.content: | # | script | what it actually does | . | 1 | generate_dak_from_sushi.py | writes contentTypes.dak into index.config.json from sushi-config.yaml plus branch/repo context — only when smart.who.int.base is a dependency and the section is absent | . | 2 | update_sushi_config.py | registers pages and menu entries in sushi-config.yaml, and writes placeholder markdown — see below | . | 3 | generate_dak_from_sushi.py, again | re-runs step 1 “with current branch context” | . | 4 | dmn_questionnaire_generator.py | emits FHIR Questionnaire resources from the DMN decision tables | . | 5 | transform_dmn.py + dmn2html.xslt + dmn.css | renders each DMN file to HTML for inclusion in a page | . | 6 | inject_translations.py | substitutes translated strings into the diagram sources before they are rendered | . Steps 1 and 2 share the workflow step “Prepare DAK environment”; steps 3–6 each have a step of their own.

1365c557a551.title: What “get it into the IG index” meant — step 2, precisely
1365c557a551.content: update_sushi_config.py does four things: . | Scans for resources — fsh-generated/resources/ (SUSHI’s output) and input/resources/ (static JSON), collecting every ValueSet and every logical-model StructureDefinition. | Writes a placeholder markdown page per resource into input/pagecontent/, as ValueSet-<id>.md and the logical-model equivalent, each carrying a <!-- DAK_API_PLACEHOLDER: … --> marker. A file that already exists with real content is left alone; the marker is how the script tells its own placeholder from an author’s page. | Registers dak-api.md in sushi-config.yaml’s pages: map, creating the pages: key if the IG has none. | Registers Indices → DAK API → dak-api.html in the menu: map, creating menu: and the Indices subsection if absent. | . So the “index” is sushi-config.yaml’s pages: and menu: maps: the IG Publisher’s Jekyll renders a page only if the file exists in input/pagecontent/ and pages: names it. Step 2 supplies both halves. Under the just-the-docs pipeline navigation is derived from sushi-config.yaml directly and the pages are folio pages, so this step has no job there. See ig-render-jekyll for what replaces it.

c4af7154e218.title: Two of these are authoring, not pre-processing
c4af7154e218.content: Steps 4 and 5 — dmn_questionnaire_generator.py and transform_dmn.py — mint artefacts rather than prepare a renderer: . | the questionnaire generator emits FHIR resources, which the Publisher validates, indexes and publishes like any other. Without it the IG is missing Questionnaires, not a page. | the DMN transform produces the only human-readable rendering of a decision table the IG has. | . They depend on nothing the Publisher does. They are content generation and belong upstream of the Publisher, as authoring steps of the DAK document kind. transform_dmn.py outputs HTML, which the JSON-only render contract does not take. Whether it gains a structured output or its HTML is treated as an embedded asset is still open.

27bf40bea202.title: Step 6 is conditional on who renders
27bf40bea202.content: inject_translations.py rewrites diagram sources before rendering because the Publisher offers no later hook. When pages render through just-the-docs, this platform’s locale layer does that for pages. Diagram sources are still rasterised outside Jekyll, so the step is still needed for them: do not remove it on the page argument alone.

c9def1c70d9a.title: Steps 1 and 3 — one fact, computed twice
c9def1c70d9a.content: generate_dak_from_sushi.py runs twice in ghbuild.yml; the second run (“Regenerate DAK configuration with current context”) recomputes the same section after the branch has been resolved. The DAK section is this platform’s own declaration, so compute it once, in the right order. Do not reproduce the double run when lifting this step.

fe04ba2b8f7c.title: What a QA report already exists for
fe04ba2b8f7c.content: Every one of these scripts instantiates a QAReporter and writes a phase report — successes, warnings, errors, files_processed, files_expected, files_missing, plus a summary with counts and a completion timestamp. The qa-report graph typology (qa-report/v1, holds: "state", cat-harness-tools schemas/sdlc/qa-report.ts) takes exactly that shape, upstream’s snake_case field names included, so no translation step sits between WHO’s producer and this platform’s consumer.

c45a841948cd.title: In the AST lifecycle: the overlay on fhir-harness’s refresh
c45a841948cd.content: smart-base’s IG is published from the AST on its cache branch (cat/fhir-harness/fhir-ast/<package id>), like every smart-* IG. The one writer of that branch is fhir-harness’s reusable ig-ast-refresh.yml (skill ig-build-pipeline, §”The AST cache lifecycle”). The plain AST exporter does not run this phase, so smart-base supplies it as an overlay; fhir-harness never names it. | The command is smart-base/scripts/dak-pre-export.sh (bun run cat smart-base:dak-pre-export). It runs steps 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6, in that order, from this checkout’s own input/scripts/. It does not repeat step 3. Steps 4–6 run only when the IG declares contentTypes.dak. Any failure fails the run. | The caller is smart-base’s .github/workflows/ig-ast-refresh.yml: fhir-harness’s template plus pre-export: bash smart-base/scripts/dak-pre-export.sh. It runs by hand, and on every push to main that changes sushi-config.yaml, ig.ini or input/**. | What the cache records. This phase rewrites the IG’s inputs (sushi-config.yaml’s pages:/menu:, placeholder pages under input/pagecontent/). fhir-harness takes the clean commit’s input digest before the command runs, puts the inputs back after the export, and records the AST against the clean commit; the prepared tree’s digest goes under the manifest’s preExport. So the cache verifies on any clean checkout, and a merge that changes no input does not make it stale. | The counterpart after the export is fhir-harness’s ig-api-gen.ts, the generic port of the post-processing schema and vocabulary generators, run over the AST by ig-site:sidecars (dak-postprocessing). | . ghbuild.yml keeps its own copy of these steps for downstream repositories; it does not write smart-base’s cache.

60c6ae814c23.title: Source of truth versus generated artefacts in a DAK repository
60c6ae814c23.content: This extends the base IG rule in ig-build-pipeline §”Source of truth versus compiled, cached and rendered output”. Two rules: . | Across knowledge layers, authority flows L1 → L2 → L3 → compiled AST / rendered site (smart-guideline-end-to-end §”The order is a rule: L1, then L2, then L3”). L1 narrative guidelines and referenced tables (library/<bib>/l1-extraction/) ground the L2 DAK components (business processes, decision-support logic, core data dictionary, L2 form wireframes, personas, scenarios, indicators, functional/non-functional requirements); those ground the L3 FHIR artefacts (input/fsh/, input/cql/). Never patch an L3 artefact or a rendered page to contradict its L2 source, or an L2 table to contradict L1 without an L1 citation. | Within the repository, hand-edit only the authored inputs — never files written by DAK pre-processing, row generators, SUSHI, the AST refresh or DAK post-processing. dak-pre-export.sh and the QA suite (qa-checkers-dak.ts isGeneratedArtefact) both draw this line: | . | Authoritative source (edit here) | Generated, cached or rendered output (never hand-edit; overwritten on build) | Producer | . | sushi-config.yaml (id, canonical, name, title, description, version, status, license, effectivePeriod, publisher, contact) and index.config.json contentTypes.dak | Legacy dak.json (read-only fallback via dak_index.py --adopt-legacy; never committed back) and fsh-generated/resources/ImplementationGuide-*.json | dak_index.py, generate_dak_from_sushi.py | . | input/fsh/**/*.fsh (ValueSet, logical-model StructureDefinition, profiles, extensions, hand-authored instances) and authored input/pagecontent/*.md | Placeholder pages input/pagecontent/ValueSet-<id>.md and input/pagecontent/<Model>.md carrying <!-- DAK_API_PLACEHOLDER: … -->, plus dak-api.md in sushi-config.yaml pages: and Indices → DAK API in menu: (reverted after AstExportCli in ig-ast-refresh.yml) | update_sushi_config.py, dak-pre-export.sh | . | Authored L2 decision-support tables (input/decision-support/**), data dictionary / requirements workbooks and L2 form wireframes | Generated Questionnaire JSON/FSH resources, rendered DMN HTML tables, and row-generated .fsh instances carrying generated from row N, Automatically generated from DAK artifacts or Autogenerated from DAK artifacts | dmn_questionnaire_generator.py, transform_dmn.py, qa-checkers-dak.ts (isGeneratedArtefact) | . | Authored BPMN / diagram sources (input/business-processes/**, input/images-source/**) and gettext .po catalogues (input/translations/**) | Translated diagram copies and rewritten <img> references in output/ | inject_translations.py, update_translated_image_refs.py | . | Cached AST (cat/fhir-harness/fhir-ast/<package id>) and sushi-config.yaml | DAK API sidecars ($SITE_WORK/ig-api/sidecars/*.schema.json, *.displays.json, *.openapi.json, .jsonld vocabularies), dak-api.html, openapi/index.html, stripped Library JSON (strip_library_binaries.py, strip_library_content.py), and input/pagecontent/smart.liquid.md / output/smart.liquid.html (generate_smart_liquid.py) | dak-postprocessing, ig-site-sidecars.ts | .

9ae71ca95b38.title: Version numbering: DAK SEMVER and how an IG’s version relates to its DAK’s
9ae71ca95b38.content: index.config.json contentTypes.dak.version (schemas/dak.ts DakDeclarationSchema, mirroring input/fsh/models/DAK.fsh) and sushi-config.yaml version both use exact MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: . | Increment | Bumps the DAK (contentTypes.dak.version) | Bumps the L3 IG (sushi-config.yaml version) | . | major (X+1.0.0) | Breaking L2 change in any of the nine DAK component types (DAK.fsh): removing or incompatibly redefining a core data element (dataElement), business process (businessProcess), decision-support table (decisionSupportLogic) or clinical rule, indicator (indicator) numerator/denominator, persona (healthInterventions), scenario (userScenario), L2 form wireframe (form), or functional/non-functional requirement (requirement); or rebasing onto a new L1 WHO guideline edition that invalidates prior L2 logic or data elements | Breaking L3 conformance change per ig-build-pipeline §”Version numbering: SEMVER for a FHIR IG” (removing/renaming a canonical resource, tightening cardinality or bindings, incompatible CQL/operation signature change, fhirVersion change, or breaking dependency major bump), or any major bump in the DAK it encodes | . | minor (X.Y+1.0) | Backward-compatible L2 addition: a new persona, scenario, BPMN workflow, DMN decision table or rule row, optional data dictionary element, L2 form wireframe, indicator or requirement; or extending an L2 value set without invalidating existing rows | Backward-compatible L3 addition (new profile, logical model, extension, ValueSet, CodeSystem, Library, PlanDefinition, Measure, Questionnaire, optional element/slice, or narrative page), or any minor bump in the DAK it encodes | . | patch (X.Y.Z+1) | Backward-compatible L2 editorial or bug fix: typos, descriptions, labels, translations or diagram layout; correcting a DMN cell or data dictionary description to match the existing L1 source without changing data-element semantics or workflow structure | Backward-compatible L3 fix (narrative prose in input/pagecontent/**, translations, example fixes, CQL/FML bug fixes preserving declared inputs/outputs and clinical intent, or rendering fixes), or any patch bump in the DAK it encodes | . How an IG’s version relates to its DAK’s: . | DAK and L3 IG in one repository (contentTypes.dak + contentTypes.ig) — lockstep. index.config.json contentTypes.dak.version, sushi-config.yaml version (and publication-request.json version on a release) carry the same MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH and matching status (draft | active | retired). Both move to the higher of the two increments: L2 minor with L3 patch is minor; an L3 major with L2 unchanged is major. | Update both files in the same commit. Step 1 seeds contentTypes.dak from sushi-config.yaml only when it is absent (if read_dak_section(repo_root) is not None: return), so editing version or status in sushi-config.yaml alone leaves contentTypes.dak stale. | . | Standalone L2 DAK and downstream L3 IG (l3-fhir-authoring). When the DAK (contentTypes: { dak }) and the IG (contentTypes: { ig }) live in separate repositories, each has its own MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH series; a major or minor bump in the DAK requires at least the same bump in the IG release that adopts it. | Adapted / country DAKs and IGs (l2-dependency-choice, l3-dependency-choice). The adaptation pins the upstream WHO DAK and IG in sushi-config.yaml dependencies: (and index.config.json dependencies) at an exact released version (bun run cat check:published-refs); its own contentTypes.dak.version and sushi-config.yaml version follow its own release series. | .

d650df9782ed.title: Data modelling — the entities, before the fields
d650df9782ed.content: One question, and everything else follows from it: . What are the things, and what is true of each of them exactly once? . A model is wrong in a way no schema check can catch when a fact that belongs to one thing is written on another. Typical shapes: a fact about a capability (what substitutes for it) copied onto every skill that uses it; a fact a BPMN diagram already states executably (which role takes over) repeated on a skill; a field naming performers in a vocabulary that resolves against nothing. Each is a field on the wrong entity, or a second copy of a fact that already has a home. Modelling first catches them, and costs far less than unwinding them later.

9d99bc5db82f.title: The procedure
9d99bc5db82f.content: 1. Name the entities, as nouns a domain expert already uses . Not the tables you expect to build. If the people who do this work say “attestation”, the entity is Attestation, even when it will be stored beside something else. A name you invented is a name nobody will look up. Stop when two candidate entities have the same identifier. They are one entity with two names, and carrying both is how a codebase ends up with a Role registry and an actor-id vocabulary that do not resolve against each other. 2. For each entity, say what identifies it . An entity with no identifier is an attribute of something else — that is the test, and it is decisive. If you cannot say what makes two of these the same one, you have found a field rather than a thing. 3. Put each fact on the entity it is about . For every fact, ask whose property is this? The question that settles the hard cases: . If this entity disappeared, would the fact still be true of anything? . What substitutes for X survives the disappearance of every skill that uses X, so it belongs to X. What this skill does when X is missing does not — it is the skill’s. 4. State cardinality in both directions, and mean it . “One attestation per report” and “one report per attestation” are different claims, and a model that states only the first cannot tell you whether a re-signature is an update or a second row. Write both. Where the answer is “many”, say what ORDERS them or admits there is no order. 5. Say which facts are derived, and never store those . A derived fact stored is a cache, and an unvalidated cache is worse than no cache. If a value can be computed from the model, computing it is the declaration — the role a process falls back to, for example, is recoverable from the diagram that executes it. 6. Declare it where a tool can read it . A model in prose is a proposal. A model in the declaration is a model. In this repository that means a graph typology in <name>.json, a Zod schema under the declared schemas directory, and a node kind that kg-export knows — placement is the skill that decides which. And ship a reader in the same change, because a field that is only documentation goes inert. A field with no consumer is not a model, it is a comment with punctuation. 7. Model VARIATION as inheritance, and earn a new kind with BEHAVIOUR . Two things are nearly the same. Do they get one type with a discriminator, two types, or one type and an override? . A new KIND is earned by a BEHAVIOUR difference — a consumer has to DO something different. Everything else is an OVERRIDE on an inherited default. So the default posture is inherit everything, override anything. A variant declares what it CHANGES; every unstated field comes from its parent. A variant that states no new behaviour is not a new kind, however different it looks. The test is on the consumer, not the values. Ask: does any reader of this model take a different code path? Different colours, sizes, labels or thresholds are the same behaviour with different inputs — one kind. Different FIELDS, different units, or a field whose meaning changes — the reader must branch, and that is a kind. Worked example: Theme . Theme dresses three surfaces: sticky notes, a website, a print publication. | variant | kind? | why | . | iris-web vs the default web theme | no | different hex values, same fields. Nothing branches. An override. | . | publication vs sticky | yes | a sticky theme’s geometry is {minWidth, padding, fontScale} across laptop \| mobile \| card; the WHO style guide states A4 \| A5 \| A5 landscape with trim size and margin, and no column width anywhere in 66 sections. minWidth means “before the grid reflows” — a fixed page does not reflow. A renderer MUST branch. | . Reusing {minWidth, padding, fontScale} for print, reading minWidth as trim width, would typecheck and mean nothing. A shape that typechecks is not a shape that models. And the palette stays SHARED across all three kinds, which is the other half of the rule: three kinds each with their own palette vocabulary would be three spellings of “accent colour”, free to disagree about what an accent is. What inheritance costs, and what it must not hide . A required field stays required after resolution, never before. “All three layouts, or invalid” is a property of the RESOLVED variant; a declaration that states one and inherits two is complete. Checking requiredness on the declaration instead is how inheritance turns into optionality by accident. And an inherited value is still a fact somebody must be able to trace. A variant that overrides a value cites why, the same as any other asserted fact — otherwise the model records what the value is and loses where it came from, which is the failure the uses[] rule exists to prevent elsewhere. 8. Point from the dependent at the general node . A relation between two entities is written on ONE of them. Write it on the entity that DEPENDS, pointing at the one it depends on. A general, reused node never holds a field naming the things that use it. The test is the step-3 question applied to the relation: if every user of this node disappeared, would the node still be complete? A skill with no task implementing it is still a skill; a task with no skill is not a task. So the pointer lives on the task. | relation | written on | never on | why | . | a task implements a skill | the BPMN task (<bootstrap.processes:skill ref>) | the skill | a skill is reused by many tasks in many processes; listing them makes every new process an edit to the skill | . | a voice speaks for a role | the voice (activeIn.roles) | the role (voice) | a role is what an actor does in a lane; how it sounds is a separate, swappable thing | . | a lane names a role | the lane (partitionElementRef) | the role (lanes) | the role names diagrams it cannot know about | . | a user story is for a role | the story (role, in scenarios/stories.json) | the role (useCases) | stories are added by whoever writes them, not by editing the role | . | a Tool satisfies a skill | the Tool (satisfies) | the skill (scripts, validators, mcpServices) | several Tools may satisfy one skill, and a script is added without editing the skill | . | a skill or capability discharges a requirement statement | the skill’s front matter or the capability (satisfies: req:<id>#<key>) | the statement (satisfiedBy) | a requirement is written once; what discharges it arrives later | . | a skill says how to read a graph typology | the skill’s front matter (graph-typologies:) | the kind (skill) | a kind is registered once; skills that read it come and go | . | a skill takes and produces a contract | the skill’s front matter (input:, output: — a path into the instance or an https IRI) | a directory named after the skill | the skill can then say its contract is elsewhere, and a contract no skill names is visible as unclaimed | . | a test checks a skill’s contract | the test run (skill, with its cases checked against the skill’s input:/output:) | the skill | tests come and go; the contract does not | . Prose counts. A skill body that says “the only step of initialize-harness” knows its caller just as surely as a field does, and goes stale the same way. Say what the skill does, not who calls it; the caller’s own declaration says the rest. The general node owns its CONTRACT. What a skill takes and returns is a fact about the skill, so it is declared there: an input and an output schema reference, each either a KG schema or a pinned external schema. Tasks, Tools and tests point at the skill and are checked against that contract. That is how a general node stays complete without naming its users. Declare which nodes are general, and let the audit hold the line. Which nodes are general is a modelling decision, so it is written down: the schema declaration’s doc comment carries @general. The general nodes are Role, Skill, Requirement statement, Graph typology, Capability, Actor and Process. kg:audit’s arrow-direction criterion then reports two things: a @general schema whose @ref names a declaration that is not general, and a BPMN <folio:…> element pointing from a process at anything but a skill, role, decision table, convention or precondition. It cannot see a bare string field with no @ref (step 9 is how those become visible) or prose, so a clean run is a claim about declared pointers only. Prose may name a dependent; data may not. The rule governs references, the things a tool follows. A general node’s prose can still name a dependent to explain itself. For example, a process’s documentation may say “feature-staging.yml publishes the branch” so the reader knows why a step exists; deleting such an explanation loses the reason a step exists. If the relation matters to a tool, it must also exist as data held by the dependent, like a workflow’s # bpmn: line. The prose then explains that data and does not replace it. What prose cannot do is notice a rename, so kg:audit’s advisory prose-names-resolve criterion lists a named path whose directory exists and whose file does not. A bare name that nothing in the repository carries is left undetermined, because it could be a run’s output, a folio’s file or an example. 9. Make every cross-node reference a typed KG reference . A reference is a claim that another node exists. A bare string makes that claim in a vocabulary nothing resolves: a typo, a rename or a deleted node reads exactly like a valid name. So a field that names another node holds a KG reference: the target’s kind and id, resolvable in the knowledge graph, and projected by kg-export as an @id link, never a literal. The IRI that link carries is <doc dir>/<kind>/<id>, never ….jsonld#<kind>/<id> — minted by the exporter, not by the model; kg-export §”Subject IRIs — a path, not a #fragment” owns that rule. Use the helpers that already exist rather than inventing one: . | helper | shape | for | . | KgRefSchema (schemas/kg/carried-note.ts) | {kind, id, note?} | any KG node | . | TaskRefSchema (schemas/kg/carried-note.ts) | {process, task} | a BPMN task: the pair, never a bare task id | . | VoiceRefSchema (schemas/content/voices.ts) | {instance?, voiceId} | a voice, possibly in another instance | . | SkillNameSchema (schemas/tools/tool-types.ts) | kebab id | a skill id, where a whole ref is not needed | . | module#Export, instance:module#Export (parseValidatorRef) | string with a checked grammar | a schema | . A reference that crosses into another instance says which instance. And a reference is resolved by a check, not trusted: the audit that reads the field fails on one that points at nothing. Free text stays free text only when it is not a claim about another node: a description, a note, a persona. Free text that names things the graph cannot point at is a reference that should be a node.

cf61ed8d3020.title: What falsifies a model
cf61ed8d3020.content: Write these down as you go and check them at the end. A model nobody tried to break is a diagram. | test | what it catches | . | name two instances that differ only in a field you called an identifier | the identifier is not one | . | find a fact you would have to update in two places | it is on the wrong entity, or duplicated | . | find a relation whose cardinality changes under a plausible future | the model states today’s data, not the domain | . | count the facts nothing reads | the part you modelled for its own sake | . | find two kinds whose consumers take the SAME code path | one of them is an override wearing a discriminator | . | find a required field a variant can never state | requiredness is being checked before resolution, not after | . | delete every user of a general node; is it still complete? | a field on the general node names its users (step 8) | . | rename a node; does anything still read as valid? | a reference is a bare string, not a KG reference (step 9) | .

a3e6fc86add4.title: What this skill is NOT
a3e6fc86add4.content: Not a storage design. Tables, files, indices and formats come after, and a model that assumed one of them has usually smuggled a storage constraint in as a domain fact. Not domain content. folio-assistant is the platform. A model of clinical recommendations, FHIR profiles or any one folio’s vocabulary belongs in that folio — this skill is the procedure, and the procedure carries no subject matter. See the platform-boundary rule in placement.

b0ffbbf46c52.doc: A decision is not a finding, and neither is a substitute for the other
b0ffbbf46c52.title: A decision is not a finding, and neither is a substitute for the other
b0ffbbf46c52.content: A finding is an observation — a checker, an agent or a person saw something. A decision is an act about a set of findings: approve, request changes, reject. The gate reads the decision; the record has to carry both, because the interesting cases are exactly where they disagree. Schema: schemas/sdlc/qa-review.ts.

db3ccdf765a0.doc: A decision is not a finding, and neither is a substitute for the other
db3ccdf765a0.title: Overruling is recorded, not erased
db3ccdf765a0.content: A finding is immutable once raised. To disagree with one, overrule it in the decision — the finding stays where it was, and the overrule names an audit note saying why. Editing or deleting the finding instead leaves the next reader unable to tell a defect that was considered and accepted from one nobody saw. checkReview enforces the two halves of that: . | a decision carries at least one audit note — why this outcome, not another; | an approve over a critical or blocking finding that is not overruled is a reported problem. Overrule it with a note, or do not approve. | .

553bcd386db8.doc: A decision is not a finding, and neither is a substitute for the other
553bcd386db8.title: Two axes, and you say which one you are speaking on
553bcd386db8.content: critical | major | minor is what kind of breakage it is — a machine can assign it. blocking | suggestion | praise is what you are asking of the gate — only judgement can. They do not map onto each other: a checker has no way to say praise, because its only good outcome is silence. So a mechanical finding carries a severity, a human finding carries a weight, and neither gets defaulted into the other.

61db34f88fa2.doc: A decision is not a finding, and neither is a substitute for the other
61db34f88fa2.title: Writing the note
61db34f88fa2.content: Three sentences is usually enough. Say what you decided, what you decided it over, and what makes that safe. Then cite. The lean-ref-resolves failure on thm:transfer-bound is stale: the declaration moved to Folio.Transfer in the refactor and the checker’s index predates it. The Lake build is green on the current head, which is the question the criterion was asking. Overruled; the criterion’s index is the thing to fix, tracked separately. cites: test/results/lean-build.witness.json; content/ch3/thm-transfer-bound.qa.json @ lean-ref-resolves . A rationale with no citation is an assertion, so cites may not be empty. Cite the node, not a description of it: a witness under test/results/, another finding, a .qa.json / .kg-qa.json / .script-qa.json sidecar, an attestation under test/attestations/, a block label, a file range, a bib key, a workflow instance under beans/workflows/. Pin a derived QA citation to its commit. A file under test/results/ is a working copy: its record is the entry the CI job qa-publish stores on the orphan qa-reports branch, keyed main/<sha>/ or pr/<n>/<sha>/. Cite it as qa-reports:main/<sha>/<path> — the same locator bun run cat qa:fetch --ref reads — or the citation dangles once the file leaves main. A judgement in test/attestations/ stays on main and is cited by path.

afb2f0419687.doc: A decision is not a finding, and neither is a substitute for the other
afb2f0419687.title: The agent assembles the citations; the human is still the author
afb2f0419687.content: Searching the corpus for what supports a rationale is clerical work and an agent should do it. Given a decision and the findings it is about, propose citations and say what each one shows: . | Start from the finding’s own evidence and walk what it points at. | Look for a witness that answers the same question the criterion was asking — a green build, a passing round-trip, a recomputed number. | Look for a prior decision on the same criterion; a standing overrule is usually the right precedent to cite. | Quote at the locator, so a citation that goes stale is visible as stale. | . Record yourself in proposed_by, never in author: the reasoning belongs to whoever made the decision, and a tool recorded as author misattributes a judgement it did not make.

903486dfeed4.doc: A decision is not a finding, and neither is a substitute for the other
903486dfeed4.title: Citations you could not resolve are not citations you checked
903486dfeed4.content: resolveCitations returns resolved, dangling or not-checked, and not-checked is what you get with no corpus resolver, or from a resolver that could not answer — a shallow clone, an absent submodule. Report it as its own state. A note whose citations were never checked is not a note whose citations are good.

80313380ec09.doc: The comparison goes BEFORE the question, not inside the options
80313380ec09.title: The comparison goes BEFORE the question, not inside the options
80313380ec09.content: interaction-modality §4.1 fixes the order — context → options → recommendation → question — and requires each option to carry what it costs. This says what “the comparison” has to contain, and where it has to live. Not to be merged with decision-audit. That records why a decision was made, after the fact, and governs overruling a QA finding. This is about what a person is shown before they decide; a skill that tried to be both would be read at the wrong moment.

4fa4fafdc4b0.doc: The comparison goes BEFORE the question, not inside the options
4fa4fafdc4b0.title: Why not in the option descriptions
4fa4fafdc4b0.content: A selection tool gives each option a short label and a short description. The trade-offs do not go there: . | A reader sees one option at a time, and a comparison is reading the rows against each other. | There is no room. Every trade-off gets compressed to its headline, and the second-order consequences are the first thing cut. | It cannot be re-read. The preamble stays in the transcript; a focused option label does not. | .

f072bc0c050e.doc: The comparison goes BEFORE the question, not inside the options
f072bc0c050e.title: What a comparison contains
f072bc0c050e.content: Per option, five things: . |   |   | . | What it does | the mechanism, in one line | . | Pro | what it buys, stated as a benefit rather than an absence of harm | . | Con | what it costs to do | . | Downstream impact | what it changes for everything else, afterwards | . | Reversibility | how expensive it is to undo once taken | . Then, once, for the set: the recommendation with its reasoning, and the default that applies if nobody answers. Cost and downstream impact are different . Cost is what the change takes: files touched, tests to rewrite, hours. Downstream impact is what the world looks like afterwards: what becomes easy, what becomes hard, what a future contributor now has to know, which other decisions are now foreclosed or forced. A cheap change with a large downstream impact reads best when only cost is shown. Say both, separately. Reversibility . opening-brief triggers on irreversibility and surprise rather than size, and the same measure applies here. Two options with identical cost and impact are not equivalent if one can be undone in an afternoon and the other is load-bearing within a week. State it per option.

89da96bfb7cf.doc: The comparison goes BEFORE the question, not inside the options
89da96bfb7cf.title: Where it lives
89da96bfb7cf.content: In the prose that precedes the question. A table is usually right — the columns above are a table’s columns, and a table is the one layout that shows rows against each other. The options in the selection tool are then LABELS for choices already explained. A label names the option and, at most, restates its headline. A reader who has read the preamble should be able to choose from the labels alone; a reader who has not should find nothing new hiding in them. If the labels are where the information is, the comparison was never made.

65862c7e1fb8.doc: The comparison goes BEFORE the question, not inside the options
65862c7e1fb8.title: When this does not apply
65862c7e1fb8.content: A small, reversible choice does not earn a table: the reader would pay attention for something that did not need it. The trigger is the same as opening-brief’s: would getting this wrong be expensive or surprising? If no, recommend and proceed. One-option “decisions” are not decisions. If the honest comparison has one viable row, do not manufacture alternatives to fill a table. Say what you are doing, say why the obvious alternative loses, and proceed.

e9c58c87743a.doc: The comparison goes BEFORE the question, not inside the options
e9c58c87743a.title: Done properly, it also answers the count rule
e9c58c87743a.content: interaction-modality §4.1 requires that with several decisions open you ask one in full and give a count for the rest. A full comparison is what “in full” means. The rest get a number, never a row from a table they cannot see.

b1bddf641195.title: Decision methodology selector
b1bddf641195.content: Input: a decision context — what is being decided, how many alternatives, how many criteria, available data, time constraints, stakeholder count, reversibility, uncertainty level. Output: a ranked list of applicable methodologies, each with: . | the methodology name and its graph-node id | why it fits this context (matched applies-when) | why it does NOT fit the alternatives (matched not-for) | complexity rating | data requirements | .

0c060abc2208.title: Relationship to methodology-adoption
0c060abc2208.content: methodology-adoption carries the protocol — four questions asked in order, the first yes decides. This skill carries the implementation: given that the protocol routes the decision to a category (computable, evidence-grading, decision-record, decision-analysis), which specific methodology in the graph serves that category best for this context? . methodology-adoption names the lane; this skill names the runner.

fed854aad087.title: Decision context schema
fed854aad087.content: A decision context has these dimensions. Not all are required — an agent provides what it knows and the selector grades against what is declared. | dimension | type | when it matters | . | questionType | "computable" \| "evidence-grading" \| "decision-record" \| "decision-analysis" | Always — from methodology-adoption §”Choosing which applies” | . | alternativeCount | number | MCDM methods scale differently | . | criteriaCount | number | AHP pairwise comparisons grow as n² | . | criteriaWeightsKnown | boolean | Some methods derive weights, others require them | . | dataType | "quantitative" \| "qualitative" \| "mixed" | Aggregation methods need numbers | . | stakeholderCount | number | Group methods (Delphi, ANP) vs solo | . | timeConstraint | "minutes" \| "hours" \| "days" \| "weeks" | Eliminates complex methods | . | reversibility | "reversible" \| "costly" \| "irreversible" | Higher stakes → more rigorous method | . | uncertainty | "low" \| "moderate" \| "high" \| "deep" | Bayesian methods for deep uncertainty | . | sequential | boolean | True when decisions recur or adapt over time | .

24f50d661a4a.title: Method families and when to use them
24f50d661a4a.content: 1. MCDM aggregation methods . When: multiple alternatives scored against multiple criteria, quantitative data available, goal is a ranking. Source: Wang & Rangaiah, “Multi-Criteria Decision-Making: Aggregation-Type Methods” (arXiv:2509.06388). | method | best for | avoid when | complexity | . | SAW (Simple Additive Weighting) | First pass, well-understood criteria, all benefit-type after normalisation | Criteria on incomparable scales without good normalisation | Low | . | MEW (Multiplicative Exponent Weighting) | Criteria with exponential importance differences | Any criterion value is zero (product collapses) | Low | . | AHP (Analytic Hierarchy Process) | Weights unknown, need stakeholder consensus on priorities | >9 criteria (pairwise comparisons explode: n(n-1)/2) | Medium | . | ANP (Analytic Network Process) | Criteria have interdependencies (feedback loops) | Simple independent criteria (overkill) | High | . | COPRAS | Benefit and cost criteria naturally separated | All criteria same direction | Medium | . | MOORA | Quick ranking with ratio normalisation | Need for weight derivation (requires pre-set weights) | Low | . | FUCA | Alternatives close in score, need tie-breaking | Very few alternatives (<3) | Medium | . | WASPAS | Combines SAW + MEW for robustness check | When SAW and MEW agree (no added value) | Medium | . 2. Probabilistic / sequential decision methods . When: decisions recur, data arrives over time, exploration-exploitation trade-off matters, experiments are costly. Source: Kristiadi, “Introduction to the Analysis of Probabilistic Decision-Making Algorithms” (arXiv:2508.21620). | method | best for | avoid when | complexity | . | Multi-armed bandits (UCB, Thompson sampling) | Repeated choice among options with unknown payoffs | One-shot decisions | Medium | . | Bayesian optimisation | Expensive-to-evaluate black-box functions, few evaluations | Cheap evaluations (just try them all) | High | . | Tree search (MCTS) | Sequential decisions with branching outcomes | No natural tree structure | High | . | Contextual bandits | Payoff depends on observable context | Context is not available or not meaningful | Medium | . The source backs bandits and Bayesian optimisation only: the ingested version has no tree-search chapter and does not mention contextual bandits, so those two rows are UNSOURCED. 3. Social / behavioral decision methods . When: multiple stakeholders, group consensus needed, behavioral biases must be accounted for. Source: Ravichandran, “Algorithmic Approaches to Sequential Decision-Making and Social Epistemology” (arXiv:2607.20636) — for grit-aware evaluation only. Delphi and nominal group technique come from the group-consensus literature and are UNSOURCED here. | method | best for | avoid when | complexity | . | Delphi method | Expert consensus without groupthink | Time pressure (<1 day) | Medium | . | Nominal group technique | Structured brainstorming → voting | >15 participants | Low | . | Grit-aware evaluation | Decisions requiring sustained investment | Reversible/low-stakes | Medium | . 4. Classical decision methods — UNSOURCED . When: well-understood problem structure, textbook applicability. No source in this repository. Nothing in library/ covers cost-benefit analysis, decision trees, game theory or expected utility, and no methodology node renders any of them. The rows below are textbook recall, not adopted method — see §”What this does NOT cover”. | method | best for | avoid when | complexity | . | Cost-benefit analysis | Monetisable outcomes, policy decisions | Non-quantifiable values | Low | . | Decision trees | Sequential binary/multi-way choices with probabilities | Too many branches (>50 leaves) | Medium | . | Game theory / minimax | Adversarial settings, zero-sum contexts | Cooperative settings | High | . | Expected utility | Single decision under known probability distributions | Deep uncertainty, unknown distributions | Low | . 5. Hybrid / distance-based MCDM — UNSOURCED . When: reference-point comparison (ideal solution), outranking rather than scoring. No source in this repository: the ingested MCDM source covers aggregation-type methods only, not outranking (ELECTRE, PROMETHEE) or distance-based (TOPSIS, VIKOR) methods. The rows below are textbook recall — see §”What this does NOT cover”. | method | best for | avoid when | complexity | . | TOPSIS | Ranking by distance to ideal/anti-ideal solution | Criteria weights uncertain (use AHP first) | Medium | . | ELECTRE | Partial ordering, incomparability is valid | Need a total ranking | High | . | PROMETHEE | Preference functions on each criterion | All criteria are simple linear | Medium | . | VIKOR | Compromise solution for conflicting criteria | Stakeholders refuse compromise | Medium | .

9ab4535332bd.title: What this does NOT cover
9ab4535332bd.content: |   | methods | backed by an ingested source | . | §1 MCDM aggregation | 8 | yes — mcdm-aggregation | . | §2 probabilistic | 4 | 2 of 4 — bandits and Bayesian optimisation | . | §3 social / behavioural | 3 | 1 of 3 — grit-aware evaluation | . | §4 classical | 4 | no | . | §5 distance-based / outranking | 4 | no | . | total | 23 | 11 | . An unsourced row is not thereby wrong: these are standard methods and their guidance may be good. It means nobody here has read a source for it, no methodology node renders it, and methodology-adoption’s “never adopt a method by naming it” applies. The selector returns a FAMILY, plus prose. MethodologyRecommendationSchema requires methodologyId — the methodology’s name from its front matter — so a recommendation must name a node in the methodology graph. The graph’s nodes are families and adopted processes (mcdm-aggregation, probabilistic-decision-analysis, adequacy-for-purpose-modelling, kepner-tregoe, dmn, swot, madr, raci/rasci, …); no individual method in the tables above has a node. So the selector returns a methodology node that exists and names the within-family method in rationale, as prose. The 23 rows are material for that prose, not a menu of returnable answers, and no individual method gets a node. | methodologyId is always resolvable. Every value the selector can emit is a node in the graph, so a consumer that follows the id finds a document. Never invent an id for a method: an id that names no node sends a consumer to a methodology that does not exist. | An unsourced row may still be named in prose, and must be named as what it is. “Of the distance-based family, TOPSIS is the usual first reach — note that nothing in this repository’s library covers it” is honest; “use TOPSIS” as a returned recommendation is not. | A request that lands wholly outside the sourced families gets a refusal, not the nearest fit. SelectionResultSchema carries the explanation for when no methodology fits. An agent asking for an outranking method is told none is adopted here. | . These families are entirely absent, even as recall: ambiguity and robust decision-making (maximin under unknown distributions), real options, voting rules and social choice, multi-objective optimisation proper (Pareto fronts rather than scalarisation), and satisficing / bounded-rationality methods.

e1105425bbd5.title: Selection algorithm
e1105425bbd5.content: function selectMethodology(context: DecisionContext): MethodologyRecommendation[] { // Step 1: Route via methodology-adoption protocol const lane = routeByQuestionType(context); // Step 2: Load methodology graph nodes const nodes = readMethodologyGraph(); // Step 3: Classify each node against the context const classified = nodes.map(n => ({ ...n, matchTier: classifyFit(n, context), // primary | secondary | excluded rationale: explainFit(n, context) })); // Step 4: Return primary matches first, then secondary. Excluded are named // but NOT recommended — per methodology-adoption, refusals are stated. return classified.sort((a, b) => tierOrder(a.matchTier) - tierOrder(b.matchTier) ); } .

44783ab91862.title: Rules
44783ab91862.content: . | Never blend. The output is one or more methods, each whole. A composite is a house method that §methodology-adoption forbids creating here. | Name refusals. Every recommended method comes with its avoid when, matched against the context. If a method’s avoid when fires, say so rather than omitting silently. | Cite the source. Each recommendation names the paper or standard the method comes from. | Report no-match. If no methodology fits, that is the output — §”If none fits, that is a finding, not a licence.” | The graph is the catalogue. Do not recommend methods not in the methodology graph. If a paper describes a method worth adopting, the output is a recommendation to ingest it via §methodology-adoption, not to use it directly. | .
