dada4b5e482f.title: Role
dada4b5e482f.content: Run the scanner, read its output, and produce a ranked workplan of loops that cross the FFI / subprocess boundary per item. Narrower than compute-audit: performance only.

ff40fbce2dd4.title: When to use
ff40fbce2dd4.content: . | “audit FFI” / “ffi roundtrip” / “native-script ping-pong” / “back-and-forth” | “where are we crossing the FFI boundary in a loop” | “find wall savings via consolidation” | After landing a new native kernel (sweep for callers stuck on per-item APIs when a batch exists or could be added) | Before optimising a script that calls a native extension or a native binary via subprocess | .

b0305d5d6dd0.title: What the anti-pattern looks like
b0305d5d6dd0.content: A script loop that calls a native function per iteration, then does script-side combine (arbitrary-precision accumulation, symbolic ops, dict-merge, etc.): . # ANTI-PATTERN — N FFI crossings + N script-side combines total = mp.mpf(0) for item in items: val = native.compute_one(item, q) # ← per-item FFI crossing weight = table.get(item) # ← script-side lookup total += weight * mp.mpf(str(val)) # ← script-side combine . The same compute as a single FFI call: . # CONSOLIDATED — 1 FFI crossing, script only stamps the result result_str = native.compute_all(items, q, dps) return mp.mpf(result_str) .

b5325edcacdd.title: Why the cost is non-trivial
b5325edcacdd.content: Each crossing pays: an FFI acquire/release (small fixed cost, larger for bigger args/returns); marshalling the args into the native side (allocation + per-item type conversion + serialising big numbers to decimal strings); marshalling the result back; and the script-side combine work in the loop body (often far slower than the equivalent native ops). For large N these add up to a dominant fraction of the wall.

d823ac142727.title: Workflow
d823ac142727.content: . | Survey — run the scanner (below) to enumerate scripts containing native-extension or subprocess calls inside a loop. | Classify each finding: . | P-F1: Per-item FFI in a loop. for x in items: native_fn(x). | P-F2: FFI + script-side combine. P-F1 plus an accumulator that should have stayed on the native side. | P-F3: Decimal-string shuttle. Per-item FFI where the return is a decimal string the loop re-parses to arbitrary precision. | P-F4: Subprocess-per-item. A native binary invoked per item via subprocess.run — the same anti-pattern via stdin/stdout. | . | Pick the fix (cheapest first): . | F-A. Use an existing batch API if one exists. | F-B. Add a batch API if none exists — enumerate internally on the native side and parallelise there; expose a single binding that returns a vector of results (a decimal-string variant for arbitrary precision). | F-C. Push the combine into the native side + return one scalar. Use this when the script-side combine loop is non-trivial. | F-D. Keep the script loop if N is small (< ~10) AND per-call work is large (seconds per item) — FFI overhead is negligible. Document the exemption in a code comment. | . | Verify equivalence at the target point — every consolidation must match the per-item version at the floor tolerance on a representative input set. No silent precision loss. Add a cross-check that runs the old per-item path and the new batch path on each test input and asserts rel.diff < floor tolerance. | Bench — report wall before/after on a real input; the commit message should include a small table. | .

fce5936ee5bf.title: Scanner (manual, until automated)
fce5936ee5bf.content: Run from the repo root; adapt the native-call token to the project: . # P-F1: native call inside a `for` block grep -rnB4 "native\." computations/*.py 2>/dev/null \ | grep -B0 "for " | sort -u # P-F2: per-iteration call + an accumulator grep -rnA5 "native\." computations/*.py 2>/dev/null \ | grep -B1 "mp\.mpf\|total +=\|sp\.Float" | sort -u # P-F4: subprocess.run([native_bin, ...]) in a loop grep -rnB4 "subprocess\.run(" computations/*.py 2>/dev/null \ | grep -B0 "for " . For each candidate, open the file at the cited line. The static scan has false positives (e.g. a loop that merely builds a single native input is fine). Keep a catalogue of offenders with their fix and a status column recording when each is discharged.

2867be462c10.title: How to add a new batch API (F-B)
2867be462c10.content: . | Native kernel: add a compute_all(...) that enumerates the work internally and parallelises (data-parallel map → collect). | Binding layer: add a wrapper returning a vector of (key, value) or (key, decimal-string) pairs (the string variant for arbitrary precision). | Build manifest: bump the version (minor for a new public API). | Caller: replace the loop with the batch call. | Cross-check at the target point on a representative input — floor tolerance. | Bench before/after. | Audit-doc the change. | .

7dae27a69a3a.title: Anti-pattern in subprocess form (P-F4)
7dae27a69a3a.content: A binary that takes one input spec and returns one output is fine — not P-F4. P-F4 fires when the script loop invokes the binary per item. The fix is the same as F-B: have the binary accept a list of specs and return a list of results in one invocation, or expose the kernel as a binding and skip subprocess entirely.

0a576cb002aa.title: Skill output
0a576cb002aa.content: Produce a markdown table: . | file:line | pattern | native api | N | fix | est savings | . Plus a prose summary noting which fixes are mechanical (F-A, F-D) vs require native-side work (F-B, F-C). No code changes from the audit pass itself — the agent that acts on the audit is compute-author for the native side and a follow-up PR for the script side.

eb971edeb9f1.title: Out of scope
eb971edeb9f1.content: . | Numerical correctness changes (use compute-audit). | Inner-kernel performance — see compute-author.md. | Architectural overhauls that change the compute graph — roadmap-level decisions, not audit-level. | .

8a222ce620cf.title: References
8a222ce620cf.content: . | compute-audit.md — the broader correctness/performance catalogue (this skill is the FFI-specific complement). | compute-author.md — guidance for writing new compute that avoids these anti-patterns up front (see its native↔script boundary-cost rule). | .

a9b0af86bd14.title: fhir-client-operations
a9b0af86bd14.content: Skill id: fhir-client-operations · Package: fhir-client · Instance: fhir-harness .

e378a598b161.title: Provenance — read this first
e378a598b161.content: |   |   | . | Library | @topologyhealth/smarterfhir 0.4.3 (package.json) | . | Source | https://github.com/TopologyHealth/SMARTerFHIR | . | Pinned commit | 506463af4bd82848f414649dac608d578c8aae44 (2025-12-02) | . | License | Apache-2.0 — LICENSE, package.json and the README agree | . | Built on | fhirclient ^2.5.2; types from @types/fhir (fhir/r4) | . Every method below is from src/Client/BaseClient.ts and the vendor subclasses beside it, at that commit. You obtain a client from ClientFactory — see smart-launch. If the pinned commit moves, re-read the source before trusting a signature here.

03f60e2d7ed4.title: What a client is
03f60e2d7ed4.content: BaseClient is abstract; ClientFactory returns one of EpicClient, CernerClient, SmartHealthClient, ECWClient, AthenaClient, AthenaPracticeClient, MeditechClient, chosen from the server URL. It holds the underlying fhirclient Client as the public, read-only fhirClientDefault.

0ec2c8734ecb.title: The operations it has
0ec2c8734ecb.content: | method | what it does | . | getPatientRead(): Promise<R4.Patient> | reads the launch-context patient (fhirClientDefault.patient.read()) | . | getEncounterRead(): Promise<R4.Encounter> | reads the launch-context encounter | . | getPractitionerRead(): Promise<R4.Practitioner> | reads the signed-in user; throws "User is Not a Practitioner" otherwise | . | requestResource(resourceID: string, requestOptions?: RequestInit) | a GET through fhirClientDefault.request({ url }); only requestOptions.headers is forwarded; the result is cast to R4.Resource | . | create<T>(r4Resource: T, patientId?, encounterId?, additionalHeaders?): Promise<T> | POSTs a new resource after hydration (below) | . | createPatient(patient: R4.Patient): Promise<R4.Patient> | create(patient) | . | hydrateResource(fhirClientResource, r4Resource, patientId?, encounterId?) | fills in missing references without sending anything | . | createReferenceArrayAuthor(): Promise<Author> | { author: [{ reference: "Practitioner/<user id>" }] } | . | getR4Endpoint(): URL, getEMRType(): EMR | the server URL and the vendor | . Search has no dedicated method. The only route in SMARTerFHIR is requestResource with a search URL, which returns whatever the server sent — a Bundle — typed as R4.Resource. Paging is not handled. import * as R4 from "fhir/r4"; const patient = await client.getPatientRead(); // search: a relative URL resolved by fhirclient against the server base const bundle = (await client.requestResource( `Observation?patient=${patient.id}&category=vital-signs`, )) as R4.Bundle<R4.Observation>; // write: subject, encounter and (for DocumentReference etc.) context are added if absent const created = await client.create<R4.Observation>({ resourceType: "Observation", status: "final", code: { text: "Body weight" }, valueQuantity: { value: 70, unit: "kg" }, }); .

f17ba593272f.title: Hydration — what create adds for you
f17ba593272f.content: Before POSTing, create calls hydrateResource, which uses the lists in src/Resource/resourceUtils.ts: . | subject → Patient/<id> when the type is in the subject list (Observation, Encounter, DocumentReference, Communication, QuestionnaireResponse, …) and the resource has no subject. | encounter → Encounter/<id> when the type is in the encounter list (Observation, Condition, Procedure, MedicationRequest, ServiceRequest, …) and has none. | context → { encounter: [Encounter/<id>], period: { start: now, end: now } } for ChargeItem, DocumentReference, MedicationAdministration, MedicationDispense, MedicationStatement. | . The ids come from patientId / encounterId if you pass them, otherwise from the launch context; a missing launch-context id throws "id not found". The test is 'subject' in resource — a key present with undefined counts as present and is not hydrated.

53d3aad84899.title: Per-vendor differences
53d3aad84899.content: . | Epic (EpicClient): create always sends Prefer: return=representation and does not accept an additionalHeaders argument. | Cerner (CernerClient): adds author: [Practitioner/<user>] when absent; requestResource always sends Accept: application/fhir+json and ignores the caller’s requestOptions. | The other five subclasses only set EMR_TYPE. | .

96a0af3d9153.title: Errors
96a0af3d9153.content: . | create failures are re-thrown as new Error("It failed with:" + reason) — the original error object, and any OperationOutcome on it, is flattened into a string. Log reason before this point if you need the outcome. | A create response with no resourceType is treated as a fetch response and its .body is returned instead. | Reads and requestResource add no handling: whatever fhirclient rejects with propagates unchanged. What those errors look like is fhirclient’s contract and is not specified by this source. | .

88f6ace0034d.title: What the library does NOT do
88f6ace0034d.content: . | No update, patch, delete, conditional create, or transaction/batch — the only write is create (POST). Anything else means dropping to client.fhirClientDefault, i.e. fhirclient directly, outside this library’s hydration and headers. | No read-by-id or search helper, paging or _include handling — use requestResource. | No validation or profile conformance — Transformer.toFhirClientType and toR4FhirType (src/Resource/transformer.ts) copy keys verbatim; they do not transform content. | R4 only — every type is from fhir/r4. | .

2b043758b6ee.title: Pitfalls
2b043758b6ee.content: . | On Cerner, create’s patientId and encounterId are ignored for hydration. CernerClient.hydrateResource takes two parameters and calls super.hydrateResource without the ids, so the launch-context patient and encounter are used. Set subject/encounter on the resource yourself when they differ. | requestResource is typed, not checked. A search returns a Bundle and an error body may return an OperationOutcome; both arrive as R4.Resource. Test resourceType before narrowing. | Hydration depends on launch context. In a launch with no encounter context, creating a type from the encounter list throws "id not found" unless you pass encounterId or set encounter yourself; with context, the launch encounter is attached without comment. | The write must be in scope. Default EHR-launch scopes for Epic and SMART are only launch online_access plus openid fhirUser (see smart-launch); no resource scope of any kind is requested. Pass the scopes you need to the SmartLaunchHandler constructor rather than expecting a create or a read to be authorised by the defaults — what a server grants without them is the vendor’s policy, not something this source determines. | .

bf3e8f13f45c.title: fhir-ig-create
bf3e8f13f45c.content: Skill id: fhir-ig-create · Package: fhir-ig-base · Instance: fhir-harness . A request to create a FHIR IG can be met in two ways: in a new repository, or inside the folio of a repository that is already harnessed. Work out which the user means and act on it. This is the IG-shaped half of getting-started, which triages “create a folio” in general. Read that skill’s §1 for how facts are gathered and §3 for how a question is put. This skill does not restate them. It adds the one fork getting-started has no branch for: an IG that starts inside a repository and may leave it later.

5f2d21e9d5e5.title: When a harness above this one specialises it
5f2d21e9d5e5.content: An IG built on a harness that needs this one (for example one that adds its own pre- and post-processing, theme and layout rules) may carry its own creation skill that specialises this one. If the request names such a harness’s kind of guide, ask skill_list for that skill and run it instead. It will route back here for every step it does not change. This skill names no such harness, on purpose: the bare FHIR layer knows nothing above it.

cc368c6a9810.title: 1. Read three facts — read-only, before anything is written
cc368c6a9810.content: | fact | how | values | . | inHarness | a <name>.json instance declaration at the working directory’s root (describeRepository membership harness) | yes / no | . | hasIg | an IG source already present: a sushi-config.yaml or an ig.ini at the root | yes / no | . | statedWhere | what the user said about where it goes | new-repo, in-repo, existing-ig, unstated | . statedWhere is unstated until the user has said it. “Make me an IG” states nothing about where. “Start an IG in its own repo” states new-repo. Do not infer it from the repository you happen to be in.

8f275b0db5dc.title: 2. Decide
8f275b0db5dc.content: | statedWhere | inHarness | hasIg | route | . | stated | any | any | what they said | . | unstated | no | yes | existing-ig: hand to repo-conversion, scan first | . | unstated | no | no | new-repo: the only route that answers itself | . | unstated | yes | any | ask, with default in-repo | . The question, when the table says ask . Put it as numbered options, four at most, recommended first, with the default stated. Load interaction-modality first; for some users a typed answer is not available at all. Where should the new IG live? . | Inside this repository, as a staged sub-KG (recommended). Cheapest to start and to change your mind about. It can move to its own repository later, and nothing outside this repository changes until you say so. | In a new repository of its own. Creating it is visible outside this repository, so I will ask once more before I create anything. | Over an IG repository you already have. I scan it first and show you what I find before importing anything. | Tell me more. | . Default if you do not answer: 1. Nothing outside this repository is touched. Why in-repo is the default: every step of it is reversible with git revert. A guide is staged in place first, and its repository is created only once that rehearsal is green: a repository is the first irreversible act, so it is not the first act. Then ask the name, as a short slug, offering the one derived from what they said as option 1.

bc07d2763d56.title: 3. Route
bc07d2763d56.content: in-repo — a staged sub-KG . The lifecycle is sub-kg-lifecycle and its process sub-kg-lifecycle.bpmn; this is what its stage 1 means for an IG. | Scaffold the declaration and the seam: bun run cat init-folio --staged <name> --title "<title>" --repository <owner>/<name> --needs fhir-harness. It writes <name>/<name>.json (repository is the planned home, and livesAt is this repository) and an empty <name>/platform.ts, and nothing at the repository’s root. Never --instance here: that scaffolds a whole repository. | Declare the graphs as their files arrive. An IG’s graphs are typically ig-ast, fhir-artifact-index and docs with igSite: true. Route every platform import through platform.ts: an empty seam on day one costs nothing, and retrofitting one later means rerouting every import. | Get the IG source, one of: . | authored here: sushi-config.yaml and input/ under the instance, authored with l3-fhir-authoring; | an IG already published elsewhere: mount or fork its source repository. Its artefact index and navigation are not ingested or committed: bun run cat ig-index:build writes them at publish from the IG’s AST and its own sushi-config.yaml. | . | Build its site from a local checkout: bun run fhir-harness/scripts/stage-ig-sites.ts --work <dir> --baseurl <baseurl> --only <name> --source <ig repo checkout> (ig-build-pipeline, ig-render-jekyll). | Seed the plan: one work-plan item for the IG, under the epic the work belongs to, after the existence check in todo-manager. | . From there the IG grows in place, and leaves only through sub-kg-lifecycle’s two owner confirmations. new-repo — its own repository . | Confirm before creating. Creating a repository is outward-facing and is not undone by a revert, so the question in sub-kg-lifecycle §”7 and 12” is asked first, with default “not yet”. The owner may create it themselves; a session without the permission hands over with agent-handoff. | Mount, don’t declare. The repository gets an index.config.json naming the layer it builds on (this one, or an overlay above it such as the WHO SMART Base IG) as a remote instance with consent, and the index.lock.json remote-mount.ts writes. No <repo>.json and no submodule: an IG repository needs no harness of its own. The same index.config.json declares the repository an IG source with contentTypes.ig and its include list, the paths this harness reads. Start with the paths the IG holds: usually sushi-config.yaml, ig.ini, input/fsh/, input/pagecontent/, input/includes/, input/images/. ig-build-pipeline §”What this layer reads” has the rules and the legacy warning. | Then steps 3 to 5 of in-repo, at the root. | Ask the two build questions of §”4. Who starts a build” before the first push; a repository forked from an upstream IG is the usual case. | Copy the site templates, unchanged. templates/ig-repo-site/ holds ig-ast-refresh.yml and site-publish.yml; copy both into .github/workflows/, as they are. An IG repository’s site is built from the AST cache (§”The AST cache lifecycle” of ig-build-pipeline), and ig-ast-refresh.yml is its one writer. Without it the repository has no site, and stage-local.ts refuses with no cache branch for this IG. The first refresh is dispatched once on the default branch by the owner, or by an agent the owner names for that run. Until it has run, the repository’s preview is not built anywhere: say so and ask. Do not stage it on another repository’s site instead (feature-staging, Which site). | . existing-ig . repo-conversion scans first and imports second, never the other way round. After the import, mount its layer through index.config.json as in new-repo step 2 (no declaration of its own), declare contentTypes.ig with an include list of the paths the harness should read, then ask the two build questions in §”4. Who starts a build”: an existing IG repository almost always carries build workflows that publish on every push. Then new-repo step 5: copy the site templates if they are missing.

79d7a1cd5043.title: 4. Who starts a build
79d7a1cd5043.content: Two questions for the owner, asked whenever an agent adopts an IG repository (existing-ig or new-repo above, or repo-conversion over a repository with a sushi-config.yaml or ig.ini), and whenever it notices automatic builds in an IG repository it is already working in. Every other skill that adopts, onboards or converts an IG repository points here. Why: inherited fork workflows can publish previews on every push and pull request, including to another organisation’s Pages site. 4.1. Detect, read-only . List every workflow under .github/workflows/ whose on: includes push, pull_request, pull_request_target or schedule and that builds or deploys a site: it runs the IG Publisher, pushes to gh-pages (or another pages branch), or uses a Pages deploy action. For each, record: . | field | what | . | file | the workflow path | . | automatic triggers | which of the four, with their branch filters | . | what it publishes | full build, branch preview (branches/<name>/), PR preview | . | where it publishes | the repository’s own Pages site, or a target outside it (another repository’s pages branch, another organisation’s github.io) | . | called by others | whether it declares workflow_call, and whether another repository calls it | . Report any deploy target outside the repository’s own Pages site, even if the owner keeps every trigger. If nothing matches, say so in one line and skip to 4.3. 4.2. Ask whether to disable the automatic triggers . Put it per interaction-modality: the detection table first, then this question: . This repository publishes to gh-pages automatically: (the table from 4.1). Should those builds keep running on their own? . | Manual only (recommended). I change each listed trigger to workflow_dispatch, so a build runs only when someone starts it from the Actions tab. I keep workflow_call wherever another repository calls the workflow, and I leave what is already on gh-pages untouched. | Manual only, and remove the workflows nobody calls. As 1, but a workflow with no caller and no remaining use is deleted from .github/workflows/ rather than kept as a manual one. | Keep them as they are. Nothing changes; I record the finding (and any out-of-repository target) in the work plan. | Tell me more. | . Default if you do not answer: 1. The default is 1: a build workflow stays defined (runnable from the Actions tab) but does not run on its own; disabling a trigger is reversible. Option 3 is for an owner who says so. Whichever option is chosen: . | Turning automatic BUILDS off never turns harness CHECKS off. The harness checks are a separate workflow, a caller of cat-harness-tools’ layer-pr-checks.yml on pull_request (index-config, “A harnessed repository runs its checks on its own pull requests”). It stays on. | Never delete gh-pages content as part of this. Removing published previews is a separate question, asked separately, with what would go and how big it is, per deletion-requires-confirmation. Option 2 deletes a workflow file, which git revert restores; it deletes nothing the workflow published. | . 4.3. Ask whether to render the IG with the just-the-docs site . Do you want this IG rendered as a just-the-docs site, with the harness’s navigation, search and language bar, on this repository’s own Pages site? . | Yes (recommended). I install the folio site workflow, manual trigger only, and tell you how to run it. | No. The IG Publisher output stays the only rendering. | Tell me more. | . Default if you do not answer: 1. The default is yes: the Publisher’s HTML is opaque to every harness surface (see ig-render-jekyll), and a manual-only workflow publishes nothing until run. On yes: . | Mount, don’t declare, as new-repo step 2: index.config.json names the layer as a remote instance, with "site": {"landing": "<that layer>"} (without it the route refuses rather than guess among the mounted layers) and contentTypes.ig. | Keep one workflow that calls the upstream IG build workflow (the route recognises ghbuild.yml, and fhirbuild.yml beside one). It is the recipe the publish mirrors, and it stays workflow_dispatch only. | Copy the site templates, as new-repo step 5. site-publish.yml is workflow_dispatch only; its first job, ast, calls this layer’s reusable ig-ast-refresh.yml, then it runs bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/stage-local.ts --repo ., the command every agent-run repository publishes with: . | it builds the site from the IG’s cached AST with the steps the mounted layers provide (ig-build-pipeline §”The IG repository’s site route”), and runs no Publisher; | it publishes main at the root (keeping branches/, _render-log/ and branches/) and any other branch as a preview under branches/<branch>/; | --plan prints what it would do and --dry-run builds without publishing; do not use --bare-ig; | an IG that needs steps beyond the layers’ declares site.build inline in its index.config.json entry, never in a <instance>.config.json; | the menu is read from sushi-config.yaml at build time; nothing is committed for it. | . | Tell the owner how to run it: Actions tab → “Site publish (by hand)” → Run workflow, on the branch to publish, with plan ticked first. The site lands at the repository’s own Pages URL; the template reads the base path from the repository name. | Sibling and dependency sites. If the IG has sibling sites (other IGs on the same platform) or depends on another IG with its own site, set the repository variables FOLIO_SITE_SIBLINGS (site URLs) and FOLIO_SITE_DEPENDENCIES (owner/repo@ref). The run then reports each sibling built with a different platform, and re-runs the dependencies’ Site publish (by hand) after a publish, which needs a FOLIO_SITE_DISPATCH_TOKEN secret; without it the run summary says what was not rebuilt. Why: sites built by hand drift to different platform versions. Every build writes folio-build.json at its site root (scripts/site-build-stamp.ts), so a deployed site can be compared without rebuilding it. A sibling whose stamp cannot be read is reported as not checked, never as matching. The report is a message, not a gate. | . 4.4. Say what the pull request will fire . A pull request that changes a workflow still runs the base branch’s pull_request_target workflows, because pull_request_target runs the workflow file from the base. So the PR that disables an automatic preview fires that preview one last time. Say so before opening the PR, and offer the two ways round it: cancel those runs as soon as they start (gh run cancel <id>), or, with the owner’s agreement, push the workflow change straight to the working branch rather than through a PR. Once the change is on the base branch, later PRs are quiet. No BPMN activity covers IG repository adoption, so these steps are not in a diagram; publishing the adopted site, and refreshing its AST, is ig-ast-cache.bpmn. When one is drawn, 4.2 and 4.3 are the owner’s lane and 4.1 is the agent’s, with 4.2’s “manual only” default as the gateway’s default flow.

dc6107908b31.title: Anti-patterns
dc6107908b31.content: . | Creating a repository because the request said “new”. “A new IG” is not “a new repository”. Ask. | Running init-folio --instance inside a harnessed repository for an in-repo IG. It writes AGENTS.md, .mcp.json, a beans store and a session hook into a subdirectory. --staged is the in-repo mode. | Hard-coding a publisher’s identity here. Template, chrome and publication target belong to a harness above this one. | Skipping the seam because the IG has no code yet. The first test that imports a platform helper is the first climb. | Typing a workflow the templates already hold. Copy templates/ig-repo-site/ as new-repo step 5 says; a hand-written set that misses ig-ast-refresh.yml leaves the repository with no site. | .

f1d9856463a3.title: fhir-questionnaire-wireframe
f1d9856463a3.content: Skill id: fhir-questionnaire-wireframe · Package: fhir-ig-authoring · Process: questionnaire-wireframe-review.bpmn (Process_QuestionnaireWireframeReview). Show a built FHIR Questionnaire the way a person will meet it — a mid-fidelity wireframe at web and mobile width, and a live form — have it reviewed as a design, check that it says what the wireframe it was derived from says, and take change requests on either side back through authoring. Sourcing. What a Questionnaire means is defined by the FHIR specification and the Structured Data Capture IG; what the live form supports is defined by NLM’s LHC-Forms. This skill states how the two are wired in this harness.

bee2e43aedb0.title: Rules
bee2e43aedb0.content: . | The renderer is NLM LHC-Forms, vendored into the site: never a CDN at runtime. Its BSD-style notice travels with the vendored files. | The field ↔ item check is scripts/check-wireframe-questionnaire.ts (Tool check-wireframe-questionnaire). It knows nothing about any one IG; a layer above uses it by name. | Either side may be edited. A change request says whether the Questionnaire or the wireframe was changed, and the agent brings the other back in line. Neither is regenerated from the other. | .

c2c5fef6c25c.title: Inputs and outputs
c2c5fef6c25c.content: fhir-harness/schemas/skills/fhir-questionnaire-wireframe/: . | in — questionnaire (required: one built JSON path; several are several runs), mode, wireframe, renderer, assetDir, suggest, issueForm, channels, branch | out — the output shape of wireframe-design-review (use, topic, assetDir, candidates[] each with its source HTML, web and mobile screenshots and their staging links, chosen, changedAssets, stagingLinks), plus renderer, fidelity[] (the checker’s findings per layout), sdcChecks[] (step 4b) and changeRequests[] (issue URL, which side was edited, status). | . stagingLinks is an inline copy of cat-harness schemas/staging-comparison.schema.json, as every contract carrying it keeps one; changedAssets is the staging preview graph’s changed-assets record, with three kinds of its own: questionnaire-wireframe, questionnaire-rendering, questionnaire-screenshot.

a8f9e29e09c6.title: Roles
a8f9e29e09c6.content: | role | does | . | fhir-modeller | authors: renders, runs the checks, applies change requests | . | business-analyst | reviews the form against the workflow it serves | . | clinical-sme | reviews what the form asks and in what order | . | build-pipeline | the mechanical steps: rendering, screenshots, the fidelity check | .

5983f844e066.title: Steps
5983f844e066.content: . | Read the built Questionnaire JSON, never FSH: fsh-generated/resources/Questionnaire-<id>.json, or the IG’s published Questionnaire-<id>.json. FSH is what the author wrote; the JSON is what every renderer and reader receives, so it is what is judged. | Render. | A mid-fidelity wireframe: one field per answerable item, in item order, each carrying data-element="<id>" (the item’s definition, or its code) and sitting in a data-layout="web" or data-layout="mobile" subtree. Monochrome, the item’s own text, no placeholder text — the rules of wireframe-design-review step 2. | A form view: the same JSON in <lhc-forms>, from the vendored LHC-Forms build, on the IG site’s Questionnaire form page (build-ig-site). | . | Screenshots at web and mobile width with the cat-harness Tool wireframe-check (1280×800 and 390×844; renders, no-overflow, no-placeholder). A candidate missing either viewport does not enter review. | Fidelity, when an L2 wireframe exists — the form was designed first and the Questionnaire derived from it: . bun run fhir-harness/scripts/check-wireframe-questionnaire.ts <wireframe.html> <Questionnaire.json> . Each layout is judged on its own: a field with no item, an item with no field, an item naming no data element, a data element twice, the first place the order differs. Exit 0 faithful, 1 a finding, 2 cannot tell — and 2 is never a pass. The findings go in fidelity[], per layout. This is fidelity, not design: a faithful form can still be a poor one. 4b. SDC build checks, with CSIRO’s libraries (Apache-2.0; used for checks, not UI), Tool sdc-checks: . bun run fhir-harness/scripts/sdc-checks.ts --ast output-ast --fixtures input/tests/questionnaires [--out <dir>] . | check | library | passes when | . | assemble | @aehrc/sdc-assemble 2.0.3 | an assemble-root’s sub-forms all resolve in this IG; --out writes the assembled Questionnaire, so assembly is a build step too | . | template-extract | @aehrc/sdc-template-extract 1.0.16 | extraction from the fixture’s response.json yields every resource in extract-expected.json | . | populate | @aehrc/sdc-populate 4.7.2 | FHIRPath pre-population from populate-context.json gives the answers in populate-expected.json | . | behaviour | @aehrc/questionnaire-test-toolkit 0.1.0 | the IG’s behaviour.test.tsx passes. Warn-only: the toolkit is early, and needs its React and Smart Forms peers installed with the IG’s tests | . The fixtures are the IG’s, one directory per Questionnaire id. Nothing is fetched from a server. not-applicable, no-fixture and could-not-determine are said, and never read as a pass. The results go in sdcChecks[], one entry per Questionnaire. | Review by wireframe-design-review, as-is use for a form that exists, design use for one being designed: blind, per criterion, at both viewports, adjudicated where reviewers disagree. That skill is the method; this one does not restate it. | Stage by feature-staging, and ask for review with staging-review: one deep link per rendered Questionnaire and wireframe, before and after. Where the request goes — the conversation, an issue, the pull request — is a judgement, and more than one may be right: staging-review’s deep-link rule, point 5. | Change requests come in in one of two ways, and both end as an issue: . | ✍ suggest, in its Questionnaire mode, on the form page: the reviewer edits the Questionnaire or the wireframe and the editor opens an issue; | the questionnaire-change issue form, filled by hand. | . Each goes to content-feedback for triage (to public-comment when a review round is open), then to l3-fhir-authoring, which edits the side the request did not touch so the two agree again, then back to step 1. changeRequests[] records each issue, which side was edited, and where it stands. | .

0c6abad615a2.title: The change-request payload
0c6abad615a2.content: What the ✍ editor writes into the issue’s body, and what the issue form asks for, by these field ids, when it is filled by hand: . | field id | holds | . | questionnaire | the Questionnaire’s canonical URL or Questionnaire/<id> | . | edited | questionnaire or wireframe: the side the reviewer changed | . | patch | an RFC 6902 JSON Patch over the built Questionnaire, its paths annotated with the item’s linkId | . | items | a readable before/after table of the items that changed | . | source | the FSH file and line the item comes from, when known | . | rationale | why | . The issue form is templates/ig-repo-site/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/questionnaire-change.yml, which an IG repository copies to .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/, as it copies the workflows beside it. It is for people filing by hand: the ✍ editor does not open it, because GitHub ignores a prefilled body when template= names an issue form, and the patch would be lost. The editor opens a plain issue whose body carries everything. A pre-filled link longer than about 7000 characters is too long for GitHub; the body then goes to the clipboard and a stub issue opens, as the ✍ runtime does.

72e4bec2f484.title: The form view and the ✍ Questionnaire mode
72e4bec2f484.content: build-ig-site writes one page per Questionnaire in the IG’s AST, Questionnaire-<id>-form.html, through scripts/questionnaire-form.ts: . | the form, drawn by the vendored LHC-Forms build (scripts/assets/vendor/lhc-forms/<version>/, its NLM LICENSE.md beside it, vendored.json recording the npm tarball and a SHA-256 per file) from a rendered copy of the built JSON, questionnaires/Questionnaire-<id>.json. The source Questionnaire is never changed. Nothing is loaded from another origin; | ✎ (the FSH source the AST names), 📣 (feedback) and ✍ (suggest a change), through the platform’s edit-links recipe and a #fa-edit-cfg block whose suggest.profiles names the mode for the ✍ runtime’s mode registry, [{ id: "questionnaire", module, extensions: [".json"], kinds: ["questionnaire"] }], beside the mode’s own builder, sw, fhirVersion, source and slug. The form host carries data-suggest-mode="questionnaire" and data-block="questionnaire:<id>"; | a plain open in CSIRO Smart Forms link-out, as a rendering cross-check. Nothing of it is embedded. | . The ✍ Questionnaire mode is scripts/questionnaire-mode.js, a plain ES module with no build step. It exports the three roles the ✍ suggest runtime’s mode registry calls (cat-harness-tools EDIT_LINKS_RUNTIME), by these names: . | export | does | . | open(host, ctx) → { get, dispose } | ctx is { text, sourceText, sourcePath, why, src, path, label, kind, repo, branch, config, status(msg) }: text the BUILT Questionnaire JSON (the host’s data-suggest-text), sourcePath / sourceText the FSH it was built from, why the reader’s reason (live). A panel: which side was edited (the Questionnaire or its L2 wireframe), and a raw-JSON fallback; with config.suggest.builder, the self-hosted NLM Form Builder in a window, its updateQuestionnaire / closed result kept (its API.md hand-back). Progress goes to ctx.status. get() is awaited on Submit, never polled, and is ctx.text itself while nothing was edited; dispose() closes the builder window | . | check(before, after, opts) | findings [{ severity, message }], from checkSuggestion below; an error blocks Submit | . | issue(before, after, ctx) | { title, body } and no template: the side edited, the FSH source link (ctx.sourcePath, anchored on the Instance: line found in ctx.sourceText), the page, the item table and the JSON Patch with each operation’s linkId. Not the Why: the runtime appends **Why:** to a mode’s body that lacks it, so the mode writing one too would file it twice | . The side edited and the builder’s round-trip baseline reach check and issue through the session open keeps. Everything else is ctx’s: the mode reads no Why from the dialog’s DOM and does not re-derive the source path from the page. Which path opens it. The form page’s host names the profile (data-suggest-mode), the source in the repository (data-src, the .fsh file) and the URL of the BUILT text the mode edits (data-suggest-text, questionnaires/Questionnaire-<id>.source.json, the unexpanded copy the IG compiled; not the copy LHC-Forms renders, whose value sets were expanded). A runtime with the mode registry serves any host that names its mode: it fetches the built text as ctx.text, reads the source as ctx.sourceText, and its dialog offers a Form | FSH switch: the Form pane is this mode, the FSH pane edits the source as text and files a source diff with the reader’s Why. Without such a runtime, the form page’s loader (scripts/templates/ig-pages/questionnaire-form.js) opens the mode itself, with the same ctx (built text fetched from data-suggest-text, sourcePath, a live why; no sourceText), its own Why field, withWhy to append the Why as the runtime does, and issueUrl for the link. Where the runtime has put its ✍ link in the host, the page’s own link hands the click to it. The self-hosted Form Builder, and no cross-site call . The editor is the NLM Form Builder (formbuilder-lhcforms 12.9.0), self-hosted. The site makes no cross-site call. | The builder is vendored unmodified (scripts/assets/vendor/formbuilder-lhcforms/). The site serves a rewritten copy of its index.html, also as window-open.html (its hand-back route): jQuery from this site (vendor/jquery/3.6.0), the Google font rules removed, and a guard that registers the service worker and reloads before anything else loads. | The service worker (scripts/terminology-sw.js, scoped to the builder; the mapping is the pure scripts/terminology-map.js) answers every request to another origin from this site: . | request | answer | . | clinicaltables /api/loinc_items/v3/search | the IG’s terminology index, in the CTSS shape. LOINC comes only from the IG’s cache; a code it does not hold shows “not in this IG’s terminology cache; add it via the FSH source” | . | clinicaltables /api/ucum/v3/search | the full UCUM list (vendored @lhncbc/ucum-lhc definitions) | . | lhcforms-static /lforms-versions/… | the vendored LHC-Forms | . | lforms-fhir.nlm.nih.gov (import and export), anything else | a local error saying it is disabled on this site | . | The terminology index is written at build time by scripts/terminology-index.ts (Tool terminology-index) from the IG’s own restored cache: output-ast/expansions.json and input-cache/txcache/ (ig-build-pipeline, §”The AST cache lifecycle”). | The form view needs no terminology server either: each item’s answerValueSet that the expansions hold becomes answerOption in the rendered copy. The source Questionnaire is unchanged; a value set the cache does not hold is reported. | A code the cache lacks is added through the FSH source. A ✍ change request can carry it as free text. | .

06481542c1eb.title: The suggest checker
06481542c1eb.content: checkSuggestion(before, after, { wireframe }) in check-wireframe-questionnaire.ts is the checker a suggest editor runs on the reviewer’s edit, in the editor-checker shape { errors, warnings }: . | errors are syntax only — not JSON, not a Questionnaire; | warnings never block, and only what the edit introduces is reported, computed against the editor’s own round-trip of the original: a duplicate linkId, an enableWhen naming no item, and the fidelity findings of step 4 when a wireframe is given. | . It is not declared as an editor-checker profile (contentType: questionnaire; a folio-editor-checker/v1 node naming open, check and issue with extensions: [".json"]): the editor-checkers typology is declared by folio-assistant-sci, which this layer does not need. The page config names the profile directly (QUESTIONNAIRE_PROFILE in questionnaire-form.ts).

7a331bb465ef.title: What this skill does not do
7a331bb465ef.content: . | It does not build the IG: l3-fhir-authoring and ig-publication do. | It does not regenerate one side from the other on its own. Which side is the source of a change is the change request’s to say. | A clean fidelity check is not a design review, and a clean design review is not conformance: fhir-validation still decides that. | .

789532215dd6.title: Processes that run this skill
789532215dd6.content: | process | step(s) that name it | . | Questionnaire wireframe review | Read the built Questionnaire JSON; Render the wireframe and the LHC-Forms view; Check field for field; Review the staged form and wireframe | . | SMART Guideline end to end | Review each L3 asset (before / after if adapted) (calls a sub-process) | .

ea92f481b62a.title: fhir-validation
ea92f481b62a.content: Skill id: fhir-validation · Package: fhir-ig-authoring · Named by l3-fhir-pipeline.bpmn (Validate against profiles, Build pipeline — SUSHI · validator · IG Publisher lane) and ig-incremental-build.bpmn (Validate the cone (fhir_validate), Publisher + validator services (JVM) lane). Validate an IG’s FHIR artefacts against the profiles and packages they claim to conform to. Sourcing. Conformance is defined by the FHIR specification and by the packages an IG depends on; the validator is HL7’s. This skill states how it is invoked in this harness and what each outcome is allowed to mean.

169cd7bea50c.title: Inputs and outputs
169cd7bea50c.content: fhir-harness/schemas/skills/fhir-validation/: . | in — igRoot (required), validationLevel, targetProfiles | out — overallStatus (required), sushiResult, publisherResult, conformanceResults | . SUSHI compiling is not conformance. FSH can compile to JSON that the validator then rejects, so a green sushiResult with an unrun publisherResult is not a pass.

a673442d357c.title: The binaries
a673442d357c.content: The package declares these capabilities (providesCapabilities in package-manifest.json); each is defined, with its detection command, in scenarios/capabilities/: . sushi --version # sushi-compiler (requires node-runtime) java -jar "${FHIR_VALIDATOR_JAR}" -version # fhir-validator (requires java-runtime) java -jar "${IG_PUBLISHER_JAR}" --version # ig-publisher (requires java-runtime) . fhir-validator is the standalone validator, distinct from ig-publisher, which builds a whole IG. An authoring loop runs the validator on single resources between builds; a release is cut from the publisher.

f8e742761d74.title: When a package host refuses you
f8e742761d74.content: SUSHI and the Publisher resolve the IG’s dependencies: from packages.fhir.org. Where that host is refused, the failure looks like a broken IG and is not one. Ask for the remedy: . bun run cat tools:remedy packages.fhir.org # → fhir-cache-seed-npm, with its command . Every network-dependent Tool declares remedies per host it reaches (check:tools enforces it), and fhir-harness/scripts/ig-cache.sh doctor prints the same answer for each host it finds unreachable. For packages.fhir.org it is fhir-cache-seed-npm --sushi-config sushi-config.yaml, and for versions npm does not carry, --mirror from a repository that fhir-package-mirror filled on a machine that reaches the host. Pin that repository with --mirror-commit <full 40-character SHA>: git cannot fetch an abbreviated SHA from a remote, and the seeder refuses one. A cloud session can fill the mirror without a person’s device, through a GitHub Actions runner: push a claude/mirror-* branch that edits packages.txt in the mirror repository, wait for its mirror.yml run, merge, re-seed. SUSHI also adds packages that sushi-config.yaml does not list, such as hl7.fhir.uv.tools.r4#latest. A #latest needs the registry to name a version, so offline it fails with errors that look like the IG’s own (for example logical-target … does not exist), even with the package in the cache. Serve the mirror as a registry on localhost, answering GET /<name> with dist-tags.latest and GET /<name>/<version> with the tarball, and run FPL_REGISTRY=http://127.0.0.1:<port> sushi build .. Check which version latest resolves to: it is the mirror’s highest, which is only right when the mirror holds the current release. Do not report “SUSHI cannot run here” before running tools:remedy. A refusal that tools:remedy answers with none is “could not determine” in the sense of the next section: say so, with the reason it gave.

71f3fba2867c.title: A capability that is absent did not pass
71f3fba2867c.content: If a probe fails, overallStatus is not a pass with an empty findings list. It is “could not determine”, and it is reported as such: a clean run over a validator that never started looks exactly like a clean IG.

5f85dbf08f48.title: Validating a cone
5f85dbf08f48.content: ig-incremental-build.bpmn validates a restricted cone — the artefacts a change touches — rather than the whole IG, and reports the cone it chose. That is a latency optimisation for the authoring loop. It does not gate a release: the full publisher build in l3-fhir-pipeline.bpmn does. Do not let a green cone stand in for a green IG: a profile the change did not touch can still be broken by it.

702aae5ad8ed.title: After validation
702aae5ad8ed.content: Quality gates on the aggregate are quality-control; publishing is ig-publication. A validator’s verdict is an input to the QC reviewer’s decision, not the decision.

fe44af08aec5.title: Processes that run this skill
fe44af08aec5.content: | process | step(s) that name it | . | Incremental IG build | Validate the cone (fhir_validate) | . | L3 FHIR IG pipeline | Validate against profiles | .

308c43a26817.doc: Figure rebuild: a figure is data, not a picture
308c43a26817.title: Figure rebuild: a figure is data, not a picture
308c43a26817.content: A folio built from an L1 entry must carry every figure its source declares, and carry it as data rather than as a picture. Two things go wrong otherwise: . | Figures go missing silently. A vector arm that matches only Fig. and Figure misses a handbook that writes Fig 1., and nothing compares the publication’s declared figures with the folio’s blocks unless figure:coverage does. | Figures arrive as pictures. A figure block whose file is vfig-pNNN.png has a caption, a page and glossary links in the KG. Its boxes, arrows and labels are pixels: no query can reach them. | . The rebuild form is picked by figure type (step 2).

c62f5b79a954.doc: Figure rebuild: a figure is data, not a picture
c62f5b79a954.title: The steps, after the folio is seeded
c62f5b79a954.content: . | Every declared figure has a block. Run bun run cat figure:coverage --entry <library>/<doc-id> --folio folio/<doc>. A missing figure is a bug in extraction or seeding. Fix that (re-run the vector arms, inspect, place the block) rather than excluding it. The one legitimate block exclusion is content the folio may not copy, such as a third-party figure used by permission. It is signed off by a person (scope: "block"), and the folio says in prose what the figure was. | Classify each figure by what it draws, by looking at the render, never by its labels alone (see l1-document-ingestion, “the text layer is not the figure”): . | The figure draws | Rebuild as | Where it lives | . | actors, systems, components, layers of an architecture | an ArchiMate view | the reference architecture the folio mounts (e.g. smart-ra tools/archimate-dth/), linked from the block’s meta.figureViews | . | a workflow with tasks, gateways, lanes | BPMN 2.0 | the folio’s processes/, or the DAK it is adapted from | . | a decision or a transition rule | DMN 1.3 | processes/decisions/ | . | classes, attributes, cardinalities | FHIR logical models (FSH), drawn as a UML class diagram generated from them | the upstream IG (e.g. smart-pcmt), else a litlfred FSH repo | . | a graph of named boxes and arrows | find what the boxes ARE (processes, actors, systems) and model it as ArchiMate elements and relationships | the reference architecture | . | phases, layers, nested shapes, a tree, a staircase | an SVG generated from data: a data file plus a generator Tool. The DIIG phases chart is the worked example: diig-phases-figure/v1 data on the L1 library entry of each publication that prints it, drawn by Tool diig-phases-svg | the data on the source’s L1 library entry; the folio commits the SVG, and adds only its own tiles in a diig-phases-adaptation/v1 file | . | a table of values drawn as a picture | a table block | the block | . | a country example, a photograph, a screenshot, a third-party figure | keep the cited picture (scope: "rebuild" exclusion, signed off) | unchanged | . One source, never a copy. Every rebuilt figure is generated from, or links to, ONE schema-backed source: an ArchiMate model, a BPMN or DMN file, a FHIR logical model, or a data file whose labels are glossary IRIs. A figure that appears in several publications (the DIIG phases chart, the SMART Guidelines layers, the ANC workflow) has one source in the layer they all mount, and each folio points at it. Content that already lives upstream (smart-pcmt’s FHIR models for dth-pc) is linked, never re-typed. | Start from the drawing’s own structure. pdf-vector-figures.py already records, per render, the labelled boxes (assembly.boxes) and which open strokes join two of them. That is a draft node and edge list. Check it against the render: the assembly does not know arrow direction or meaning, and a label in white space belongs to no box. | Keep the picture as evidence. The rebuilt block cites the PDF page and keeps meta.source.file pointing at the crop, so a reviewer can compare. Record how it was made in meta.source.method: archimate-view, bpmn, dmn, fhir-logical-model, generated or redrawn, plus generator when a script draws it and the source’s path or IRI. | Assert nothing the figure does not draw. A rebuild is a transcription of the drawing. A relation the figure does not draw is not added, and counts, dates and country facts stay cited source content, never model facts (the L2 DTH workplan rule: no empirical claims in formal content). smart-ra’s dth_sc.py states the same rule in its view documentation. | Re-run the check. --require-computable fails while any figure is still a picture or only linked, so a folio can adopt it as a gate once the rebuilds are done. | .

40b9e08e2222.doc: Figure rebuild: a figure is data, not a picture
40b9e08e2222.title: Routes by figure type, in detail
40b9e08e2222.content: A workflow picture becomes BPMN XML . A figure drawn in BPMN notation (lanes, events, gateways, tasks, groups, subprocesses), such as the ANC workflow in dth-pc Fig. 6 and dth-sc Fig. 7, is transcribed into a .bpmn file. | Look for the source’s own BPMN first. If the publication it is adapted from (a DAK, a DTH, an IG) publishes the process as .bpmn, mount or cite that file; never redraw it. Otherwise transcribe it: WHO smart-anc, for example, publishes no .bpmn for its ANC workflow. | Transcribe exactly what is drawn. Keep the source’s activity numbers and names as task ids and names (10.5 Nutrition supplementation), the lanes, the gateway labels on their flows, a group as bpmn:group, and a subprocess as bpmn:subProcess. Include bpmndi coordinates taken from the render, so the diagram looks like the source. | What the figure emphasises becomes data, not colour. The purple outline on “connections to the supply chain” becomes a marker on those tasks, an extension element or a documented category, so a query can find them. | Shared processes live once, in the layer the folios mount (dth-sc for the supply chain handbooks), and each folio’s figure block points at that file. | Validate with the cat-harness bpmn-authoring checks, then render the SVG with the same tool the folio uses for its own processes. | . A data model becomes FHIR logical models, rendered as UML . A class diagram with attributes and cardinalities (dth-pc Fig. 9: Generic Product, Trade Item, Regulated Trade Item) is a data model. | Find the newer computable source first. dth-pc’s data model is carried forward in smart-pcmt: Product and ProductAuthorization logical models. Link to those, cite the handbook figure as the original, and list the differences rather than hiding them. Read WHO and smart-* repositories; never change them. | Only where no source exists, transcribe it as FSH Logical: models in a litlfred repository. sushi must run without errors before the commit. | Draw the figure as a UML class diagram generated from the StructureDefinitions, never from the picture. Show each entity as an IG-style structure tree, using the FHIR layer’s logical-model-schemas and ig-ast-render. | In mapping tables, every FHIR path links to the spec page for its version (https://hl7.org/fhir/R5/<resource>-definitions.html#<Resource.path>), and every entity links to its logical model or profile. State the FHIR version when the source and the mapping differ (smart-pcmt is 4.0.1; dth-pc maps to R5, where InventoryItem first exists). | . A layered or phased chart becomes an SVG generated from data . Charts such as the SMART Guidelines L1–L5 layers, the DIIG phases, nested strategies or a cost tree are not graphs. Write their content as a data file: layers, boxes, their text, and which feeds which. Then generate the SVG with a Tool. The DIIG phases chart is the worked example; the data lives in the L1 library: . | Each published version is transcribed once, as diig-phases-figure/v1 data on that publication’s L1 library entry, under figure-data/. DIIG Fig. 1.1.1 lives on 9789240010567-eng, and the product catalogue handbook’s Fig. 4 lives on 9789240116191-eng. | A folio that adds its own tiles (dth-hrh) writes only those tiles in a diig-phases-adaptation/v1 file that adapts the published version. | Tool diig-phases-svg (bun run figure:diig-phases) draws either one. The folio commits the SVG and records the data file in meta.source.generated. | The SMART Guidelines approach chart (L1–L5 layers and their country adaptations) follows the same pattern: smart-guidelines-approach-figure/v1 data (the product catalogue handbook’s Fig. 5 is on 9789240116191-eng), drawn by Tool smart-approach-svg (bun run figure:smart-approach). | A source’s own wording stays as printed, typos included (“prioritise outcomes”); a correction is a review comment, not an edit to the data. | Labels are SVG <text>, never pixels, so they can be searched, translated and read aloud. | A label that names a glossary concept (L1 Narrative, Digital adaptation kit, Localisation) links to the SKOS term, an <a href> around the text. | . Mermaid is a rendering, never a source . Mermaid is a drawing language, not a schema. Nothing downstream consumes it: no KG import, no validator, and the document site does not render it. Its node names are local strings with no IRI, so they cannot link to a glossary term, an ArchiMate element or a FHIR model. A hand-written .mmd is therefore a second copy of content, which the one-source rule forbids. Mermaid may appear only as a view GENERATED from a schema-backed source, when it lays out better than the native renderer, and then the generated text and SVG are build output, not authored files. Drop the flattened figure text from the prose . Page-level seeding puts a figure’s text layer into the prose block of its page (“Fig. 1: Product master data Product identifier, Name, …”). That text is neither prose nor a figure. Once the figure has a block, remove its text from the prose, from the caption line to the end of the figure’s labels. The labels live in vector-labels.json and, after a rebuild, in the computable source. The l1-coverage check is unaffected, because figure labels are not normative sentences. Link table cells . Tables seeded from a publication hold names that the folio already defines. Link them: . | a chapter or section name links to its section anchor in the folio; | an organisation or role (Ministry of Health, National Regulatory Authority, Central Medical Stores, Data officer) links to its glossary term, and through that to the ArchiMate actor or role the term maps to; | a cross-reference to a figure or table (“Fig. 9”) links to the block. | . Match names only on an exact glossary label or altLabel. A cell with no match stays plain text and is listed for review. A guessed link is worse than none. Example data becomes FHIR example instances . A figure or table that shows example records, such as products, packs or identifiers with quantities, is instance data and not a drawing. Examples are dth-pc Fig. 11 (packaging variations) and the NPC01101001 table. Write the records once as FSH Instance:s of the upstream logical model (InstanceOf: Product, Usage: #example) beside that model. The figure or table is then generated from the compiled instances. For dth-pc these instances are in litlfred/smart-pcmt. The instances carry only what the source prints: . | A value the model requires but the source omits gets data-absent-reason#unknown, never a plausible guess. | Numbers that do not add up in the source are transcribed as printed, and the mismatch is listed in the PR. | A column with no clean element is left out and listed, not forced. | . A repeated activity header comes from the step records . A bar that repeats over each activity, such as INPUTS / STEPS / RESOURCES / OUTPUTS in dth-pc, is a view of that activity’s step-table record. Generate it from the record. Each input and output links the BPMN data object it names, and nothing is typed into the bar.

b366d623a50e.doc: Figure rebuild: a figure is data, not a picture
b366d623a50e.title: Reviewing the classification
b366d623a50e.content: An agent proposes, and a person decides. Review happens either in the folio’s Contributor Log sheet or in a GitHub issue, and the result always lands in the folio’s figures.json by a PR. | Propose. An agent looks at each figure’s render and vector-layer structure. It proposes a route from the table in step 2 and an upstream source to reuse, if one exists, and gives its evidence. | Review in the sheet. Write one row per figure, or per batch, to the Contributor Log’s Agent tab, one row per change set. The script copies the rows across, so the sheet needs no new columns: . | Title: Fig N: route | Selected Sections: the section that holds the figure | Feedback: Decision needed: <question>, followed by lettered options with the recommendation marked | Agentic status: Needs human | . An Editor accepts the recommendation by setting Ready for agent to Yes, or types another letter. The steps are in review-sheet-script, “A question to people goes in the sheet”. | Or review in an issue. One issue per figure, labelled figure-route, holding the same question. The row’s Issue column and feedback-issue.ts keep a sheet row and its issue linked, so either one can start the review and the decision closes both. | Record. Accepted routes are written to figures.json in a PR, with who approved each one. figure-coverage then holds the folio to them. | .

dcbd3417318e.doc: Figure rebuild: a figure is data, not a picture
dcbd3417318e.title: Reading the report
dcbd3417318e.content: | State | Meaning | . | missing | declared by the publication, no block in the folio | . | excluded | no block, by a signed-off scope: "block" exclusion | . | picture | only crop or image blocks | . | linked | a picture whose block links a model view; the view may not draw the whole figure | . | computable | a diagram or table block, or a figure block with a rebuild method | . | cited | kept as a picture on purpose, by a signed-off scope: "rebuild" exclusion | . As in l1-coverage, an agent may propose an exclusion, but only a person signs one off. Declared figures are read with cat-harness-tools declaredFigureCaptions, the same reading check:l1-complete uses, so the two checks agree on what the publication declares.

b02e16fdf668.doc: Filing a source: what Dublin Core carries, and what it does not
b02e16fdf668.title: Filing a source: what Dublin Core carries, and what it does not
b02e16fdf668.content: This is the librarian’s half of intake. A file lands in uploads/; describing what it is is filing, and deriving structure from it is library-ingestion (uploads-and-library-are-two-stages-of-one-pipeline).

04c3cd2dfce6.doc: Filing a source: what Dublin Core carries, and what it does not
04c3cd2dfce6.title: The line, and it is drawn by the vocabulary
04c3cd2dfce6.content: folio-assistant-core/docs/source/guides-document-ingestion/how-much-of-this-does-dublin-core-carry.md is the source of truth; in summary: . Dublin Core covers the bibliographic layer well — dcterms:title, creator, date, language, identifier, hasPart, format, extent. A per-folder record and an archive’s part/whole structure sit comfortably there. It does not cover the derived layer. A narrative description of a figure, a transcript, a back-translation confidence, a sheet’s column headers, and above all the provenance of a generated narrative are not dcterms terms. The house rule (schemas/jsonld.ts): . generalising is sound; inventing is not. Where an existing vocabulary has the term, use it. Where it does not, the term goes in this project’s own namespace, not into an approximate dcterms one: consumers read a dcterms term by DCMI’s definition, not ours.

805d369130b5.doc: Filing a source: what Dublin Core carries, and what it does not
805d369130b5.title: What is NOT decided, and must not be decided from memory
805d369130b5.content: Which vocabulary to reach for beyond Dublin Core is not yet decided. PROV-O is the obvious candidate for provenance. Do not mint a prov: term because it sounds right: read the published specification, or leave the fact in this project’s namespace and say why. The same applies to Dublin Core itself: before using a dcterms term not listed above, read the DCMI specification (refinements and range constraints) rather than inferring it from the name.

0bf012ac7c00.doc: Filing a source: what Dublin Core carries, and what it does not
0bf012ac7c00.title: What to record at INTAKE, and what waits
0bf012ac7c00.content: Filing captures how the thing arrived, which nobody can reconstruct later: . | fact | why it cannot wait | . | where it came from — the URL, the query, the person | a file in a queue has no origin written on it | . | when it was captured | the web changes; “now” is not recoverable next week | . | how it was captured | a PDF print and a crawl are different artefacts (see archiving-web-pages) | . | what came with it | assets, sidecars, the parts of a multi-file capture | . | the identifier the source claims for itself | a DOI or an arXiv id is the publisher’s identity, not ours | . The .extraction.json sidecars in an instance’s uploads/ model most of this — container, method, capturedAt, producer, readAt, assets[]. Read one before designing a new shape. Everything else — sections, structure, OCR, derived narrative — is the ingestion engine’s and is recorded in library/<bib-slug>/.

7925aab8b9f2.doc: Filing a source: what Dublin Core carries, and what it does not
7925aab8b9f2.title: A sidecar is not a document
7925aab8b9f2.content: <source>.extraction.json describes the capture of <source>: metadata about a queued unit, not a queued unit. A file that describes another file in the same queue is not itself waiting to be ingested. An orphan sidecar, one whose source has gone, must stay visible in the queue view.

c1e2d8e58acb.doc: Filing a source: what Dublin Core carries, and what it does not
c1e2d8e58acb.title: Identifiers are claimed, not assigned by us
c1e2d8e58acb.content: A DOI, an ISBN, an arXiv id and a WHO publication number are the publisher’s identity for the thing. Record them as dcterms:identifier values with their scheme; do not normalise them into one string, and do not treat the absence of one as a defect. A working paper legitimately has none. The slug under library/ is ours and is a different kind of name: it is how this corpus addresses the item, and every knowledge-graph reference resolves through it. Do not derive one from the other silently: record the mapping.

d0c0516c8c45.doc: Filing a source: what Dublin Core carries, and what it does not
d0c0516c8c45.title: A folio whose bibliography is CSL-JSON
d0c0516c8c45.content: A folio that cites its sources as CSL-JSON (references/<key>.json or <folio>/schema/references.ts) and joins uploads to references in its source ledger already holds the bibliographic facts. Do not re-type them into records by hand: declare a catalogue directory and run the catalogue-from-references Tool (bun run cat catalogue:from-references <instance> --apply). It writes one record and one item node per entry the ledger joins to exactly one reference, leaves every other entry alone, and judges no licence (every gate stays unknown). The reference stays the source of truth: change it and re-run, never edit the generated record.

25850ae97b41.title: Finding software — get it, do not route around it
25850ae97b41.content: The container is the agent’s to provision: installing usually takes one command, and a workaround produces the wrong output quietly.

720ea380c4ae.title: The rule
720ea380c4ae.content: A missing program is a step, not a stop. When a script says it needs something: . bun run cat software:ensure --for cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-ocr.py # what that script needs bun run cat software:ensure tesseract pdftoppm # by name bun run cat software:check # report only . scripts/ensure-software.ts walks a ladder per entry and stops at the first rung that leaves the thing present (checked by presence, never by exit code): . | rung | how | offered when | . | present | command -v, or import for a Python module | always checked first | . | apt | apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends, one apt-get update and retry on failure | apt-get exists and the agent is root or has passwordless sudo | . | pip | python3 -m pip install, with --break-system-packages on an externally managed interpreter | the entry names a pip package | . | GitHub release | the asset for this platform at a pinned tag, verified against its sha256 before unpacking, into ~/.local/bin | the entry declares one | . Every attempt is printed, including the rungs not offered and why. Exit 0 means everything asked for is present.

541451d8d614.title: What not to do instead
541451d8d614.content: . | Do not substitute. A cached OCR text, a weaker backend, a skipped step, a “could not determine” you could have determined: each produces output that reads as the real thing. If the right tool cannot be installed, say which rung failed and how (the tool prints it), and stop. | Do not install by hand and move on. If a script needs something the table does not list, add an entry to scripts/software.json — how to get it, its licence, and usedBy — so the next agent’s --for finds it. The tool refuses an undeclared name (exit 2) for exactly this reason. | Do not download an unpinned or unverified binary. A GitHub entry carries a tag (never latest) and a sha256 per platform, taken from the release’s own checksums file; the table’s test enforces both. | A licence is recorded, not a reason to refuse. PyMuPDF is AGPL: it is installed into the environment to RUN tools and is never vendored or shipped (see pdf-structure.py’s licence note). The entry says so. | .

73d3a8c7c6a4.title: When a rung is blocked by the network
73d3a8c7c6a4.content: That is blocked-build-dependencies: read the refusal (curl -sS "$HTTPS_PROXY/__agentproxy/status") before working around it. What an agent container typically reaches: . | route | result | . | apt (Ubuntu archive), PyPI, npm | open | . | github.com/<o>/<r>/releases/download/<tag>/<asset> | 200 — the GitHub rung works | . | raw.githubusercontent.com | 200 | . | git clone https://github.com/... | works | . | codeload.github.com archives, github.com/<o>/<r>/raw/... | 403 | . | api.github.com | unreliable — find a tag with git ls-remote --tags instead | .

dce3bb551abc.title: A missing tool for the WHOLE environment
dce3bb551abc.content: When every new session will need it, the durable fix is the environment’s setup script (the person’s cloud environment settings), not each agent installing it again. Say so to the person once, with the line to add — bun run cat software:ensure --for <script> covers it — and carry on installing it in this session meanwhile.

e105d6c3e938.title: Flushable containers
e105d6c3e938.content: A flushable container is a named store whose whole point is that it keeps things. A trash you can recover from, a review preview somebody has not looked at yet, a console log you read back after a failure. The accumulation is the feature, which is why none of them can be solved by simply not writing. Three containers share the rule, which is why it is general rather than three copies of one rule: . | container | what it holds | “flush” means | . | fsh-guts | deprecated pages, scripts, proposals — “the trashcan that is kept” | a real, irreversible delete. It is the last stop | . | staging previews | one built site per open branch, under branches/<slug>/ on the publish branch | removal from the publish branch — recoverable by re-running Feature Staging | . | console log | what a run printed | truncation | .

ce37d065022c.title: Three actions, and they are not three wrappers on one
ce37d065022c.content: Each answers a different question, and a container that offers only one of them is missing capability rather than keeping things simple. | Flush all — “I do not need any of this.” One decision, whole container. The cheapest to build and the easiest to regret, so it is the one that most needs the confirmation rule below. | Trim to limit — “keep what fits.” Mechanical, and it needs two things the container must declare: a total order and which end is expendable. See below — that end is not always the same. | Select to prune — “I need to look first.” The only action that can spare an item a rule would have taken, which is exactly why it cannot be dropped as redundant. A rule that is right 95 % of the time still needs a way to be overruled on the other 5 %, and select is that way. | .

6cc7cd858c0d.title: The expendable end is declared, not assumed
6cc7cd858c0d.content: Trim-to-limit on previews and trim-to-limit on a console log discard opposite ends, and this is the specialisation most likely to be got wrong. | A preview is most useful when newest. The oldest is the one nobody is reviewing any more, so trimming drops the oldest. | A console log is often most useful at its oldest retained line, because the first error is the cause and everything after it is consequence. Dropping the oldest to make room is how a log keeps 10,000 lines of cascade and throws away the one line that explained it. | . So a container declares which end trim takes. A shared trim that assumes “drop oldest” is correct for two of the three cases here and silently wrong for the third, and wrong in the direction that destroys the evidence.

90801471a069.title: The badge has three states, and the third is not “fine”
90801471a069.content: Over-full is a declared state and gets a badge — including the trash. A container you can recover from is the one whose size a reader stops thinking about, so fsh-guts is the one that most needs the badge rather than the one that needs it least: nothing else in the interface says it has grown, and the whole premise of keeping deleted things is that nobody is watching them. So does under. And so does could not determine — a container whose size could not be read is not under its limit, it is unmeasured: “‘Could not read gh-pages’ is never ‘0 MB of previews’“. A badge that shows a number it could not obtain is worse than no badge, because a reader acts on it.

feb10e8224ee.title: Never flush without explicit confirmation
feb10e8224ee.content: This inherits deletion-requires-confirmation.md whole: an agent never removes a durable artefact on its own initiative, it reports what would go — with sizes and ages — and waits to be told. Two container-specific sharpenings: . | fsh-guts is the strictest case in the system, because it is where deletes already went. AGENTS.md makes “delete” mean “relocate to fsh-guts”, which is what makes deletion reversible everywhere else — flushing fsh-guts is therefore the only truly irreversible delete, and the one confirmation that cannot be inferred from context. | Recoverability changes the bar, and it is the container’s job to say so. A staging preview is regenerable by re-running Feature Staging, so confirming its removal is a smaller decision than confirming a fsh-guts flush. A container that does not declare its recoverability forces every flush to be treated as the worst case, which is how a useful action becomes one nobody dares run. | .

3789cba6c4f0.title: Liveness gates the prune, and “cannot tell” spares the item
3789cba6c4f0.content: An item can look dead and be live. A branch with no open PR may have been committed to minutes ago by a session that reuses one branch across a run of PRs: “no open PR” is not a synonym for “abandoned”. So a container declares its liveness signals, a prune candidate must fail every one, and a signal that could not be evaluated spares the item rather than condemning it. For previews those signals are open-pr, unmerged-branch and recent-commit (30 minutes — the shortness is the point).

5a017541c3d1.title: A limit below the floor is not a limit, it is a permanent alarm
5a017541c3d1.content: A limit must sit above its floor — concurrent users × item size. A limit beneath its own floor cannot be satisfied, so it fires constantly, and a signal that always fires becomes invisible. When the floor exceeds the limit, the finding is about item size or the limit, never about pruning more aggressively. When you look at item size, look for duplication before content. Staging previews built with an absolute baseurl of /…/branches/<slug> carry the slug on every page, so git’s content-hash deduplication shares nothing between them: N previews store N copies of a site identical apart from its own address. A container over its limit is a question about the container, and “prune more” is the one answer that never asks it. But “make the references relative” is not the fix. A reference is either an address or a name, and only addresses may be relativized. A stylesheet href is an address; a JSON-LD @id or a JSON Schema $ref is a name, and a relative one resolves against the retrieval URL — so the graph’s identities become a function of how the file was fetched, and an out-of-band validator has no base at all. Deduplication is not worth buying with identity; identity references are left byte-for-byte alone, and what remains is a real floor, answered by a limit whose basis states it.

a079882fda53.title: Adding a container
a079882fda53.content: Declare, do not infer: . | what it holds, and whether the contents are recoverable and how; | its limit, with a basis that names the floor; | the order and which end trim takes; | its liveness signals, and that an unevaluable signal spares; | which of the three actions it offers, and what each does specifically. | .

8b137f4c4249.title: Not built yet
8b137f4c4249.content: The viewer — a counter, an over-full badge and a select dialog — is separate work: it is UI, and a select dialog must meet the accessibility rules. The staging mechanism is a preflight plus a dispatchable cleanup path, because a label-based remedy cannot reach the previews the check finds. This skill is the concept those two implement, not a third implementation of it.
