1dc9ec707864.title: Reading GitHub state — resolve the ref, do not compose the URL
1dc9ec707864.content: Skill id: github-state-inspection · Package: sdlc-core . Every question of the form “is it published?”, “why is this 404?”, “did that deploy?” has an authoritative answer in a ref, and a misleading one in an HTTP request. This skill says which to reach for and in what order.

50156a7bb4a2.title: The rule
50156a7bb4a2.content: A published URL is LOOKED UP in the publish ref’s tree. It is never built from the source path. cat-harness/docs/guides/agent-onboarding.md publishes to /docs/cat-harness/guides/agent-onboarding.html: the layer segment moves from in front of docs/ to behind it. Anyone composing the URL from the source path gets a 404 and concludes the page is missing. Source paths also move, and some pages (proposals, for one) are kept in the repository but deliberately unpublished. A URL composed from a remembered source path can assert a page exists where the repository has decided none should.

5e8386f1dc13.title: First check for ANY deployment question
5e8386f1dc13.content: Look at the branch. Not the site. git ls-remote origin refs/heads/gh-pages # does the publish ref exist at all git fetch origin gh-pages git ls-tree --name-only FETCH_HEAD # what is at the root git ls-tree -r --name-only FETCH_HEAD | grep -i <thing> # where does it actually live . For a staging preview, the subtree is branches/<branch-slug>/, and git ls-tree --name-only FETCH_HEAD branches/ lists every branch with a live preview. The slug replaces / with -: claude/festive-galileo-s7ibx0 becomes branches/claude-festive-galileo-s7ibx0/. The MCP GitHub tools answer the same question without a fetch — get_file_contents with ref: "refs/heads/gh-pages" and a directory path returns the listing. Use whichever is to hand; both read the ref, which is the point.

bf6feaf78632.title: Present on the ref is not the same as SERVED — read the Pages deployment
bf6feaf78632.content: The step above is authoritative for what exists. It is not authoritative for what a reader gets, and the gap between them has a mechanism worth knowing. Pages-from-a-branch publishes through a pages build and deployment run, and a new push to the publish ref cancels the run already in flight. So a commit can sit on gh-pages with the file plainly there while the last successful deployment is an older tree. git log --format='%h %ad %s' --date=iso -10 origin/gh-pages # how fast is the ref moving . and the deployments themselves, which only the API has: . actions_list method: list_workflow_runs workflow_runs_filter: { branch: "gh-pages", event: "dynamic" } . Read conclusion per run, not just the newest — cancelled is the one that misleads, because nothing is red and yet nothing shipped from that commit. Each staging deploy pushes two commits about ten seconds apart, the payload (staging(<slug>): from <sha>) and then render-log: rendered …, and the second reliably cancels the first’s build, so on a busy publish ref many recent deployments read cancelled. So when a preview 404s and the file is on the ref: . | Check whether a deployment has succeeded since the commit that added it. A cancelled newest run with an older success means the tree being served predates your push. | Check whether your subtree survives in that older tree too — on a ref this busy, git cat-file -e <commit>:<path> over the recent commits answers “was it ever missing” directly, and a path present at every one of them rules the ref out as the cause entirely. | Only then is the question about Pages rather than about the repository, and it is a wait-or-escalate, not a fix. | . What this does not license. A cancelled run is an explanation to verify, never one to assert: it is equally consistent with a page that is serving fine. From a container that cannot reach the host, the honest report is the mechanism plus what you could and could not establish — not “it is probably propagation”.

9a6ed57e5cec.title: Why curl is not the first check, and often not evidence at all
9a6ed57e5cec.content: Three distinct failures produce an identical-looking result, and only one of them means the page is missing: . | what you see | what it can mean | . | 404 | the page is not published — or your URL was composed wrong | . | 000, CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403 | the agent’s proxy blocks the host. Says nothing about the site | . | 200 on a stale page | the deploy has not run yet; the old build is still served | . In a Claude Code container, outbound HTTPS goes through a proxy that blocks github.io. A curl against a Pages URL from here returns 000 and a 403 tunnel error regardless of whether the page exists, so “could not determine” from a fetch is no answer when the ref holds one. “Could not determine” is a third state and must never be rendered as a pass — but it is also not a place to stop when another source can determine it. Reach for the ref first, and a fetch only to confirm something the ref cannot tell you (that a redirect works, that a asset loads).

7ea959ce1aea.title: CI state — read check RUNS on the head sha
7ea959ce1aea.content: Commit statuses and check runs are different APIs and this repository uses the second. pull_request_read with method: "get_status" returns {"state":"pending","total_count":0,"statuses":[]} on a PR whose eight checks are green, because there are no legacy statuses to report. Use method: "get_check_runs". Further traps: . | Check the sha. A check_suite.completed event names a head_sha that may already be superseded by your own later push, and the staging workflow’s own commits appear as shas that are not PR heads at all. Compare against the PR’s current head before concluding anything. | mergeable_state: "unknown" means GitHub has not finished computing it, not that the PR is fine. "dirty" is a real merge conflict and is work now. | “No suite failed” over ZERO suites is not a pass, and neither is a clean run list that is only PART of the check set. See below. | . A clean check set and a COMPLETE check set are different questions . A check_suite.completed event says no third-party suite is still running or failed. Its own harness note admits the gap: suites with no runs, cancelled suites and legacy statuses are not covered; verify the PR’s overall state before acting. So the event is evidence about the suites that EXIST, and silence about the ones that do not yet. The same hole exists one layer down: a classifier that guards only the EMPTY run list passes a PARTIAL one — one clean run where thirteen are owed reads as PASS — 1 check(s) completed clean. So before reading a clean check set as green, ask whether it is the whole set. check:head-has-run answers it — coverageFor reconciles the runs against the workflows the tree itself declares, and mergeStateForHead returns conflicted for the case below. bun run cat ci:watch composes both. Do not build a second reconciliation; two answers to one question are free to disagree. Four causes of an absent-or-inert run, which must not collapse into one silence. The fourth is not an absence: the run exists, it completed, and it executed nothing. | cause | how it reads | what to do | . | a conflicted head | no pull_request run is published AT ALL — the forge mints no refs/pull/N/merge, and a pull_request run checks that ref out | merge the base in. The checks are not slow; they are never coming | . | a filtered trigger that owed no run | genuinely nothing was due | stay silent — loosening this produces false fires | . | a run never created, unexplained | a workflow the tree declares on: pull_request has no run and the head is mergeable | a finding, not a wait | . | a bot-actor push | the runs EXIST and are completed, with conclusion: action_required — approval was owed and never given, so no job ran | read the dispatched run instead; see below | . A draft PR is a fifth reading of the same silence: Code-quality gates does not fire from pull_request while a PR is a draft, so a draft head owes those runs no more than a filtered trigger does. Mark it ready, do not dispatch. conclusion: action_required is not a failure, and not a pass . Counting conclusions makes this invisible. action_required is a terminal conclusion that is neither success nor failure, so a predicate written as conclusion != "failure" reads it as fine and one written as conclusion == "success" reads the head as merely incomplete. Neither says what is true: the workflow was reached, approval was owed, and no job body executed. A head pushed by a bot actor gets pull_request runs that are all action_required; a head pushed by a session gets runs that execute. The merge-forward bot does not void the gates. With no MERGE_MAIN_TOKEN set, merge-main.yml dispatches both gating workflows — code-quality-gates.yml and jsonld-gen-check.yml — so the merge commit is proved by CI rather than trusted; Feature Staging is left alone because it is preview-only. Such a head shows the pair pull_request: action_required beside workflow_dispatch: success, on the identical head sha. So the rule for reading a head is by workflow and sha, never by event: a workflow_dispatch run of an owed workflow on the exact head is proof, and after a merge-forward it is arguably better proof, because the branch tip already contains the base and the dispatch tests the merged content rather than a synthesised merge ref. check:head-has-run already reads it this way, so do not add an event filter to it. MERGE_MAIN_TOKEN is a convenience, not a correctness fix: it makes the PR’s own runs fire on the bot’s push instead of needing a dispatch. Do not hand-push commits to “restore” gates that already ran. Ask whether the BASE moved before calling any verdict non-deterministic. A pull_request run tests the head merged with main as it was at push time, so main moving flips verdicts in both directions with no change to your branch — a green head can become a red merge commit, and a red check can turn green when a sibling’s fix lands. That is not a flapping gate.

3a3c4e0b714e.title: Order of resort
3a3c4e0b714e.content: . | The ref — git ls-tree / get_file_contents. Authoritative for what exists and where. | The API — check runs, PR state, branch list. Authoritative for what happened. | The workflow run — actions_list / get_job_logs. Authoritative for why it happened. | An HTTP fetch — last, and only for what the first three cannot answer. From an agent container, treat a failure as a proxy result until proven otherwise. | . From a cloud agent container, use REST. The proxy blocks GraphQL, so gh pr view and other GraphQL-backed gh commands fail; gh api repos/... works. Actions log blob URLs return 403 through the same proxy, so read logs with the GitHub MCP get_job_logs (return_content, tail_lines), not by fetching the URL it would hand you.

538ba93b46b9.title: Role
538ba93b46b9.content: Maintain the project-wide glossary of defined terms. Builds the glossary.json index from every block’s defines: [...] field, generates the chapters/glossary.tex chapter, writes the same terms as a SKOS scheme for the glossary page, and gates CI with --check mode.

2199d8bf3b72.title: The SKOS scheme
2199d8bf3b72.content: The builder also writes <glossary dir>/paper-<paper>.glossary.json, a folio-glossary/v1 scheme, into the glossary directory declared by the instance that holds the paper. Core’s glossary page reads it through collect() and shows the paper’s terms, in the instance’s namespace, beside every other scheme. The rules (status by provenance, verbatim definitions, the slug as notation) are in glossary-terms. The paper’s scheme is unordered: its terms are shown A–Z. A glossary whose terms must be read in a logical order declares ordered: true and gives each term requires; see glossary-terms §”Ordered glossaries” — do not sort one of those. --check also fails when the scheme is stale, when two slugs would mint one term IRI, or when another document in the directory holds the scheme id. A scheme not written yet is reported and does not fail.

8a2bb46cde50.title: When to invoke
8a2bb46cde50.content: . | A user mentions: glossary, defined terms, defterm, refterm, defines[], “build glossary”, “regenerate glossary”. | After any block’s defines: [...] field is added, modified, or removed. | As part of content-validation whenever a chapter is validated end-to-end. | .

ea2eb50f3e7f.title: Tools
ea2eb50f3e7f.content: | Command | Purpose | . | cd content && bun run pipeline/build-glossary.ts <paper-dir> | Generate glossary.json + chapters/glossary.tex + the SKOS scheme | . | cd content && bun run pipeline/build-glossary.ts <paper-dir> --check | CI gate — non-zero exit on duplicates or out-of-date JSON | . | cd content && bun run pipeline/glossary-candidates.ts <paper-dir> | Phase C: propose candidate owner blocks per slug → glossary-candidates.json (gitignored) | . | cd content && bun run pipeline/apply-glossary-curation.ts <paper-dir> | Dry-run: show edits implied by glossary-curation.json | . | cd content && bun run pipeline/apply-glossary-curation.ts <paper-dir> --write | Apply curated defines: [...] insertions to chosen .ts files (idempotent) | . | cd content && bun run pipeline/codemod-refterm.ts <chapter-dir> | Dry-run: preview :refterm[…] backfill in a chapter | . | cd content && bun run pipeline/codemod-refterm.ts <chapter-dir> --write | Apply backfill to disk | . | cd content && bun run validate <paper-dir> | Includes the five glossary-term validation rules | . | cd content && bun run validate <paper-dir> --strict | Adds term-mention-coverage (bare-text mentions) | . pipeline/… above is the FOLIO’s own path. build-glossary.ts and codemod-refterm.ts live in folio-assistant-core/scripts/, beside the schemas/glossary.ts they read. A folio that vendors its own content/pipeline/ copy uses it. A folio that does not reaches them through the glossary_check and codemod MCP tools, whose resolver searches the folio, then the platform, then folio-assistant-core/scripts/. Curator web UI (Phase C) . /folio/glossary-curator.html?paper=<paper-dir> is a propose-and-pick interface served by the folio-assistant HTTP server. | The page calls GET /api/glossary/candidates (which runs proposeCandidates() and returns the same data as glossary-candidates.json). | The author clicks one candidate per slug (or “skip for now”), then hits save to POST /api/glossary/curation, persisting the decisions to <paper>/glossary-curation.json (committed). | The agent then runs apply-glossary-curation.ts --write to insert the chosen defines: ["…"] fields into each owner block’s .ts file, followed by codemod-refterm.ts <chapter> --write to backfill :refterm[…] mentions. | . Roles: GET is open; POST requires collaborator or higher.

2fc643036fbf.title: Authoring contract
2fc643036fbf.content: Every term registered in any block’s defines: [...] field must be wrapped at every occurrence: . | Defining occurrence (exactly one block): :defterm[Visible] / :defterm[Visible]{#slug} in .md; \defterm{slug}[{Visible}] in .tex. | Reference occurrences (every other mention, anywhere in the project): :refterm[Visible] / :refterm[Visible]{#slug} in .md; \refterm{slug}[{Visible}] in .tex. | . Plain text and \emph{} are not permitted for a defined term once its slug appears in any defines[] list.

8626d3646923.title: Validation rules (Phase B)
8626d3646923.content: | Rule | Severity | Trigger | . | defterm-declared | error | :defterm[X] whose X is not in this block’s defines[] | . | defterm-marked | warning | defines[] entry with no :defterm[X] in the .md | . | refterm-resolves | error | :refterm[X] not declared in any block’s defines[] | . | defterm-unique | warning | Same slug declared by multiple blocks | . | term-mention-coverage | warning (--strict) | Bare-text mention of a known slug not wrapped in :refterm[…] | .

98b90c0f84d6.title: CI integration (formal-pipeline tie-in)
98b90c0f84d6.content: If the project has a formal-proof pipeline (e.g. Lean), the glossary build can regenerate a synonyms module from glossary.json, emitting abbrevs to library synonyms: . -- Auto-generated from glossary.json — do not edit by hand. namespace Project.Glossary open CategoryTheory abbrev MonoidalCategory := CategoryTheory.MonoidalCategory abbrev BraidedMonoidalCategory := CategoryTheory.BraidedMonoidalCategory -- For non-library synonyms, emit a `def ... := sorry` stub -- with a `-- Ref: [manuscript]` comment. end Project.Glossary . abbrev is preferred over def so that elaboration sees the library type definitionally. The formal-proof CI re-runs --check after this file is regenerated. Enable the strict-mode validator (--strict) in CI only after the first :refterm backfill batch lands.

500b6e0f9284.title: Glossary Build
500b6e0f9284.content: Generated from folio-assistant-core/skills/library/cataloguing/glossary-build.md — do not edit here. ✎ Edit this page’s source .

a1774d6fedd3.title: Glossary terms
a1774d6fedd3.content: A glossary can reference external SKOS schemes, and that is the preferred way.

e2c178856b88.title: Where terms go
e2c178856b88.content: Core declares the glossary directory in folio-assistant-core.json. Its graph typology is perInstance, so every folio built on core has a glossary/. Each *.glossary.json is one SKOS concept scheme, $schema: "folio-glossary/v1" (folio-assistant-core/schemas/glossary.ts).

3b9dfb9adf22.title: Reference first, define second
3b9dfb9adf22.content: | you have | write | . | a term somebody else already defines in SKOS (ISCO-08, an EU authority table, a W3C vocabulary) | a local term with exactMatch (or closeMatch, broadMatch, narrowMatch) to the external concept IRI. Do not copy its definition. | . | a list of external terms this folio uses | members: the external concept IRIs, emitted as a skos:Collection | . | a whole external scheme | a remoteGraphs entry in the declaration with graphTypologies: ["glossary"]: known about, not held | . | a term only this folio defines | a local term with prefLabel, definition, and notation for its code | .

6a840d66133b.title: Three states, never two
6a840d66133b.content: . | authored: a person wrote or approved the definition. It must have one. | candidate: extracted from a source and not yet curated. It may have no definition, and the page marks it. | could-not-extract: the source names a term the extractor could not read. It carries a reason a person can act on. | . A candidate is never presented as a definition. An extractor writes candidates; only a person moves one to authored. A paper’s definition block counts as that person: its author wrote the definition and marked it (see “A paper’s glossary” below).

b69a9d476209.title: How a term is linked: the workflow
b69a9d476209.content: Terms are linked across the glossary, the narrative and the knowledge graph with a few shared joins, not a framework. One join key: the SKOS term (its id, or its IRI from another instance). Everything else points at it, and nothing copies it. | thing | how it names the term | . | the defining site | the term’s source: its glossary row (an L1 section line, or the document’s glossary table block). One node-kind structure for every term. | . | a narrative block that explains the term at length | the block’s defines: [<term id>] (and :defterm[...]{#id} inline). Provenance, not a second definition. | . | other uses in prose | nothing to write: matched at build time (term-passages.ts) and linked by --link-terms | . | an acronym | notation on the term, never a second list. The acronyms table is drawn from it (glossary:table). | . | an organization | focus (W3C ORG), shared ones in smart-ra organizations.glossary.json | . | an ArchiMate element | the element’s skosConcept property (glossary-archimate.ts) | . | a BPMN lane or task, DMN decision, skill, Tool | the generated candidate schemes (glossary-extract.ts); exactMatch when one is the same concept | . | a FHIR code | exactMatch / closeMatch to the CodeSystem concept; the code stays a CodeSystem | . | an external glossary | exactMatch to its IRI, members, or a whole scheme in remoteGraphs | . Where terms come from. | Ingesting a source (L1, DTH, DAK): bun run cat glossary:from-source reads its glossary and abbreviations sections into verbatim candidate terms with source: <file>#L<line> (l1-document-ingestion). No per-handbook script. | Authoring in the narrative (dth-hrh): the glossary file is edited, and the chapter is drawn from it (glossary:table, or the folio’s own build). A block that explains a term lists it in defines. | External: reference, don’t copy (below). | . What a reader gets. Every authored-scheme term has a page (glossary:page, glossary/instance/<instance>/<scheme>/<term>/). It shows the definition and acronym, Defined in (its glossary row), broader, narrower (computed), related terms, matches, ArchiMate elements, and In the narrative: the blocks that explain it, then those that use it. A Capitalized label in prose links to that page when the document build passes --link-terms, which dth-init sets for every DTH. Warnings, never failures. bun run cat glossary:links reports a source that is missing from a mounted layer, and a defines id that no scheme holds. With --all it also lists terms the narrative never uses. The acronym report is glossary:acronyms.

b4b0ea5e568a.title: Conventions
b4b0ea5e568a.content: Every folio follows these; none re-decides them. The instance namespace. A term’s IRI is <instance namespace>glossary/<scheme id>/<term id>. The instance namespace is built from the instance’s declaration (iriBase, version, and the stub of a sub-instance) by instanceNs in folio-assistant-core/scripts/glossary-page.ts; schemeIri and termIri are in folio-assistant-core/schemas/glossary.ts. For example: . | instance | namespace | . | folio-assistant-core | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant-core/v0/ns/ | . | ihris (its own site) | https://litlfred.github.io/ihris/ihris/ns/ | . The namespace is never the asset’s path: moving the asset must not move the term. A term is minted by the instance that owns its source. A scheme and its terms live in the namespace of the instance whose root holds the SOURCE ASSET, not of the instance whose glossary/ directory holds the file: . | In a folio with sub-instances, that is the sub-instance (instanceNs(<sub-stub>), under the folio’s own publication root). It is never the root instance, even when the glossary/ directory is declared at the root. In ihris, a term drawn from ihris-manage is minted in ihris-manage’s namespace, not ihris’s. | A code list extended by several packages belongs to the instance that DEFINES it. Say so with the scheme’s own source (a repository path in that instance). Each term’s source still points at the package that contributed it. | A scheme whose terms are sourced in several instances and that names no defining source is refused, never guessed: split it, one scheme per instance. folio-assistant-core/glossary/ holds two platform schemes for that reason, core’s and cat-harness’s. | No two instances share a namespace, and a scheme IRI is unique across every instance. | . check:glossary enforces all of this (schemeOwner and collect in glossary-page.ts, and the checks in glossary.test.ts); glossary-extract.ts mints extracted terms by the same rule. When a check fails, fix the generator or split the authored scheme. Never edit the output. One ConceptScheme per code list. This follows schemas/code-list.ts (codeListToSkos): “a code is addressable and two lists may share a code without sharing a concept”. The same code in two lists gives two concepts. A relation between them is a SKOS match, never a merge. The basis of a match is recorded, never assumed. A match comes from a mapping the repository verified, such as a FHIR ConceptMap whose equivalence implies one: . | equal/equivalent gives exactMatch; | wider/subsumes gives broadMatch; | narrower/specializes gives narrowMatch; | nothing else gives a match. | . Any other basis needs the owner’s explicit acceptance. One example is a ValueSet that binds a local code list to the external code system itself, so that the local code is the external code. Once accepted: . | the scheme’s description names the basis and the ruling; | the builder lists the accepted systems explicitly; | QA recomputes the matches from the same source. | . ihris’s ISCO-08 lists to ESCO are the worked example. An IRI built from a publisher’s pattern but never dereferenced says so.

99b0e6c48369.title: Then
99b0e6c48369.content: bun run cat glossary:page writes the index, docs/glossary/index.md (the authored terms with A–Z and a filter box, the counts, the sources, schema.org DefinedTermSet JSON-LD, and a link to every asset type’s page), one page per asset type at docs/glossary/<type>/index.md (skills, tools, bpmn-activities, dmn-decisions, schema-fields: that type’s extracted terms, with A–Z and a filter box), and one SKOS JSON-LD file per scheme under docs/assets/glossary/. Each term is on exactly one page. bun run check:glossary is the gate: it fails on a document that does not validate, on a stale page, and on a page over its size budget (64 KB for the index, 1 MB for an asset type’s page). A page over budget is split further, never given a bigger budget. The harness’s swimlane-role terms (swimlane-glossary, the swimlane-glossary skill) are one more source the page links to, not copies of.

bdc8a19d1241.title: Extracted terms
bdc8a19d1241.content: glossary:page also extracts a candidate term from every knowledge-graph asset that carries a title and a description (folio-assistant-core/scripts/glossary-extract.ts): skills, Tool nodes, BPMN tasks and call activities, DMN decisions, and schema fields with a doc comment. One scheme per asset type per instance (kg-skills, kg-tools, kg-bpmn-activities, kg-dmn-decisions, kg-schema-fields), written to generated/<instance>/<type>.glossary.json inside core’s glossary/. | They are generated. Never edit them: fix the asset, then re-run. | The kg- scheme prefix is reserved for them. An authored scheme that takes it fails check:glossary. | A definition is the asset’s own text, verbatim. An asset with no description gives a candidate with no definition. | To promote one, author a term in a glossary of your own with a definition you have checked, status: authored, and the same source. | BPMN lanes and roles are not extracted: the swimlane ledger carries them. | Extracted terms are on their asset type’s page, never on the index, and each carries the “candidate, extracted” badge. Only authored terms go into the schema.org DefinedTermSet, which is on the index. | .

82e4b1394cb4.title: Ordered glossaries — logical order, not A–Z
82e4b1394cb4.content: Some glossaries (bootstrap’s, for one) are read top to bottom: each term is defined only by terms above it, and never by itself. Do not sort them A–Z. | ordered: true on a glossary says its terms array IS the order. Each term’s requires lists the local ids its definition uses; the schema refuses one that is later, itself, or not in the glossary. checkDeclaredOrder (schemas/dependency-order.ts) is the same check for any authored order. | In SKOS the order is a skos:OrderedCollection (memberList as an RDF list), each use is dcterms:requires, and isDefinedBy — the schema or standard that defines the term — is rdfs:isDefinedBy. | On the page an ordered scheme is its own numbered section at the top of the index, with its “Uses” links, and is not repeated under the A–Z bar. | A schema whose $defs carry uses IS an ordered glossary, read by termsOfSchema in glossary-page.ts: the definitions stay in one place, the schema, and the glossary cannot drift from it. They are authored, not candidate: a person wrote and approved them in the schema’s source, and the collector only reads them out. | The uses list is authored, not inferred. A text matcher over the definitions is a guard that the list and the prose agree (graph.test.ts); a word can appear without being used as a term. | .

8b5cb46eae33.title: Translation: authored terms only
8b5cb46eae33.content: bun run cat glossary:pot writes one gettext template per scheme that has an authored term, to translations/<locale>/glossary/<instance>--<scheme>.pot under cat-harness’s declared translation-sources directory, beside the BPMN templates in processes/, through the same pipeline (formatPot, the same timestamp-blind comparison); the translation status page counts them. bun run cat glossary:pot:check is the gate. | Only authored terms are extracted: prefLabel, each altLabel, and the definition, in the source language (en when given per language). A candidate reaches a template once a person promotes it. | The term’s IRI is the translator comment, never a msgid. It stays the same in every language; only labels and definitions are translated. | translations/<locale>/glossary.po is a different file (terminology hints for translation-block-qa). Do not confuse it with the glossary/ directory. | . Translations and the per-locale pages . A translation is a .po beside its template: translations/<locale>/glossary/<instance>--<scheme>.po. bun run glossary:page reads every such file (readGlossaryTranslations, through glossary-pot.ts’s potPath) and produces two things: . | a page per locale, docs/<locale>/glossary/index.md, listing every authored term with its translated label, alternative labels and definition. An entry with no translation shows the source text marked (untranslated) — never silently English, never dropped — and the page states how many terms are fully translated; | language-tagged SKOS: the published <instance>--<scheme>.skos.jsonld carries skos:prefLabel and skos:definition once per language (@language), the source as en. | . check:glossary covers both, stale and orphan alike. A translation is UNOFFICIAL until a person signs it off. Every glossary .po says so in its header and records Last-Translator: folio-assistant agent (drafted, unofficial) when an agent drafted it; every locale page carries translation_status: unverified. Keep code, identifiers and standard names (BPMN, SKOS, ODRL, PROV-O, JSON, IRI, $schema, needs) as written, and give each capitalised defined term ONE rendering per locale across every scheme.

aaba1131dbb8.title: Source glossary first
aaba1131dbb8.content: When a folio is written from a source document (a WHO handbook, say), its terms come from that source’s own glossary before anyone writes one. | Latest edition. Use the most recent edition in the library. If it lacks something an older edition has, use the older one and say so on the term. | Verbatim, as candidates. Extract every glossary entry as a folio-glossary/v1 term, status candidate, the definition copied word for word with its page. Keep the source’s spelling as an altLabel when the prefLabel is normalised. | Read the PDF when the ingest missed it. A glossary the library entry does not hold (a missed section, a missing indicator sheet) is read from the PDF, and the scheme says so. | Structure the source gives is kept. Modules, indicators and the like become concepts too, linked (broader, related) to the glossary terms they cite. | Record what the source never defines. A term the source uses but does not define is a candidate with no definition and a scopeNote saying so, not a definition we write. | Place the scheme with the source. It lives beside the document’s library entry (for WHO publications, in the WHO publications IG), so every folio that cites the source shares one scheme. | Use the source’s words downstream. Blocks, diagrams and ArchiMate names use the source’s terms and link to their concepts, not a paraphrase. | . A conflict between the source’s definition and another scheme’s is raised as an issue on the repository that owns the other scheme, quoting both. Neither is chosen by the agent.

5fa6aa439278.title: Deprecating a term: a change set, decided later
5fa6aa439278.content: Replacing one term with another (for example “Core Data Element” replacing “MDS-HRH”) is proposed, not applied. The agent records a change set with the old term, the new term, the reason, and every place the old term appears. It changes no text and no glossary entry. An agent review, started later by an editor, decides it. Once decided: . | the old term stays in the scheme, so old links still resolve, with a scopeNote saying it is deprecated and why, and related to the new term (folio-glossary/v1 has no deprecated status yet; adding one is a schema change, not part of this rule); | the folio’s own prose moves to the new term; | quoted source text is never changed: a quote keeps the term it was published with. | .

607c2b328374.title: A paper’s glossary
607c2b328374.content: The paper builder (folio-assistant-core/scripts/build-glossary.ts, skill glossary-build) also writes the paper’s terms as one folio-glossary/v1 scheme, paper-<paper directory>, into the glossary directory the paper’s OWN instance declares. The page picks it up through collect() like any other scheme, so the IRIs are in that instance’s namespace (a sub-instance’s for a paper in a sub-instance, never the root’s). | the owning block | its :defterm paragraph | status | . | kind: "definition" | found | authored: the author wrote the definition | . | any other kind | found | candidate: extracted from a theorem, remark, … | . | any | not found | could-not-extract, with the reason | . The definition is the :defterm paragraph, verbatim, with directives replaced by their labels. The slug is the term’s notation. Never edit the scheme: edit the paper and re-run the builder. An instance that declares no glossary directory gets a notice and no scheme; add { "id": "glossary", "path": "glossary/", "dependents": "reproduce", "graphTypologies": ["glossary"] }.

870e6b61a99b.title: Organizations and acronyms
870e6b61a99b.content: An organization (WHO, HL7, ISO, GS1, a national regulator) is a glossary term like any other, plus a focus: SKOS’s foaf:focus link from the concept to the organization, which is typed with W3C ORG. The concept keeps the words: prefLabel is the full name, notation is the acronym, and altLabel holds other spellings. The organization keeps the facts about the organization. { "id": "who", "prefLabel": "World Health Organization", "notation": "WHO", "definition": "…quoted from its source…", "status": "candidate", "focus": { "type": "FormalOrganization", "homepage": "https://www.who.int/", "subOrganizationOf": ["un"] } } . | type is a W3C ORG class: Organization, FormalOrganization, OrganizationalUnit or OrganizationalCollaboration. | subOrganizationOf names a local term that has a focus, or an organization’s IRI. sameAs links the same organization in another register, such as ROR or Wikidata. Give an identifier only when you have checked it; never guess one. | Without iri, the organization’s IRI is <term IRI>/_focus. | . One home per organization. An organization that several handbooks use (WHO, HL7, ISO, GS1, UNICEF, USAID) is defined once, in the shared reference architecture’s organizations scheme. A handbook lists it under members and does not copy it. An organization only one handbook names, such as a country’s regulator, stays in that handbook’s glossary. An acronym is scoped to its meaning. Use the document’s own expansion, and check it in context. In the WHO product catalogue handbook, “FDA” is the Rwanda Food and Drugs Authority, not the US Food and Drug Administration. When the document’s acronym would mislead a reader, record it as a candidate and raise it in the document’s review log. Do not fix the quoted text yourself. Finding the acronyms that are missing. The QA criterion acronym-in-glossary warns, block by block, about an acronym that no glossary the folio can see holds as a notation, prefLabel or altLabel. It warns and never fails. For the whole folio, with counts and the expansion the document gives (its abbreviations table, or “Long Name (ACR)”), run: . bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/glossary-acronyms.ts --folio folio . Each row is a candidate for a person to decide on. Words set in capitals (RESOURCES in a figure), plural forms (GTINs) and the folio’s own ids (PC-R-05) are left out.

864d35894b92.title: Architecture elements: the model drawn from the graph
864d35894b92.content: A reference architecture’s elements live in the knowledge graph, and the ArchiMate model is drawn from it, with the relationships on each glossary term. A term that names an element is a glossary term like any other, plus a focus that is the element: its ArchiMate type, and its relationships to other terms’ elements. { "id": "client-registry", "prefLabel": "Client Registry", "definition": "…quoted from the document…", "status": "candidate", "focus": { "archimate": "ApplicationComponent", "relationships": [ { "type": "Realization", "target": "client-identification" }, { "type": "Access", "target": "client-record", "accessType": "read" } ] } } . | archimate is the element type, as ArchiMate’s exchange format names it. | relationships[].type is one of ArchiMate 3.2’s eleven. target is a local term whose focus is an element, or an element’s IRI. accessType is only for Access. | In JSON-LD the element is <term IRI>/_focus, typed archimate:<Type>, and each relationship is a predicate such as archimate:serving. | . The Tool archimate-from-glossary (bun run cat archimate:from-glossary --instance <dir> --model <id> [--write] [--prune] [--check]) makes the model agree. It matches each element by its skosConcept property, never by name. It names and documents the element from the term, creates any element the model lacks (on no view: place it in Archi, or with archimate-detangle), and adds the relationships the terms list. A type that disagrees is reported, and a person decides. A relationship between linked elements that no term lists is removed only with --prune. Archi keeps the layout: no box moves. Its report counts the elements that still point at no term. An authored ArchiMate model is never a source of the glossary. Never write a term, label, definition, focus or relationship into a glossary from a model someone authored in Archi. The words come from the source documents; the model only depicts them. The one exception is a model that was ingested: received from elsewhere and held as a source under the instance’s library/. Such a model can seed the glossary once with --seed --from library/<entry>/<file>.archimate (--write to write). Every term an element of it already points at, and that has no focus yet, takes the element’s type and its relationships to the other linked elements. From then on, the glossary is the source. The Tool refuses --seed on any model outside library/. The read-only “depicted by” links on a term’s page (glossary-archimate) read the model’s skosConcept on each build and write nothing into the glossary, so they are allowed.

506e0a562c36.title: Not here
506e0a562c36.content: A clinical code system is FHIR CodeSystem/ValueSet, not a glossary: convergence stops at SKOS. A glossary term may exactMatch a clinical concept; it does not become one.

47671a618c48.title: Processes that run this skill
47671a618c48.content: | process | step(s) that name it | . | Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph | Read glossary and abbreviations into candidate terms | . | Classify and code content | Run reuse-first lookup and record candidates; Adjudicate slot codings and glossary candidates | .

50e30e0891b2.title: Glossary terms
50e30e0891b2.content: Generated from folio-assistant-core/skills/library/cataloguing/glossary-terms.md — do not edit here. ✎ Edit this page’s source .

f0566f6a38ab.title: Goal review — cold start, sweep a window, prioritise against stated goals
f0566f6a38ab.content: This is a review, not a plan. It reads everything and writes only work items for the gaps it finds. Picking up the queue it produces is pickup; declaring intent is session-intent; this skill sits before both and feeds them.

250d36eaea94.title: Inputs — four, all stated before the first read
250d36eaea94.content: | input | what it is | default if the owner gives none | . | window | the time period to sweep, as a duration or two instants | the last 4 hours | . | goals | the outcomes to prioritise against, in the owner’s words | the store’s goal milestones, offered in the closing question (§”No goals given”); only if there are none, ask, or review without a queue and say so | . | scope | which repositories and stores are in the sweep | the checkout you are in and its forge repository | . | axes | which kinds of activity to read | all six below | . Keep the owner’s wording for a goal verbatim through the whole report. A goal paraphrased by the agent is a different goal, and the reader cannot tell which one the queue was built for. No goals given — but the store may already hold them. With no goals given, list the open milestones (beans list -t milestone), each title verbatim, and offer them as the queue basis in the closing question. Say which milestones quote the owner (their body carries the owner’s own words) and which are a milestone’s wording only — a title is the owner’s words only where it says so, and presenting one as such is the paraphrase this section forbids, one level up.

1579c8da8e51.title: Cold start — before any durable read
1579c8da8e51.content: Run the instance’s cold-start line (the top of AGENTS.md), so the work-plan Tool is in hand and primed. | The line can be wrong. If it fails, the fallback Tool for the work plan still exists — find it through the tools graph, do not stop — and the failure is the first instruction gap to record. | Fetch every branch, not just the default. Most of a window’s activity is on sibling branches that have not merged. | . Then fix the window’s two edges as commits on the default branch: the last commit before the window opened and the head now. Every “before → after” measurement below is a diff between those two.

c1f34992548f.title: The six axes, and what each one can and cannot tell you
c1f34992548f.content: 1. Sibling sessions. ASK THE SESSION API FIRST. List the sessions; where it answers, it gives what no inference can — each session’s session_status, and a task_summary that carries a held question in plain text. Fall back to commit trailers when it does not answer, and report “could not determine” when neither does. Never present the fallback as the method. Reading the listing. It is ordered by creation, not activity, so in-window sessions are interleaved with ones last active weeks earlier. Page until a whole page was created before the window opened, then stop — a session cannot be updated before it exists, so no later page can hold an in-window row. A reader who does not know the order either stops at page 1 or pages forever. The listing is large (~75 KB per 40 sessions): parse it, do not read it, and note the JSON sits inside an untrusted wrapper line. Read status_bucket / session_status and task_summary; a summary on a session that requires action is a held question — quote it, it is the sweep’s most valuable line. The trailer route, for when it is needed: the durable identity of a session is the trailer it leaves on its commits. Sweep the window’s commits across all branches for those trailers, group by session, and record for each: commit count, first and last commit, and the branches whose tip it wrote. A session’s state is then read from its branch: an open proposal that is green, red, conflicted, or one that merged. Say plainly that this is inferred. 2. Branches. Refs with commits in the window, each with its count ahead of the default branch and its tip session. A branch that is ahead by zero has merged; one ahead by sixty-five is a workstream the default branch cannot see (axis 4 says why that matters). 3. Change proposals (pull requests). Two lists: closed in the window, with merged distinguished from abandoned; and open, sorted by last update. For each open one, read the merge state, the CI outcome on the current head, the last comment, the reviews, and whether the body or last comment carries a question to the owner — quote the question. “Green” means every check on the head passed; a head with no checks is not green. 4. The work plan. Diff the store between the window’s two edges: items added, and every status transition (todo → completed, in-progress → completed, todo → in-progress, anything → scrapped). Then two measurements the store’s own status field cannot give you: . | Claims without activity — items in-progress with no change in the window. in-progress records a claim; it does not record that anyone is working (bean-coordination §”A quiet claim”). | Items that exist only on a branch. The store is committed per branch, so a long-running proposal can carry an entire epic the default branch has never seen. Sweep the open branches’ stores too, or the review is blind to the largest workstream. Compare against origin/main, never a bare main — the local ref is whatever this container last checked out, and nothing moves it. A session fetches origin/main and fast-forwards its own branch; the local main just sits there, often thousands of commits stale, and a count against it can be wrong by two orders of magnitude in the direction that manufactures a crisis. And if you cannot confirm the baseline is fresh, report could not determine rather than a count. An unverifiable baseline is not a measurement — §Rules, rule 1, applied to the ref. Confirming it is cheap: . # Resolve the default branch, then FALL BACK — `origin/HEAD` is unset in some # clones, and without the fallback this exits 128. # `session-start-coord-sweep.sh` does the same. DB="$(git symbolic-ref --short refs/remotes/origin/HEAD 2>/dev/null | sed 's@^origin/@@')" [ -n "$DB" ] || DB=main git fetch origin "+refs/heads/$DB:refs/remotes/origin/$DB" git rev-list --count "refs/heads/$DB..origin/$DB" # 0 = the local ref is usable . An explicit refspec, not a bare git fetch origin $DB: the bare form updates refs/remotes/origin/$DB only when remote.origin.fetch happens to cover it, and exits 0 when it does not. Then compare by work item ID, never by file diff against a merge base. Even with a fresh origin/main, git diff --diff-filter=A origin/main...origin/<branch> -- beans/defs diffs against the merge base, which predates everything main gained since — so the count of “added” work items inflates with how far behind the branch is. The check, ids on the branch minus ids anywhere on main (archive included): . ids() { git ls-tree -r --name-only "$1" beans/defs | sed -n 's#.*/folio-assistant-\([a-z0-9]\{4\}\)--.*#\1#p' | sort -u; } comm -23 <(ids origin/<branch>) <(ids origin/main) # beans on the branch and nowhere on main . A large file-diff count from a far-behind branch is the stale-base signature, not a hidden epic — measure by id before reporting either. | . 5. Issues. Updated in the window, and the full open set for classification. Measure it; do not expect a size. 6. CI on the default branch. Runs in the window by workflow and outcome. A red default branch reclassifies every “stalled” proposal, so read this before judging any of them. Compare the tool’s span with the window. check:ci-health reads the last 100 runs and says what span they cover (“100 recent run(s) spanning 13.4h”), which can be shorter than the window. The uncovered part is could not determine (rule 1), reported as such with its extent. To cover it, page the forge’s workflow-run listing for the default branch by created back to the window’s start (the actions_list tool, or GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runs?branch=<default>&created=>=<start>); check:ci-health takes no --since. Where a check fails, sidecars and generated files are the first suspect — for instance a QA sidecar not regenerated after its skill was edited.

d016f0de1616.title: Classify against the goals — judgement, marked as judgement
d016f0de1616.content: For each goal, in this order: . | Assign the items from every axis that advance it. Assignment is a judgement; say so once, and quote the item’s own title so the reader can disagree. An item can serve two goals; a goal can have none. | Critical path — the items in dependency order, from what the goal waits on first. Read dependencies from item bodies, not from the blocked_by field alone: dependencies are often only prose. | Blocked on the owner — items whose next step is a decision. Quote the question verbatim from the item; a paraphrase is a second question. | Done in all but name — items whose body says everything is finished but whose status is not completed. Report them; never resolve a sibling’s item (bean-coordination). Where the body says “not resolving unilaterally, awaiting the owner”, that is the owner’s line to close, and it is the same rule seen from the other side. | Effort — S (under an hour of agent work), M (a session), L (several sessions or an epic), with “blocked” as a separate mark, because a blocked S is not small. | Contradictions — two items or rulings that cannot both be followed. Name both and stop there; the owner reconciles them. | . Goals that are not in the store are a gap. If the owner’s goals exist nowhere as objects — no milestone, no epic carrying the goal’s words — every future review re-does this classification from scratch. Record that as a work item and offer the fix as an option; do not create the objects unasked.

78d9575393d1.title: Output — three parts, in this order
78d9575393d1.content: 1. Synopsis of the window. Counts first, each with how it was measured: proposals merged and abandoned, still open by state (green, red, conflicted, stale); work-plan transitions by kind; items added; claims without activity; issues touched; CI outcome on the default branch; sessions seen and how. A count in prose without its measurement is a claim (turn-reporting); a table is the right shape. 2. A priority queue per goal, ordered by the critical path. One line per item: id, what it is in six words, effort, what it waits on. Split into do now (nothing waits on the owner), owner decides (with the question), and close or scrap (done in all but name, superseded, expired notices). 3. The instruction gaps, each as a work item. A gap is anything the instructions said that the sweep could not do as written, said two ways, or did not say at all. Create the item with the measurement in its body and the rule it concerns named; parent it to the process epic. Do not create one per stale item — that is a queue entry, not a gap. Then one question, selectable. The queue will surface several owner decisions. Ask one in full — context, options, recommendation first and marked, a stated default — and give a count of the rest (interaction-modality §4.1). A reader on a low-dexterity profile (interaction/) answers by choosing a number.

10893a5a7423.title: Rules
10893a5a7423.content: . | Could not determine is never rendered as clean. Sessions the API cannot see, a store on a branch you did not fetch, a check that did not run — each is reported as unknown, and unknown outranks “nothing found”. | Measure at the window’s edges, not from prose. A body that says “nothing remains” is evidence; the status field is a claim; a count you remember from an earlier turn is neither. But a COMMITTED CHECK’S OUTPUT is not prose, and re-deriving it is strictly worse than quoting it. A check’s finding was produced by code with a test behind it; your inline version of the same question has neither. So quote the finding and name the check that produced it — bun run cat health, check:anchor-names, whatever it was — and re-derive only what no committed check answers. A re-derivation that finds MORE items than the instrument hands the owner a larger permission than any instrument justified, and deletion-requires-confirmation assumes the list put to a person is true. Where the rule exists as code (stagingSlug in schemas/sdlc/staging.ts, for a staging slug), import it. Not the same as “read the published survey” below. That is about a SIBLING’S sweep and the reason is duplicated effort. This is about an instrument’s computed finding and the reason is correctness — a wrong number reaching a person who acts on it. | Read the owner’s rulings out of the items and carry them forward. An item can be blocked only in name — the ruling already in a sibling’s body. Quote it and move the item to do now. | A window boundary is an artefact. A bulk edit just before the window makes everything look untouched; a bulk edit inside it makes everything look active. Say when a count is dominated by one commit. | Generated files inflate every count. Diff stats, files changed and commits touched all double where sidecars, exports or rendered diagrams regenerate; count the authored change and say the rest is generated. | The report is not durable; the gaps are. The synopsis lives in the turn and, if it must outlive the session, on the issue that asked for it. The work items are what the next agent inherits. | Do not pivot into the queue. The owner asked what to do next, not for it to be done; the first queue item is the next question, and picking it up is a separate, declared intent. | .

bea4733a565c.title: What falsifies a review
bea4733a565c.content: . | A proposal the review called green that a reviewer finds red on the same head: the CI read was of the wrong commit. | An item the review placed on a goal’s critical path that the owner says serves a different goal: the assignment was a paraphrase. | A “stalled” session that was in fact mid-turn: the inference from its branch was stated as fact. Re-read axis 1; the word is inferred. | .

acbe95c6b28a.title: Read the published survey before deriving one
acbe95c6b28a.content: bun run cat survey:owed first, so that parallel sessions do not each re-derive the same sweep. The command answers in four states, and each says what you owe: . | it says | you do | . | none published | the whole window is yours. A determined empty, not an error. | . | covered | read the survey; do not re-derive it. | . | a delta | survey only to..origin/main — normally a handful of commits. | . | unusable | a published survey’s upper edge is unreachable here (rewritten history, another branch). Survey the whole window. | . When you finish a sweep, publish it: . bun run cat survey:publish --from <sha> --by <session> --axis beans="…" --axis ci="!not looked at, and why" . An axis written name=!reason records one you did not cover. That is a first-class answer: a survey of four of six axes is useful, and a reader must be able to tell which two it says nothing about; recording only what you did lets a partial survey read as a complete one. The window’s two edge commits are recorded, so staleness is decidable rather than guessed. An unreachable upper edge is reported as unusable and never as covered, because siblings trust a covered survey instead of looking. This does not claim the window and does not divide the axes between sessions. It is an artefact: one session writes what it found, and a later one decides for itself whether that still covers its question.

e5f08783b1f8.title: Tools this skill reaches for
e5f08783b1f8.content: Reached through the tools graph the instance declares, never by a remembered path: the work-plan CLI and its manual fallback; the forge API for proposals, issues and CI runs; version-control history for trailers, branch tips and the window’s edges; and the session API where it can see siblings. Where one is absent, the axis it serves is reported as could not determine.

e17dd3ba9f35.title: grade
e17dd3ba9f35.content: Skill id: grade · Package: authoring-who-smart-guidelines · The grading SYSTEM that evidence-appraisal applies when a folio declares GRADE. Origin: the GRADE Working Group (gradeworkinggroup.org); Evidence-to-Decision frameworks per Alonso-Coello et al., BMJ 2016; WHO applies it through the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. evidence-appraisal is the procedure and names no system; the folio declares one. GRADE applies to certainty of evidence for a health recommendation, over the body of evidence answering one PICO question — not to platform or architecture decisions, which are kepner-tregoe, recorded per madr. Every value below is a code. Each vocabulary is a folio-code-list/v1 in this instance’s code-lists/, with a definition and source per code, published as SKOS beside the glossary. Record a code, never a paraphrase: . | list | codes | . | grade-certainty | high · moderate · low · very-low | . | grade-rating-down | risk-of-bias · inconsistency · indirectness · imprecision · publication-bias | . | grade-rating-up | large-effect · dose-response · plausible-confounding | . | grade-etd-criterion | the twelve Evidence-to-Decision criteria | . | grade-recommendation-direction | for · against | . | grade-recommendation-strength | strong · conditional | .

e01b76fb954f.title: It has a slot waiting
e01b76fb954f.content: folio-assistant-core’s processes/content/evidence-retrieval.bpmn frames the question as PICO, retrieves candidates across three classes, and runs Task_AppraiseGrade — “Certainty of evidence per the grading system the folio declares.” GRADE fills that slot when declared; the diagram does not name it.

3e81cf927967.title: Certainty, in four levels
3e81cf927967.content: High · Moderate · Low · Very low — the certainty that the true effect lies close to the estimate. Randomised trials start High and observational evidence starts Low; then: . | rated down for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, publication bias; | rated up for a large effect, a dose-response gradient, or where plausible confounding would have reduced an observed effect. | . The grade attaches to the body of evidence per outcome, never to a citation. A single paper does not have a GRADE; the BPMN task sits after the join, not inside the fan-out. Record every rating-down and rating-up with the code that moved it — a certainty with no reasons cannot be re-examined.

453f4c4c7328.title: Evidence-to-Decision: certainty is one criterion of several
453f4c4c7328.content: A recommendation does not follow from certainty alone. The EtD framework for clinical and public-health recommendations judges each criterion explicitly: problem priority · desirable effects · undesirable effects · certainty of evidence · values · balance of effects · resources required · certainty of the evidence of required resources · cost-effectiveness · equity · acceptability · feasibility (twelve, per Alonso-Coello et al. 2016). Then a recommendation carries a direction (for / against) and a strength (strong / conditional). Strength is not certainty. A strong recommendation can rest on low-certainty evidence when the balance of effects is decisive, and a conditional one can rest on high certainty when values differ across populations; hence two code lists, not one score.

80100354e8a7.title: What this platform must not do with it
80100354e8a7.content: . | No numeric aggregation of EtD criteria. The framework judges each criterion and argues the recommendation; it does not sum them. | could not determine is not very-low. Absent evidence and low-certainty evidence are different findings with different actions. evidence-retrieval ends such a case at EndEvent_GapRecorded (“Gap recorded, no recommendation”); evidence-appraisal names it a third state. | No empirical claim enters a formal proof. A graded body of evidence supports a recommendation, never a theorem. In a paper folio the two live in different block kinds and must not be joined. | .

c4fda7a22c4e.title: Refusals
c4fda7a22c4e.content: . | Never grade a single citation. The body, per outcome. | Never report a recommendation without its direction and strength. One without the other is not a GRADE recommendation. | Never table it in DMN. See dmn — tabling asserts a repeatability the method denies. | .

94f9d4119d5f.title: Graph detanglement — the practice, not the migration
94f9d4119d5f.content: Skill id: graph-detanglement · Package: graph-management . A repository grows until part of it wants to leave. Sometimes the reason is size, sometimes it is semantic — “split only where consumers or cadences differ” (docs/concepts/architecture/migration-plan.md). Either way the move is the same and the mistake is the same: treating the split as a migration to be executed rather than a practice to be run. This skill is the practice. Its subject is any graph with directed edges whose nodes are being partitioned: TypeScript modules into repositories, blocks into chapters, skills into packages.

55fd6c0d5404.title: The one rule, at four scales
55fd6c0d5404.content: At block scale — pipeline/qa-criteria-registry.ts, the detangler-no-dependency-cycle criterion: . “a cycle is reorder-invariant — when two blocks each uses: the other, or a longer loop closes, NO chapter ordering removes the forward edge. A cycle signals a genuine structural tangle: prune one dependency edge, merge the mutually-defining blocks, or factor the shared content into a third block both depend on.” . At repository scale — scripts/repo-partition.ts, the gate’s own failure message: . “A repo may not import one that depends on it. Either the CLASSIFICATION is wrong — check the target’s layer before the importer’s — or the import is.” . At knowledge-graph scale — kg-detangle.ts (bun run cat kg:detangle), over the instance stack each <instance>.json declares in needs. The repository and knowledge-graph scales share ONE verdict function, schemas/kg/layer-direction.ts. An edge is wrong-direction exactly when its target layer is not among what the source layer declares it may reach — ALLOWED for repos, needs plus itself for instances — and no reasoned permit names it. An instance with no needs is undetermined, reported in its own column, never read as clean. The function stops at direction: whether an allowed edge is a restatement or essential is the adjudicator’s call, so those edges stay unclassified with the verdict as their basis. The direction count is the one detangle number that is GRADED, and it is graded in a gate of its own — bun run cat kg:detangle:direction, blocking in CI. Everything else this tool measures stays pinned: kg:detangle:check fails on a stale or orphaned sidecar and never on a number, because the carve is an adjudication a person makes and grading it would be the tool overruling the adjudicator. A module’s bucket is taste. An edge whose target layer is not among what the source layer’s <instance>.json says it may reach is a contradiction between two declarations, which no adjudication makes consistent, so it is the one thing here a machine may refuse. Two flags, two scripts, two CI steps, so a red run says which question broke. Two things that gate reports and refuses to grade, both because grading them would be grading a could-not-determine: . | undetermined edges — an endpoint’s instance declares no needs. Failing on these would be the gate deciding a layering nobody declared. | the denominator — the count is over the edges that resolve. Dangling refs are excluded before any edge is classified, so a 0 is “0 among the edges that resolve”. The gate prints the excluded count and its breakdown, so a pass cannot hide an edge that failed to resolve. | . It is not check:partition’s second opinion. That tool’s root is one instance, so it partitions a future layout by path rule among that instance’s own modules; this checks the present layout against declared needs across instances. Either can be green while the other is red, and Phase I.1 of the migration plan needs both. At term scale — a glossary declared ordered (logically tight, non self-referential). Each term’s requires must point UP, and checkDeclaredOrder in schemas/kg/dependency-order.ts names every forward, self and missing use. It is the block-scale rule with terms for blocks: a forward requires is a forward edge, and two terms defined by each other are a cycle no ordering removes, so the moves are the same three — drop the use, merge the two terms, or factor the shared idea into a term above both. The rule and its form on the page are in glossary-terms §”Ordered glossaries”. Same rule, four scales, two vocabularies. Prune, merge, or factor into a third are the only three moves, and “the classification is wrong” is the fourth possibility the block- and term-scale versions do not have because a block’s chapter is not in doubt the way a module’s layer is. Everything below is machinery for finding out which of the four you are looking at.

3182f5145d3e.title: The four stages, and each is a gate
3182f5145d3e.content: Nothing moves until the stage before it measures zero. The stages are not advice about sequencing; each is a state the graph is in. 1. Declare in place . The sub-graph is declared where it already sits. Still inside the repository, still connected, nothing moved. The declaration gains a directory entry with its graphs[] kinds; a sub-graph that owns its own layout gains a nested declaration (beans/beans.json, todos/todos.json) whose paths resolve against its own directory, so the whole graph relocates by moving one folder. Declaring is cheap and extracting is expensive. The methodology graph typology is defined by exactly this property: “extractable (somebody else’s work, adopted, so it lifts out with its declaration when the field moves on)”. 2. Detangle . Drive cross-edges toward zero. This is the long stage and the rest of this skill is about it. 3. Isolate . The sub-graph carries its own declaration, its own namespace, its own published artefact. bootstrap/ is the demonstrated case: its own declaration, its own bootstrap: namespace — the prefix IS the stub, see kg-export §”A prefix is the stub” — its own graph document. 4. Extract . Only once edges are zero and the declaration stands alone. A directory move rather than a file-by-file sift. The five-point gate is in docs/concepts/architecture/migration-plan.md Phase II and is not restated here. For a Knowledge Graph leaving as its own repositories — a content repository and a tools repository — the rest of the method, from splitting the tools out to the cutover, is kg-separation and its process kg-separation.bpmn.

50f42dcceaa0.title: The seventeen moves
50f42dcceaa0.content: Measurement . 1. Read the unassigned column before the edge count. A low edge count over an unclassified corpus is the same false comfort as a green check over an empty one: “these are not cross-edges — they are edges this tool declined to judge. Do not read them as clean.” The same false comfort at a different join is covered-is-not-reachable: a skill showing as covered is not evidence that its code is reachable. Read that skill before concluding a corpus is covered. 2. The count rises when the measurement improves, and that is correct. Folding previously-unjudged edges in raises the wrong-direction count. A detangling count that only ever falls is not being measured honestly. 3. Quote both numbers, not only the one that improved. An edge can move rather than vanish. 4. An assignment is verified by re-running, never by being locally reasonable. The obvious move, even the one the tool’s own message asks for, can raise the count. Ordering . 5. Move the shared target first, then the importers. Classifying leaves before their shared schema targets adds edges; moving the targets first does not. 6. A schema moves with its script, or you mint the edge you meant to retire. 7. Declaration and readers first, files second. Update the declaration and every consumer while the files are still where they are, verify green, and only then git mv. The reverse order makes every gate red at once with no way to tell which failure is which. 8. Some fixes are two steps and only work in one order. Reclassifying handlers alone can make the composition root cross the line to mount them; a step that is edge-neutral by itself (resolving routes by variable specifier) can be what makes the reclassification a net win. Judgement . 9. Read what a module is FOR, never what directory it sits in. Layer is not by directory, and a name says what something is for while an argument list says what it does. 10. The triage question, in either of two equivalent forms. “Does it act on the PLATFORM or on CONTENT?” and “does it need a folio to have anything to do?” A sharper cut: needed to RUN a process is tooling; DESCRIBES one is core. And for the renderable side: if it renders, it is not the harness’s. 11. Check the TARGET’s layer before the importer’s. The gate’s failure text says so. 12. A keyword classifier gives false signals on filenames, and will keep reclaiming. fsh in fsh-guts.ts matches the FHIR-Shorthand keyword; content in content-type.ts sends marker machinery to core. Every keyword assignment is provisional against a read of the module, and removing a misclassification needs an exact entry rather than deleting the old one, because a rule that classifies by name will keep reclaiming it. 13. Inverting a dependency does not remove the edge if the new holder sits in the same layer. 14. The fix is not an exemption, it is the right owner. An exemption is what you write when ownership is genuinely ambiguous, and then it carries its reason inline. Enforcement . 15. A check is an error only once its count is zero, and enforce per axis. Turning a red gate on teaches the next agent to append || true (see the ruff comment in code-quality-gates.yml). 16. Watch the new gate FAIL before trusting it. Re-introduce the defect deliberately and see exit 1. A gate that cannot fail is indistinguishable from one that passed. 17. Merge main before trusting a local green; CI builds the merge ref. A gate that passes locally and fails in CI can be a newer, stricter gate on the merge commit, not flakiness.

a2f2fe71f872.title: Declare a falsifier, and mean it
a2f2fe71f872.content: State in advance the result that would show the classification wrong (for example, “if classifying these RAISES the cross-edge count, the classification is wrong rather than the tool”). When it fires, read the new edges rather than arguing them away, and change the plan. A falsifier that never fires is decoration.

dfd59700ac58.title: Measurements that are not measurements
dfd59700ac58.content: . | A measurement you know to be inconclusive is not a measurement. If an earlier rule (an exact list consulted first) means your change never applied, say the experiment was inconclusive. | An edge that several passes called intractable is an edge nobody read. Open the file before deferring it. | A grep that under-reports reads exactly like a clean result. A pattern like from "\.\./*skills/ cannot match ../../skills/, and an export {} block can hide consumers that tsc finds. | Enumerate dispatch points before proposing a mechanism. It is how you find the ones already built, and as an audit it survives a bad hit rate where a choice between guesses does not. | .

a20512b9639d.title: What the metric will not tell you
a20512b9639d.content: From the editorial side, measured on a real corpus: . “an unconstrained search cleared 66 of 236 forward references — and a narrative review of its 53 moves found 18 of them made the paper worse. Reducing the metric and improving the reading are different objectives, and they diverge often enough that the difference is not a rounding error.” . “Expect the reviewed yield to be roughly a third of what the raw metric promises, and prefer it.” . So: a guard is not an objective. Pinned nodes, atomic families and container boundaries constrain the search, and split and merge are never auto-dischargeable — they rename things and ripple through every reference.

5cffee9862af.title: Related
5cffee9862af.content: . | graph-rendering — drawing the graph being partitioned, with each group’s detangle numbers beside it. The UML overview pages show them per sub-graph. | placement.md — the sibling SOP, for where a NEW node goes. 2efe8a923b76.title: Processes that run this skill
