e1f153265acf.title: Asking the person — the canonical rule (STRICT, read this first)
e1f153265acf.content: This box is the ONE rule for putting any question or decision to the person. Every other copy (AGENTS.md, the .claude/skills/interaction-modality stub, the ask-well.sh hook, project instructions) points here. If a copy disagrees, this box wins. Every question goes out TWICE, in this order: . | A chat message that states the whole question on its own. What is being decided and why, every PR / work item / link it touches (each id glossed), what happens next, and every option with its letter, a one-line explanation, its trade-off, and which one you recommend. Say what you will do if no answer comes. | Then the tappable card with the same option letters and labels, so the answer is one tap. | . Every question tool counts, whatever the host calls it: AskUserQuestion (Claude Code), request_decision / the “Decision” card (Claude projects), a button card from post_widget, or any selection box a later host adds. Why both, and why the chat copy comes first. Once answered, a card shows only the option that was chosen, and a dismissed card shows nothing. The chat text is the only record of what was asked. This overrides host guidance that says the opposite. The Claude projects request_decision tool tells the agent “Ask once, and do not repeat the question in a message.” Write the full question in the chat anyway, then post the card. Never: . | a card with no full question and options written before it; | a request for a typed reply (“answer 1y 2n”, “reply A or B”): the owner has very limited hand function, and typing is the cost this rule removes; | a pointer instead of the question (“see the card”, “see the issue”). | . If no card tool exists in this host, post the numbered options in chat, say the card tool is unavailable, and keep each answer to a single short choice. In the processes, this box is the skill ask-the-person (input and output schemas) and the subprocess Process_AskThePerson: compose, write in the chat, offer the card, then record the answer or proceed on the default. A diagram step that puts a question to the person is a callActivity with calledElement="Process_AskThePerson", so the association is visible in the diagram rather than remembered. The rest of this skill is the reasoning and the detail: §4.1 for what the context must contain, §4.2 for the form.

73c0b0be8fef.title: 0. The failure this prevents
73c0b0be8fef.content: An agent that asks a good question in an unusable form has asked nothing. The usual shape of it: a long open prompt — “Tell me about the folio you have in mind, what content types you expect, and how you’d like it organised” — sent to somebody for whom typing is slow and painful. The reply comes back short, the agent reads shortness as low engagement, and asks another open question. @litlfred, this repository’s owner, has very limited hand function. Every question put to that user is to be answerable by selecting, not by typing: numbered or lettered options, a recommended default stated first, and the work proceeding on that default when no answer comes. Free text is always available and never required. Generalise the rule rather than special-casing the person: . A question’s cost is paid by the person answering it. Design the question so the cheapest possible answer is still a complete one.

47317d9c09e9.title: 1. The modality profiles
47317d9c09e9.content: Four axes, independent — a user can be on more than one. | profile | what changes | detection signal | . | low-dexterity | Every question is a selection. Options numbered. One recommended default, first, marked. Never more than ~4 options. Batch decisions so one answer covers several. Long-running work is announced, not confirmed. | user says so; very short replies to open questions; typos of a kind that cost effort to fix; voice input artefacts | . | low-vision | Large type in anything rendered. No information carried by colour alone. Short lines. Tables kept narrow or replaced by lists. ASCII diagrams avoided — they do not survive a screen reader or a 200 % zoom. | user says so; requests to enlarge; screen-reader artefacts | . | audio | Answers read aloud cleanly: no code fences in prose, no tables, no “see the diagram”, spell out identifiers on first use, one idea per sentence. Questions asked one at a time. | the channel is voice; the user is dictating | . | plain-language | Shorter sentences, domain jargon expanded on first use, no nested clauses. Independent of disability — it is also the right default for a second-language reader. | user asks for simpler wording; the folio’s audience | . The default profile — nobody has said anything — is ordinary chat with selectable options wherever there is a genuine choice.

146e339a7370.title: 2. Detecting it without an interrogation
146e339a7370.content: The detection must not itself be an unusable question. So: . | Read cat-harness/memory/interaction.json first. If it says, you are done. Never re-ask what is recorded. | Read the channel. A voice session is audio without asking. A terminal session is not. | Offer once, as options. At first contact and not again: . How would you like me to ask you things? . | Options I can pick from (recommended — fewest keystrokes) | Ordinary chat | Read aloud / voice | Large type | . (No answer is fine — I’ll use 1.) . | Watch for the signal you were not given. Consistently one-word answers to open questions, or an explicit “hard to type”, moves the user to low-dexterity and is recorded, so no future session re-learns it. | . Never ask a user to name a disability. Ask what form they want the conversation to take. The profile is about the interface, not about them.

2437ccad276c.title: 3. Where the preference lives
2437ccad276c.content: cat-harness/memory/interaction.json, committed, so every sibling session reads it rather than asking again. { "$schema": "https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/schemas/interaction.json", "users": { "litlfred@ibiblio.org": { "profiles": ["low-dexterity"], "note": "Very limited hand function. Every question selectable; never require typing.", "source": "stated by the user" } }, "default": { "profiles": [] } } . source is required and is one of stated by the user, inferred from behaviour, or set in the site settings. An inferred profile is honoured and is labelled as inferred, so it can be corrected. 3.1 Who is typing, outside GitHub too . An entry is keyed by a handle, and the session has to work out whose handle it is before the entry can apply. Identity is (provider, handle), GitHub first. One resolver answers for every host: bun run cat auth:login --all (cat-harness-tools/src/core/identity.ts). It prints every identity the session can see, each bare and as provider:handle: . | provider | read from | vouched for by | . | github | the auth Tool’s own resolver: a token, or GITHUB_ACTOR in Actions | GitHub | . | gitlab | GITLAB_USER_LOGIN, only inside GitLab CI | GitLab | . | claude | the agent host’s signed-in account | the agent host | . | any | CAT_HARNESS_PERSON, provider:handle[,…], for this session only | nobody: the person says so | . | any | the user-level store’s identities, and the chosen entry of its profiles | nobody: the person says so | . | git | git config user.email, then user.name | nobody: self-asserted | . So an entry may list gitlab:<handle> or claude:<email> among its aliases, and a person with no GitHub token is still recognised. A self-asserted identity is enough to choose how to TALK to someone, never enough to AUTHORIZE them. Permissions take only what GitHub vouched for (task-authorization §”Asking who you are”). When nothing matches, that is a third state. It is neither “no preference” nor a guess. The session-start sweep says it could not determine who is typing, and applies the strictest profile on record until told otherwise, so an account switch never drops an accommodation. Which agent host runs the session is reported too (cat-harness-tools/src/core/agent-host.ts), because most hosts tell a command nothing about the person. Of Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Codex, Cursor, Antigravity and the Copilot CLI and coding agent, only Claude Code passes the account (CLAUDE_CODE_USER_EMAIL, in its cloud sessions). On the others the resolver adds a note saying the host passes no account, and the person is found from a forge token, CAT_HARNESS_PERSON, the user-level store or the git author. The markers are the ones two independent detectors agree on; a new host is one row in that file’s table. Several people. On a shared machine each person has their own home directory, so their own user-level store. In a shared session or under a shared login, CAT_HARNESS_PERSON names who is typing now. A person with several accounts on one provider lists each one in the store, as entries or as identities: { "github": ["litlfred", "litlfred-bot"] }; every one is a match key, and an entry marked active: true comes first. When the keys match more than one person on record, the sweep says so and the session applies the strictest of their profiles, never the first one listed. Several people in one store. identity.json may hold named profiles, profiles: { "<name>": { identities, interaction } }. The one in use is the profile CAT_HARNESS_PROFILE names, else the store’s activeProfile, else the one whose identities match CAT_HARNESS_PERSON, else the only one. With several profiles and nothing to choose between them, the resolver reports a third state, ambiguous-multi-user, and applies the strictest interaction profile on record until someone says who is typing. The same state is reported when the session matches several people in interaction.json whose profiles differ. A preference that must not be committed lives in the user-level store, ~/.config/cat-harness/identity.json (or $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/…, or the path in CAT_HARNESS_USER_CONFIG), under interaction. It is per machine and never in the repository. The sweep prints it, marked as not committed.

4b7af6ad022a.title: 4. Asking a question well
4b7af6ad022a.content: §4.1 is what the question has to contain; §4.2 is what shape it has to take. A question can pass every item in §4.2 and still be unanswerable, because none of those say what the options mean. 4.1 Context before the question (STRICT) . Order matters, and it is: context → options → recommendation → question. Never the question first with the explanation available on request. The test is one sentence, and it is checkable in a single pass: . Can the reader answer without opening anything? . If answering needs them to open an issue, a file, a diff or a scrollback, the question is not ready. A link is where somebody goes for more; it is never where the terms are defined. And when a link IS the right thing — a rendered page the reader has to see for themselves — it points at the page, not at the site it is on. The rule and where the page list comes from: staging-review §”The deep-link rule”; the failure it also hides: continual-progress §”Link the PAGE, never the site root”. Six parts, in order: . | What is being decided, in plain words — stated as what will differ depending on the answer, not as the name of the decision. | Every identifier expanded on first use. A work item id, an option name you coined, a field, a Lean declaration, a file path: all opaque without their gloss, above all an option name you coined yourself, because it feels defined to you. | The options, compared — what each does, its pro, its con, what it changes downstream, and how reversible it is. Laid out here, in the prose, where the rows can be read against each other; a selection tool shows one option at a time, so trade-offs written into its labels are not a comparison. decision-comparison carries the columns, why cost and downstream impact are different things, and when a decision is too small to deserve a table. | Your recommendation, and why, stated first and marked. See §4.2. | What happens if they say nothing. Then do that. | The question itself, last. | . This binds every place a decision is handed to the person, not only an explicit question tool: the end-of-turn “next” line, a work item’s ## Done when, a PR body asking the author to choose, a comment on an issue. Those are where it is most often broken, because they feel like reporting rather than asking. A PR body as a whole, not only its question, is governed by pr-description. The prose does not travel — the question object must stand alone (STRICT) . The six parts above assume the reader is in the conversation, reading the prose that precedes the question. Often they are not. A question asked by a background session, a cloud session, a subagent or a scheduled run reaches the person through a channel that carries only the structured fields — the question text, the option labels, the option descriptions. Everything written around the call stays in a transcript the person would have to go and open. The asker’s analysis stays in its own transcript, and a relay has to reconstruct it. So the test grows one clause: . Can the reader answer without opening anything — including the session that asked? . Put in the structured fields everything needed to choose: . | field | carries | . | the question | what will differ depending on the answer, with every identifier expanded. Never a bare noun phrase — “kupb scope” is a topic, not a question. | . | each option’s description | that option’s own consequence and how reversible it is. A reader comparing two options must be able to do it from the two descriptions alone. | . | one option’s description | what happens if they say nothing, marked as the default and phrased as what you will then do. | . The comparison table still belongs in the prose, where rows can be read against each other, but nothing may be load-bearing only in the prose. Two things this rules out: . | A question whose context sits in the paragraph above the call. Correct in a live conversation, invisible through a relay. | An option label carrying the trade-off and a description carrying nothing — or the reverse. A label is a handle; the description is the argument. | . The question goes in the chat too — both, every time (STRICT) . The rule above makes the structured fields stand alone. This is its mirror: the chat must stand alone as well. Every question handed to the person is written in the chat, as text — the question, the numbered options, the recommendation and what happens with no answer — and asked through the selection tool. Neither copy may depend on the other. A question asked only in the selection tool vanishes with one stray tap; for a person with limited hand function a stray tap is the ordinary case. A dismissal is not an answer. The tool reports a dismissed box as “do not proceed”, and the right move is exactly that: proceed on nothing. The question stays open in the chat text, and the next turn re-asks it through the selection tool when the person indicates it was accidental — never treat the dismissal as a choice of any option, including the default. (The stated default governs silence over time, not a dismissal.) . Two things this rules out: . | A question that exists only inside the selection tool. One dismissal, one connection drop or one client that does not render the box, and the decision is gone with no trace in the conversation. | A chat that says “see the question below”. A pointer to the box is not the question; if the box goes, the pointer points at nothing. | . And when you are the one relaying somebody else’s blocked question: say that you are relaying, and say where the answer has to be given. An answer typed at the relay does not reach the asker. The reverse direction, a sibling getting its question to the agent that is talking with the person, and the answer back, is hand-back-to-discussion. Worked example . Unanswerable — every content word is undefined, no option has a cost, and there is no recommendation: . next — cross-agent skill install + prefix. I’d want your call on prefix-at-rest vs prefix-at-install before writing anything. The same decision, askable: . Next up is installing this platform’s skills into whichever agent is running (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor), so each one can load them. Skills would get an fa- prefix so their names cannot collide with the host agent’s own commands: /fa-beans-tui rather than /beans-tui. One decision shapes everything else — where the prefix gets applied: . | When a skill is installed into an agent (recommended) — files in this repo keep their plain names, and the prefix is added as they are emitted. Nothing here has to change. | In this repository itself — rename every skill file. That touches the package manifests, every skill ref in the BPMN diagrams, two doc generators and every cross-reference between skill bodies, and is painful to reverse. | . Say nothing and I will take (1) when I start. A pending question is not a STATUS — ask it (STRICT) . “Stream 3 is blocked on four questions” is not a report. It is a question you declined to ask. Naming a block, linking to where it lives and summarising it still leaves the person unable to answer with a click. Whoever can put the question to the person owns asking it. A question does not “belong to” the session that blocked on it: if you can act on the answer — and an agent with repository access usually can — ask it. If you truly cannot act, ask anyway and carry the answer back. Pointing somewhere is the failure mode, not the fix. “Answer it in that session” moves the whole cost of the decision onto the person. Reserve it for what genuinely cannot be done from here, and say plainly that it cannot. When several are pending, ask the most consequential in full and give a count for the rest — never “which question would you like me to ask?”. §”More than one decision pending” below carries that rule. More than one decision pending — ask ONE, count the rest . The six parts above are per decision. When several are open, stating all in full is a wall, and naming them compactly is a teaser. Ask the one that is actually next, in full. For the others, give a COUNT and no option names. Two other decisions are waiting; I will put each properly when it is next. A count says work is queued without inviting an answer to a question whose terms the reader cannot see. There is no “just listing what’s open” exemption. A wrap-up that names a decision has handed it over, whatever the framing sentence says. Either the options and their costs are there, or the name comes out and a count goes in. Enforced, not remembered — the layers . A rule that depends on being remembered is not enforced. So: . | layer | what it does | what it cannot do | . | .claude/skills/interaction-modality/ | makes this skill offerable by name | triggering is probabilistic; it helps an agent already thinking about asking well | . | PreToolUse on AskUserQuestion → scripts/ask-well.sh | prints the six parts at the one moment the rule certainly applies, on every agent and every session | it sees the tool call, not the prose written before it, so it REMINDS and never blocks — a gate that cannot tell must not refuse | . | schemas/process/decision-request.ts | makes the comparison unomittable: no optionals, so a decision with two options and one comparison does not parse, and renderDecision emits the prose table and the selection from ONE object so they cannot drift | it cannot tell a good con from a lazy one, and does not try — it checks that the question was asked, never that the answer is honest | . | Stop → scripts/decisions-named-not-asked.ts | reads the turn that just ENDED and names the paragraph that handed decisions over bare (e.g. a closing list of open item ids) — the one path the layers keyed on a question tool cannot see | it reads prose, so it is a heuristic; it reminds and never blocks, and a paragraph that happens to carry a comparison suppresses it | . None of these is sufficient on its own. bun test cat-harness-tools/scripts/tests/decision-request.test.ts asserts each refusal, and the Stop hook’s fixtures are real turns rather than invented strings. The posture, and the condition that revisits it . The hook reminds; it does not gate. A gate that refused a well-formed question because the schema turned out too narrow would cost the person the one channel they use to correct an agent. So: . | The hook reminds. It never blocks, and a question always reaches the person, well-formed or not. | renderDecision is the house style for any decision with more than two options, or any decision whose options differ in cost rather than only in kind. Write the object, render the prose, then offer the selection. | Gating is revisited on EVIDENCE, not on a date. | . The condition: twelve RENDERED decision records. bun run cat health reports bean-rendered-decision-records — work items whose decision actually went through {@link renderDecision}, detected from the five-row table it emits. At twelve, a person can read them and judge whether the schema fits the decisions this repository actually has. An ## Options heading is NOT a rendered decision, because work items carry considered-options sections as ordinary practice, so their count grows without anyone using the schema. The counter is a health metric over beans/, not a second store, because a parallel store of decision objects would be a count free to disagree with the work item store’s. The record goes in the work item it belongs to, under ## Options, where madr.md’s two-option floor and bean-thin-decision-records govern it; renderDecision composes the chat message. The unit is WORK ITEMS, not decisions: hasRenderedDecision is a per-bean boolean, so twelve means twelve different work items. The unit is not changed, because moving it without moving the number is a silent re-calibration. A deferral with no trigger is not a deferral: it is indistinguishable a month later from a decision nobody made. 4.2 Form — the checklist . Before any question, all five: . | Could this be a selection? If the answer set is finite, make it one. | Is there a recommended option, and is it first and marked? A user who does not want to decide should be able to pick the first thing and be right. | Is it four options or fewer? Beyond that, split the question. | Does no answer have a safe meaning? Say what you will do if they say nothing, then do that. Silence must never block the work. | Is it blocking at all? Do everything that does not depend on the answer first, and ask at the point where the answer is actually needed. | . And the negative rule: do not ask a question whose answer you could look up. Every fact getting-started reads from the filesystem is a question not asked. This is the largest accessibility win available, and it is invisible. 4.3 After the answer — a ruling is a skill edit, not just an applied answer . The asking is half the loop. The answer comes back, and if it settles how a kind of thing is decided rather than only this one, it is a rule and it is written into the skill that governs it in the same turn: the rule and its reason in the narrative, the quote and date in the skill’s provenance log. Otherwise the next session asks again. The rule, the three questions that identify a rule-level answer, and why it needs no permission: symbiotic-interaction §2. It applies to any author correction, not only to answers to questions asked here.

1b836365a857.title: 5. Driving the questions from DMN — one logic, four surfaces
1b836365a857.content: Guided questions driven by DMN logic, across modalities, are two separable things: . What to ask next is a decision. It belongs in a DMN table alongside folio-intent.dmn: inputs are the facts known so far, output is the next question’s id (or none, when enough is known). It is authored by whoever owns the process, is reviewable as a table, and is the same for every user. How to render the question is the modality. Options as a numbered list in chat, as spoken alternatives one at a time over audio, as large-type radio buttons on the site. The DMN table never learns about any of this. facts ──▶ [ next-question.dmn ] ──▶ question id ──▶ renderer(profile) ──▶ user ▲ │ └──────────────────── answer recorded as a new fact ─────────────────────┘ . Four properties over an agent improvising the interview: . | The question set is finite and reviewable. You can read the table and know every question the agent can ask. | It terminates. A table whose output can be none has a stopping condition; an improvising agent does not. | Asking becomes obligatory rather than optional. This is the trick folio-intent.dmn already uses: ask is an outcome of the table, so the agent cannot route past it; an agent that decides for itself whether to ask will, under pressure to be helpful, decide not to. | A question skipped is auditable. The facts are recorded; you can replay the table and see which rule fired. | . The limits, stated so nobody is surprised: the FEEL subset this repo implements covers equality, comparison and one-of — no ranges, no not(), no function calls (src/workflow/decision-table.ts). A genuinely open question — “what is this paper about?” — is not a decision and does not belong in a table. And conversation is not a wizard: a user must always be able to say something the table did not anticipate, which is what option 5 of the intent question is for.

b4d49f99df8e.title: 6. Grounding — what this follows
b4d49f99df8e.content: The rules above are the subset of published accessibility guidance that a conversational agent can actually keep. Named so they can be checked rather than taken on trust: . | WCAG 2.2 AA is the baseline for anything rendered — the docs site, the viewer, a generated PDF. The success criteria that bite hardest here: 1.4.4 Resize text (200 % without loss), 1.4.3 Contrast, 1.4.1 Use of Colour (never colour alone), 2.4.7 Focus Visible, 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions. | WCAG 2.2’s newer criteria are the dexterity ones: 2.5.7 Dragging Movements, 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) — 24 × 24 CSS px — and 3.3.7 Redundant Entry, which says do not make someone enter the same information twice. §3’s committed preferences file is 3.3.7 applied to a conversation. | Cognitive accessibility (WCAG 3.1, and W3C’s COGA guidance) is what §4’s “four options or fewer” and plain-language profile come from. | EN 301 549 is the procurement standard that makes WCAG AA a legal requirement in EU public-sector contexts; Section 508 does the same in the US. Folios published for public-sector use land in those contexts. | Authoring Tool Accessibility Guidelines (ATAG 2.0) is the one most often missed: it covers tools that produce content, which is what this platform is. Part A is the tool being usable; Part B is the tool helping the author produce accessible output. The alt-text and heading-order checks a folio’s QA sweep should carry are Part B. | .

02a0e8ff4bc4.title: 7. The settings surface
02a0e8ff4bc4.content: The published site carries a settings control (gear, top right) writing the same four profiles to localStorage, so a reader who is not the author still gets large type or reduced motion. It is per-viewer and per-browser by construction — it never reaches an agent. cat-harness/memory/interaction.json is the agent-facing record and the site control is the reader-facing one; keep them separate.

c2650595bca2.title: 8. Anti-patterns
c2650595bca2.content: . | The question first, the context on request (§4.1), typically in the private vocabulary the agent built while working. “Happy to explain if useful” does not repair it. | Asking someone to describe their disability. Ask about the interface. | Re-asking what cat-harness/memory/interaction.json records (WCAG 3.3.7). | A “quick open question” because the option list felt like overkill. The list is cheaper for the person answering. | Blocking on an answer with no default. State the default, act on it. | Treating an inferred profile as a diagnosis. It is a rendering choice, labelled inferred from behaviour, and the user overrules it. | Accessibility as a rendering concern only. The largest win is §4’s last rule — not asking at all — and no stylesheet delivers it. | .

1f47272177ac.title: The IRIS CDN Exporter
1f47272177ac.content: The exporter is an agent role plus a set of deterministic scripts. The scripts (scripts/iris-cdn/) move bytes. The agent plans, reviews and reports. It never holds the signing key and never pushes to a WHO repository. Processes, all in processes/: . | Process | When | What | . | iris-cdn-initial-load.bpmn | once, run by hand with a stated budget | every record and every bitstream, in resumable batches | . | iris-cdn-nightly.bpmn | every night, 02:00 UTC | only the items IRIS reports as changed | . | iris-cdn-reconcile.bpmn | Sundays, 04:00 UTC | catches withdrawals, which REST does not report, and checks for drift | . | iris-cdn-sign-publish.bpmn | called by the three above | BagIt bag, detached JWS (ES256), did:web key, verify | . What each process does is in docs/iris-cdn-export.md; where it runs, what it writes where, and its secrets are in docs/iris-cdn-deployment.md; signing is skill iris-cdn-signing; reading changes from IRIS is skill iris-rest-feed.

33bbd7a546f7.title: The no-churn rule
33bbd7a546f7.content: Content that has not changed is not rewritten, re-uploaded or re-signed. Each step says how: . | Canonical records. A record is written as JSON with sorted keys, LF line endings and no fetch timestamp inside it. If the canonical bytes equal the held ones, the file is not rewritten. | Content-addressed bitstreams. A bitstream is stored under its SHA-256. An object that already exists is never downloaded, uploaded or overwritten again. | Sorted graph output. The graph is rebuilt in full, and N-Quads partitions are written sorted, so a partition with no changed item comes out byte-identical and is not re-uploaded. | Date-free manifests. bag-info.txt has no Bagging-Date, so the tag manifest of an unchanged payload is byte-identical. | An empty diff ends the run. No commit, no new signature. | . A step that cannot meet its rule reports it. It never hides it.

59d6873c090d.title: What the agent does
59d6873c090d.content: . | Plan the initial load as one batch per collection page, with the checkpoint in state/initial-load.json in the Cloudflare git repository. | Review each run report and open a bean for each anomaly: a change count far from the recent median, a quarantined bitstream, a verification whose verdict is unknown, or a partition over its size ceiling. | Never widen scope. Only the owner changes what is exported, its budget or where it is stored. | .

41b4e04862d6.title: What the agent must not do
41b4e04862d6.content: . | Push to any WHO/* repository. | Treat a short listing as a mass withdrawal (see iris-rest-feed). | Delete a published object. A withdrawn item is marked withdrawn, and its bytes stay addressable because a citation to them may exist. | Put an upstream count into prose. Counts come from the catalogue and the run reports. | .

b2bb1ea8dc14.title: Processes that run this skill
b2bb1ea8dc14.content: | process | step(s) that name it | . | IRIS CDN initial load | State scope and budget, with denominators; Plan batches by community and collection; Fetch bitstreams not already held; Store bytes under SHA-256 (skip if held); Commit the batch checkpoint; Quarantine and report the mismatch; Review the load report; open beans for gaps | . | IRIS CDN nightly change ingest | Fetch only bitstreams whose checksum changed; Write canonical records into the library; Review the run report; open beans for anomalies | . | IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation | Treat the listing as faulty; escalate | . | Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release | Store new objects (never overwrite) | .

39d4a8b56cdc.content: The code is scripts/iris-cdn/bag.ts and scripts/iris-cdn/signing.ts. The process is processes/iris-cdn-sign-publish.bpmn.

9f3c00415f03.doc: Signing and verifying an IRIS CDN release
9f3c00415f03.title: Standards used, and nothing else
9f3c00415f03.content: | Piece | Standard | . | Package and digests | BagIt 1.0, RFC 8493: bagit.txt, bag-info.txt, manifest-sha256.txt, tagmanifest-sha256.txt | . | Signature | JWS compact serialization with a detached payload, RFC 7515 Appendix F | . | Algorithm | ES256, ECDSA on P-256 with SHA-256, RFC 7518 §3.4. It is the same curve as WHO’s signing DID key. EdDSA (RFC 8037) is accepted when verifying | . | Public key | JWK, RFC 7517, as publicKeyJwk | . | Trust chain | x5c in the JWK (RFC 7517 §4.7): X.509 certificates, leaf first, ending at one issued by WHO’s signing key | . | Key publication | W3C DID Core 1.0 document, verificationMethod of type JsonWebKey (W3C Controlled Identifiers 1.0) or JsonWebKey2020, which is the form WHO’s own DID uses. Both are accepted | . | DID method | did:web | . No draft standards are used. A new one needs the owner’s explicit approval.

4f3ab3aa2f68.doc: Signing and verifying an IRIS CDN release
4f3ab3aa2f68.title: What is signed
4f3ab3aa2f68.content: There is one release signature, over the bytes of tagmanifest-sha256.txt, plus one signature per changed library item (below). The tag manifest pins the SHA-256 of every other tag file, and manifest-sha256.txt pins the SHA-256 of every payload file. Signing the tag manifest therefore covers the whole bag. The tag files live in the release git repository; the payload files live in R2 under sha256/<aa>/<digest>. The signature is stored beside the tag manifest as tagmanifest-sha256.txt.jws, in the form <header>..<signature>. The empty middle segment is the detached payload. The protected header is {"alg":"ES256","kid":"did:web:…#<key>"}. ECDSA signatures are randomized. Signing the same bytes twice gives two different signatures, so unchanged content is never re-signed: an unchanged night produces the same tag manifest and gets no new signature.

3ceab9325ec5.doc: Signing and verifying an IRIS CDN release
3ceab9325ec5.title: A signature on each library item
3ceab9325ec5.content: Every library item has its own manifest at items/<handle>/manifest-sha256.txt, in the same line format as the BagIt payload manifest. It lists the item’s record, records/<handle>.json, and every file under bitstreams/<handle>/. The item’s detached JWS is stored beside it as manifest-sha256.txt.jws. | An item verifies on its own. Fetch its manifest and JWS, verify the JWS against the DID document and its x5c chain, then check each digest. | The release signature proves completeness. The item manifests and their JWSs are payload files, so the release tag manifest pins them all. Nothing can be added or removed without breaking the release signature. | Only changed items are signed. If an item’s manifest bytes did not change, its existing JWS is kept (signItems in scripts/iris-cdn/run.ts). A metadata-only edit changes the record digest, so that item is re-signed while its PDF digest stays the same. | .

7d1aab6dd8a2.doc: Signing and verifying an IRIS CDN release
7d1aab6dd8a2.title: Where the key comes from
7d1aab6dd8a2.content: The verifier resolves the kid’s DID from the web, never from the package: . | did:web:<cdn-domain> resolves to https://<cdn-domain>/.well-known/did.json, and did:web:<cdn-domain>:iris resolves to https://<cdn-domain>/iris/did.json. The DID must be stable, because the DID is the signer’s identity. | When the DID document lists assertionMethod, the key must be in it. A retired key stays in verificationMethod so that old releases still verify, but it is removed from assertionMethod. A signature by that retired key on a new release then fails. | . If the DID document cannot be fetched, the verdict is unknown, not failed and not verified. A portal that cannot check says so. The trust chain. Our key’s publicKeyJwk.x5c holds the certificates that end at one issued by the key in WHO’s signing DID, did:web:raw.githubusercontent.com:WorldHealthOrganization:tng-participants-prod:main:WHO:signing:DID. The verifier is given WHO’s public key as its anchor, as the variable IRIS_CDN_TRUST_ANCHOR_JWK in CI. With an anchor, a key with no x5c fails. run.ts verify refuses without the anchor or IRIS_CDN_DID: the verdict is unknown and it exits non-zero. Called without anchors, verifyDetached reports the chain as not-checked, never as verified. No other trust anchor is assumed. A trust list, such as GDHCN via WHO SMART Trust, could only be an additional route to the same DID document, never a replacement for it.

94db319819c1.doc: Signing and verifying an IRIS CDN release
94db319819c1.title: Key custody and rotation
94db319819c1.content: . | The private key is a JWK (kty: EC, crv: P-256, x, y, d). It never goes into git, a log or a bean. It is the GitHub environment secret IRIS_CDN_SIGNING_JWK in environment iris-cdn-release, which only jobs on main can read. | The key already exists. The subordinate key is already published in a DID document, with x5c up to WHO’s signing DID, before the exporter runs. That publication is offline and outside these processes. No CI job issues certificates or edits the DID document. | To rotate: . | Add the new key to the DID document and to assertionMethod. | Publish the DID document. | Sign the next release with the new key. | Take the old key out of assertionMethod, and keep it in verificationMethod. | . | The DID document is built in a fixed order, so republishing it with the same keys writes the same bytes. | .

ce818da57f0c.doc: Signing and verifying an IRIS CDN release
ce818da57f0c.title: Verifying by hand
ce818da57f0c.content: In a checkout of the release git repository: . # 1. tag files against the tag manifest sha256sum -c tagmanifest-sha256.txt # 2. the release signature, with the key resolved from did:web IRIS_CDN_DID=did:web:<cdn-domain> IRIS_CDN_TRUST_ANCHOR_JWK='<WHO public JWK>' \ bun scripts/iris-cdn/run.ts verify --release <checkout> --no-revert . Payload digests in manifest-sha256.txt are checked against the objects at https://<cdn-domain>/sha256/<aa>/<digest>, not against files in the checkout.

65ccfc6f00e0.title: IRIS, DSpace and Dublin Core
65ccfc6f00e0.content: Every claim here is read off one captured record: the DSpace full item record for wpr-rdo-2020-003-eng, transcribed at catalogue/records/wpr-rdo-2020-003-eng.dc.json. Nothing is asserted from general knowledge of DSpace. Where this file and the record disagree, the record wins. The type is folio-assistant-core/schemas/dublin-core.ts. It is generic: Dublin Core is ISO 15836 and DSpace is a platform. This file covers only what IRIS does with them.

f4d769f0e764.title: Scale
f4d769f0e764.content: From IRIS’s storage report (By Location → Entire Site) and home page, read 2026-09-20: . |   |   | source | . | items | 273,559 | the home page’s search placeholder | . | files | 1,057,223 | the storage report | . | storage | 361.55 GB | the storage report | . | top-level communities | 8 | the storage report | . Items and files are different denominators, so catalogue/catalogue.json carries them in separate fields, totalItemsUpstream and totalFilesUpstream. That is 3.86 files per item, because an item carries several bitstreams. totalBytesUpstream is derived: the report prints two decimals and no byte count, so the value is round(361.55 × 1024³), good to about ±5 MiB. It is GiB rather than GB because every per-community figure the report prints (238.58, 19.72, 34.84, 26.14, 25.71) reproduces exactly at 2³⁰ and none does at 10⁹.

e1ebfe97abf0.title: Three identifier systems
e1ebfe97abf0.content: The worked item carries all three: . | system | value | authoritative? | . | DSpace UUID | 18892cf3-5a4f-42a4-923c-a93f4a594dec | no — IRIS’s own, stable only while this DSpace instance is | . | Handle | 10665/332098 | yes — guaranteed by the Handle System, outside WHO | . | WHO govdoc | WPR/RDO/2020/003 | no — WHO’s publication number | . The library slug wpr-rdo-2020-003-eng is derived from the govdoc, the weakest key. A tool that resolves by Handle survives the source moving. A legacy handle is live in the record, and must not be deduplicated . dc.identifier.uri appears twice: . https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/332098 ← global http://iris.wpro.who.int/handle/10665.1/14518 ← regional, merged away . Regional IRIS instances were folded into the global one and both URIs were kept. The second is a real alternate identifier, and evidence that a source host can disappear (the sourceLoss gate’s worked example).

6945dd6e51e7.title: Qualified, repeated, language-tagged
6945dd6e51e7.content: Every field is element.qualifier. Four fields repeat in this one record (dc.date.accessioned, dc.date.available, dc.identifier.uri, dc.subject.mesh), so Record<string, string> silently keeps the last value and drops the rest. There is a per-field language column, present on dc.title, dc.description and each dc.subject.mesh, absent on the author, the dates and the identifiers. An absent tag is not en: it is a value whose language nobody asserted.

d49538273b5f.title: MeSH is a controlled vocabulary, not a keyword
d49538273b5f.content: dc.subject.mesh = Publishing, Guidelines as Topic. These are NLM Medical Subject Headings, with their own identifiers and hierarchy at https://id.nlm.nih.gov/mesh/. A MeSH term can be resolved and subsumed (searching “Guidelines as Topic” should reach narrower terms); a free-text keyword can do neither. DcValue.authority records the distinction per value.

916b70a61121.title: An item is not a file: bundles
916b70a61121.content: DSpace groups bitstreams into bundles — conventionally ORIGINAL, plus TEXT (extracted), THUMBNAIL and LICENSE. Size and format are per-bitstream: the 2.68 MB in the record is the PDF’s, not the item’s. Bundles are why there are more files than items.

bf9a388797b2.title: Containment is a path, not a parent
bf9a388797b2.content: The breadcrumb: Home → 7. Regional Office for the … → Regional Office for the W… → Information products — four levels, two of them communities and one a collection. DSpace also lets an item be mapped into several collections, so “the” parent of a node does not exist. CatalogueNode.parents is a list of paths.

d8e8c3ce3812.title: What a later tool needs — as requirements
d8e8c3ce3812.content: | # | requirement | why, in one line | . | R1 | Resolve by Handle where one exists; treat UUID and govdoc as secondary | only the Handle is guaranteed outside WHO | . | R2 | Never deduplicate dc.identifier.uri | the second one is evidence of a host that vanished | . | R3 | Preserve repetition on every field, not a known list | four fields repeat in a single record; assume more do | . | R4 | Treat an absent language as unasserted, never as en | both states occur in one record | . | R5 | Carry dc.subject.mesh as a controlled value with its authority | it can be resolved and subsumed; a keyword cannot | . | R6 | Model bitstreams per bundle, with size and format on the bitstream | an item is not a file | . | R7 | Model containment as a list of paths | four levels deep, and multiple mappings are legal | . | R8 | Never infer metadata from the PDF when a record exists | OCR off a title page catalogued the WHO Editorial Style Manual as Abies | . | R9 | Record what the source says even when it contradicts the file | dc.description says 30 p.; the PDF has 33 | . | R10 | An item with no known collection carries parents: [] — never a guessed one | held-and-unplaceable is a STATE; inventing containment is unfalsifiable | . | R11 | Key a node by path when its UUID is not in the capture | an invented UUID resolves to nothing while looking authoritative | . | R12 | Keep the page captured and the identifier apart | /items/<uuid>/full is what was fetched; the Handle is what the item IS | . | R13 | A materialized claim must name bytes that EXIST, and something must check it | an unchecked claim can name no bytes and still pass as held | . | R14 | Read a storage figure in the units that round-trip its own bytes | IRIS prints “GB” for what its byte counts make GiB — a 7% error | . | R15 | Never fall back to a parent URL when an item has no upstream URI | “no upstream URI recorded” is the answer; the front page is a lie that resolves | . | R16 | A partial transcription must SAY it is partial | a truncated abstract that does not declare itself cannot be told from a short one | . | R17 | Hold what you hold: model the bitstreams whose bytes are here | the handbook lists 8 upstream; this repository has 1 | . | R18 | Do not “correct” a record that looks wrong | the English-titled editorial manual really does carry an Italian ISBN | . | R19 | A derived figure must round-trip the figure it was derived from | round(361.55 × 1024³) bytes must render back as 361.55 GiB | . | R20 | An item count and a file count are different denominators | 273,559 against 1,057,223 — a fraction built from the wrong one is off by 3.86× | . | R21 | Mint stable URIs at the extractor (Upstream Skolemization) | minting https://iris.who.int/entity/item/{handle}#{prop}_{idx} at extraction leaves no blank nodes for a later pass to resolve | . | R22 | Append-only streaming partition writes | A 300,000 item corpus cannot accumulate uncompressed in working memory; write quads directly to partition file streams | . R8: where a library entry’s title comes from . who-pub-tps-931 shows why. Its structure.json carries title: "Abies" and authors_raw: "Cpe N" — OCR noise off a scanned title page of the WHO Editorial Style Manual. 9789241548960-eng has three renderings of one title from the PDF (Handbook forGuideline Development 2nd edition from joined title lines, GRC Handbook - second edition from PDF docinfo, and the real one) and no authority among them. The IRIS record settles both. A library entry’s title is taken, in order, from: . | the catalogue record: dc.title of the Dublin Core record that the catalogue node naming the entry (libraryId) points at through metadataRef; | referenced.json identity.title; | the PDF Info /Title (structure.json metadata.docinfo.Title), only when it is not junk such as Microsoft Word - …, a file name, untitled, or an arXiv stamp; | the slug, which check:library-qa then reports as title-missing. | . The page-1 front-matter parse is never a title. It may still feed search and the section files’ doc_title. The manifest records which source won as meta.title_source (for example dc-record) and where it came from as meta.title_from, so R8 can be checked. The resolver is cat-harness-tools/pipeline/library-title.ts; the library-ingestion skill carries the full rule.

64fc95ad0efe.title: Covers: an artefact we made, filed where IRIS files its own
64fc95ad0efe.content: The replica’s home page shows a cover beside each item in its Recent Submissions strip, and each library entry page shows it too. None of them came from IRIS. Each is page 1 of the item’s PDF, rasterised by cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-cover.py and filed as a THUMBNAIL-bundle bitstream — the bundle name DSpace uses for the thumbnails it generates. Nothing downstream can tell the two apart from the bundle name, so the bitstream’s materialization.note must say the cover was derived here. The PDF is either held in this repository or, for a referenced item, fetched by the iris-cover-pdfs GitHub workflow, matched against the sha256 its ORIGINAL bitstream records, rendered and discarded. Only the cover PNG is committed. folio-assistant-core/scripts/gen-covers.ts (bun run iris:covers) renders only covers the catalogue asks for: a node declares the THUMBNAIL bitstream and the script supplies the bytes. It refuses to write bytes for a THUMBNAIL whose materialization.note does not declare the derivation, since a tool cannot attest to its own output. bun run iris:covers:check compares the bytes, the recorded sha256 and the recorded pixel dimensions, re-rendering where the PDF is held. That is R13 for covers. A cover whose PDF is not held can be verified but not re-rendered. The WHO emblem is masked on covers . The site chrome carries no WHO mark until the replica is published under WHO. Covers are shown with the WHO emblem and wordmark blanked to flat grey before the PNG is written, so the committed bytes never contain it. Each THUMBNAIL bitstream declares the blanked rectangles and the reason as maskedRegions. A title that contains “WHO” is not masked: it is the work’s name. A cover whose publication gates block it is shown as cover withheld, not no cover.

9f437bfe7094.title: Getting a record
9f437bfe7094.content: DSpace 7 exposes /server/api/discover/search/objects, paged and filterable by dsoType, scope and facets; communities are listed at /community-list. The calls this repository makes, and what live IRIS accepts, are in iris-rest-feed; the code is scripts/iris-cdn/rest-feed.ts. A record derived from a PDF rather than transcribed from IRIS must be marked derived, so it can be replaced wholesale when the real record arrives with nothing downstream having believed it. Enumeration cost, subsetting and the characterisation that decides whether IRIS may be cited at all are in who-iris/sources/who-iris.json.

a874f8287d7b.doc: Oxigraph multi-graph search for WHO IRIS
a874f8287d7b.title: Oxigraph multi-graph search for WHO IRIS
a874f8287d7b.content: The IRIS catalogue and its Dublin Core records are compiled into named graphs and queried with Oxigraph: natively in Bun at build time, and as WebAssembly in a browser. One SPARQL query can then join Dublin Core properties, catalogue containment and bitstream access gates — which DSpace Discovery cannot do in a single call.

1a3cc764d614.doc: Oxigraph multi-graph search for WHO IRIS
1a3cc764d614.title: Build and query
1a3cc764d614.content: # Build from catalogue/nodes and site/dublin-core into dist/oxigraph/ bun run scripts/build-iris-oxigraph.ts # Build from exported DSpace records (the CDN release's records/ tree) bun run scripts/build-iris-oxigraph.ts --records <dir> --out <dir> # Load dist/oxigraph/who-iris-dataset.nq and run sample searches and facets bun run scripts/iris-oxigraph-search.ts bun test scripts/tests/iris-oxigraph.test.ts . scripts/iris-oxigraph-search.ts exports IrisOxigraphEngine (loadSpine, loadCommunity, searchSpine, complexSearch, facetCounts). The CDN exporter (scripts/iris-cdn/run.ts) calls the build over exported records and publishes each output file as graph/<file>.

63ebc7ade903.doc: Oxigraph multi-graph search for WHO IRIS
63ebc7ade903.title: 1. Graphs and files
63ebc7ade903.content: The build writes, sorted and de-duplicated so unchanged inputs give byte-identical files: . | Tier 1, the spine — <https://iris.who.int/graph/spine>, in who-iris-spine.nq and .nq.gz. Hierarchy (dspace:Community, dspace:Collection), item Handles, titles, first creator, issued date, and bitstream descriptors with copyright verdicts. Loaded first. | Tier 2, one partition per community — <https://iris.who.int/graph/community/{id}>, in iris_who_int_graph_community_{id}.nq and .nq.gz. The full Dublin Core of that community’s items: MeSH authorities, abstracts, spatial coverage, govdoc numbers, ISBNs. Mounted on demand. | Catalogue and metadata graphs — <https://iris.who.int/graph/catalogue> and <https://iris.who.int/graph/metadata>, each in its own iris_who_int_graph_{catalogue,metadata}.nq(.gz), and merged in who-iris-dataset.nq and .nq.gz for server-side use and integrity checks. | subgraph-manifest.json — the spine and each community partition, with file names, quad counts and item counts. | queries.json — prepared SPARQL queries. | . Namespaces . | dspace: = https://iris.who.int/ns/dspace# — catalogue terms (Item, inCommunity, hasBitstream, fileName, …). | dspaceNs: = https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant-core/v0/ns/dspace/ — Dublin Core value terms, including authority. | . No binary bytes in the graph . PDFs, cover images and archives are never stored as literals. A bitstream node carries only: . | dspace:fileName (e.g. "WPR-RDO-2020-003-eng.pdf") | dspace:mediaType (e.g. "application/pdf") | dspace:fileBytes (integer) | dspace:copyrightGate — the copyright gate’s verdict, e.g. "permitted" | . The bytes are fetched from the CDN.

221a1f23a3a2.doc: Oxigraph multi-graph search for WHO IRIS
221a1f23a3a2.title: 2. Requirements
221a1f23a3a2.content: | # | Requirement | Why, in one line | . | OX-1 | Mint stable URIs at the extractor (https://iris.who.int/entity/item/{handle}#{prop}_{idx}); the build fails if any blank node remains | no multi-document collisions, every node addressable, no normalizer pass | . | OX-2 | Store zero binary bytes in RDF | keeps WASM memory small; binaries are static files on the CDN | . | OX-3 | Join across named graphs with explicit GRAPH blocks | separates containment and rights from bibliographic description | . | OX-4 | Use Handle URIs as the item subject (https://hdl.handle.net/...) | identity resolves outside WHO’s servers | . | OX-5 | Treat bitstream rights as access gates | results can be filtered by whether the PDF may be downloaded | . | OX-6 | Partition by community | a client fetches only the slice it needs | . | OX-7 | Never scan whole-corpus text in SPARQL | full text belongs in a static inverted index | . | OX-8 | Preserve controlled-vocabulary authorities (dspaceNs:authority) | distinguishes MeSH headings from free keywords | . | OX-9 | Append-only streaming partition emission | bounded memory at 300,000 items. Not met yet: buildIrisDataset holds and sorts every quad in memory; StreamingPartitionWriter is defined but unused | .

f4f13a1b5c5d.doc: Oxigraph multi-graph search for WHO IRIS
f4f13a1b5c5d.title: 3. SPARQL recipes
f4f13a1b5c5d.content: Recipe 1: multi-condition search . Items in the Western Pacific community, issued in or after 2000, with a subject containing “guidelines”, and a PDF whose copyright verdict is permitted. PREFIX dcterms: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/> PREFIX dspace: <https://iris.who.int/ns/dspace#> PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> PREFIX rdf: <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#> PREFIX xsd: <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> SELECT DISTINCT ?handle ?title ?creator ?issued ?pdfName WHERE { # 1. Join Dublin Core Metadata GRAPH <https://iris.who.int/graph/metadata> { ?handle dcterms:title ?title ; dcterms:creator ?crNode ; dcterms:subject ?sNode . ?crNode rdf:value ?creator . ?sNode rdf:value ?subject . OPTIONAL { ?handle dcterms:issued ?issued } } # 2. Join Catalogue Hierarchy & Access Gates GRAPH <https://iris.who.int/graph/catalogue> { ?handle dspace:inCommunity ?comm ; dspace:hasBitstream ?bs . ?comm rdfs:label ?commLabel . ?bs dspace:mediaType "application/pdf" ; dspace:fileName ?pdfName ; dspace:copyrightGate "permitted" . } # 3. Multi-Field Filter Evaluation BIND(IF(BOUND(?issued), xsd:integer(SUBSTR(STR(?issued), 1, 4)), 0) AS ?year) FILTER ( CONTAINS(LCASE(?subject), "guidelines") && CONTAINS(LCASE(?commLabel), "western pacific") && (?year >= 2000) ) } ORDER BY DESC(?year) . Recipe 2: facet counts . Item counts per subject term and its authority. PREFIX dcterms: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/> PREFIX rdf: <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#> PREFIX dspaceNs: <https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant-core/v0/ns/dspace/> SELECT ?subject (COUNT(DISTINCT ?handle) AS ?itemCount) ?authority WHERE { GRAPH <https://iris.who.int/graph/metadata> { ?handle dcterms:subject ?sNode . ?sNode rdf:value ?subject . OPTIONAL { ?sNode dspaceNs:authority ?authority } } } GROUP BY ?subject ?authority ORDER BY DESC(?itemCount) ?subject .

f6b0263d851c.doc: Oxigraph multi-graph search for WHO IRIS
f6b0263d851c.title: 4. Browser pattern: spine first, communities on demand
f6b0263d851c.content: import oxigraph from 'oxigraph'; // Where the graph files are served from, e.g. a release's graph/ directory. const BASE = '<graph-base-url>'; async function gunzipText(resp: Response): Promise<string> { const stream = resp.body!.pipeThrough(new DecompressionStream('gzip')); return new Response(stream).text(); } const store = new oxigraph.Store(); // 1. Fetch the spine and the manifest const [spineResp, manifestResp] = await Promise.all([ fetch(`${BASE}/who-iris-spine.nq.gz`), fetch(`${BASE}/subgraph-manifest.json`), ]); const manifest = await manifestResp.json(); // 2. Load the spine: hierarchy, title search and rights filtering work now store.load(await gunzipText(spineResp), { format: 'application/n-quads' }); // 3. Mount a community when the user selects it. load() adds its named // graph without clobbering what is already in the store. async function mountCommunity(commId: string) { const partition = manifest.tiers.tier2_communities.partitions[commId]; if (!partition) return; const resp = await fetch(`${BASE}/${partition.fileGz}`); store.load(await gunzipText(resp), { format: 'application/n-quads' }); } // 4. Run a prepared query locally for (const binding of store.query(myPreparedQuery)) { console.log(binding.get('title').value); } .

0edbb1d24161.doc: Reading IRIS changes over DSpace REST
0edbb1d24161.title: Reading IRIS changes over DSpace REST
0edbb1d24161.content: Changes are read from the DSpace REST API only. REST has no change feed with deletions, so a nightly walk is paired with a weekly reconciliation. The code is scripts/iris-cdn/rest-feed.ts; its tests run on fixtures in scripts/tests/iris-cdn.test.ts.

e3eb98dc4e8a.doc: Reading IRIS changes over DSpace REST
e3eb98dc4e8a.title: What live IRIS accepts
e3eb98dc4e8a.content: . | Discovery offers only five sortOptions: score, dc.title, dc.date.issued, dc.date.accessioned, dc.date.available. sort=lastModified,DESC returns HTTP 422. | Changes are found with a Solr range query instead: query=lastModified:[<isoZ> TO *]. | The bound must be a Z-suffixed UTC timestamp. A +00:00 offset returns totalElements: 0. | .

8d24da2f8b58.doc: Reading IRIS changes over DSpace REST
8d24da2f8b58.title: Endpoints
8d24da2f8b58.content: | Use | Request | . | Changed items since cursor | GET /server/api/discover/search/objects?dsoType=ITEM&query=lastModified:[{isoZ} TO *]&sort=dc.date.accessioned,DESC&page=N&size=100 | . | Weekly full item listing | GET /server/api/discover/search/objects?dsoType=ITEM&sort=dc.date.accessioned,DESC&page=N&size=100 | . | Collection-scoped batch (initial load) | GET /server/api/discover/search/objects?dsoType=ITEM&scope={collectionUuid}&sort=dc.date.accessioned,DESC&page=N&size=100 | . | Communities / collections with parent | GET /server/api/core/{communities|collections}?page=N&size=100&embed=parentCommunity | . | One item with its files and collection | GET /server/api/core/items/{uuid}?embed=bundles/bitstreams&embed=owningCollection | . | Bundle bitstreams beyond page 0 | GET /server/api/core/bundles/{bundleUuid}/bitstreams?page=N&size=100 | . | A file’s bytes | GET /server/api/core/bitstreams/{uuid}/content | .

fe9888eb1e36.doc: Reading IRIS changes over DSpace REST
fe9888eb1e36.title: Nightly: changedSince(cursor)
fe9888eb1e36.content: . | Normalise cursor to UTC Z (new Date(Date.parse(cursor)).toISOString()) and run the range query above. | Page through the matching result set. | The cursor is inclusive: an item modified at that instant is read again, not missed. Re-reading an unchanged item writes the same bytes. | Return the items oldest first, de-duplicated by UUID. | . The cursor is the newest lastModified read, kept in state/cursor.json. A failed night does not advance it.

ec5aded42498.doc: Reading IRIS changes over DSpace REST
ec5aded42498.title: Metadata changes without the PDF changing
ec5aded42498.content: A PDF may stay the same while its Dublin Core changes. Records and files are handled separately: . | A record is re-read whenever its item appears in the walk. A PDF is re-fetched only if its DSpace MD5 changed. | Communities and collections are re-read in full every night (allContainers). A renamed collection changes no item, and DSpace 7 does not expose lastModified for these. An unchanged one serializes to the same bytes. | The weekly metadata check. The weekly listing pages carry each item’s metadata. metadataSha hashes it canonically, and any item whose hash differs from the one last ingested is re-read. That catches edits that did not move lastModified, without one fetch per item. | .

dfac32ad5817.doc: Reading IRIS changes over DSpace REST
dfac32ad5817.title: Weekly: allItems and withdrawnOrHidden
dfac32ad5817.content: . | List every item ID Discovery returns. | Compare that list with the IDs the library holds. | Guard. If more than 1% of held items are missing, the listing is treated as faulty and nothing is marked. Possible causes are a paging fault, an outage or a Solr reindex. | Re-fetch each missing item by ID. Mark it withdrawn only if IRIS confirms it: withdrawn: true, or a 404 (gone), 401 or 403 (private). | .

086a03266653.doc: Reading IRIS changes over DSpace REST
086a03266653.title: Fixity
086a03266653.content: DSpace reports an MD5 checkSum for each bitstream. Downloaded bytes must match it before their SHA-256 is recorded. A mismatch quarantines the bitstream and reports it. It is never retried silently.

7798fc0b7829.doc: Reading IRIS changes over DSpace REST
7798fc0b7829.title: Politeness
7798fc0b7829.content: Requests are made one at a time, with a User-Agent that names the project and its repository, and back off on 429 and 503. The initial load is paced to the budget stated in Task_StateBudget (processes/iris-cdn-initial-load.bpmn), including maxRequestsPerSecond.

b99adcf8a3a8.doc: Reading IRIS changes over DSpace REST
b99adcf8a3a8.title: Processes that run this skill
b99adcf8a3a8.content: | process | step(s) that name it | . | IRIS CDN initial load | Harvest a batch of item records (REST) | . | IRIS CDN nightly change ingest | Read the cursor of the last published run; List items changed since the cursor; Fetch the changed records and bitstream lists; Commit the advanced cursor | . | IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation | List every item id IRIS reports; Compare with the ids the library holds; Re-check each missing item by id; Mark confirmed items withdrawn (keep bytes) | .

3128897c7f44.title: Working an issue — announce, then re-check
3128897c7f44.content: Two rules. Both exist because your view of an issue and everyone else’s diverge the moment you start, and neither side can see that it has happened.

6bdd97dcec23.title: Announce the branch when you create it, not when you finish
6bdd97dcec23.content: Comment on the issue with the branch name, the process and phase, and the work items claimed — at creation. Before it, run the collision review in coordinate §”Starting new work”. A summary posted after the work lands is not a substitute. Until the first comment appears, a sibling session and a human both see an issue with nobody visibly on it, which is precisely the state the work plan exists to prevent and the one no sibling can detect. Announce once, on the single edge into implementation. A process that loops back into implement re-enters on the same branch, and re-announcing each time is noise that trains the reader to skip the announcements that matter.

e4655425d62b.title: Re-check the issue while you work
e4655425d62b.content: Checking once at session start is not checking. Requirements change while you are heads-down, and the comment that changes direction is the one you are least likely to see. Track what you have already read as two marks, not one: . | a comment-id high-water mark, and | the newest edit timestamp — because an edited comment keeps its id, and an edited requirement is a changed requirement. A high-water mark alone cannot see an edit at all. | . With no stored mark, everything counts as unseen. A fresh container has read nothing, and defaulting the other way is exactly how the comments that change direction get skipped — silently, because nothing distinguishes read from never looked.

601748ddf0f8.title: When the new material is a large chunk of work, stop
601748ddf0f8.content: Do not fold it into the current run. Say that this is a good stopping point for review, link the artefact, and confirm priorities before continuing. Absorbing it buries a scope change inside a diff nobody asked for, and spends the author’s next review on work they have not agreed to. A large new ask is a decision to hand back, under the usual discipline — context, options with their costs, a marked recommendation, then the question.

2ed040389d72.title: What an issue is for, against its neighbours
2ed040389d72.content: They are not synonymous, and conflating them is how an agent closes something it had no standing to close: . |   | what it carries | . | issue | stakeholder sign-off | . | change proposal | code review | . | work item | work-plan tracking | . Never close an issue without explicit authorisation from the analyst or stakeholder. Whether work is done is a judgement, and an agent must never assume completion on its own say-so — the same rule that stops you closing a work item a sibling is mid-flight on. That authorisation may be given in advance: an issue-close waiver, which names the issues it covers and expires. It is the stakeholder answering the same question earlier, which is the whole of what this rule asks for — never the agent supplying the judgement itself. confirmation-waiver.md. After each round of implementation, post a summary on the issue, not only on the change proposal: what was accomplished, what remains, and links to the updated content for review.

58d15aac7a2c.title: Milestones and decision points go on the issue, as they happen
58d15aac7a2c.content: A round can be long, and the owner follows the issue, not the session or the PR. So between round summaries, post on the issue at two kinds of moment: . | A milestone — a result the owner would want to know before the round ends: a method lands, a benchmark number moves, a tool turns out not to run here, an approach is replaced because measurement reversed it. | A decision point — whenever you put a choice to the owner in the chat, put it on the issue too, in the same shape: context, options with their cost, the marked recommendation, and what happens if nobody answers (interaction-modality). A choice made only in the chat leaves no record where the next reader looks. | . Not every push: a push is reported on the PR. An issue update is for what a stakeholder would act on. Each update must be readable on its own, because it is read days later without the session: status, approach in a line, findings with their numbers and provenance, what landed, and next steps — and a link to the previous update rather than a restatement of it.

4db932c04c4c.title: A sign-off on the issue becomes a record
4db932c04c4c.content: When a requirements document is signed off on its issue — approved, amended, rejected, deferred or cancelled — the comment is the evidence, not the record. The record is a requirement-signoff attestation in the attestations graph (test/attestations/requirement-signoff/<set>.attestations.json): who (kind, id, actor), at, scope, outcome, the stage it moves the requirement set to, the reason, and evidence — the comment’s permalink, …/issues/<n>#issuecomment-<id>. A sign-off given in chat is quoted on the issue first, dated, so the evidence link exists. The agent writes the record of a person’s decision; it never writes one for a decision nobody made, and check:requirements refuses approved or accepted without a human one.

95d74b0acd8a.title: Before you publish that something does not exist (STRICT)
95d74b0acd8a.content: An issue comment is published, and a false claim in one costs more than a missing true one: it sends the next reader off to verify an accusation, and the correction never reaches everybody the original did. So before an issue comment, PR body or commit message asserts that a file, a function or somebody’s cited precedent does not exist, re-read it from the remote — git show origin/main:<path> — in a command of its own, and check the open branches when the claim is nobody has built this. Grepping your checkout answers “is this in my base”, not “does this exist”, and a git fetch earlier in the same compound command is not a barrier when siblings merge every few minutes. bean-coordination §”Re-derive from the REMOTE” has the two guards. For the third case, a path that exists only on an open PR’s head, ask the open-work-lookup Tool.

3b8d78362205.title: When the work has a BEAN and no issue (STRICT)
3b8d78362205.content: A round summary is owed either way. With no issue, it goes on the change proposal AND into the work item — the work item is the durable artefact a sibling reads, and a summary that exists only in a PR thread is invisible to the work plan on main. And a work item that has an issue carries the link BOTH ways: a reader arriving at either object has to be able to reach the other, and a check reports the ones that cannot. When to open an issue at all is crdm-detect §”Issue association” — scan before creating one, and never create one without permission. This section is about what is owed once the work exists, not about manufacturing an issue for every work item.

b07ed3ef6c3d.title: Knowledge graph affordances — browse, materialise, instantiate, copy-into-folio
b07ed3ef6c3d.content: A person or an agent arriving at any conformant instance has four verbs available on what they find: . | browse — explore the graph, its subgraphs, its skills, its processes, its schemas and its assets without mutating anything. | materialise — pull a remote harness closure or a subscribed subgraph onto local disk at a pinned commit or recorded digest. | instantiate — scaffold a new folio or harnessed repository from the harness so it can author and publish its own graphs. | copy-into-folio — take a node or asset from a knowledge graph into your own folio (assets[] or folio/), stamp KgAsset.source provenance, and edit, comment or raise todos on your copy. | .

b798cd3e2a4a.title: The four verbs and their capability floor
b798cd3e2a4a.content: Three of the four verbs write, and an agent in a read-only container, a viewer on a static site, or a session without repository credentials cannot perform a write. Each verb therefore declares its capability requirement up front and degrades cleanly rather than failing halfway through a procedure. | verb | write capability required | process | governing skills | Tools | read-only degradation | . | browse | none (git-read or published HTTP/files only) | — (stateless read) | kg-navigation, directory-conventions | skill-list, skill-fetch, search-graph, get-neighbors, kg-graph-export | none needed — browse is the read-only floor and must remain completely useful with zero write capabilities | . | materialise | one of git-push, github-api, github-connector (to persist lock/record changes; local worktree write for --staging) | mount-dependency.bpmn, materialize-remote.bpmn | remote-mount, materialize-remote, kg-subscription | remote-mount (mount:remote), mount-from-lock, kg-retrieve-npm | run bun run cat mount:remote --plan or mount:remote:check to inspect the resolved closure and digests without writing | . | instantiate | one of git-push, github-api, github-connector | getting-started.bpmn, repo-conversion.bpmn | folio-init, getting-started, repo-conversion | folio-init (folio_init / bun run cat init-folio) | run folio-init with --dry-run (dry_run: true) to emit the full manifest and file plan as Markdown without touching disk or remote refs | . | copy-into-folio | one of git-push, github-api, github-connector | copy-into-folio.bpmn (for KG assets); copy-out-materialized.bpmn (for materialized library items) | kg-affordances, copy-out-materialized, directory-conventions | declaration-resolution (check:declared-assets), witness-conformance | inspect the upstream asset in place via browse, and emit the target KgAsset declaration snippet (with source pre-filled) so the user can apply it where they have write access | .

b6f62ca63a6d.title: Why browse requires zero write capability
b6f62ca63a6d.content: browse is the read-only floor of every conformant knowledge graph: . | On a published site (gh-pages or a CDN), browse reads the exported JSON-LD graph (kg.jsonld), the per-subgraph visualisers, and the rendered BPMN/DMN surfaces over plain HTTP. | In a checkout with an MCP server attached, browse uses skill-list, skill-fetch, search-graph and get-neighbors. | In a bare filesystem checkout with no server and no network, browse reads <name>.json at the instance root, resolves directories[] and assets[], and reads the files directly (kg-navigation). | . No step of browse may require git-push, github-api or github-connector. If a browse tool or visualiser refuses to run because write credentials are absent, that is a defect in the tool.

aeb736b9a065.title: Checking write capability before a writing verb
aeb736b9a065.content: Before starting materialise, instantiate or copy-into-folio, determine which write capability the current environment holds (scenarios/capabilities/): . | git-push — a working tree with push access to the target repository’s remote (git push --dry-run succeeds). | github-api — a GH_TOKEN / GITHUB_TOKEN or gh auth status capable of creating commits, branches or pull requests via the GitHub API. | github-connector — an MCP GitHub connector (push_files, create_or_update_file, create_pull_request) attached to the session. | . The three states of the capability check are kept distinct: . | Available (git-push, github-api, or github-connector present): proceed with the writing verb using the corresponding tool path. | Absent (probed and none of the three is present): take the read-only degradation branch (--plan, --dry-run, or in-place inspection plus an exportable snippet). Never silently drop the provenance or leave a half-written tree. | Could not determine (the probe itself failed for an environmental reason, such as an unreachable host): report could-not-determine with the probe error; do not report the capability as absent and do not attempt a blind write. | .

e70a5beface2.title: copy-into-folio and KgAsset.source provenance
e70a5beface2.content: When a folio owner or authoring agent copies an asset from an upstream knowledge graph into their own folio to adapt it, comment on it or raise todos against it, the process is copy-into-folio.bpmn. Like copy-out-materialized, copying a knowledge-graph asset into a folio is two writes and a refusal: . | Never touch the source graph. The upstream instance is read-only from the copier’s point of view; the arrow runs out of the source lane and never back. | Copy the bytes and declare the asset in the target folio’s <name>.json assets[]. A file copied into an undeclared scratch path is invisible to check:declared-assets and to the folio’s visualisers. | Stamp KgAsset.source (AssetSourceSchema in schemas/kg/kg-node.ts) on the target folio’s KgAsset entry: | . { "id": "adapted-guideline-table", "src": "assets/adapted-guideline-table.json", "role": "guideline-table", "source": { "instance": "litlfred/example-ig", "path": "assets/guideline-table.json", "ref": "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567" } } . The three states of KgAsset.source . KgAsset.source ({ instance, path, ref? }) is how the graph tells a copy from original work: . | source state | meaning | . | present, and ref matches upstream | copied from instance at path and current with that upstream commit | . | present, and ref differs or is omitted | copied from instance at path, either adapted locally since ref or taken without a commit pin (staleness is checkable only when ref is recorded) | . | absent (undefined) | authored in this instance — a third state, never “copied from an unknown place” | . A copied asset MUST carry source: without it the copy is indistinguishable from locally authored work, and nothing downstream can reconstruct which instance it came from. Working on the copy in the target folio . Once the asset is declared in the target folio with KgAsset.source stamped and verified by bun run cat check:declaration-resolution (check:declared-assets), it is ordinary writable content of the target folio. The folio owner can edit it in place, attach review comments, or raise todos (todo-manager) against it without disturbing the upstream knowledge graph.
