689e3631f0a8.title: Merge-conflict patterns — what a merge may resolve on its own
689e3631f0a8.content: bun run cat merge:main is the command; sdlc/processes/merge-base.bpmn is the process it executes, called from Task_PrepareMerge in code-change-review.bpmn. The patterns themselves are data in cat-harness-tools/scripts/merge-conflict-patterns.ts. This page says what each one is FOR, so a reader can tell a deliberate refusal from a gap. Most main-into-branch merges that conflict do so only on generated files, and every one of those resolves the same way — take the base’s copy, regenerate — so resolving them by hand costs an agent a round and the PR another CI run for nothing.

fc1c49770188.title: The three rules that make it safe
fc1c49770188.content: . | All or nothing. Every conflicted path is classified before anything is touched. One refusal ABORTS the merge and restores the tree. Resolving nine generated files and leaving one authored conflict half-done reads as progress, and is not. | Proved, not assumed. After resolving, bun run cat regen asks the checks the CI workflow runs (under merge:main, those whose inputs either side changed since the fork point; --full-regen asks every one) and runs each stale one’s writer until the tree settles. Anything unrepaired aborts the merge. No pattern names its own check: the gate set is derived from the workflow and cannot drift, a hand-kept list of check names can. | Classify with the BASE’s patterns, not your tree’s. pathClass reads PATTERNS from the checkout it is running in. A branch that forked before a pattern was declared therefore classifies by the OLD declaration, and every path in a newly-declared family reads authored — the one verdict that routes work to a person. | . A path that no pattern names is refused. Adding automation is adding a pattern, deliberately, with its reason — never widening a glob on a hunch. Applying rule 3 . A stale tree can be wrong in either direction. A pattern the base has added makes it over-report authored conflicts, which sends a person work the base already declares mechanical. A pattern the base has narrowed, reordered or retired makes it under-report: it takes a side on a path the base now refuses. So git fetch, and classify with the BASE’s own merge-base.ts (from a worktree of the tools at the base, git worktree add --detach <dir> origin/<base>), run against your checkout with --root <your checkout> --base origin/<base> (add --dry-run to classify and change nothing). merge-main.yml does the same: it checks out main’s tools and runs main’s merge-base.ts --root on the PR’s branch. The number that decides whether a human is needed must come from the declaration the merge will actually be resolved under.

ceeec19c589d.title: A merge round — run each check ONCE
ceeec19c589d.content: Most of a round of folding main into a PR is the same question asked twice. What each step costs and adds: . | step | cost | what it adds | . | merge:main, including its own regen | 5–10 min — regen 238–309 s with nothing stale, 601–639 s when a writer runs | THE regen; rule 2 above | . | skill:register | 1–2 min | the derived artefacts the merge left owed | . | a standalone regen after merge:main | 4–5 min | nothing for the merge — same tree; it can only add a pair already stale on both parents, which CI reports anyway | . | full local bun run cat gates | ~24 min (1429 s), nearly all bun test (~21.8k tests) on 3–4 local cores | what CI’s sharded run says in ~5 min, 4 ways | . | regen again in a fresh checkout, to prove a no-op | 4–5 min | what CI’s own clean checkout already proves | . The timings in this section were recorded by 2026-10-08, when cat-harness was seeded. Re-measure with bun run cat measure:merge-round before you quote them. Three of five rows repeat a measurement somebody else, or the same command, has already made. So: . When every conflict is generated — the trimmed round . “Generated” means every conflicted path was resolved by a declared take-base, region or sidecar pattern below, and the merge brought in no authored change of yours to reconcile. | bun run cat state:mount, then bun run cat merge:main. merge:main’s regen IS the regen. Do not run another one after it. | bun run cat skill:register until bun run cat skill:register:check passes. The chain can need two passes: one writer’s output is another’s input. | Targeted checks, and only these: . | skill:register:check and kg:detangle:check — the two reds a generated-only merge actually hit in CI; | subgraph:jsonld:check — a merge or edit that changes a skill also changes its payload hash; skill:register does not run subgraph:jsonld, so run the writer (bun run cat subgraph:jsonld) when the check is red; | check:declared-paths (never with --update here) and check:process-index; | bun run typecheck, and bun run cat lint at 0 errors; | the deletion audit — git diff --name-status --diff-filter=D HEAD^1 HEAD -- '*/test/results/*' must list only files main itself deleted. A gitignored-but-tracked file is dropped by a merge silently, local checks stay green because the writer recreated it on disk, and CI’s fresh checkout fails. merge:main refuses such a drop itself (§”When one side deleted the file”); after a hand merge, restore each one main still tracks with git checkout HEAD^2 -- <path>; | submodule pins equal to main’s — git ls-tree HEAD bootstrap bootstrap-tools against git ls-tree origin/main bootstrap bootstrap-tools. Not git submodule status: merge-queue §”git add -A after a merge silently reverts the submodule gitlinks” says why it cannot see this; | the fsh-guts mount is not committed — git diff --stat origin/main HEAD -- fsh-guts is empty; | git merge-tree --write-tree origin/main HEAD reports 0 conflicts, with the exit status captured on the next line (prepare-merge step 4). | . | Push, never with force. CI’s sharded run is the full gate set. Skip the local full bun run cat gates and the fresh-checkout regen for this kind of merge: each repeats something CI does better. | . When it is NOT generated-only — keep the full local run . An AUTHORED file conflicted, or the merge touched code (a script, test, schema or workflow that conflicted or that you reconciled by hand, on either side): run the full local bun run cat gates before pushing, and read prepare-merge §”What a green LOCAL run entitles you to claim” before quoting it. The targeted list above is chosen for a merge that changed only artefacts with one right answer; it cannot see a semantic conflict such as an import of a module the other side moved (merge-queue §”A train admits only members that STACK cleanly”). Four things a round needs to know . | merge:main has no “continue after a manual fix” mode. When one path blocks it, it aborts and restores the tree (rule 1). Do its steps by hand: git merge origin/main, fix the blocking path, then resolve each declared path by its own pattern’s strategy, never with one command for all of them, and stage each with git add -f <path>: . | take-base: git checkout --theirs <path> when main kept the file; git rm <path> when main deleted it, since a modify/delete has no stage to check out (§”When one side deleted the file”). | owned-tree: take each parent’s committed blob, as takeOwnedTree does (§”subgraph-index and subgraph-payload”). Never --theirs: in a rename/rename it writes conflict-marked bytes under a hash name. | readme-generated-regions: edit the conflict markers in place, hunk by hunk, as resolveGeneratedRegions does. A hunk inside a generated region may take either side, because regen rewrites the region. A hunk outside one, or one that moves a region boundary, is an authored conflict. Never --theirs: it replaces the whole README and drops the branch’s own edits to it, including the ones git merged cleanly. | . Then run the regen it would have run, and both droppedInMerge checks it would have run: once after resolving, and once after regen and git add -A, before committing. Each path git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=D HEAD lists must be one main deleted since the merge base, and each path git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=D MERGE_HEAD lists must be one the branch deleted since the merge base. After regen, a writer’s own deletion also passes, but only when the file is gone from disk too. | Give the regen a long leash. Cold, it needed ≥1200 s of wall time (recorded by 2026-10-08; bun run cat measure:merge-round re-measures). Run it in the background rather than under a default 2-minute tool timeout, which kills it part-way and leaves a half-written tree. | merge:main commits with git’s default message. Amend that commit to add the session’s trailers (git commit --amend) before pushing — it is your unpushed commit, so this is not a rewrite of shared history. | Do not fold main in while another big PR is minutes from landing. Wait for it. Merging now buys a second round the moment it lands (merge-queue). | .

4e8f3fee25b6.title: A pattern is not always the answer — ask what the file’s record is
4e8f3fee25b6.content: Read this before declaring a pattern for a path that already has one. The registry answers how a conflict is resolved. It never answers whether one arises, and reaching for it a second time on the same path is the move to stop and check. A declared pattern settles a file whose content is a function of the TREE, and settles nothing about one whose content is a function of the machine that built it — there, take-base is a loop. This section is about a third case: the content is tree-determined, the pattern does resolve it, and the path still conflicts on every merge. The LSI indexes are the example: a one-sentence edit to one skill rewrites most of skills.lsi.json (an SVD rotation is globally sensitive), so the file conflicts on nearly every merge, and the pattern only makes each conflict cheap — and no check on main judges those bytes. So the question to ask is not which strategy, it is: . What is this file’s record, and is main it? . | main is the record — an authored file, or a generated one a reader navigates to by name. Declare the pattern; that is what the registry is for. | main is not the record — the file’s record is the qa-reports entry for its commit, or a build output, and the copy on main is a duplicate kept in step by a gate. Then take it off main, and keep the declaration for the branches still carrying it, where the base has deleted the file and take-base resolves that too (see the next section). | Part of it is, and part is not — the common case, and the one to look for before concluding either of the above. Cut by what each value is a function of: a value the TREE determines stays committed and is reviewable; a value determined by some other artefact’s CONTENT is produced where that artefact lives. docs/lsi/index.md is the worked example — front matter, prose and the verdict table stay, each index’s size, poles and findings go — and the front matter is why it could not be taken off whole: it declares the harness tile, so an uncommitted page is a page with no way in. | . The trap on the way out. Taking a page off its store and leaving it committed can make it worse: a page computed from qa-reports at main reads the latest published entry, so the committed copy goes stale whenever anyone else pushes. Whatever stays committed must be computed from the tree.gitattributes reached the same conclusion from the -merge side and states it plainly: “Removing these conflicts, rather than tidying them, needs the files off main altogether.” Two things make that safe rather than merely tidy, and both are checks, not care: every reader must already cope with the file’s absence, and something must still PRODUCE it where its record lives — qa:refresh decides that per writer, so a family can be removed on its own.

d0d0caab14b3.title: When one side deleted the file
d0d0caab14b3.content: A modify/delete conflict has no stage for the side that deleted it, so checkout --theirs (or --ours) has nothing to take. Every resolving strategy takes the base’s side of the deletion instead: its copy when the base kept the file, git rm when the base removed it — takeBase in merge-base.ts. Regeneration recreates the file if it is still produced. Classification is by path, so an authored path in a modify/delete conflict is refused exactly like any other conflict on it. The owned-tree patterns are the exception. They read which parent commits hold the path rather than which stages exist, because in a rename/rename “no stage 3” does not mean the base deleted anything (see subgraph-payload below). Taking a deletion is the ONLY way a merge may drop a path, and merge-base.ts checks this before every merge commit. droppedInMerge compares the index with the merge base and both parents. A path either parent tracks that the result lacks is a drop, unless one side deleted it since the merge base. A path both parents hold, or one a side added, must survive. The check runs twice. Right after resolution, before anything else is staged, every drop is refused. After regen and add -A, only a drop the disk still holds is refused, because a writer may delete what it owns: subgraph:jsonld replaces a content-addressed payload when the merge changes its node, and its :check proves that. The check exists because of the gitignored-but-tracked files under */test/results/. Once one of them leaves the index, regen rewrites it on disk and git add -A does not stage it again, since it is now untracked and ignored. The failure signature is green locally, red in CI, with the check reporting the file missing (“has none”). git add -A is not what removes such a file: it only fails to restore one that something else (such as a git rm) already removed from the index. The refusal line says when the dropped file is still on disk, which is the case that local checks cannot see.

9bec0bbb9044.title: The patterns
9bec0bbb9044.content: kg-qa-manifest — take the base, regenerate . **/test/results/**/kg-qa.manifest.json. One per instance (hosted ones one level deeper), holding only the auditor’s script hash, so any change to kg-audit.ts restamps every one at once. It holds no attestation. qa-results — take the base, regenerate . **/*.qa-results.json. Whole-artefact QA results, rewritten whole by their producer. They change whenever any finding does. derived-results — take the base, regenerate . kg-qa sidecars, LSI indexes, detangle sidecars, tool-run records and translation-qa sidecars under test/results/. Recomputed from the whole corpus, so any concurrent skill or schema change touches them. Attestations live in test/attestations/, which no pattern names and a merge therefore refuses; test/results/ is not committed on main, and a branch still carrying a sidecar takes the base’s side. The LSI half is untracked on main; the globs are kept for branches still carrying it (§”A pattern is not always the answer”). auto-docs — take the base, regenerate . The generated docs index pages, already -merge in .gitattributes. One page per directory, so a new file anywhere changes one. uml — take the base, regenerate . Generated overview diagrams and their SVGs. prov-qaqc — take the base, regenerate . The PROV-O QA/QC report (docs/prov-qaqc/) and its per-instance logs (docs/assets/prov/). Generated WHOLE from the workflow instances under beans/workflows/, so any branch that records an instance — which every branch doing process work does — rewrites the index page and adds a .prov.jsonld. The globs are instance-agnostic (**/docs/prov-qaqc/**), like derived-results and unlike glossary: a dependent folio runs prov:qaqc over its own instances and writes the same two shapes under its own root. It names no check of its own, per rule 2: regen runs prov:qaqc because check:prov-qaqc is a workflow gate, and a pattern that named its own check would be a hand-kept list able to drift from the workflow. glossary — take the base, regenerate . The generated glossary and LSI pages: whole-corpus aggregates where concurrent term additions always collide. The LSI page’s per-index detail is added by the docs-site build rather than committed, and what is left is a function of the tree. The glossary page has no equivalent split: every number on it is a term count over the whole corpus, so there is no half that only the tree moves. That is the second branch of §”A pattern is not always the answer” — main is still the glossary page’s record, and declaring the strategy is all there is to do. translated-glossary — take the base, regenerate . cat-harness/docs/{ar,es,fr,ru,zh}/glossary/index.md. The per-locale glossary pages glossary-page.ts writes whole beside the English one (check:glossary), so they collide exactly when it does. Only the glossary page is named: the rest of each locale directory is authored translation, and a locale no generator writes (de/) is refused. viewer-pages — take the base, regenerate . docs/external-schemas/index.md, docs/methodologies/index.md, docs/processes/*.md, docs/qa/index.html and docs/translation-status/index.html: whole-file viewer pages, each with its writer’s --check in the CI workflow (external-schemas:viz, methodologies:viz, processes:viz, state:visualizer, translation:status). A new schema, diagram or translation anywhere rewrites them. It also holds state:visualizer’s other pages, docs/{beans,todos,health, issue-marks,swimlane-glossary,uploads}/index.html, each headed “Generated by scripts/state-visualizer.ts”. docs/uploads/index.html is the viewer OF uploads/, not an upload, and the uploads refusal’s **/uploads/** would catch it; first match wins, so the viewer entries sit above the refusal. docs/fsh-guts/index.md is not committed: it is derived from fsh-guts/, which is kept on a branch, so it is built at publish by derive:publish and a merge cannot meet it. That is the general answer for any derived page whose input lives on a branch — see directory-conventions §”The storage clock” — and is better than a take-base pattern, which only makes the collision cheap. The archive itself (fsh-guts/**) is kept content and stays refused. viewer-namespace — take the base, regenerate . docs/cat-harness/{catalogue,folio,library,schemas,uploads,voices}/**: the pages gen-library-viz, gen-folio-viz and gen-schema-viz place through viewerPlacement, each rewritten whole from the corpus and checked by its :viz --check. As above, its uploads/ pages render uploads rather than being them. auto-docs/ under the same prefix keeps its own auto-docs entry. navbar-include — take the base, regenerate . docs/_includes/generated/**: the navbar/footer include written whole by gen-navbar-include.ts (navbar:include --check). Any new page, graph or tile rewrites it. Its authored neighbours in docs/_includes/ stay refused. viewer-nav-qa — take the base, regenerate . test/results/viewer-nav/viewer-nav.qa.json: check-viewer-nav’s mechanical layout verdict over every viewer page. Recomputed from the pages, and it carries no reviewer’s attestation. handler-index — take the base, regenerate . docs/cat-harness/published-graphs.md, the handler’s index of every published graph and declared viewer, written whole by gen-handler-index.ts (handler:index:check). Any new graph or viewer rewrites it. skos-glossary-export — take the base, regenerate . **/docs/assets/glossary/*.skos.jsonld: the published SKOS export, written whole by glossary:export (glossary-export.ts, gated by glossary:check). Every instance’s export restamps whenever any declared role, skill or term moves, so two PRs that touch unrelated skills still collide here. It is not the ledger, and that distinction is the whole safety argument. glossary-ledger.json carries forward: glossary-export.ts reads the prior ledger and preserves a concept’s earlier names as skos:hiddenLabel, so taking one side would drop a term’s history. The ledger sits one level up from generated/ and matches no glob here — verified, and pinned by a test. This is .gitattributes’s rule applied to a resolver: the test is not is it generated but does its producer carry anything forward.skos.jsonld does not match site-data’s cat-harness/docs/assets/**/*.json — .jsonld is not .json — which is why it needed its own entry rather than falling through. glossary-generated — take the base, regenerate . **/glossary/generated/**: the per-instance generated glossary JSON, same writer and same check as skos-glossary-export. The glob stops at generated/, so the sibling ledger is untouched. skill-instructions — take the base, regenerate . **/docs/reference/skill-instructions/**: skill instruction bodies, written whole by skills:docs (gen-skill-docs.ts’s OUT_DIR, gated by skills:docs:check). Never hand-edit it. Safe because emit() is compare-or-write with no merge — under --check it compares and records drift, otherwise it writes the content whole — so nothing is carried forward from the file on disk. The authored neighbour is the skill itself. skills/**/*.md is the SOURCE these pages are generated from and stays refuse; a test pins that pair, because resolving the generated copy while taking a side on the source is the mistake this entry would otherwise invite. docs-pages — take the base, regenerate . The cat-harness/docs/**.md pages gen-docs-pages.ts writes whole from the authored blocks under cat-harness/docs/source/<slug>/ (docs:pages, gated by docs:pages:check). Each one says so in its own front matter: . generated: scripts/gen-docs-pages.ts — do not hand-edit; run `bun run cat docs:pages` . Safe because nothing is carried forward. emit() is compare-or-write: the only read of a prior page is inside its --check branch, for the comparison, and every other read in the script is of an INPUT (readBlock over docs/source/, BPMN XML, manifests). Its one walk of the output directory skips files carrying the generated marker. Confirm the writer by reading the script, not by how whole-file it looks. Gated on EXACT content, which is why take-base is verifiable rather than merely convenient. The generator’s own docblock says a difference in a page is “somebody who added a node, renamed a block, ran a first sweep, or moved a sidecar, and did not regenerate”. So after take-base, docs:pages:check proves the regenerated page is right — the resolution is not trusted, it is checked. The slugs are ENUMERATED, not globbed, and that is deliberate. cat-harness/docs/*.md and guides/ mix generated pages with authored ones (architecture.md, index.md, agent-onboarding.md, …). A directory glob would take a side on authored prose — the one thing a resolver must never do. The cost is that a page added to docs/source/ is refused until its slug is declared here, which is the safe direction to be wrong in, and a test reads the pages’ own front matter from the TREE so the enumeration cannot go quietly stale. That test must read the front matter, not the file: the generated body of this skill, docs/reference/skill-instructions/merge-conflict-patterns.md, quotes the marker in the code fence above, and a detector that reads a quotation as a declaration finds its own documentation (audit-coverage). That page’s front matter names gen-skill-docs.ts, and skill-instructions is declared before docs-pages, so the first match gives it the right owner. The authored neighbour is the source, and it stays refused. cat-harness/docs/source/process-publication-workflow/every-workflow-in-the-repo.md is the hand-written INPUT for docs/process/publication-workflow.md. Even when both sides only added rows, a union of additions is a property of that instance and not of the path. A test pins the pair, and pins that nothing under content/ is claimed at any depth. health-report — take the base’s measurement . test/health/results/*.health-report.json. Not a derivation of the tree but a measurement of external state (publish branch, clone size, the work plan), written by bun run cat health and refreshed daily on the base by the health-check workflow, so the base’s copy is simply the newer measurement and a branch’s older one carries nothing worth keeping. check:harness-state judges its producer hash; if the merge changed the producer, bun run cat health rewrites it. qa-witnesses — take the base, regenerate . test/results/witnesses/**: witness projections (qa-witness/v1) and page verdict indexes, written by gen-docs-pages.ts from the kg-qa sidecars and the live subject. A projection, never an attestation, and the docs-site build regenerates them at publish. pot-templates — take the base, regenerate . translations/**/*.pot: gettext templates extracted from the English pages by pot-for-pages.ts (translation:pot:check), so every edit to a source page rewrites its template in every locale. The .po files beside them are authored translations and stay refused. site-data — take the base, regenerate . Generated site data indexes under docs/assets/**/*.json and docs/_data/. subgraph-index and subgraph-payload — owned tree, regenerate . **/docs/subgraph/** holds the subgraph JSON-LD indexes. **/docs/payload/sha256/** holds the content-addressed payloads (<hex> is the sha256 of its bytes, with a <hex>.json sidecar beside it). bun run cat subgraph:jsonld writes both directories whole, and it deletes every file in them that it did not write. Any skill edit rewrites an index and moves a payload. Why not take-base. When both sides change one node’s payload, git reads it as a rename/rename. The base’s hex goes to the branch’s hex on one side and to main’s hex on the other. Git leaves the old name at stage 1 only, the branch’s new name at stage 2 only, and main’s at stage 3 only. Both new stages hold git’s three-way merge of the two bodies, with conflict markers. So take-base fails in two ways: . | It reads “stage 2 only” as “the base deleted it” and git rms the branch’s new payload. That is a path the branch added, so droppedInMerge refuses it at the resolved checkpoint. | checkout --theirs writes marked bytes under a name that is the hash of other bytes. | . The owned-tree strategy (takeOwnedTree in merge-base.ts) reads the parents’ commits, never the stages. For each path: . | it takes the base’s committed blob when the base has the path; | it takes the branch’s committed blob when only the branch has it; | it removes the path only when neither parent has it, which is a deletion both sides made. | . The resolution therefore drops nothing a parent holds, and every kept payload holds the bytes its name hashes. The orphan it keeps is the writer’s to remove. The writer is named in the pattern as prunedBy: "subgraph:jsonld", a writer and not a check: regen still derives the check from the CI workflow. When regen runs that writer, the writer deletes the orphan. Both droppedInMerge checkpoints still hold, and they are why this works. The resolved checkpoint sees no drop. The staged checkpoint sees the writer’s deletion of the superseded payload, a path the branch added, and allows it because the disk no longer holds it either. That is the legitimate replacement of a content-addressed payload, which a single post-regen check would have refused. The test fixture in merge-base.test.ts covers this, and so does its refusal sibling, which shows that take-base on the same merge is refused. Adding another owned-tree pattern needs a writer that deletes what it did not write. Without one, the kept orphan survives regen, and only the writer’s :check can catch it. The test requires every owned-tree pattern to name a prunedBy script that has a :check twin. Under --no-regen (a merge train), the orphan stays in the member’s merge commit until the train’s final regen. navbar-rail-data — owned tree, regenerate . **/docs/assets/navbar/rail-*.js is the navbar’s shared rail data. Each file is named rail-<hash>.js after the content hash of the rail JSON it carries (lib/harness-rail.ts), so a changed rail is a new file and the old one is orphaned. bun run cat navbar:assets deletes every rail file no committed page names, and navbar:assets:check fails on one. Both sides of a merge add their own hash, which is why this is owned-tree and not take-base, for the same reason as subgraph-payload above. The neighbours navbar.js and navbar.css are not covered: they have fixed names and a byte-for-byte check, and stay refused. seed:ready reads the same declaration: deleting or renaming an owned-tree path is not a move of the layer, because a regen renames it anyway. readme-generated-regions — hunk by hunk . Directory READMEs mix authored prose with generated regions (<!-- kg:subgraph:begin --> … :end -->) whose file counts and listings change on every concurrent addition. A hunk inside a region takes the base’s side and the generator rewrites the region; a hunk in authored prose, or one that moves a region boundary, refuses. File-count churn is resolved here; the README keeps its exact counts. standalone-baseline — take the base, regenerate NOTHING . cat-harness-tools/scripts/standalone-baseline.json, check:standalone’s list of accepted standalone failures. It is the one take-base pattern with no regeneration, because it is a ratchet. Re-measuring after a merge would write any new standalone failure into the list unreviewed, which is exactly what the gate exists to stop. Git conflicts on it only when BOTH sides changed the list, so taking the base is fail-closed: if this side’s change was a new failure, its CI goes red until its author runs bun run standalone:baseline on purpose; if it was a fix, all that is lost is a shorter list, and the check reports it. beans — refused, by declaration . Before you go looking for the other session, check whether there is one. A beans/defs/** conflict has two causes and they need different handling: . | cause | how to tell | what to do | . | two sessions edited one work item | the default branch’s claim note names a branch that is not yours | a coordination question — talk to them | . | one session: the claim landed on the default branch, the completion stayed on the branch | the note names your own branch | no coordination needed; keep the completing value and the note | . The second is beans:claim’s normal path, not an edge case: it pushes the claim to the default branch so a sibling sees it before your PR exists, and your branch then edits the same work item to finish it. claim-bean.ts brings the claim COMMIT into the claiming branch after the push: a fast-forward when the branch has nothing of its own yet, otherwise a merge commit. The claim is then in the branch’s merge base, so finishing the work item merges cleanly (copying only the claim’s text still conflicts on updated_at, and a conflicted PR gets no CI at all). The conflict therefore means the claim could NOT be brought in: a detached checkout, local edits in the way, or a merge that would conflict. beans:claim says so (NOT in this branch's history) and falls back to the text mirror (mirrorClaimNote). Resolve the remainder by merging the default branch in, or by keeping the completing branch’s value and the note — and never by unioning the front matter, since a duplicated updated_at is check-bean-front-matter’s recorded defect. Work item definitions are authored work-plan state; two sessions editing one work item is a coordination question (bean-coordination). artefact-verification — refused, by declaration . scripts/artefact-verification.json, the per-check consumer-verification declaration. This is the entry that exists to stop a sweep, not to resolve one — and the one most likely to be globed by mistake, because it reads like a generated sidecar (under scripts/, a .json, its key set derived from package.json). Two facts, either one sufficient: . | task-io.ts classifies check:artefact-verification as TREE_READER, which has no outputs. No script writes the file, so regen has no writer to run and take-base is a silent discard rather than a resolution. | Its own _comment requires every none entry to carry a reason, in prose, and says the file “may only SHRINK”. A branch that adds a gated check adds an authored sentence — precisely what taking base would drop. | . So a conflict here is a genuine editorial merge: both reasons are wanted, and which survives is a judgement. Human merge is the cost of the file’s shape, not a hole in this catalogue. The falsifier: if a --write is ever added that composes the derived key set and carries existing reasons forward, the file becomes regenerable and this entry becomes take-base. Nothing today wants such a writer, and adding one to make merges cheaper would be building a mechanism to serve the merge tool rather than the gate. uploads — refused, by declaration . Uploaded source material: provenance-bearing input, never regenerated.

4e98b0fcbf05.title: Adding a pattern
4e98b0fcbf05.content: . | Measure first: replay recent merges with git merge-tree --write-tree and look at what the conflicting lines are, not just which files. | Add an entry with its why and the narrowest glob that covers it. Order matters: the first match decides. | Add a test that the unsafe neighbour is refused, not only that the case resolves. | Add a section here. | .

151e6b061bcb.title: In CI — opt in with the merge-main label
151e6b061bcb.content: .github/workflows/merge-main.yml, which lives in the folio-assistant index and not in this repository, is a second CALLER of the same command, never a second resolver. It runs main’s merge-base.ts --root on the PR’s branch (rule 3). It runs on a push to main, when the label is added, when a labelled PR is marked ready for review, and by hand: . | A sweep (a push to main, or a dispatch naming no PR) merges only a labelled PR that CONFLICTS with main. A PR that merges cleanly is skipped, because its pull_request CI already tests the merge ref (owner ruling 2026-11-05, branch-freshness). Adding the label, or a dispatch naming the PR, still merges a clean one. | Same-repository PRs only, and never a draft. A labelled draft is picked up when it is marked ready. | Runs queue; they are not cancelled in progress. For one PR, runs started by a push to main queue behind each other. A run of any other event (the label, ready-for-review, a dispatch) cancels an earlier run of the same event. Runs of different events can run at once, and the one that pushes second is rejected without overwriting anything. | It pushes only a proved merge, as a fast-forward of the branch it checked out; if the author pushed meanwhile the push is rejected and nothing is overwritten. | A refusal pushes nothing and lists the ✗ paths in its comment. Adding a pattern stays a person’s change, made here. It does NOT label the PR: a label asserting “a person is needed” outlives the condition that set it (merge-queue §”A hold has an EXPIRY and a trigger, or it outlives its reason”). The reason lives in the comment, which is dated and names the run. | A declared resolution that FAILS is a refusal too, not an unexplained red job. If taking the base or resolving a region throws, merge-base prints ` ✗ [: could not resolve] — <git's first error line>` and aborts, so the bot's comment names the path and the error. Staging a conflicted path uses `git add -f` in both resolvers (git exits 1 when staging an unmerged ignored path), safe because the path is one git listed as unmerged. `regen` reporting an unrepaired check is still a red job: that is a defect for a person to read, not a conflict. | One comment per PR, edited in place on every run — except a run that was cancelled (a newer label or ready-for-review run superseded it) or whose merge step reported no status, which leaves the comment untouched. The text is composed by cat-harness-tools/scripts/merge-main-comment.ts, which is unit-tested. | The merge commit is still judged by CI: pushed with the PUSH_BRANCH_TRIGGERING_CI credential (the harness GitHub App, or a repository secret of that name) when one is available, otherwise followed by a dispatch of code-quality-gates.yml on the branch, because a GITHUB_TOKEN push triggers no workflow. | . GitHub runs no pull_request CI on a conflicted PR, and main can move faster than an agent round. Use the label on a PR that is waiting on review rather than on its author; leave it off a branch somebody is pushing to.

b4a6e3b2bdeb.title: When a merge-train member is refused: bean, hand back, or dispatch
b4a6e3b2bdeb.content: A train is built in one of two ways, and they treat conflicts differently. The automated train (bun run cat merge:train, which merge-train.yml runs; the workflow is proposed in folio-assistant#2960) runs merge-base.ts --no-regen for each member, then one bun run cat regen, then one CI run. A conflict that a declared generated-path pattern covers is resolved at train time, and a conflict in a hand-written file refuses the member (owner ruling 2026-11-05, “Resolve generated only”; merge-queue §”The automated merge train”, proposed in cat-harness#1053). A steward’s hand train admits only members that stack with no conflict at all (merge-queue §”A train admits only members that STACK cleanly”), so it refuses a conflicted member before merging it. In either train, a member is also refused when the train’s combined result fails a gate that the member alone did not fail. The steward drops it and the train goes on without it. sdlc/processes/merge-refusal.bpmn executes what happens to the dropped member. The author’s side, the queue and the bounce-back are merge-queue; the hand-back format is the agent-handoff skill. A refusal has one of three causes: a conflict on a path refused by declaration (two PRs editing one work item, say), an authored or undeclared path, or a gate the combination fails that each member passed alone. Each refusal becomes a work item, because a PR comment or a chat message leaves nothing in the work plan to say it happened. 1. Open one bean per refused PR, and check before you create . beans create dedupes on nothing (see todo-manager §”Check before you create”). The title carries the PR number, so the check is exact: . beans list --json --search 'title:"Merge refused: #1822"' \ | jq -r '.[] | select(.title | startswith("Merge refused: #1822 ")) | select(.status != "completed" and .status != "scrapped") | .id' . | An open work item already exists for this PR: do not create a second one. Add the new refusal to it under ## Attempts with --body-append (never --body-file, which replaces the body). | Otherwise create one: type: bug, titled Merge refused: #<n> <first refused path or gate>. --parent and the create are one action (todo-manager §”After you create”). | . The parent is the epic or story the PR’s own work belongs to, not the steward’s epic. Find it in this order: the work item the PR’s branch adds or claims (git diff --name-only origin/main...<head> -- beans/defs/), then a work item id in the PR body or commit messages. Parent the refusal under that work item’s parent when the PR’s work item is a task, or under the PR’s work item itself when it is an epic or story. Then mark it --blocking <the PR's bean>. Only when the PR names no work item at all does it go under the steward’s own merge-gate epic, and the work item body says so. The body records what the owning session needs in order to act without asking: . PR #1822, head <sha> (the sha the train used), dropped from train `<train name>` (its other members, and the base sha it merged onto). ## Refused - `cat-harness/scripts/gen-library-jsonld.ts`: authored conflict, no declared pattern. Overlaps #1881, which is already in main. ## Done when - [ ] the PR's head merges main with `bun run cat merge:main` and no refusal, and CI is green on that head - [ ] the PR re-enters a train with a new `ready: <sha>`, and lands . For a combined-gate refusal, list the gate, its first failing line, and which other members the train held, because the fix may belong to either side. 2. Hand it back to the owning session, with a fail condition . The owning session is the one in the PR’s Claude-Session: trailer, or in its body. Hand the work item back to it in agent-handoff form: the steward is the coordinator and verifier, the owning session is the executor, and the owner rules on anything authored. The work item carries: . | ## Roles: steward (coordinator, verifier, closes), owning session (executor), owner (authored conflicts, any exception). | ## Report to: the PR. One line per event: <id>: started, <id>: done <sha>, <id>: blocked <why>. | ## Done when: as above. The verifier is the next train, not the executor’s own log. | ## Fails if, the fail condition, which is when the steward takes the work item back: . | no started line on the PR within 4 hours (these hours are as of 2026-10-08, when cat-harness was seeded; merge-manager-watcher acts at 2+ hours and merge-queue calls a PR stale after 24, and the owner decides which governs); | or no push to the PR branch within 24 hours; | or the owning session is gone: archived, failed, or unknown to get_session; | or the executor reports blocked on something it cannot settle. | . | . Send the hand-back to the session itself (send_message), as one line that names the work item and the branch, never the instructions. The instructions are in the work item, on the branch. After that, the steward does not edit the work item, except to add a further refusal (§1), record a dispatch (§3) or close it (§5). Anything else it learns goes to the PR (agent-handoff §1). The fail condition is a takeover, not a reminder, and that differs from agent-handoff §7 on purpose. There, the executor is in another environment and the coordinator cannot do the step, so an expiry only means asking again. Here, the work is in this repository and an agent can do it, so a missed deadline moves to §3. The one thing that is never done is putting a second writer on a branch whose first writer may still be live: before taking over, read the work item’s holder note and the PR’s last push (bean-coordination §”A quiet claim”). 3. When no live owner can be reached, dispatch one agent . If the owning session is gone, or the fail condition has fired, dispatch one agent on the PR’s branch (dispatch-agent). One agent is not a swarm; a second one is, and needs the owner’s per-swarm permission (swarm-management). Its budget is modest: one fix, one push, one report. | It may do what the patterns would have done had they been declared: bring main in with merge:main, regenerate, and fix a gate failure that has one mechanical answer. It pushes merge commits only, and never force-pushes. | It may not decide an authored conflict. Two sibling PRs editing one work item, one script changed differently on both sides, or a page over its budget only in combination: each of these is a choice between authors. The agent writes the question to the owner on the PR, with both sides quoted, the options and a default, and stops (interaction-modality §4.1). | It signs ready: only once it is the owning session. merge:guard takes the PR’s own session from the last session id in the PR body (signingSession in merge-guard.ts), and accepts a ready: <sha> marker only from that session. When the owning session is gone, the agent becomes the owner the way merge-queue §”Stalled for days” step 3 describes, with the owner’s go-ahead as there. It edits the body’s session line to its own session, records “taken over from . (gone)", and then marks the PR ready and signs. The steward never edits that line to itself, and never signs: while a Merge Manager is active, check 2 refuses a merging session that marked the PR ready itself. | The dispatch is recorded on the work item by the steward, before the agent starts: ## Attempts, with the date, the reason the fail condition fired, the agent’s session or task id, and the budget. | . Two failed attempts with the same cause go to the owner instead of a third dispatch (agent-handoff §7). 4. Comment on the PR once, and edit that comment . One comment per refused PR, edited in place as the work item moves on, as merge-main.yml does with its own comment. It names the work item, the head sha, the train, the refused paths, and who holds the fix (the owning session, a dispatched agent, or the owner). A second refusal of the same PR updates the same comment. Remove ready-to-merge (merge-queue). 5. Close the bean when the PR’s fate is settled . The steward is the verifier, so the steward closes: . | the PR lands: completed, with the merge commit as evidence; | the PR is closed unmerged: scrapped, with the reason and a link. The work item is never deleted (bean-coordination). | . A fix that is pushed but has not landed does not close the work item. The member must survive a train first. A refusal work item left open after its PR has gone is a stale hold.

885725f77c60.title: Processes that run this skill
885725f77c60.content: | process | step(s) that name it | . | Merge the base branch in | Classify every conflicted path against the declared patterns; Resolve each by its declared strategy; Abort, restore the tree, list what was refused | . | A refused merge-train member | Record the refusal on the bean; Comment on the PR once, linking the bean; Hand back, with a fail condition; Merge main in, regenerate, fix mechanical gates; Re-enter a train on the new head | . | A merge train | Hand it back (calls a sub-process); Hand the culprit back (calls a sub-process) | .

9d1ade8e0d4f.title: Merge manager watcher — the loop that runs the merge-steward role
9d1ade8e0d4f.content: The merge manager is the agent that holds the merge-steward role on one or more repositories (actor merge-manager). The role says what the steward may decide. The skills say how: what lands next (merge-queue), how it lands (merge-to-main), conflicts (merge-conflict-patterns), shared branches (ref-stewardship), and full runners (saturation-meta-merge). This page covers the loop that runs them: when to look, what to read, and where each reading leads. The process is sdlc/processes/merge-manager-watch.bpmn.

14a3805f317a.title: Am I the active merge manager?
14a3805f317a.content: Exactly one live session holds the lane on each repository. It holds the lane when the owner gave it the lane, or when it took the lane over from a stalled holder (stalled-agent-triage) and told the owner. On taking the lane, it says so to the coordinator, so that every sibling knows where to send PRs. On handing it over, it says to whom. A session that cannot tell whether a merge manager is active asks the owner (merge-queue, §”When no Merge Manager is active”). A memory that one existed yesterday does not count, either way.

58f0722983ad.title: What wakes it
58f0722983ad.content: . | A timer, every 10 minutes while the merge window is open, and hourly outside it. This is a backstop, not the main signal. | A PR event on a subscribed PR: ready for review, CI finished, review submitted, merged or closed. Subscribe to every open non-draft PR in the repositories it holds. | A main run finishing, green or red. | A sibling’s message, for example “ready”, “hold”, or “done”. | . Never poll in a loop inside a turn. End the turn and let the next event wake it.

38dae48d00b0.title: What it reads each time (live, never stored)
38dae48d00b0.content: . | The open PRs: draft or ready, head SHA, mergeable state, owed checks, and whether any open decision is waiting on the owner. | The runner queue on each repository: queued and in-progress runs, and the age of the oldest queued run. | The latest main push run on each repository, and its verdict. | The owners of the PRs: the last push or comment by each owning session. | .

c09aeda71a66.title: Where each reading leads
c09aeda71a66.content: | Reading | Process | . | A ready PR that stacks, with green owed CI | merge-train (Process_MergeTrain) | . | Queued runs 60+ minutes old with nothing landed, or the owner says runners are full | saturation-meta-merge: offer the card, never run without the owner’s tap | . | A PR whose owner has not pushed or answered for 2+ hours | stalled-agent-triage: tell the owner and take it over | . | main red | The fix goes to main as its own PR first; an automated post-merge-regen repair PR, when one is open, lands with priority (merge-queue §”Merge steward procedure: post-merge verification”). Trains wait for main to be green | . | Nothing to do | End the turn with no message | .

c9f4a2c6bb16.title: Keeping the swarm in step
c9f4a2c6bb16.content: . | Hold. Before any batch landing (a train or a meta-merge), message every sibling that pushes to the repositories involved: what is about to land, and “hold pushes, merges and run cancels here until done”. | Done. After the landing, post “done” with what landed and what is still open. Post it even when the owner chose not to go ahead. A hold with no “done” is an outage. | Hand back. A PR that cannot land (conflict, protected path, red) goes back to its owner with the reason, on the PR’s own thread or work item. It is never fixed inside the train. | Report. After every landing, report to the owner: what merged, the main verdict on each repository, and any open decision. Keep it to one message. | .

5f5248c9c63e.title: Safety rules (STRICT)
5f5248c9c63e.content: These come from the role; the watcher is the step that acts on them: . | Merges happen only on the owner’s explicit OK. A card tap counts, and it names each PR. A sibling’s or coordinator’s request does not count. | Never merge committee content, change sets (CS-), or held subscriptions/ trees. Never touch WHO or smart-* upstream repositories. | Never push .github/workflows/ changes without the workflows permission. | Never cancel a main push run that has already started. | Never skip, disable or quarantine a test to get to green. | .

54719aec518d.title: What this does not do yet
54719aec518d.content: . | The timer is each session’s own scheduled check-in. No workflow wakes the merge manager yet. | The readings are made by hand with gh api. A merge:watch tool that prints the four readings in one table is follow-up work. | .

fe9c307ab6b4.title: Processes that run this skill
fe9c307ab6b4.content: | process | step(s) that name it | . | Merge manager watch: wake, read the queue live, route | Read PRs, runner queue, main verdict and owners | . | Saturation meta-merge: land the ready PRs when the runners are full | Broadcast the hold to siblings; Post done to every held sibling | .
