bf209ef0e14f.title: Overview
bf209ef0e14f.content: This skill imports external mathematical papers into the content object system. It handles three input formats: . | PDF upload — stored in uploads/<paper-id>/, OCR/text-extracted | LaTeX source upload — stored in uploads/<paper-id>/, parsed directly | arXiv reference — fetched via arXiv API, source downloaded to uploads/ | . The output is a new paper directory under content/ with properly typed content objects (.ts + .md triples), ready for formalization.

0c5cebce2511.title: When to Use This Skill
0c5cebce2511.content: . | User says “import paper”, “add paper from arXiv”, “upload PDF/LaTeX” | User provides an arXiv ID (e.g. 2301.12345) or URL | User wants to incorporate external results into the formalization | Proof-writer skills need to reference external theorems | .

aa2083be54dd.title: Import Pipeline
aa2083be54dd.content: Phase 1: Acquisition . | Source | Action | . | PDF file | Store in uploads/<paper-id>/original.pdf | . | LaTeX file(s) | Store in uploads/<paper-id>/ preserving structure | . | arXiv ID | Fetch metadata via API, download source tarball to uploads/<paper-id>/ | . Preferred fetch path: when the session network allows arxiv.org, use the paper-search-mcp MCP server rather than raw curl / WebFetch: . | Tool | Use for | . | paper-search-mcp.search_arxiv(query=…) | resolve an author/title to an arxiv ID + canonical metadata (title, authors, year, abstract, primary category) — feeds import-meta.json | . | paper-search-mcp.download_arxiv(arxiv_id, output_dir="uploads/<paper-id>/") | fetch the PDF to uploads/ with the canonical arxiv-id-named filename — single call, no shell | . | paper-search-mcp.read_arxiv_paper(arxiv_id) | parsed text body for downstream environment extraction (Phase 2) — useful when PDF OCR is brittle | . | openalex-paper-search.get_work(doi=…) | metadata-only path for papers without an arxiv preprint (paywalled or pre-arxiv era) — fills the same import-meta.json shape | . Sandboxed sessions (Claude-Code-on-the-web with the github-only allowlist) cannot reach arxiv.org / api.openalex.org; the MCP servers stay configured but fail soft. In those sessions, queue the actual fetch onto scripts/upload-bib-papers.sh running on a normal-network machine (handoff documented in bib-qa.md §Batch intake pipeline). All uploads are committed to the repo under uploads/ for reprocessing. Metadata is stored in uploads/<paper-id>/import-meta.json: . { "source": "arxiv", "arxivId": "2301.12345", "url": "https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.12345", "title": "...", "authors": ["..."], "fetchedAt": "2026-03-22T...", "format": "latex", "files": ["main.tex", "macros.tex", "..."] } . Phase 2: Environment Extraction . Scan LaTeX source (or extracted text from PDF) for formal environments: . \begin{theorem} ... \end{theorem} → TheoremBlock \begin{definition} ... \end{definition} → DefinitionBlock \begin{proposition} ... \end{proposition} → PropositionBlock \begin{lemma} ... \end{lemma} → LemmaBlock \begin{corollary} ... \end{corollary} → CorollaryBlock \begin{conjecture} ... \end{conjecture} → ConjectureBlock \begin{example} ... \end{example} → ExampleBlock \begin{remark} ... \end{remark} → RemarkBlock \begin{proof} ... \end{proof} → ProofBlock . Also extract: . | \label{} → used for cross-references | \ref{} / \cite{} → mapped to uses[] dependencies | Sectioning (\section{}, \chapter{}) → chapter/section structure | Custom theorem environments (\newtheorem{thm} etc.) | . Important: This phase requires user interaction. Present extracted blocks to the user for review before committing: . | Show count of each kind found | Let user preview, rename, skip, or re-classify blocks | Let user define the paper ID and chapter structure | . Phase 3: Content Object Generation . For each confirmed block, generate: . | .ts manifest — using content/schema/builders.ts: import { theorem } from "../../schema/builders"; export default theorem({ label: "thm:imported-main-result", title: "Main Theorem (Smith 2024)", uses: ["def:imported-widget"], tags: ["imported", "arxiv:2301.12345"], meta: { source: "arxiv:2301.12345", originalLabel: "thm:main", originalSection: "3.2", importedAt: "2026-03-22T..." } }); . | .md content — the environment body converted from LaTeX to project markdown conventions: . | Inline math: $...$ (preserved) | Display math: $$...$$ | Complex TeX: fenced ` ```tex ` blocks | Cross-refs: [text](#label) with imported prefix | . | . Phase 4: Lean Stub Generation (Optional, User-Confirmed) . User selects which blocks to formalize. For each: . | Generate .lean file with declaration stub + sorry: -- Imported from: arXiv:2301.12345, Section 3.2 -- Ref: [smith2024] https://doi.org/10.xxxx/xxxxx /-- Main theorem from Smith (2024). -/ theorem imported_main_result : ... := by sorry . | Update .ts manifest (use the package-qualified ref URI; see cat-harness-tools/schemas/lean-packages.ts for package names): lean: { ref: "<paper-pkg>:<Paper>.Imported.Smith2024.imported_main_result" }, status: "stated" . | Every sorry MUST have a -- Ref: comment citing the source paper. | . Phase 5: Todo Suggestions (NOT Auto-Created) . The importer suggests todos to the user but does NOT create them automatically. Suggestions are presented in the UI for user confirmation: . | “Formalize proof of [thm:imported-X]” — when a theorem has no .lean | “Verify statement of [def:imported-Y]” — for all imported definitions | “Connect [thm:imported-Z] to existing [thm:main-result]” — when dependency analysis suggests a relationship | “Add CSL-JSON entry for [source]” — if citation not in references.ts | . Only when the user explicitly confirms a suggestion does it become a todo in the feedback system.

f65fa772d503.title: Integration with Proof-Writer Skills
f65fa772d503.content: How proof-writers use imported papers . The formalizer, proof-triage, and category-theory skills can: . | Search imported blocks via tags: ["imported"] — when stuck on a sorry, or when planning a formalization | Reference imported theorems in uses[] of main paper blocks | Look up original context via meta.source and the upload files | Cite sorry’d proofs with the imported paper’s reference | . Cross-paper dependency tracking . When a block in one paper uses a block from another paper, use qualified references with the target paper’s directory name: . // In the main paper, referencing another paper in the folio export default proposition({ label: "prop:some-derived-result", uses: [ "rem:some-local-remark", // same paper (bare label) "other-paper:cor:foo", // cross-paper (paper-dir:label) ], }); . Syntax: . | Same paper: bare label ("def:foo") | Same folio: "paper-dir:label" ("other-paper:cor:foo") | External folio: full URL ("https://folio.example.org/viewer/#/view/paper-id") | . The validation pipeline (uses-resolve in constraints.ts) skips qualified refs — they are resolved at folio level, not per-paper. Folio registration and viewer URL . Every imported paper must be registered in content/folio.ts: . paperRef({ dir: "other-paper", title: "Title of the Imported Paper", url: "/viewer/#/view/other-paper", // viewer route tags: ["algebra"], }), . The url field enables: . | Cross-paper link resolution in the viewer | CSL-JSON URL field for folio-hosted citations | Read-only import of external folios for referencing | . Bibliography integration for imported papers . When the imported paper has a folio viewer URL, include the URL in its CSL-JSON entry in content/schema/references.ts: . ref({ id: "smithjones2004", type: "article-journal", author: [ { family: "Smith", given: "Alice" }, { family: "Jones", given: "Bob" }, ], title: "On the structure of widgets", issued: { "date-parts": [[2004]] }, URL: "https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0409565", }), .

f1a0213efa1b.doc: Paper voice audit and watcher rules
f1a0213efa1b.title: 1. Proof bodies and mathematical hedging (one-voice-audit)
f1a0213efa1b.content: . | Proof bodies share the default scholarly voice. Both narrative .md files and proof bodies (.lean formal-proof docstrings and expository proof comments) must use third-person scholarly register unless the block carries tags: ["non-scholarly-voice-exception"] with a rationale in notes. | Mathematical hedging phrases (Criterion 11). In addition to generic hedges, flag paper-specific patches that substitute for a derivation: simplifies the paper, provides the (mathematical framework|natural setting|canonical (duality|basis|framework)), and gives a canonical (functor|grading|ordering). Keep a phrase only when it is the canonical mathematical term of art (for example essentially surjective for a functor) or carries the explicit exception tag. | Category E — pdflatex Unicode crashes. Characters such as ↦ (U+21A6), ⁻ (U+207B), √ (U+221A), ─ (U+2500), ✅ (U+2705), ·, and ² crash pdflatex unless mapped in the preamble. Replace them with LaTeX math commands (\mapsto, ^{-1}, \sqrt{}, \cdot, ^{2}) or strip box-drawing characters; add \newunicodechar to the preamble only when a glyph is used corpus-wide. | Category H — Conditional-theorem banner exception. Migrate status banners such as > **Status: theorem (sorry-free)...** to authorNotes on the .ts manifest, except **Theorem (conditional on [conj:X])** banners that are structural parts of the theorem statement — keep those in prose. | Category J — Precision propositions. Empirical-fit phrasing (within X%, matches to Y ppm) is removed from published blocks unless the block itself is a proposition whose formal statement establishes a precision bound. | Kickbacks and proof trimming. In expository proofs, phrases like “We have shown…” or “It remains to verify…” that serve as proof structure require author judgement rather than mechanical deletion. For proofs containing genuine work-tracker language disguised as exposition, route to proof-conciseness. | .

f25347e6b5eb.title: Path containment — two questions that look like one
f25347e6b5eb.content: src/core/safe-path.ts is the implementation. The two checks are not interchangeable: . | you have | you want | use | . | a URL path (/a/b.html), possibly percent-encoded | the file it names inside a root | resolveWithin, then realPathWithin | . | a single identifier (paperId, a slug, a work item id) | one path segment, or a refusal | safeSegment / joinSegments | . | a path you are about to write that does not exist yet | containment despite an absent leaf | writableWithin | . Why not one function. resolveWithin relies on a URL pathname beginning with /, so normalize absorbs leading .. against the root and traversal by spelling cannot escape it. An identifier has no leading slash, so a/b passed to it resolves to a contained nested path. When the caller meant one directory, contained is not the question, and a collapsed check would accept it. The lexical check is the weaker half. resolve is string arithmetic and never touches the filesystem, so a symlink inside the root pointing out of it passes. realPathWithin catches it. writableWithin walks up to the nearest existing ancestor, because a target that does not exist yet has no realpath to compare.

4898fbbc66bf.title: Rules for a sink
4898fbbc66bf.content: Enumerate the sink shape, not a list of instances. Every join() reached from a request is a sink; a fix aimed at the sinks an audit listed leaves the ones it did not. Check every external value. A function that takes two external values (say paperId and rootName) needs both checked, which is why joinSegments checks every segment rather than the first. Check the value you were given, not the fallback. id = paperId || file.name.replace(/[^a-z0-9-]/gi, "-") sanitises only the branch nobody attacks. A file name needs basename AND safeSegment, in that order. basename reduces ../../etc/passwd to passwd, but basename("..") is "..", which is not a name. Either alone admits something. Ask where each element of a parsed structure came from. A list of member names read from a stored manifest was written from user input, so validating the identifier alone leaves a read reachable through a member name. Where a member may legitimately sit in a subdirectory, the check is realPathWithin (containment), not safeSegment. A refused read and a refused write behave differently. A reader that already returns [] for “nothing there” returns [] on refusal and logs, since a traversal attempt and a typo look identical in an empty array. A writer throws, because a refused write has no correct no-op: the caller believes the item was saved. The gate, and what it cannot do . scripts/tests/server-path-sinks.test.ts is a source ratchet: it proves the guard has not been deleted, never that a value is checked on every path to a sink. It asserts its own non-vacuity, because a renamed server would otherwise make every not.toContain pass.

19ed5e6e8006.title: pcf-consent
19ed5e6e8006.content: Skill id: pcf-consent · Package: fhir-ig-authoring · Instance: fhir-harness · Modules: schemas/pcf-consent.ts (consentToOdrl, decide, evaluatePcfPolicy, PCF_IMPLICIT_POLICY_SETS), schemas/iti-108-consent-client.ts (findAccessConsents, Iti108ConsentClient), schemas/odrl-to-fhir-r5-permission.ts. Model patient privacy consent directives in FHIR Implementation Guides, translate them into W3C ODRL 2.2 policies, and evaluate three-valued access-control decisions (permit | deny | unknown). Standards and scope: . | Specifications: IHE IT Infrastructure Technical Framework Supplement — Privacy Consent on FHIR (PCF) 1.1.0 (Trial Implementation, 2023-08-04) and HL7 FHIR R4 Consent (Trial Use, FMG maturity level 2). | Profiles: IHE PCF Basic (IHE.PCF.consentBasic) and Additional PurposeOfUse (IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate: extended HL7 PurposeOfUse codes and nested provision exceptions). The translator also handles IHE.PCF.consentAdvanced security-label sensitivity tags when declared. | Referenced by canonical URL only: never copy or re-author IHE PCF StructureDefinitions or ValueSets in an IG; pin the upstream packages in sushi-config.yaml and reference IHE profiles and value sets by their canonical URLs. | No IUA claim: do not claim conformance to IHE Internet User Authorization (IUA), and do not profile ITI-71 / ITI-103 OAuth token exchange; HTTP Authorization headers on ITI-108 reads are passed through opaque to the transport. | Trust-anchor neutral: any consent-bearing workflow or verifiable link depends on an abstract trust anchor (a national PKI, a regional federation, did:web, the Global Digital Health Certification Network (GDHCN), …); none is hardcoded. | .

142aa2f6d312.title: 1. Model — Authoring IHE PCF 1.1.0 Consent in a FHIR IG
142aa2f6d312.content: 1.1 Package dependencies in sushi-config.yaml . An IG that profiles, instantiates, or references IHE PCF consent directives or Verifiable Health Links pins the upstream IHE packages in sushi-config.yaml and references their artefacts by canonical URL only: . dependencies: ihe.iti.pcf: id: ihe_iti_pcf uri: https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/ImplementationGuide/ihe.iti.pcf version: 1.1.0 ihe.iti.vhl: id: ihe_iti_vhl uri: https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/ImplementationGuide/ihe.iti.vhl version: 1.0.0-comment . FHIR R4 Consent in an R5 IG (could-not-determine): ihe.iti.pcf@1.1.0 is an R4 (4.0.1) package. When an R5 (fhirVersion: 5.0.0) IG compiles against it and SUSHI or the IG Publisher rejects cross-version R4-in-R5 profile resolution, report that cross-version outcome explicitly as could-not-determine with the exact tool diagnostic rather than silently dropping the dependency or hand-copying the profile. 1.2 Canonical URLs (never re-declared locally) . Reference the IHE PCF profiles, value sets, and HL7 code systems by their canonical URLs exported in fhir-harness/schemas/pcf-consent.ts: . | Artefact | Canonical URL | Constant in schemas/pcf-consent.ts | . | PCF Implementation Guide | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF | PCF_IG_CANONICAL | . | PCF Basic Consent profile | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/StructureDefinition/IHE.PCF.consentBasic | PCF_CONSENT_BASIC_PROFILE | . | PCF Intermediate Consent profile | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/StructureDefinition/IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate | PCF_CONSENT_INTERMEDIATE_PROFILE | . | PCF Advanced Consent profile | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/StructureDefinition/IHE.PCF.consentAdvanced | PCF_CONSENT_ADVANCED_PROFILE | . | PCF Basic Purpose ValueSet | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/ValueSet/BasicPurposeVS | PCF_BASIC_PURPOSE_VS | . | PCF Advanced Security Tag ValueSet | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/ValueSet/AdvancedSecurityTagVS | PCF_ADVANCED_SECURITY_TAG_VS | . | HL7 v3 ActReason (PurposeOfUse) | http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-ActReason | HL7_ACT_REASON_SYSTEM | . | HL7 v3 Confidentiality | http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-Confidentiality | HL7_CONFIDENTIALITY_SYSTEM | . | HL7 v3 ActCode | http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-ActCode | HL7_ACT_CODE_SYSTEM | . | HL7 v3 ParticipationType | http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-ParticipationType | HL7_PARTICIPATION_TYPE_SYSTEM | . | HL7 ConsentScope | http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/consentscope | HL7_CONSENT_SCOPE_SYSTEM | . | LOINC Privacy policy / Consent | http://loinc.org (59284-0) | LOINC_SYSTEM / LOINC_CONSENT_CODE | . 1.3 Required structure of a PCF Consent instance . Every conformant IHE PCF 1.1.0 Consent resource carries: . | meta.profile: one of IHE.PCF.consentBasic, IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate, or IHE.PCF.consentAdvanced (detectPcfProfile(consent) inspects meta.profile and falls back to structural inspection). | status: "active" for an enforceable consent directive ("draft", "proposed", "rejected", "inactive", and "entered-in-error" carry no active permissions or prohibitions). | scope: http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/consentscope#patient-privacy. | category: includes http://loinc.org#59284-0 (Consent). | patient: reference to the Patient subject (Patient/<id>). | dateTime and performer (the consenting patient or authorized representative, which becomes the ODRL assigner) and organization (the custodian organization). | sourceReference or sourceAttachment: the signed paper/electronic consent artifact or questionnaire response. | policy: policy[].uri naming the overarching privacy policy (such as one of the four IHE PCF Volume 1 §1:53.2.1 implicit policy URIs). | provision: root provision (type: "permit" or "deny"), purpose codings from http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-ActReason (TREAT, HPAYMT, HOPERAT in BasicPurposeVS, or extended PurposeOfUse codes such as HRESCH, CLINTRCH, BIORCH, PUBHLTH, ETREAT, BTG, PATRQT), optional period, actor, action, dataPeriod, data, securityLabel, and optional nested provision.provision exceptions. | . No draft purpose vocabularies: W3C DPV is a Community Group report and is refused (dpv:* or /dpv returns false in isKnownHl7PurposeOfUse). Always use HL7 v3 ActReason PurposeOfUse codes.

b1cb98c925f7.title: 2. Translate — consentToOdrl() and the Four Implicit Policies
b1cb98c925f7.content: consentToOdrl(consent, options) in fhir-harness/schemas/pcf-consent.ts translates a FHIR R4 Consent into a W3C ODRL 2.2 Set policy (PcfOdrlSet). 2.1 Field-by-field mapping (Consent → ODRL Set) . | FHIR R4 Consent element | ODRL 2.2 Set element | Translation rule | . | id + meta.versionId | uid | consentPolicyUid(consent) → urn:ihe:pcf:consent:<id>:v<versionId> (or urn:ihe:pcf:consent:<id> when unversioned). | . | performer[0] (fallback patient) | assigner | The party granting or withholding consent. | . | status !== "active" | permission: [], prohibition: [] | Non-active consents emit an empty Set, which evaluates to "unknown" (or defers to implicitPolicy). | . | provision.type ("permit" / "deny") | permission / prohibition | Root provision defaults to "permit" when provision.type is omitted, per FHIR R4 Consent.provision.type. | . | provision.purpose[] (v3-ActReason) | constraint (odrl:purpose) | Each HL7 PurposeOfUse code becomes { leftOperand: "odrl:purpose", operator: "odrl:isA", rightOperand: code }, so ontological parent codes (TREAT, HRESCH, ETREAT, …) permit their sub-concepts (CLINTRL, BTG, CLINTRCH, BIORCH, …) via broaderOrSelf over HL7_PURPOSE_OF_USE (IHE PCF Vol 3 §3:5.8.2). Non-HL7 local project codes become odrl:eq. Multiple purpose codings expand into one rule per purpose (logical OR). | . | provision.period (start, end) | constraint (odrl:dateTime) | period.start → { leftOperand: "odrl:dateTime", operator: "odrl:gteq", rightOperand: start }; period.end → { leftOperand: "odrl:dateTime", operator: "odrl:lteq", rightOperand: end }. Date-only bounds (YYYY-MM-DD) expand to 00:00:00.000Z (start) and 23:59:59.999Z (end). | . | provision.actor[].reference | assignee | One rule per actor reference; defaults to ANYONE ("*") when actor is omitted. | . | provision.action[] | action | "read" → "odrl:display", "correct" → "odrl:modify", "access" / "collect" / "use" / "disclose" (and default) → "odrl:use". | . | provision.data[] (meaning: "instance") | target | Direct resource references (DocumentReference/ex-doc, Observation/ex-obs) become rule targets. | . | provision.data[] ("authoredby" / "related") | constraint (pcf:author / pcf:encounter) | meaning: "authoredby" → leftOperand: "pcf:author"; meaning: "related" → leftOperand: "pcf:encounter". | . | provision.dataPeriod | constraint (pcf:dataPeriod) | Clinical data creation/effective period (odrl:gteq / odrl:lteq on pcf:dataPeriod). | . | provision.securityLabel[] | constraint (pcf:securityLabel) | Confidentiality / sensitivity tags (R, V, ETH, PSY, SDV, HIV, …) become odrl:eq or odrl:isAnyOf on pcf:securityLabel. | . | Nested provision.provision[] | permission / prohibition + conflict | Child provisions inherit parent period (intersected via mergePeriods). A root permit with nested deny exceptions sets conflict: "odrl:prohibit". A root deny with nested permit exceptions (e.g. dissent except for Break-Glass BTG) sets conflict: "odrl:perm". | . 2.2 The four IHE PCF Volume 1 §1:53.2.1 implicit-policy Sets . When a patient has no explicit active Consent on file (or when their explicit Consent has expired), IHE PCF Volume 1 §1:53.2.1 and §1:53.4.2.4 define four overarching jurisdictional baseline policies, exported in PCF_IMPLICIT_POLICY_SETS and resolved by getImplicitPolicySet(uriOrAlias): . | Canonical URI (PCF_POLICY_*_URI) | Alias(es) | Constant | Semantics | . | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/Policy-basic-normal | "basic-normal" | PCF_IMPLICIT_BASIC_NORMAL_SET | Permit Clinical Treatment: permits odrl:use when odrl:purpose isA TREAT (including ETREAT, BTG, CLINTRL, POPHLTH); non-treatment purposes return deny. | . | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/Policy-all-normal | "all-normal", "opt-out" | PCF_IMPLICIT_ALL_NORMAL_SET | Permit All Authorized (opt-out baseline): permits odrl:use when odrl:purpose isA PurposeOfUse. | . | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/Policy-break-glass-only | "break-glass-only" | PCF_IMPLICIT_BREAK_GLASS_ONLY_SET | Break-Glass Only: prohibits all uses except when odrl:purpose isA BTG (medical patient-safety override). | . | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/Policy-deny | "deny", "opt-in" | PCF_IMPLICIT_DENY_SET | Deny All (opt-in baseline): prohibits all odrl:use until an explicit active Consent permits access. | .

257adb3b878f.title: 3. Decide — Three-Valued Evaluation, ITI-108 Reads, obtainConsent, and PROV Citations
257adb3b878f.content: 3.1 decide() and evaluatePcfPolicy() (permit | deny | unknown) . decide(consentOrPolicy, req, options) in fhir-harness/schemas/pcf-consent.ts evaluates a PcfDecisionRequest (actor, actorRoles, actorGroups, action, and scope / top-level purpose, dateTime, target, securityLabel, dataPeriod, author, encounter): . | Active explicit Consent governs: if one or more active, non-expired Consent resources (or translated PcfOdrlSets) are supplied, any deny across them returns "deny" (odrl:prohibit), any "permit" (with no "deny") returns "permit", and unresolved scope operands return "unknown". | Missing Scope Operand is "unknown", never "permit": if a rule constrains odrl:purpose, odrl:dateTime, pcf:securityLabel, target, or assignee and the request omits that dimension, evaluation yields "unknown". Under conflict: "odrl:perm" (such as a root deny with a Break-Glass permit exception), if the exception’s constraint is unresolved, evaluatePcfPolicy() returns "unknown" rather than prematurely denying before purpose is supplied. | Expired or absent Consent: . | If options.implicitPolicy is provided, decide() falls back to the configured implicit-policy Set (IHE PCF Vol 1 §1:53.2.2 & §1:53.4.2.5). | If no implicitPolicy is configured: an expired active Consent returns "deny", and an absent or non-active Consent returns "unknown" — never a silent "permit". | . | . 3.2 Reading consents via IHE ITI-108 (findAccessConsents) . findAccessConsents(query) and Iti108ConsentClient in fhir-harness/schemas/iti-108-consent-client.ts implement the IHE ITI-108 (Find Access Consent, [ITI-108]) RESTful search transaction (GET <baseUrl>/Consent) as a Consent Consumer: . | Search parameters (buildIti108SearchUrl): patient / patient.identifier, status (defaults to "active"), actor, purpose, security-label, period, date, data, _profile, and _count. | Client-side validity filtering (evaluateConsentValidity / filterIti108Bundle): every Bundle.entry.resource of type Consent is verified against FhirConsentSchema. Entries whose status !== "active", whose patient does not match the queried patient, or whose provision.period is expired (end < now) or future-dated (start > now) are excluded from consents and recorded in ignored[] with a structured Iti108IgnoredReason ("not-active", "expired", "not-yet-valid", "patient-mismatch", "invalid-period", "invalid-consent"). | Third-state failure handling (status: "unknown"): network failures, DNS errors, request timeouts, non-2xx HTTP responses, malformed JSON, non-searchset payloads, or OperationOutcome errors return { status: "unknown", reason, detail } — never an empty consents: [] that a caller could mistake for “no consent on file”. When passing an ITI-108 result into decide(), check result.status === "unknown" first and propagate "unknown". | . 3.3 Fulfilling odrl:obtainConsent duties on DSAs via injected createPcfConsentEvaluator . cat-harness/schemas/content/odrl.ts holds no FHIR resource types or pcf:* keys. A Data Sharing Agreement (@type: "Agreement") carrying an { action: "odrl:obtainConsent" } duty evaluates consent through an injected consentEvaluator: createPcfConsentEvaluator(consents, options) callback from fhir-harness/schemas/pcf-consent.ts, which returns { verdict, consent: { id, versionId, uid } } to permits() / permitsWithConsent() / decideWithConsent(): . | DSA + no Consent (or unreachable ITI-108 registry) → "unknown": when odrl:obtainConsent is due and no active matching PCF Consent (or consent-verification record) is provided, permits() returns "unknown". | DSA + matching deny Consent (or expired Consent) → "deny": when the patient’s PCF Consent denies the requested actor, action, purpose, or target, the decision is "deny". | DSA + matching active permit Consent → "permit": when an active, in-period PCF Consent permits the request’s actor, action, purpose, and target (and any other DSA constraints and duties hold), permits() returns "permit". | . 3.3a Consent rules for agreements . Four rules govern consent-based agreements. Rules 2 and 4 are enforced here; rules 1 and 3 are authored in the agreement itself (the dsa document kind and its lifecycle process in folio-assistant-core). | Legal basis. An agreement carries odrl:obtainConsent only when consent is its legal basis. Agreements resting on treatment, public-health law or a research waiver carry no such duty, and this evaluator is never asked. | Version pinning. A Consent names the agreement’s fixed-version URL in R4 Consent.policy.uri. createPcfConsentEvaluator counts a Consent only when that URI equals the agreement’s version (the agreement policy’s uid, or agreementPolicyUri); consentsCitingAgreement() is the filter. An amendment that widens use is a new version URL, so the old Consent no longer counts. An amendment that narrows use needs no new consent: pass the agreement’s DCAT 3 version chain as agreementVersions (each version’s ODRL policy and its dcat:previousVersion), and an older Consent still counts while every step back to its version is a narrowing amendment. isNarrowingAmendment() decides that from the ODRL rules alone: every newer permission sits inside an older one (same or narrower action, same target and assignee, each older constraint matched by one at least as tight, each older duty kept), and every older prohibition and obligation remains. A widening step, a missing version or anything it cannot compare (such as inheritFrom) stops the walk, and new consent is needed. | Plain language. Every agreement that needs consent publishes a plain-language summary, hashed with the agreement. That summary is what the person consents to. | Scale. The jurisdiction picks one of PCF’s implicit default policies (opt-in or opt-out) and passes it as implicitPolicy. Registry reads may be cached: new Iti108ConsentClient(base, defaults, { ttlMs }). An entry ends at its TTL, at the earliest provision.period.end of its Consents, or when consentWithdrawn(id) is called for one of its Consents. | . 3.4 Citing Consent.id + Consent.meta.versionId in PROV-O decision records . Every consent-based access decision recorded in the hash-chained W3C PROV-O decision log (cat-harness/schemas/content/prov.ts, cat-harness-tools/src/workflow/prov-record.ts) must cite the exact Consent resource version used: . | Use extractConsentCitation(consent) / consentPolicyUid(consent) from fhir-harness/schemas/pcf-consent.ts to obtain { id, versionId, uid, status, patient, performer, policyUris }. | Include the translated consent policy uid (urn:ihe:pcf:consent:<id>:v<versionId>) in "cat-harness:underPolicy" on the prov:Activity decision record alongside the governing DSA Agreement uid, and record the Consent’s id and meta.versionId citation so any auditor can verify which version of the patient’s consent directive was in force when the decision hash (cat-harness:recordHash chained via cat-harness:previousHash) was computed. | . 3.5 One-way renderer: ODRL 2.2 Agreement to FHIR R5 Permission (output only) . HL7 FHIR R5 Permission (Trial Use) is output only: W3C ODRL 2.2 is the source of truth and nothing reads Permission back. schemas/odrl-to-fhir-r5-permission.ts provides odrlAgreementToFhirR5Permission(agreement, options) and fhirR5PermissionToFsh(permission, options): . | FhirR5PermissionSchema and its required value-set code lists are built from hl7.fhir.r5.core#5.0.0’s StructureDefinition-Permission.json and CodeSystem-*.json (permission-status, permission-rule-combining, consent-provision-type, consent-data-meaning), so no field outside FHIR R5 Permission is ever invented. | Maps conflict (prohibit / perm) to combining (deny-overrides / permit-overrides); assigner to asserter; shared dateTime constraints to validity; the agreement’s fixed-version uid and dcterms:source to justification.evidence / justification.basis; permission / prohibition to rule.type (permit / deny); target to rule.data.resource; assignee, action (consentaction), and purpose (HL7 v3-ActReason PurposeOfUse) to rule.activity; and delete duty roughly to rule.limit (v3-ActCode#DELAU). | Every ODRL 2.2, DCAT 3, or SPDX term with no exact home in FHIR R5 Permission (including @type, profile, inheritFrom, spdx:checksum, isA, exclusive lt/gt bounds, elapsedTime, refinement, and duties or duty constraints) is returned explicitly in dropped: DroppedOdrlTerm[] rather than dropped silently. | .

4185833e12a3.title: Inline PDF viewer — a pinned pdf.js, installed at build time
4185833e12a3.content: Skill id: pdf-inline-viewer · Package: ui-core · Tools pdf-viewer-install, pdf-viewer-embed · Code cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-viewer.ts . A lightweight inline viewer for PDFs on a CDN: search, scroll, jump to page, print and download. pdf.js is copied onto the built site (not loaded from a CDN) and loaded lazily.

3b41185edaec.title: The two acts, and which Tool does each
3b41185edaec.content: | act | who does it | Tool | . | put the viewer into a built site | the site workflow, once per build | pdf-viewer-install | . | show one PDF on one page | a page generator, once per page | pdf-viewer-embed (TypeScript: embed() from pdf-viewer.ts) | . docs-site.yml and feature-staging.yml both run the install right after mount-instance-docs.ts, passing --allow for the repository owner’s cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/<owner>/ and raw.githubusercontent.com/<owner>/. Nothing of pdf.js is committed. The viewer lives at <site root>/assets/vendor/pdfjs/ in the built site only.

911e9a4bfcc9.title: May this page embed this document? The publication gate decides, not you
911e9a4bfcc9.content: An embed is a link that also renders. So it follows the same rule as the download link: if the bitstream’s publication gates (copyright, restrictions) are not permitted, the page gets no viewer: the embed returns nothing whenever the download link would be withheld, and the page says only “held here, not published”. Never embed a document to “just preview” it. A preview is publication.

7a1a19e93a78.title: Why the viewer opens only allowlisted hosts
7a1a19e93a78.content: The pdf.js generic viewer refuses a cross-origin ?file=. That is validateFileURL, whose error is “file origin does not match viewer’s”. It refuses so that a hosted viewer cannot be pointed at any document and lend it the host’s address. Our PDFs are on a CDN, not on Pages, so the build adds a shim (folio-open.js) that opens ?src= instead. It opens a URL only when the URL starts with an --allow prefix, or is on the viewer’s own origin. Anything else is refused on screen and never fetched. | A prefix is a prefix, not a substring. https://evil.example/cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/<owner>/x.pdf is refused, and a unit test pins that. | An empty allowlist is a usage error, not a default. Forgetting --allow would otherwise ship a viewer that refuses every CDN document while the build reports success. Write --allow same-origin-only when that really is what you want. | .

6764ed943b77.title: Three things measured rather than assumed (pdf.js 6.4.299)
6764ed943b77.content: All three are listed under binds in the pdfjs entry of upstream-pins.json, so a version bump re-checks them. | The modern build needs a very new browser. It calls Map.prototype.getOrInsertComputed. Chromium 140 lacks it, threw during startup and never opened the document. The install uses the legacy build, which carries its own polyfills. | webviewerloaded fires on parent.document when the viewer is framed by a same-origin page, and on its own document only otherwise. An embed on this site is the same-origin case, so a listener on document alone never fires and the frame stays empty. The shim listens on both, and checks detail.source. | defaultUrl is the tracemonkey sample paper. The shim sets it to empty, so a missing or refused ?src= shows an empty viewer rather than somebody else’s document. | .

a97794659739.title: The embed, and what it does when it cannot work
a97794659739.content: . | Site root from the browser. One generated page is served at several depths (/<folio>/, /folio-assistant/<folio>/, /branches/<branch>/<folio>/). The caller passes the route pattern, using the folio-mount.ts convention (group 1 is the root), and the inlined client applies it. A page off the route gets a frame saying so, never a 404 inside the frame. | Lazy. The frame is pointed at the viewer only when it comes within 200px of the viewport. This uses an IntersectionObserver, because how engines treat loading="lazy" on a script-set src varies. A reader who never scrolls there downloads nothing. | Plain links always. “Open the PDF on its own” and “Download” sit under the frame whether or not the viewer works. They are not a fallback that appears on failure. | .

253ec45a23d7.title: Caching: why the frame’s address carries a version tag
253ec45a23d7.content: GitHub Pages serves every file with max-age=600 through a CDN, so a hard reload can still be answered from a copy up to ten minutes old. | The frame’s address ends &v=<rev>.<deploy>. <rev> is VIEWER_REV, a hash of the pinned release, the shim and the patch. <deploy> comes from the host page’s document.lastModified, which Pages sets at deploy time. So the frame is exactly as fresh as the page around it. A reader who sees the new page gets the new viewer. | The shim is fetched as folio-open.js?v=<rev>, so a change to it cannot be masked by a cached copy. | Where a server sends no Last-Modified (a local preview), the browser reports the current time, so the frame is simply never cached there. That is correct, just slower. | . The outer page itself is outside this. If the green staging banner shows an older commit than the deploy, the whole page is a cached copy. Wait out the ten minutes, or use a private window.

f9f02f297a0d.title: The site’s own post-build passes leave the viewer alone
f9f02f297a0d.content: viewer.html is Mozilla’s markup with one <script> added. minify-site.ts skips it (rewriting it would ship bytes no pdf.js release contains), and check:duplicate-ids and publish-verify’s html-unique-ids count it out of scope, not passed. It declares id="buttons" twice upstream. That finding is real, and nobody here can fix it without forking pdf.js. They ask isVendoredViewer(), so there is one answer to “is this ours”. The two passes that INJECT into every page skip it too. These are the staging banner and the standalone navigation rail; otherwise both draw inside the PDF frame. Any new pass that writes into every *.html in _site owes the same exclusion. standalone-rail.test.ts and pdf-viewer.test.ts each assert it for the existing two.

b6c43b5eaf8d.title: Cost
b6c43b5eaf8d.content: About a 7 MB download per build, adding about 12 MB (404 files) to the built site. The size matters most for staging previews, each of which carries its own copy on gh-pages. bun run cat health reports the size of gh-pages. Nothing is added to a clone.

05d3cac017b2.title: Verifying a change here
05d3cac017b2.content: Unit tests (cat-harness-tools/scripts/tests/pdf-viewer.test.ts) run the shipped shim and client against stubs: the allowlist, the parent-document listener, the root derivation at three depths, and lazy loading. They cannot check that pdf.js opens, searches and prints. For that, install into a scratch site with --zip, serve it, and drive it in a browser (see rendered-verification). Check, and screenshot for the author: the page count shows, a search finds matches, the page box jumps, print and download are present, and a narrow viewport does not load the viewer until it is scrolled to.

539be45e918e.title: /pending-show — what is this session working on?
539be45e918e.content: Quick status display. Read-only. Run any time to answer “where am I?” or “what did I say I was going to do?”.

2b54716453d6.title: What it shows
2b54716453d6.content: In order: . | Current branch + PR. Branch name, PR number (if open), PR title. | Work items list. Current in-progress or todo work items for this session (via beans list). | Goal scope. From STATUS.md: which goal(s) the current PR touches. | Master ledger intent. The “INTENT” cell of the current session-log row in docs/coordination/<goal>.md. | .

a42b16c8a574.title: Output format (compact)
a42b16c8a574.content: ## Session pending — 2026-01-01 14:32 UTC Branch: claude/<feature-slug> PR: #1580 — <PR title> Beans (via `beans list`): [epic-123] Session tracker (In Progress) [task-124] Subtask 1 (Completed) [task-125] Subtask 2 (In Progress) Goal: <goal-slug> (also touches: <other-goal>) Ledger intent (docs/coordination/<goal>.md): (1) create ledger + STATUS.md, (2) coord with #1577, .

b1a3f567524d.title: Implementation
b1a3f567524d.content: This is a thin reader. No writes. Sources (read order): . | git branch --show-current | mcp__github__list_pull_requests({head: "<branch>"}) for PR number | Run the CLI tool beans list to find tasks matching the current scope. | STATUS.md — find row where “Active PRs” contains current PR | docs/coordination/<goal>.md — find session-log row for current branch | .

293af080bd5f.title: When to invoke
293af080bd5f.content: . | User asks “what are you working on?” / “what’s left?” / “status?”. | Mid-session checkpoint — ensure ledger is consistent with Work items state. | Before a context handoff (compaction event, end of session). | .

b80ef19f90db.title: Pickup Skill
b80ef19f90db.content: Continue work on existing open change proposals — pull requests (PRs) — with minimal wasted tokens. This skill exists because the expensive failure mode is acting on a remembered or assumed branch name / scope and then re-discovering reality mid-task. The cure is: resolve ground truth first, in one batch, then dispatch. Read repo-root AGENTS.md first. This skill operates under the branch/PR workflow, the project’s production-vs-exploratory and content validation discipline, and CI-billing-failure rules. It does not override them.

f0af9bfbb8f7.title: Hard rules
f0af9bfbb8f7.content: . | NEVER trust a remembered branch name or PR title. A PR number is the only stable handle. git ls-remote / a branch you “recall” is not — branch names drift and a PR number you were given may map to a different PR than its scope suggests. Always resolve head.ref, title, and body checklist by reading the PR (the read change proposal forge-operation Tool) for the literal number before doing anything. | A review targets a commit SHA — re-verify the nit is still live. Gemini/Copilot review the commit at review time. Later commits on the branch may have already fixed the flagged issue. Before “fixing” anything from a review, grep the current file: if eval( / the unused symbol / the dead dict is already gone, reply noting it’s resolved — do not re-apply or hallucinate a fix. | Verify the file before trusting any description of it — including the review’s, the PR body’s, and your own earlier read if the output looked corrupted. Read the real bytes (capture to a temp file and Read it if terminal display garbles output). | Commit-early in every sub-agent. Long sub-agents hit idle/stream timeouts. A sub-agent that explores for 80 tool-calls then dies without committing loses everything. Brief sub-agents to commit after the first substantive edit and push after each commit. | Classify CI before diagnosing it. Multiple jobs failing in ≤5 s with identical started_at is the GitHub Actions billing signature, not a code failure (integration-watcher §5f). Do not push retrigger commits; note it and move on. Real failures take ≥30 s. | Never merge. Merge needs explicit user permission via /prepare-merge. This skill prepares and reports; it does not merge. | .

16acc32061eb.title: Arguments
16acc32061eb.content: /pickup <PR#> [<PR#> ...] # full pickup: discover + dispatch each /pickup <PR#> --reviews-only # just apply the safe review-nit fixes /pickup <PR#> --discover-only # print the resolved brief, do not dispatch . With no arg, ask the user which open PR(s) to pick up (offer the recently-updated claude/* PRs, listed with the list change proposals forge-operation Tool).

e1841bb45429.title: Procedure
e1841bb45429.content: Step 0 — Load tools . Resolve the forge-operation Tools from the tools graph, picking the node for the forge the checkout’s remote is on (skills-and-tools). This skill uses read change proposal (details, check runs, reviews, review comments), list change proposals, comment on change proposal and request review. Where the session offers the Tool’s MCP arm, those tools are deferred — load them before Step 1; otherwise its shell arm serves. If neither is reachable, say so and stop: a PR not resolved is not ground truth. Step 1 — Resolve ground truth (ONE batched pass per PR) . For each PR number, in a single message issue parallel calls: . | read change proposal → head.ref (the REAL branch), title, body (checklist), base.ref, mergeable_state, state. Act on mergeable_state only when it reads dirty. This endpoint can serve a merged PR’s PRE-MERGE view for a long time, so clean and unknown can both be describing a PR that is already gone; unknown additionally means not computed yet rather than cannot be determined. For “has this landed?”, ask git: git merge-base --is-ancestor origin/<head> origin/<base>. | its check runs → CI state. | its reviews and review comments → review bodies + inline threads (these are often rate-limited; tolerate failure and proceed with what you have). | . Parse the body for unchecked - [ ] items — that is the work queue. Classify CI per Hard Rule 5. If --discover-only: print, per PR, the resolved branch, title, unchecked checklist items, CI verdict (billing/real/green), and open review nits. Stop. Step 2 — Triage review nits into safe vs unsafe . Safe class (auto-apply after re-verifying live per Hard Rule 2): . | eval( / exec( → ast.literal_eval (or a real parser). | Unused function / import / variable / dict removal (dead code). | Obvious typos in comments/docstrings. | f-string / format trivialities, missing r on regex literals. | . Unsafe class (never auto-apply — AskUserQuestion or defer): . | Anything touching math/numerics, a witness value, or a canonical formula (production-vs-exploratory discipline applies). | Anything changing a formal statement, a proof, or a content validation invariant. | Architectural / multi-file refactors, API changes. | A reviewer suggestion that conflicts with the PR’s stated intent. | . Step 3 — Dispatch one worktree sub-agent per PR . For each PR with non-trivial remaining work, spawn a background Agent(isolation: "worktree", run_in_background: true). The brief MUST contain (filled from Step 1, not assumed): . | the resolved branch name (git fetch origin <ref> + git checkout -B <ref> origin/<ref>; “do NOT create a new branch”); | the literal PR title + the unchecked checklist items; | the relevant AGENTS.md discipline pointers for that PR’s domain (content validation / production-vs-exploratory / formal-proof / precision-goals — whichever apply); | commit-early-and-push instruction (Hard Rule 4) with the session URL line for commit bodies and 4× exp-backoff push retry; | “validate before pushing content (bun run validate <paper>); never add a status field; do NOT open a new PR (it exists); do NOT merge”; | “if blocked on a bad premise / a gate / a missing toolchain, STOP and report — do NOT fabricate work or numbers.” | . Keep each brief single-focus where possible; a sub-agent with one clear deliverable is far less likely to time out than one with a broad survey. For purely mechanical review-nit fixes, do them inline (Step 4) rather than spawning an agent. Step 4 — Apply safe review-nit fixes inline . For --reviews-only or small nit batches, do it in the foreground via a temp worktree (keeps the working branch clean): . git worktree add -f /tmp/pick-wt <resolved-branch> # edit in /tmp/pick-wt, re-verify the nit is live first python3 -c "import ast,sys; ast.parse(open(P).read())" # syntax gate for .py # run the script/test if cheap, to confirm no behavior change git -C /tmp/pick-wt commit -am "<msg>"; push with retry git worktree remove --force /tmp/pick-wt . Commit message: style(<area>): <fix> — address <reviewer> review. Commit body ends with the session’s attribution lines. Step 5 — Reply frugally + report . | Reply to a review only if it resolves the thread or raises a question — be frugal. For “already fixed in a later commit” nits, one short note is enough; don’t reply per-nit. | If Copilot’s review errored (“unable to review”), request its review again (the request review forge-operation Tool). | Report per PR: resolved branch, what was done / dispatched, commit SHAs, CI verdict, blob URLs (.md primary), and any blocked items with reasons. Never claim a formal artifact compiles/verifies unless a checker actually confirmed it; say “verification pending” otherwise. | .

19b802190c35.title: Worktree hygiene
19b802190c35.content: Sub-agent worktrees are auto-locked while running. After completion, git worktree prune then git worktree remove --force .claude/worktrees/agent-<id> for finished ones. Remove any /tmp/*-wt you created. Never rm -rf a tracked path to “clean up” — check git ls-tree first (a path tracked on base is not leftover junk).

2e9fe5208a0d.title: Anti-patterns this skill prevents
2e9fe5208a0d.content: | Anti-pattern | Cost seen | Guard | . | Dispatch on assumed branch name | 3× ~10 min wasted sub-agents | Hard Rule 1 / Step 1 | . | Re-fix an already-fixed review nit | hallucinated edits | Hard Rule 2 / Step 2 | . | Trust corrupted tool output | wrong edit target | Hard Rule 3 / Step 4 | . | Sub-agent times out uncommitted | full progress loss | Hard Rule 4 / Step 3 | . | Diagnose billing CI as a code bug | retrigger churn | Hard Rule 5 / Step 1 | . | rm -rf a base-tracked dir | deleted real files | Worktree hygiene | .

693c849b159b.title: Placement — decide where it goes before you write it
693c849b159b.content: One question, answered before the first file exists: . Which instance owns this, which of its declared graphs does it go in, and what kind of node is it? . An agent that starts writing and works the answer out afterwards produces a node in the wrong repository, under a hardcoded path, named by a composed string. All three are silent: the tests pass, and the damage lands on the next consumer. This is a decision procedure. Four steps and a stop. Run it in order; the later steps are meaningless if an earlier one is a guess.

0ed753311a56.title: Step 1 — which instance?
0ed753311a56.content: folio-assistant is the platform, not the content. It holds skills, schemas, the pipeline and the MCP server an agent uses to author a folio — a paper, a WHO SMART Guideline, an IG — and the folio lives in a separate repository. Ask of the thing you are about to write: . Does this name, assume, or default to one folio? . A paper directory, a document title, a badge URL, an owner/repo, a Lake library prefix, a workflow filename, a simulator path, a licence block, a vocabulary, a constant with a subject-matter value. If the answer is yes, it does not belong in platform code. There are three destinations, not two, and collapsing the third is the common mistake: . | destination | what goes there | test | . | the platform | the mechanism, parameterised | the same code is correct for every folio | . | the folio’s tree | the subject matter itself | a reader of that folio would look for it | . | the folio’s config | the value the mechanism reads | it varies per folio but platform code needs it | . A value that varies per folio and is consumed by platform code is a config field — <name>.config.json, <name>.json, lakefile.toml — never a literal in a script and never a file the platform has to go and find. A Lake prefix, for example, is read from lakefile.toml, and left unprefixed when no lakefile names one, because a wrong namespace is worse than none. Do not infer the instance from the directory you are standing in. Read the declaration at the repository root, carrying name, stub and directories. basename($PWD) is not an identity — a repo cloned into a differently-named directory resolves to nothing, and reports no config rather than an error.

5545fc633394.title: Step 2 — which declared graph, and where does that instance put it?
5545fc633394.content: A node’s location is not a path you memorise. Every instance declares the directories it scans in <name>.json, and each entry names the kind of graph it holds — cat-harness (skills, roles, workflows, decisions, requirements, permissions), schemas, tools, qa, beans, folio and the rest. The vocabulary is open. | Ask for a skill, do not open a file. skill_list for what exists here, skill_fetch to load one, work_plan_prime for the work plan. With no MCP, resolve the graph from the declaration (readDeclaration in schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts) and read the directory it names. | In this repository the skills graph’s path is skills/. That is a fact about this instance, not a convention you may carry to another one. Ids are stable across a relocation; paths are not. | Overrides match on the entry’s id, never on its path. An instance that sites its knowledge graph elsewhere redeclares the same id with a different path. Matching on path makes two knowledge graphs out of one relocation, and every consumer then scans a directory that is not there. | Declare only what exists. A declared-but-absent directory is worse than an undeclared one: every consumer scans nothing and reports a clean run over it. | . Full rules, inheritance order and the three read states: directory-conventions.md. The docs graph, and the filing question it answers . docs is an authorable destination like the others, and the one an agent most often forgets to consider when it derives a destination list: deriving the list is not enough if the derivation drops a declared graph. What goes there: a design-memory asset — something produced while BUILDING, rather than the thing built. kg-contribution-offer carries the one question that identifies the class and why fsh-guts is the tempting wrong answer (its content may be thrown away; a design record’s value is that it survives). WHOSE docs/ comes first, and it is Step 1’s question again. Detailed information, design and planning for a harness, feature or tool go into that harness’s docs/: docs is a declared graph, and the instance that owns the feature owns the record of why it is shaped that way. A feature’s reasoning filed in the wrong instance’s docs/ reads fine and is unreachable from the place that needs it. Then where inside it, which is this skill’s question and not kg-contribution-offer’s: . | the asset is | it files under | . | why a subsystem is shaped as it is — requirements, options, rulings | <instance>/docs/architecture/, with parent: Architecture in the front matter | . | options for a decision not yet taken, with what each costs | <instance>/docs/proposals/, kind: proposal, and a row in its index.md | . | what was FOUND — prior art, a survey, a measurement, a comparison — that informs a decision without proposing one | <instance>/docs/research-and-analysis/, kind: research, and a row in its index.md | . | how a person does a task with it | <instance>/docs/guides/ | . | how to REACH a data source the content describes — endpoints, shapes, quirks | <instance>/docs/, beside the subject it serves | . | what a declared thing IS, generated from source | <instance>/docs/reference/ — never hand-edited | . Three rules that catch the usual mistakes: . | A design record is dated and says what it was true OF. It is history, so it carries the commit, PR or issue it describes. A record written in the present tense becomes a claim about today, and goes stale invisibly. | It states what it could NOT establish. A requirement referenced but never defined, a measurement not taken: named as such. A design record that reads complete when it is not is worse than a short one. | It is prose for a person, not instructions for an agent. If you find yourself writing “the agent SHALL”, it is a skill and it is in the wrong graph. | . The line between the two, stated as a test: . A skill carries what a competent practitioner needs IN ORDER TO DO the task. Anything beyond that is documentation. Background, derivations, options not taken, an API’s full surface when the task touches three calls: real, worth keeping, and none of it needed to act. Both directions fail silently — a skill that swallows them makes every agent read a chapter to find a rule, and a rule filed in docs/ because it arrived with context is a rule skill_fetch will never serve. Inheritance . An instance inherits its dependencies’ directories and skills, deepest dependency first and root last so the root wins: declarationChain + resolveDirectories for directories, and resolveSkillDirs in schemas/kg/harness-config.ts for the cross-instance skill overlay. So a skill placed in the platform reaches a downstream folio through its declaration; never copy a skill into the folio, which mints a second copy free to drift.

7ea57cdbdf74.title: Step 3 — which KIND of node?
7ea57cdbdf74.content: The axes below are distinct. Ask the separating question; do not pattern-match on what the thing resembles. | you are about to write | ask | the two answers | . | a new content type | does it need different code, or only different rules? | different code → an adapter; only rules → a profile plus a subclass | . | something a participant is or does | must the performer know it, or may the participant do it? | know → a skill, on the lane’s role; do → a permission, on the actor | . | a participant | does it persist across processes, or is it a position inside one? | persists → an actor; a position → a role, which is the BPMN swimlane | . | a sequence of steps | does it have actors, activities and a control flow? | yes → BPMN under the workflows directory, not a Mermaid fence and not prose | . | a branch at a gateway | is the answer computed from facts, or chosen by a person? | computed → a DMN table plus a <cat-harness.processes:decision/> ref; chosen → an ordinary gateway | . | a durable fact for one agent | does it govern, or summarise what governs? | governs → a skill; summarises → a memory entry under the memory nodes | . | subject matter | would a reader of one folio look for it? | yes → the folio, as data — never the platform | . Adapter vs profile is the expensive one. Adapters (paper, dak) partition block kinds into disjoint namespaces, and adapterForKind — what QA-criterion scoping reads — must stay total and unambiguous. Profiles (document, paper) nest: every document kind is also a paper kind. Making document a third adapter would make adapterForKind ambiguous on every shared kind. Actor / role / skill / permission. One sentence carries the model — an actor performs a task in a process as a role, using that role’s skills. Permissions stay on the actor: moving them onto Role, which looks right, conflicts wherever a permission is held by some but not all actors sharing a role. Resolution rules, how to bind a lane, and how to add a role: role-model.md. Do not re-derive them here. A .md under the cat-harness path that declares its own $schema is not a skill. The audit walks that directory recursively; declaration beats location, the same contract part-of: carries. Adding a graph typology is a registry change, not a new top-level directory. If nothing in the open vocabulary fits, that is a decision to hand over (Step 5), not one to settle by creating a folder.

ea08ff852d8e.title: Step 4 — which stub? There are two, and they are unrelated
ea08ff852d8e.content: This is the step most often skipped, because “stub” reads as one word. The agent-file stub — a pointer, never a home . AGENTS.md is the agent-generic source of truth. CLAUDE.md and GEMINI.md are thin stubs whose entire content is a pointer to it; scripts/init-folio.ts writes all three for a new folio. | Never put guidance in a stub. It reaches one tool’s agents and nobody else, and the other two stubs are then quietly wrong. | And prefer not to put it in AGENTS.md either. That file’s own banner says it: it is a bootstrap pointer, and the discipline lives in the skills graph. A rule that exists only in AGENTS.md is not in the generated reference, not in the published skill docs, and not found by an agent that went looking for the skill first. | . So: new guidance is a skill. Add a pointer from AGENTS.md if it needs one, and register the skill in its package manifest. The artefact stub — resolve it, never compose it . The declaration carries stub, the filename stem of every artefact this instance publishes. artefactStub() is the one function that answers it (stub when declared, otherwise name), and renderingPath() / siteDir() derive the published paths from it: . <base>/<name>/<stub>.jsonld <base>/<name>/<stub>.json <base>/<name>/<stub>.schema.json <base>/<stub>/ docs/<stub>/ . The graph document is under the instance’s own directory, the host’s included: one rule for every layer, with subjects beside their document (instance-publication §”Which base an @id is minted against”). Compose nothing; resolve everything. A hand-written path such as /kg/ 404s, because the real path comes out of renderingPath. A naive guess is not merely fragile, it is wrong on real instances. WHO’s SMART Base IG publishes under a stub shorter than its repository name, so “the stub is the repo name” fails on the reference implementation the convention was modelled on. The declaration file itself is NOT stub-named: it is <name>.json, found by findDeclarationFile() matching a file’s stem to its own name. Everything it describes is named after the stub, because by the time you fetch those you have read the declaration that names them.

7b9471261717.title: Step 5 — when you cannot tell, stop and ask
7b9471261717.content: Placement has three states, like everything else here: determined, determined-empty (this instance genuinely has no such directory — a real answer), and could-not-determine. The third is never to be rendered as the first. Do not guess and do not pick the repository you happen to be standing in. A misplaced node is not a typo: it is a second copy of something, free to drift, that a later agent will find and believe. Hand the decision over the way interaction-modality.md §4.1 requires — context → options with what each costs → your recommendation, marked → what happens if they say nothing → the question. The test is one pass: . Can the reader answer without opening anything? . Every identifier expanded on first use. A link is where somebody goes for more; it is never where the terms are defined. I need to place <thing>, which <one sentence on what it does>. Two candidates: A. <instance/graph> — costs <what this makes harder, concretely> B. <instance/graph> — costs <…> Recommend B, because <the property that decides it>. If you say nothing I will do B and note it in the PR body. A or B? .

6da12de23afc.title: The worked failure this skill exists to prevent
6da12de23afc.content: A platform script that writes a whole README holding one folio’s title, badges and licence destroys the README of every other folio it runs in, because prose about a folio belongs to that folio. Every step above catches it: Step 1, the content names one folio; Step 2, a helper path is composed rather than resolved; Step 4, published paths are built by convention and checked against nothing. The pattern that replaces it: the folio owns the file; the platform owns the markers, and writes a section only where the README carries its marker pair (readme-sections).

e209afe5b55d.title: Checklist
e209afe5b55d.content: Before you create a skill, role, actor, workflow, decision, schema, tool or content object: . | Instance — platform, folio, or the folio’s config? Does anything in it name one folio? | Graph — which declared entry, resolved from <name>.json by id? Not a path you remember. | Kind — which side of the separating question in Step 3, and can you say why in one sentence? | Stub — if it is guidance, is it a skill rather than a stub or AGENTS.md? If it publishes, does every path come from artefactStub() / renderingPath()? | Registered — bun run cat skill:register (skill-registration), and bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/gen-skill-docs.ts run, so the published mirror is not stale. | Could not determine? Stop. Ask in the Step 5 frame. Do not default to the repo you are in. | .

7aee924436a6.doc: A plan request stops at a signed-off plan
7aee924436a6.title: A plan request stops at a signed-off plan
7aee924436a6.content: A request for a plan always gets a requirements document and a work plan, handed to the user as links for review before any implementation. This operation lives in folio-assistant-core; the methods that say how requirements are gathered (crdm, spec-kit) stay in cat-harness, and each points here.

9fadf3471cba.doc: A plan request stops at a signed-off plan
9fadf3471cba.title: The trigger — a request for a plan
9fadf3471cba.content: Any of these, in the owner’s or a stakeholder’s words, is a plan request: . | “plan”, “make a plan”, “plan the …”, “what’s the plan for …” | “approach”, “what approach would you take” | “proposal”, “propose …”, “draft a proposal” | “how would you …” | “come up with …” | . Always — content requests included. “Plan the edits to chapter 3” is a plan request exactly as “plan the new validator” is. What changes between them is which methodology governs, never whether the gate applies. A request to do a thing is not a plan request, and does not acquire one by being large. That is the opening brief’s job (opening-brief), which is said in chat and does not stop.

20a2a9479126.doc: A plan request stops at a signed-off plan
20a2a9479126.title: What to produce — two artefacts
20a2a9479126.content: . | A requirements document. Every requirement in it follows the ONE definition in requirement-definition: a statement, a conformance level, a source, at least one success criterion with its verification method, and a sign-off owner. | A work plan. Beans — one or more per requirement — each naming the req: statements it delivers and carrying a ## Done when copied from their success criteria. The rule and the shape are in requirement-definition §”The work plan is beans”. | .

d8509f5a618d.doc: A plan request stops at a signed-off plan
d8509f5a618d.title: Where they go — the methodology decides, the gate does not
d8509f5a618d.content: Which methodology governs is decided by the existing fork in crdm-detect §”Which requirements methodology”. This skill does not re-decide it, and never blends the two (methodology-adoption). | methodology | requirements document | work plan | . | crdm — stakeholder-facing, the answer depends on a folio’s subject | committed under the owning harness’s docs/proposals/ | beans on the same branch, linked from the document | . | spec-kit — platform capability, content-agnostic | the spec, posted as a comment on the governing issue (never a specs/ directory — spec-kit says why) | beans, linked from the spec comment | . Either way the issue is the review surface: a CRDM document is linked from a comment on it, a spec-kit spec IS a comment on it.

d3d816ca1555.doc: A plan request stops at a signed-off plan
d3d816ca1555.title: Hand over both as permalinks (STRICT)
d3d816ca1555.content: Every link handed to the user is an absolute GitHub permalink: . https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/blob/<sha>/<path> . — with the commit sha, never a branch name, and never a repo-relative path: . | A repo-relative path is not a link. docs/proposals/x.md in chat is clickable only when the reader’s working directory is that repository, and a person reviewing from claude.ai or a phone has none. | A branch link moves. The document the owner signs off must be the document that was reviewed; a link to blob/<branch>/ shows whatever was pushed since. The sha pins it. | . Get the sha after pushing: git rev-parse HEAD, then compose https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/blob/<sha>/<path>. An issue comment is already absolute (…/issues/<n>#issuecomment-<id>). This binds every hand-over — a turn report, a PR body, an issue comment — not only a plan; turn-reporting rule 8 points here.

84ccce2989c2.doc: A plan request stops at a signed-off plan
84ccce2989c2.title: Then STOP until sign-off is recorded on the issue (STRICT)
84ccce2989c2.content: After posting both links, the agent ends the turn. The requirements document is a requirement set at stage proposed (requirement-definition §”The document is a requirement set”). No implementation — no schema edit, no script, no skill text, no content block — until sign-off is recorded on the issue: a comment from the sign-off owner (or quoting them verbatim, with date) saying the plan is approved, or approving it with changes — and the decision is then recorded as a requirement-signoff attestation that moves the set to approved, which check:requirements refuses unless the signer is a human. Silence is not sign-off. A reaction is not sign-off. An approval in chat is real but not yet recorded: the agent quotes it on the issue, dated, before starting. What is allowed before sign-off: the requirements document and its revisions (docs/proposals/ or the issue), the beans that ARE the work plan, and the branch and draft PR that carry them — continual-progress still applies to the plan itself. This gate does not replace the methodology’s own sign-off steps. CRDM’s stakeholder sign-off (crdm-signoff.bpmn, crdm-close.bpmn) and spec-kit’s spec-before-code gate run unchanged; this is the point at which a plan request reaches them, not a second set of them. A breach is detectable . No commit outside docs/proposals/ and beans/ lands on the branch before the sign-off comment’s timestamp. A reviewer checks it by hand: compare git log --format='%cI %H' --name-only on the branch against the sign-off comment’s created_at.

0f444139de45.doc: A plan request stops at a signed-off plan
0f444139de45.title: What this does NOT mean
0f444139de45.content: . | It does not mean every request gets a requirements document. Only a request for a plan does. A request to fix a typo is a fix. | It does not mean the agent asks permission to write the plan. Writing it is the request; stopping comes after. | It does not mean the plan must be long. A two-requirement plan with two beans is a plan, and is reviewed faster than a long one. | .

086b61b6e5f8.doc: A plan request stops at a signed-off plan
086b61b6e5f8.title: Cross-references
086b61b6e5f8.content: . | requirement-definition — the one definition of a requirement, and the work-plan rule | crdm-detect, spec-kit — the methods, which point here | issue-working — what an issue is for, against a PR and a bean | .

556db6839cb6.title: The platform’s own gates — run what CI will run
556db6839cb6.content: One command: . bun run cat gates # the fast set bun run cat gates --all # plus the jobs that need a browser bun run cat gates:list # see them without running them . Run it before you push, not after CI tells you.

7d459ccaf375.title: The CI workflow is the list
7d459ccaf375.content: This skill does not list the gates, because a written list drifts from CI and a stale list reads as authoritative, so nobody checks it. bun run cat gates derives the set from .github/workflows/code-quality-gates.yml at the moment you run it, so a gate added to CI is in your next local sweep. package.json is not the authority: many of its check: scripts appear in no workflow, and running all of them would fail you on things CI does not gate. The workflow’s own comments name the scripts it deliberately excludes, with a reason beside each (for example check:ci-health is a report about main, not a gate on your diff). Read the reasons there.

a990da411c00.title: bun test green is not the gates green
a990da411c00.content: The test suite, tsc --noEmit and the *:check gates fail independently. One cause can also fail two gates at once. Run the gate set, not just the tests.

72ebaae3570b.title: …and the gates green is not the PUBLISHED PAGE green
72ebaae3570b.content: Gates read sources. A defect that exists only in a renderer’s output — for example markup that Kramdown escapes because a Liquid whitespace-strip joined two attributes — passes every gate. | Gate coverage is bounded by what a gate can look at. Ask what the gates read, not how many there are. | When your change alters a rendered page, build the page. The site build is not in the fast loop. check:escaped-markup asks one narrow version of “the output is well-formed”, and only in docs-site.yml, where _site/ exists. If the real build will not run locally (the just-the-docs remote theme 403s through the agent proxy), stub the theme and build anyway; never substitute the thing under test. continual-progress §”A template is not a page” carries the discipline. | .

f206ad7d3c5c.title: …and a green gate is not a VERIFIED FACT
f206ad7d3c5c.content: A gate can see the artefact and still answer a different question from yours. A rule that lives only in prose has a compliance ceiling nobody measures. When you write a rule into prose, ask what would fail if somebody ignored it; if the answer is nothing, you have written a wish. The measurable form is a check, a schema field, or a test. A gate’s silence is bounded by its stated scope. check:stale-paths, for example, judges two shapes — an id adjacent to an arrow, and a numbered step under a path heading — and declines everything else. Prose that merely mentions a closed work item passes it while carrying the same defect. Likewise check:ci-health labels workflow files that produced no run unjudged, not green. Green over a narrow rule is worse than red, because red is examined; a gate that does not fire is indistinguishable from one that passed. Before quoting a tick as evidence: . What does this gate say it judges, and is my claim inside it? . Read the check’s own header — every one here states its scope and its declined cases — rather than inferring the scope from the fact that it ran.

178ed2bc6e7c.title: Fast versus full is job membership
178ed2bc6e7c.content: The split is read from the workflow at run time. | fast — the typescript job. No browser. This is the inner loop. | --all — adds the jobs that install Chromium. render:bpmn:check is there because bpmn-js renders through a browser, so it can pass locally only because a browser happened to be installed. | .

8311bb4c32a0.title: Running “the gates that relate to my change” is not running the gates
8311bb4c32a0.content: Pick the gate set by JOB MEMBERSHIP, never by which gates you judge relevant. bun run cat gates --all is the whole point of there being a command. A subset chosen by an author tests the author’s model of the change, and CI tests the change; they differ precisely where the bug is. gates --all takes minutes; a red CI run costs a push cycle. A verification names a tree . A verification names a TREE, not a branch. Anything edited after the run started is unverified, however green the run was. bun run cat gates reads the WORKING TREE, not the commit. An edit made while it runs leaves the change unverified, and can make the run report failures that were never in any commit. Nothing looks wrong when this happens: the run really passed, about a different tree from the one pushed. Run the gates after the last edit, not alongside it — if you edit while they run, the run is spent and needs doing again. A skill edit is the case most likely to produce this, because a skill body has two committed artefacts generated from it. A skill edit is three files: . | file | regenerate with | . | the body, skills/<pkg>/<name>.md | — you edit it | . | test/results/kg-qa/.../<name>.kg-qa.json | bun run cat kg:audit | . | docs/reference/skill-instructions/<name>.md | bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/gen-skill-docs.ts | . The kg-qa row is a derived QA result whose record is the commit-keyed entry the CI job qa-publish stores on the orphan qa-reports branch. While a committed copy exists, kg:audit:check compares against it, so regenerate it. bun run cat skill:register does all of it in one command. A minted term needs a gloss . termIri("X") MINTS a term, and a minted term needs a gloss. Adding a new @type or a new property in kg-export.ts is therefore a TWO-file change: the emitter, and schemas/content/vocabulary.ts (CLASS_GLOSSES for a type, PROPERTY_GLOSSES for a property). ns:check refuses the half done alone. This is a different gate from the export’s own undeclared-term report: one checks that the JSON-LD @context binds the term, the other checks that the namespace DEFINES it. Both must pass, and passing the first is not evidence about the second.

bd02848f46d4.title: What a *:check failure is telling you
bd02848f46d4.content: Most of these gates compare a committed artefact against what its generator would produce now. A red one almost never means “the artefact is wrong”. It means you changed an input and did not regenerate. So the fix is to run the generator and commit its output — never to hand-edit the artefact into agreement, which makes the next regeneration noisy and detaches the artefact from its source. QA gates have a different shape. A gate over the qa graph computes and judges: --check writes nothing, and fails only on a finding that is NEW against a baseline — the committed working copy, or --against <ref> on the qa-reports branch. A missing baseline is UNKNOWN, printed and never a pass, never a fail. The four judge states are ok (0), finding (1), unknown and error (2) — JUDGEMENT_EXIT in scripts/qa-results.ts. A red one of THOSE is a real finding your change introduced; regenerating does not clear it, fixing the subject does. Which gates have this shape is in each script’s own docblock. Each *:check script has a generator beside it under the same stem; bun run cat gates:list shows the check, and the script it checks is named in the check’s own output when it fails.

ee3cc0e9a245.title: …and a green gate set is not a CLEAN RUN
ee3cc0e9a245.content: bun run cat gates snapshots the tree before the first gate and after every one, so every gate can pass and the run still exit 1: . ✗ every gate passed, and the run is NOT clean — 1 gate(s) changed the tree. The gates after the mutation were handed the repaired tree, so their verdicts describe a state you have not committed. gate-tree-mutation carries the two causes, the one command that tells them apart, and the question that settles the second: does the churning field describe the subject the artefact is about, or the run that produced it? Only the first is a reason to write.

2f1fd26d2aae.title: Three things this skill will not do for you
2f1fd26d2aae.content: It does not replace reading the failure. The runner names the failing command and the CI step it belongs to, so a local failure and a red PR are findable by the same string. Read what the gate printed. It does not tell you a gate is wrong. A gate whose purpose you cannot state gets “fixed” by being made to pass, which turns the check into decoration. Every gate in that workflow carries a comment saying what it catches; if you think one is wrong, that comment is what you are arguing with. It does not make --all optional before a push that touches a diagram. Anything under processes/ changes a rendered SVG, and the check for that is in the browser job.

f48209cb75a9.title: If bun run cat gates reports no gates
f48209cb75a9.content: It fails rather than exiting clean: an empty sweep that exits 0 is indistinguishable from a passing one. If you see that refusal, the workflow was renamed or restructured and the reader needs fixing — not the gate list.
