15a4b8232b9f.title: pr-description — a PR body a first-time reader can follow

0eae777ac7f5.title: What a PR description is for
0eae777ac7f5.content: The reader has not been here. A reviewer, the owner coming back a week later, or the next agent opens the PR cold. The description is the one place they can learn what the change is for, without the chat, the work item or the commit log. If they need any of those to follow it, it has failed. It is not a change log of commit titles turned into bullets (“fix fsh-index path”, “one file per key”): every line is true, and only the author can read it.

c50170628042.title: The sections, in order
c50170628042.content: | # | section | answers | test | . | 1 | The problem | what is wrong or missing today, concretely | a reader could explain it to a colleague without reading the code | . | 2 | Why it matters | who it hurts, and what it blocks | names a person, a process or a measured cost, not “improves quality” | . | 3 | The approach | the shape of the solution, and the alternatives set aside | says why THIS shape, not only what | . | 4 | Constraints | what the solution had to respect: owner rulings, invariants, things it must not change | each one is a reason a reviewer would otherwise ask “why not just…?” | . | 5 | The solution | what changed, grouped by idea, not by commit | a table or short list, at most one line per idea | . | 6 | How to use it | the commands, flags or pages a reader runs or opens | copy-pasteable, with prerequisites stated | . | 7 | What is not done | untested paths, known gaps, follow-ups | nothing a reviewer would be surprised by later | . | 8 | Status | the live checklist (continual-progress invariant 3) | CI state on the CURRENT head | . Scale it to the change. A one-file fix can be three short paragraphs: problem, fix, verified by. The order still holds, and so does “why”, because “why” is the section a reviewer cannot reconstruct from the diff. These are the questions opening-brief asks in chat before the work starts. The PR description is their durable form, updated with what the work found.

761223bf5b1b.title: Rules
761223bf5b1b.content: . | Expand every identifier on first use. Not “fixes wnhh” but “bean wnhh: SUSHI and the IG Publisher cannot run locally without packages.fhir.org”. Not “W7”, but “W7, the incremental rebuild”. | Every number carries its provenance: measured on which head, by which command, or carried from where. The table in opening-brief §”The four parts” applies unchanged. | Say what is not verified in its own section. Not as a hedge buried in a bullet. continual-progress §”What to do with the thing you could not verify” is the rule; this is where it goes. | A decision you hand the reader follows interaction-modality §4.1: context, then options, then a recommendation, then the question. The test is whether the reader can answer without opening anything. | Link, never paste. A long log, a full diff or a measurement table goes in a comment, a committed sidecar or a linked page. The description carries the conclusion and the link. | .

11f2667b6421.title: Updating a PR: comments, not edits
11f2667b6421.content: A reader who has already read the description must be able to trust that it still says what it said. A change they need to see goes where GitHub shows it as new, which is a comment: a push, a CI round, a review answered, a decision taken. Two exceptions are edited in the description itself: . | Status is updated in place. It has two parts, and both stay current: . | structured: the status checklist (continual-progress invariant 3), with the work item and its epic, each linked, and the CI state on the current head; | narrative: two or three sentences on where the work stands and what it waits on. | . | Scope changes are recorded, never overwritten. Keep the original problem and solution text. Add a dated entry under ## Scope history: what changed, why, who decided, and what it supersedes. Strike through (~~…~~) any original line it invalidates, instead of deleting it. A reader can then see both what was first proposed and what is being merged. | . Anything else, such as a better phrasing or a fact found later, goes in a comment.

ef12f96ce736.title: Cross-reference everything
ef12f96ce736.content: Every identifier is a link: . | thing | link to | . | work item | its file, beans/defs/<id>--<slug>.md, on the PR’s head branch | . | epic or milestone | the same, plus the work items dashboard at <site>/beans/ (for this repository, https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/beans/) | . | issue or PR | a full owner/repo#N link, never a bare #N across repositories | . | skill or process | its file, or its page under <site>/reference/ | . | a measurement | the committed sidecar or the CI run that produced it | . The dashboard has no per-bean deep link, because its epic scope lives only in page memory. A link opens the whole board, so link the work item’s file for the work item, and the dashboard for the overview.

9e8e8df596ca.title: What never goes in it
9e8e8df596ca.content: . | Credentials, tokens, internal hostnames, or anything outside the diff. The same rule as for PR templates. | Model identifiers. The footer carries the session link, not the model. | Chat shorthand that only the session understood: “per the 2y ruling”, “Q4”, “round 3”. Say what the ruling was. | .

eeffc159a0e7.title: Worked example
eeffc159a0e7.content: A PR adding an incremental-build library to the FHIR IG Publisher, before and after. | Before: “What’s in it”: twelve bullets, one per commit (“W1:”, “W2:”, “-fsh-users:”, …), then “Housekeeping”. Accurate, and unreadable to anyone who did not write it. | After: . | The problem: the Publisher is all-or-nothing, and what a build knew is thrown away. | Why it matters: folio-assistant needs a structured record of a build to detect staleness, review changes and eventually rebuild part of an IG. | The approach: a library on top of the Publisher, staged W1 to W7, with a table of what each stage adds and its state. | Constraints: the Publisher is not modified; an AST is a cache, never an authority; “cannot tell” means a full build. | How to use it: three commands. | What is not done: W7 has never run end to end, and a stray .pyc was committed. | . | .

3bfd6d8682d4.title: Relationship to other skills
3bfd6d8682d4.content: . | continual-progress owns the status checklist and the rule to open the PR at the first commit. This skill owns everything above that checklist. | opening-brief asks the same questions in chat before the work starts. The description answers them for a reader after it. | prepare-merge records gate results in the body, in the gate’s own terms, and adds them under Status. | issue-working: the issue holds the request and its sign-off, and the PR description links it in the first line rather than restating it. | .

edbc8896bb81.title: Staging links
edbc8896bb81.content: When a staging preview exists, every request this skill makes for feedback, review or sign-off carries it: one deep link per changed page, to the anchor where the change sits, with the same page on main as before. Where the skill declares an output contract, they go in its stagingLinks field. The rule, and where the page list comes from: staging-review §”The deep-link rule”.

1883b935e2cd.title: Prepare for a handover
1883b935e2cd.content: When a session stalls, what survives is what is on the remote: commits on pushed branches, PRs and their comments, and work item notes. Everything else is lost, including uncommitted edits, local-only commits, scratchpad plans, running jobs and the chat. This skill moves the parts that matter onto the remote, in an order where each step is worth something on its own if the next one never runs. Order matters. Do it top to bottom, and push after each step.

775ac9a5fb81.title: 1. Commit work in progress on its own feature branch, with a brief status
775ac9a5fb81.content: For every worktree or checkout you have changed, including subagent worktrees you own: . git -C <worktree> status --short # see what is there git -C <worktree> add -A git -C <worktree> commit -m "WIP(handover): <one-line state> Status: <what this commit holds, what is half-done, what is known broken> Next: <the next concrete step> Bean: <id> PR: <#n or none>" . | Commit on the feature branch the work belongs to. Never on main, and never on somebody else’s branch. | A red commit is fine. An unpushed one is not. Say in the message that it is WIP and what is broken, so the next agent does not take it for done. | Mid-merge? If the conflicts are resolved, commit the merge. If they are not, run git merge --abort and say so in the report: a half-resolved merge cannot be pushed, and guessing the resolution is worse than redoing it. | Generated files half-written by an interrupted regenerate can be committed as WIP. The status line must say the regenerate did not finish. | .

62aa60c4fba2.title: 2. Push every branch that has commits not on the remote
62aa60c4fba2.content: git -C <worktree> push -u origin HEAD:<branch> # never --force git -C <worktree> log --oneline @{u}..HEAD # must print nothing . | Push to the branch’s own name. A branch that never had a remote gets one with -u. | Never force-push or rebase to make a push go through. If the remote has moved, merge it in (git merge origin/<branch>) and push. | If a push is refused (permissions, a protected branch), stop and record the refusal in the report. Do not route around it. | Open a draft PR for a branch that has none (continual-progress), so the work is findable from the PR list and not only from git ls-remote. | .

a3bc1c50a5eb.title: 3. Note what cannot be pushed
a3bc1c50a5eb.content: List anything that lives only on this machine, and say for each whether it can be rebuilt: . | running background jobs (a regenerate, a test run): what they were for, and whether a re-run reproduces them; | scratchpad files: plans, logs, measurements. Copy anything worth keeping into the report or into a committed file; | local tools state: the work items fallback, caches. | . Secrets are never copied anywhere. Name them only.

b83bca875405.title: 4. Write the handover report, citing the commits
b83bca875405.content: Use the handover-report template, written as a work item note on your work item or its epic, then commit and push it: . bun run cat beans:note <bean> --title "handover: <role> <date>" \ --body-file <file> --branch <branch> bun run cat beans:notes && git add -A && git commit -m "handover: <role>" && git push . Cite every commit by SHA. For each item in the report’s “In flight” table, give the branch, its head SHA as pushed in step 2, and its PR. A report that says “the branch” without a SHA cannot be checked against reality by the triage that reads it. And write a DISPATCH LINE for every unstarted item — the fixed one-sentence form in handover-report rule 7, one line per work item, naming a branch that does not exist yet. The report is not finished without them, because a handover that hands nobody a way to pick the work up makes the next reader re-derive the dispatch.

3fb0629ed2dc.title: 5. Tell whoever coordinates
3fb0629ed2dc.content: One short message to the steward or the parent session: the bean-note path, the PRs, and the one thing most at risk. That message is a pointer. The report is the record.

75d02e54f47b.title: Done when
75d02e54f47b.content: . | git log @{u}..HEAD is empty in every worktree you touched; | every branch with work has a PR, a draft one if need be; | the handover report is pushed, and cites every head SHA; | the coordinator has the pointer. | .

fa47523fbf36.title: /prepare-merge-auto — Autonomous merge pipeline
fa47523fbf36.content: Runs the full /prepare-merge workflow PLUS: . | Sibling coordination (before starting) | Review-comment resolution (after reviews land) | Structured user questions (only when genuinely blocked) | Merge (after all comments resolved), through merge-to-main: “autonomous” covers the preparation, never the authorisation | .

fb616955c339.title: Workflow
fb616955c339.content: Phase 0: Sibling coordination . Before starting the merge pipeline, identify sibling change proposals (pull requests, PRs) whose scope overlaps this branch’s files: list the open ones with the list change proposals forge-operation Tool. For each sibling PR that touches the same files or content domain: . | Post a brief coordination comment: “Starting prepare-merge on # | ; touches . Review welcome if you'd like to check for conflicts before merge." | | Do NOT wait for responses — this is a courtesy notification, not a blocking request. | . Phase 1: /prepare-merge (steps 1–6) . Execute the full /prepare-merge skill (rebase, integrate, one-voice, build, final rebase, request reviews). All steps must succeed before proceeding. Phase 1b: Wait for reviews + status briefing . Wait for Copilot and Gemini reviews to land before proceeding. Do NOT skip ahead — the reviews are the input to Phase 2. Wait protocol (15-minute window): . | After requesting reviews in Phase 1, poll for Copilot’s check-run status every 30 seconds (up to 15 minutes) — the github Tool, read change proposal (check runs). Look for the copilot-pull-request-reviewer check run: . | "status": "queued" or "status": "in_progress" → reviewer has noticed the PR; keep polling every 30s | "status": "completed" → reviews are in, proceed immediately | No check run after 2 minutes → reviewer did not trigger for this file type (e.g. skill-only PRs with no code); proceed with 0 comments | . | For Gemini: check the PR’s issue comments with the read change proposal forge-operation Tool (comments). If a gemini-code-assist[bot] comment contains “daily quota limit”, note “Gemini: quota exhausted” and proceed without waiting further. | 15-minute hard cap: if neither reviewer has completed after 15 minutes, proceed with whatever comments have landed. Note “Copilot: timed out (15 min)” in the briefing. | . Once reviews arrive (or the 15-minute cap is reached), give the user a concise status briefing: . | PR identity: “#N — title” with clickable URL | Branch: branch-name → main | Scope: files changed, additions/deletions, commits | Review comments received: total count, by reviewer, with 1-line summary of each thread: ``` Review comments (5 total — Copilot: 3, Gemini: 2): . | [Copilot] line 42 engine.py — threshold mismatch | [Copilot] line 98 engine.py — unused variable | [Copilot] line 173 engine.py — spelling fix | [Gemini] line 15 table.md — missing citation | [Gemini] line 88 table.md — ambiguous wording ``` | . | Disposition plan: for each comment, state the planned action (accept / modify / reject / escalate) BEFORE making changes — so the user can redirect: Plan: accept 1,2,3; accept-with-modification 4; reject 5 (reason: standard term per §7a) . | CI status: green / failing / pending | . The user can reply with overrides (e.g. “reject 4”, “skip 2,3”). If no override within ~30 seconds, proceed with the stated plan. Phase 2: Resolve review comments . After the briefing (and any user overrides), triage each thread: . | Classification | Action | . | accept | Apply the suggested fix, commit, push. | . | accept-with-modification | Apply a modified version, commit with explanation. | . | reject-with-reason | Reply on the thread with the reason (e.g. “intentional — see §X”). | . | escalate | Cannot resolve autonomously — proceed to Phase 3. | . For each resolved thread, commit the fix with message: fix(PR #N): address <reviewer> thread r<id> — <1-line summary> . Push after each batch of resolutions. Phase 3: Structured user questions (only when blocked) . If any review comment requires a judgment call (ambiguous intent, architectural decision, multiple valid approaches), use AskUserQuestion with: . | Rich context per interaction-modality: . | Quote the exact comment + file path + line number | Show the current code vs proposed change (preview) | State trade-offs for each option | Default to multiSelect: true unless choices are mutually exclusive | Prefix with 🟡 | . | Batch questions — collect ALL blocked items into a single AskUserQuestion call (up to 4 questions) rather than asking one at a time. | . Phase 4: Merge . After all review comments are resolved (or the user has answered all escalated questions): . | Run bun run scripts/run-validate.ts content/<paper> one final time. | Run the merge-to-main sub-process (sdlc/processes/merge-to-main.bpmn). In order: read the head’s evidence live (CI per owed job on the head SHA, mergeability, review state and Claude Approvals where the repository runs it); a repository with no CI is none, never green; find the owner’s authorisation for THIS merge, and ask with the evidence when there is none; record it; then merge pinned to the head, with merge_method: "merge" unless told otherwise. Having invoked this skill is not the authorisation, and neither is a broad instruction such as “fix all issues until green”. | CRITICAL: DO NOT DELETE THE BRANCH EVER! If using the GitHub CLI, DO NOT pass --delete-branch. If using the GitHub API, ensure the branch is preserved. | Report the merge SHA + URL, and the authorisation it was made under. | . Phase 5: Post-merge coordination . After merge: . | Post a brief update on any sibling PRs that were notified in Phase 0: “PR # merged; updated on main. Please rebase if needed." | Unsubscribe from the merged PR’s activity. | .

b6e106bfc54d.title: Error handling
b6e106bfc54d.content: . | If /prepare-merge fails at any step, STOP and report the blocker. Do not request reviews on a broken branch. | If CI fails after pushing review fixes, investigate and fix before merging. | If the user doesn’t respond to Phase 3 questions within the session, leave the PR open with a summary comment listing the unresolved items. | .

a99ce4fc7ae8.title: Anti-patterns
a99ce4fc7ae8.content: . | Do NOT merge without resolving review comments (even if CI is green). | Do NOT merge without the owner’s authorisation for that merge, recorded (merge-to-main). Green CI is evidence, not permission. | Do NOT read “no checks” as “nothing red”. A PR with ZERO check runs renders identically to one whose checks have not started. Match the PR’s head_sha against the branch’s workflow-run list before calling it green, and re-run the workflows by dispatch when no run exists for that sha. Same rule, with the procedure, in prepare-merge.md §Guardrails; change one and change the other, because a rule kept in only one of the two is missed by agents following the other. | Do NOT squash unless the user explicitly says “squash”. | Do NOT skip sibling coordination — it prevents post-merge conflicts. | Do NOT ask trivial questions in Phase 3 — only genuinely ambiguous decisions warrant user input. | Do NOT delete the branch after merging — and not at any other time either, without explicit assent from the user or the repository owner. Same rule, same wording, in prepare-merge.md §Guardrails; change one and change the other. | .

b34011d444b5.title: Prepare-merge — get a feature branch ready to land
b34011d444b5.content: Canonical, repo-agnostic recipe for taking a claude/* (or any feature) branch to a clean, conflict-free, green, pushed state so it can be merged with no surprises. Downstream repositories vendor or sync it rather than maintaining their own copy. “Prepare-merge” is a plain-English ask, not a built-in command, so without one recipe each agent re-derives the steps, inconsistently or unsafely. “Prepare-merge” ≠ “merge”. It makes the branch mergeable and stops. It does not push to the default branch and does not merge a PR. Both are outward-facing, hard-to-reverse actions — do them only on an explicit request. The merge itself is its own sub-process with its own gate, merge-to-main: evidence on the head, the owner’s authorisation for THAT merge, recorded, then the merge. Asking for prepare-merge (or “ship it”) is not that authorisation.

ebd9eec97b54.title: fsh-guts must not reach publication
ebd9eec97b54.content: Before a branch that touches the knowledge graph ships, the published export must contain no reference to fsh-guts — not the graph typology, not the declared directory, not the skill that documents it, and not an edge naming any of them. scripts/tests/fsh-guts-unpublished.test.ts asserts it against the built artefact and runs in bun test. The mechanism is in kg-export §”fsh-guts NEVER reaches a published graph”.

727b58cd46e0.title: Recipe
727b58cd46e0.content: . | Clean + committed. git status --short must be empty. Commit outstanding work first (the container is ephemeral — uncommitted work is lost on resume). | Fetch the base + your branch (retry on network error, backoff 2/4/8/16s): git fetch origin <base> <branch>. | Integrate if the base moved. Compare git merge-base HEAD origin/<base> to git rev-parse origin/<base>: . | Equal → base hasn’t moved; nothing to do (your branch is a clean fast-forward). | Different → bring the base in, resolve conflicts, then re-run the green check. A rebase needs a force-push with lease: git push --force-with-lease — never a bare --force (it clobbers sibling pushes). | . Merge with bun run cat merge:main, never a plain git merge followed by regen. It resolves every conflict a declared pattern covers (glossaries, translated glossaries, UML, viewer pages, site data, QA sidecars), refuses the rest with the tree restored, and runs regen on the result. A plain git merge stops on those same generated files, one by one. After EVERY base merge, conflicted or not, run bun run cat regen — see §”A clean merge can produce a wrong artefact” below. If you merged with bun run cat merge:main, its regen already was that run; do not run a second one. For a merge whose conflicts were all generated, the round is merge-conflict-patterns §”A merge round — run each check ONCE”: targeted checks and a push, with CI’s sharded run as the full gate set in place of a local bun run cat gates or check:merged. An authored conflict, or a merge that touched code, still owes both. A conflict in test/results/ or test/attestations/: see §”Conflicts in test/results/ and test/attestations/” below before resolving either by hand. | Prove it merges cleanly (no assumptions): . | git merge-base --is-ancestor origin/<base> HEAD → success means a clean fast-forward, so conflicts are impossible. This alone is sufficient. | Otherwise dry-run with git merge-tree --write-tree origin/<base> HEAD (exit 0 = clean; non-zero = not clean; add --name-only to list the conflicted paths) and trust its exit code AND its first line. Exit 1 means CONFLICT only when stdout opens with the merged tree’s id — git also exits 1 for a ref it cannot merge (unfetched, mistyped), printing no tree, and that is “could not determine”, never “conflicted with nothing in conflict”. | Capture $? on the line after the command, before anything else runs — git merge-tree … >/dev/null 2>&1; rc=$?, or cmd || rc=$?. echo "base($(git rev-parse --short origin/main)) rc=$?" reports the SUBSTITUTION’s status, always 0 when the ref exists. if ! cmd; then rc=$? is the same trap: inside that branch $? is ! cmd’s status, 0. shell-exit-status.test.ts fails on either shape in a tracked script or workflow. | GitHub’s HTTP 405 “Pull Request has merge conflicts” is a backstop, not a check — it is learned at merge time, after the PR was announced clean. Do not grep the old three-arg output for <<<<<<< / “changed in both”: that false-positives on files which legitimately contain those literals (docs about merge conflicts, test fixtures, this skill). | A clean text merge is not a clean state. merge-tree answers “do the files conflict?”, not “do the gates pass on the result?”. Before asking for a merge, run bun run cat check:merged: it builds the merge with the current base in a throwaway worktree and runs the full bun run cat gates there (exit 0 passes, 1 fails, 2 could not determine — never read as clean). A generated measurement can be green on the branch, green on the base, merge without a conflict, and be stale on the result. | GitHub’s merge queue tests exactly the commit that will land; the gating workflows carry merge_group: so it works once the owner turns it on. Until then, check:merged is the agent’s half. | . | Green check. Run the project’s tests/build (here: bun test, plus bun build <file> --target=bun for type-checking touched files). Report honestly: distinguish failures you caused from pre-existing ones (diff the counts against a baseline run on the merge-base). Do not call a branch green by silently inheriting red. Then run bun run cat security:gate, by name, and quote its result. It runs every security check this repository has (workflow injection, secret leaks, lockfile and toolchain pins, QA reviewer permission, materialised fixity) plus two advisories, and refuses when a blocking check fails OR could not be run. Most of those checks are also inside bun run cat gates; naming the command here makes the merge step cover security explicitly, rather than only when the CI run before it happened to include it. Its advisories (unpinned third-party actions, dependency advisories) are reported in the PR and are not cleared by a green gate. Check the adversarial review verdict with bun run cat check:adversarial-review. On any branch with agent provenance (trailers, claude/* branch, bot committer), it verifies that an independent adversarial review verdict exists, binds to the head SHA, and covers the full diff without silent truncation. Findings are warn-only (“would have blocked”): they are recorded, as data for deciding when to promote the check to a gate, and do not hold the merge. Know what the target covered. Green is a claim about the files the build compiled, which is usually fewer than the files on disk — build targets default to a root plus its transitive imports. Confirm the files you touched were in it (artifact count vs. source count, or build the module by name), and scope any corpus-wide number you quote to what actually ran. For contentType: paper branches that touch content blocks, also run the block_pdf_render gate: . bun run scripts/render-changed-blocks.ts [--upload-drive] . This compiles a standalone PDF for every changed block and scrapes the LaTeX log; --upload-drive additionally pushes clean PDFs to Google Drive when it is configured. Exits 1 on LaTeX errors (fix required); exits 0 with warnings only (advisory); exits 2 on setup problems — including no local latexmk, which is the common case in a container. Exit 2 means the gate did not run; report it that way rather than folding it into a green. For a branch that changes a folio’s blocks, report review coverage. content-change-review.bpmn’s coverage gate (GW_Covered, table decisions/review-coverage-gate.dmn) reads the block counts below and, where the preview published a rendered-impact.json, three page counts (unreviewed pages, undetermined inputs, missed pages; see rendered-impact). Report them in the PR body, in the gate’s own terms, and a page count the preview did not publish as “not known”: . | open defects: review comments of kind defect still open or addressed, from the preview’s review-comments.json; | changed blocks with neither a verdict nor a waiver on their current version. | . Both come from one command, the folio-review-coverage Tool, run on the preview’s published files with --changeset changeset.json --blocks blocks.json --comments review-comments.json [--rendered rendered-impact.json --measured rendered-measured.json]. Its command line is the Tool node’s invoke, declared by the content layer that owns the review process. Quote its stderr summary. If the preview has no review-comments.json, or one with no verdicts field, write “not measured”, never 0. Never count resolved comments as coverage: a resolved comment is not a reviewer’s verdict on the block. This REPORTS; it does not merge or refuse. The gate belongs to the review process, and the committee decides the outcome. Say so when coverage could not be measured, because a branch passed with unmeasured coverage reads as “reviewed”. | Push the feature branch (retry/backoff as in step 2): git push -u origin <branch>. Then ask whether the push produced a run: bun run cat check:head-has-run. The push runs the fast gates first, where the pre-push hook is on. Git’s pre-push hook (installed by cat-harness-tools/scripts/git-hooks/install.sh) and, for agents, a Claude Code PreToolUse hook on git push both run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pre-push-gates.ts on the checked-out tree, before anything leaves the container (work items cat-tools-pp9g and folio-assistant-fn8q). It runs the fast gates minus the whole-suite bun test, plus only the test files whose import closure holds a file the push changed (owner, 2026-11-05: “Affected tests only”). CI still runs the whole suite. What it says: . | refused: a gate or an affected test that is green on the push’s base in this same environment is red now. Fix it, as you would a red CI job. It quotes the gates or tests and the log path; | ? gates not judged: a red it cannot attribute to this push (red on the base too, or no base outcomes recorded here), tracked files that differ from HEAD, exit 2, or no cat runner. The push goes and CI decides. A fresh container reddens some tests CI passes (no publish-time pages, a slower machine), so this is not a local green: report it as not determined, never as pass; | ✓: the fast gates passed on this tree and the affected tests with them. A record keyed by the tree is written; it names bun test as held out, so it never claims the suite. Pushing the same tree again re-runs nothing. | . A push the hook refused is never forced through with a bare --no-verify. If you must push anyway, name the reason, which is logged to .git/cat-gates/push.log: CAT_GATES_BYPASS='<reason>' git push ..., and put the same reason in the PR body. A local pass does not replace step 7: CI still runs every gate. This does not change what you do next — step 7 dispatches either way. It changes what you can honestly SAY. A push can silently produce no run, and a pull request showing zero checks is indistinguishable from one whose checks have not started (§Guardrails, “NO CHECKS IS NOT GREEN”). If the check reports no run, write that in the PR body alongside the dispatched run’s URL. Three states, and the third is not a finding: could not ask (no remote, no network, 403, 404) means nothing was established, and it must not be reported as either answer. | Dispatch the repo’s CI on the pushed branch, and fold the result into the PR. Local green is not CI green — CI runs on a cold cache, its own toolchain, and without whatever build flags you set locally. So after the push, trigger the relevant workflow against your branch (gh workflow run <wf>.yml --ref <branch>, or the actions_run_trigger MCP tool), wait for it, and put the run URL and conclusion in the PR body. Red → fix and re-dispatch. Do not open a PR citing a workflow nobody ran. If you lack actions: write and dispatch returns 403, do not quietly skip it: state in the PR that CI was not run, and give the exact command a maintainer should run. Find the workflow by reading .github/workflows/, not by name. Guessing a workflow name is how this gate gets skipped while appearing to run (a guessed name can be a publish workflow). In a repository whose workflows are all workflow_dispatch-only, nothing runs on push or PR, and “CI is green” is only ever true because someone dispatched it. Check when CI last ran (actions_list → list_workflow_runs): “there is a workflow” is not evidence anything is being checked. Many workflows document a local equivalent in their own header. Run those; they are the same check without the dispatch. Read the workflow before assuming there is no local path. | Stop here unless a PR / merge was explicitly requested. If a PR was requested, see below. | .

30af9e328b69.title: What a green LOCAL run entitles you to claim
30af9e328b69.content: The same commit can fail different tests in CI, in a clean worktree, and when the failing files are run alone, and the sets need not be nested. A green local run is not a weaker version of a green CI run — it is a different measurement, and either can be the one that is wrong. What it entitles you to say, exactly: . The gates I ran passed, on the tree I ran them on, in this environment. And what it does not entitle: . | “CI will pass.” CI tests refs/pull/N/merge, not your head — a tree neither parent holds. A staleness that exists only in the merge tree cannot be seen from any checkout. | “The gate set passed.” Only if you ran the gate set. A subset chosen by hand misses gates such as check:partition (a new script must be classified in scripts/partition/instance-rules.ts) and no check script is unrun (a new check:* needs a SCRIPT_EXEMPTIONS entry when no workflow runs it — or, for a script owned by an instance above cat-harness, a gateExemptions.scripts row in that instance’s <instance>.json). bun run cat gates derives its list from the workflow, so it cannot drift from what CI runs. | “Nothing is failing, so nothing is wrong.” A conflicted head produces no merge ref, so pull_request workflows never fire and the PR shows zero check runs. That reads as untested, not as red. | “It passed in isolation, so the failure is not mine.” Running the file alone removes the only condition under which it failed — for example a test near its time budget that crosses it only under load. | . Your environment is part of the claim, and it can be checked. Run bun run cat check:environment before trusting a run from any hand-built tree, and install dependencies rather than borrowing them: a symlinked root node_modules makes any tool that resolves a real path through it report a location this repository does not contain. Confirming the symlink is git-ignored is not enough; path resolution is a separate confound.

4837a104ed47.title: A clean merge can produce a wrong artefact (STRICT)
4837a104ed47.content: bun run cat regen after every base merge. Not only after a conflicted one — after every one. bun run cat merge:main runs it as part of the merge, so after merge:main it has already happened once and a second run re-asks the same tree. Two branches can change one committed generated file in non-overlapping places — say one adds a count field to a projection’s header and the other adds an entry to its array. Git merges them with no conflict and produces an artefact neither side would ever emit (a count that disagrees with the list). A conflict is a question. A clean merge is an assertion that the result is correct — and for a generated file that assertion is worth nothing, because git is merging text it has no way to evaluate. After a merge, RE-RUN THE GENERATORS. Never read the diff to decide whether you need to. bun run cat regen does it by asking each gate first, so its output is the set of artefacts the merge actually broke rather than a wholesale rewrite: . bun run cat regen # repair what is stale in the whole gate set bun run cat regen --fast # ...only the jobs that install no browser bun run cat regen --dry-run # report what is stale, change nothing bun run cat regen --changed <base> # ask only the pairs whose inputs changed since <base> bun run cat regen --explain # say, per pair, why it was asked or not . It asks the gates rather than regenerating everything because the gates (read from the workflow, not package.json) are the list, and because rewriting artefacts that were already correct leaves a diff that says nothing about what the merge broke. The QA working copy is part of the run — do not build it by hand around regen. Generators such as uml:overview and readme:subgraphs read the computed, ignored */test/results/ tree. Before every pass regen asks the copy’s stamp (bun run cat qa:working-copy -- --status) whether it was built from the tree as it stands, and rebuilds it if not. The paths that rebuild changed join the pass’s change set, so any pair that reads them is asked again. A failed build exits 2, and regen never grades a pass over a half-built copy. gates uses the same stamp, so the gates that follows a regen on the same tree builds nothing. It reports four states, and unrepaired is the one to read: a check that still fails after its writer ran is a real defect, not staleness, and the command exits non-zero rather than claiming a repair it did not make. So is a check with no writer. --changed asks less, and says what it assumed. A pair whose declared inputs, script sources and commands meet none of the paths changed since <base> (plus the working tree) is not asked: its answer is its answer at <base>. Undeclared and {tracked} pairs are always asked, as is any pair whose inputs cannot be determined. bun run cat merge:main passes the merge’s fork point, so a skipped pair is one NEITHER side touched, and it is current if the fork point, the branch tip or the base tip was current. merge:main -- --full-regen asks every pair. Separately, every pass after the first asks only the pairs whose inputs the previous pass actually changed (measured from git, not declared). Both cuts are only as good as the task-io.ts declarations — and, for a task owned by an instance above cat-harness, that instance’s own taskIo block in its <instance>.json. task-io.ts collects them and refuses a task declared twice, so declare a row where its script lives, never in both places. The whole-tree pairs (kg:audit:all:check, skill:register:check, kg:audit:check) still run after every merge. Submodules: check the pointers BEFORE you stage the merge (STRICT) . A base merge can roll a submodule back without a conflict, and git add -A is how. git merge updates a submodule’s gitlink in the index but not the submodule’s working checkout. If the checkout still sits at the branch’s old pointer, git add -A during conflict resolution stages that stale checkout, rolling the submodule back in the merge commit. bun run cat regen then runs against the old tools and “repairs” generated files to their old form, and CI fails in code the PR never touched. No step conflicts, and every local check against the stale submodule passes. So, after any base merge and before staging: . git submodule update --init --recursive # move each checkout to the merged pointer git diff --cached --submodule=short -- bootstrap bootstrap-tools # must be empty unless YOU bumped it . Then regenerate. Stage paths by name during a merge, never git add -A, and before pushing confirm the merge carries only your change: . git diff --stat origin/<base> HEAD # should list your files, not hundreds . A diff against the base far larger than your PR is the signal.

d3cfd0a32ae1.title: Conflicts in test/results/ and test/attestations/ — regenerate one, read the other
d3cfd0a32ae1.content: | tree | holds | durable home | on a conflict | . | <instance>/test/results/** | DERIVED verdicts — every script entry | the orphan qa-reports branch, main/<sha>/ and pr/<n>/<sha>/, written by the CI job qa-publish | take the base’s side: bun run cat merge:main does, then bun run cat regen | . | <instance>/test/attestations/** | JUDGEMENTS — every agent, human and baseline-pair attestation, qa-attestations/v1 | main, as authored content | a person reads both sides; never regenerated, never “take ours” | . test/results/ files are not committed on main, so a base merge conflicts there only for a branch that still carries a copy. merge:main takes the base’s side (the derived-results pattern in merge-conflict-patterns), which is the deletion, and regen rewrites the working copy. Do not hand-resolve one and do not regenerate one in order to “commit the result”: the record of a commit is its qa-reports entry, which no merge touches. Regenerating is a resolution, not a guess, because both writers are idempotent (sameScriptVerdict keeps a reproduced entry verbatim and ignores reviewed_at, reviewed_sha and script_commit_sha), so a sidecar is a pure function of the tree. A conflict in test/attestations/ is two judgements that disagree, and reconciling them is a person’s call. No merge-conflict pattern names that tree, so merge:main refuses it, as does qa:attestations:migrate. Keep both sides’ entries unless they are the same judgement; then run bun run cat qa:attestations:migrate:check, which exits 1 if a judgement is still only in a derived file. There is no qa:resolve-conflicts command: derived sidecars are not committed, so there is nothing for it to resolve.

cc7f7a92dced.title: Shipping is not merging — hand over on the PR itself
cc7f7a92dced.content: What happens after the handover is merge-to-main, called by merge-train.bpmn for a queued PR and by crdm-close.bpmn for a CRDM feature. When the branch is green and pushed, it reaches the Merge Steward only by its own state: label ready-to-merge, a signed ready: <head sha> comment, and no needs-merge-human. merge-queue §”Handing a PR to the queue” has the six points, and when NOT to spend CI keeping up while far back. Never post the handover anywhere but the PR.

966621719b1b.title: Opening the PR (only when asked)
966621719b1b.content: GitHub access here is via the GitHub MCP server, whose tools are deferred (lazy-loaded). At session start they appear as names only — you cannot call them until you load the schema: . ToolSearch "select:mcp__github__create_pull_request" . Then call mcp__github__create_pull_request with owner, repo, head (the feature branch), base. This “load-then-call” round-trip is by design, not a failure, and is needed once per deferred tool per session, for every mcp__github__* tool (review, comment, merge, CI status). PR body content: pr-description, written for a first-time reader. PR body convention: end with the Claude Code footer + session link (see the harness git instructions). Do not include the model identifier in the PR.

eb96f29f1f49.title: Guardrails
eb96f29f1f49.content: . | Never push to the default branch and never merge a PR without an explicit ask. Prepare-merge leaves the decision to the human. When the ask comes, the merge runs merge-to-main; a broad instruction such as “fix all issues until green” is not the ask. | In folio-assistant an agent never merges to main at all. When CI is green on every job: mark the PR Ready for review, add the label ready-to-merge, and comment ready: <head sha>. The Merge Steward session brings main in, regenerates and merges. If it reports red: fix, then re-label. The policy is in continual-progress §”Green means handed to the Merge Steward”. | Check the change against the skills that govern it before calling it ready, an agent’s PR above all. Green CI says the code does what its tests say; it does not say the change keeps the rules the owner set for that area. Read the governing skills (from the mounted layers when the MCP skill server is unreachable) and hold the diff to them: a step that, say, copies the IG Publisher’s finished HTML into a site passes every test and breaks ig-render-jekyll. A design choice the PR body describes in passing is a question for the owner when a skill already answers it, never an implementation detail to merge past. | --force-with-lease, never bare --force when a rebase rewrote history. | Honest green. Pre-existing red is reported as pre-existing, with evidence; your-change red blocks the “ready” claim. | NO CHECKS IS NOT GREEN — verify against the run list, never the PR page. A PR with zero check runs renders identically to one whose checks have not started. Both are “nothing red”. A push followed by a PR can produce no pull_request-event run for that head, the newest run on the branch being for the previous head. Waiting longer is not the remedy, because how long you wait does not predict whether a run appears, and neither is avoiding force-pushes: plain fast-forwards hit it too. So before calling a branch ready, and before any merge: . | Read mergeable_state FIRST — and believe it only when it says dirty. clean can be served stale (a merged PR’s pre-merge view), and unknown means GitHub has not finished computing it. dirty is the one value worth acting on unilaterally, because its remedy — merging the base in — costs nothing on a PR that did not need it. dirty means the PR conflicts with its base, which is very likely why nothing ran: a workflow on: pull_request: with actions/checkout@v4 and no ref: checks out refs/pull/N/merge, and a conflicting PR has no such commit. When it is dirty, merge the base branch in — do NOT dispatch. A workflow_dispatch run resolves refs/heads/<branch>, so it tests the branch, not the merge result: on a conflicted PR that is a green signal for a tree that will never exist. The workaround in step 3 is for a MERGEABLE PR whose run never fired. | Read the PR’s head_sha. | mcp__github__actions_list → list_workflow_runs, filtered by branch, and find a run whose head_sha matches. | No run for that sha → the branch is NOT ready, whatever the PR page shows. Say so in those words rather than “checks pending”, and re-run them with mcp__github__actions_run_trigger → run_workflow against the branch. | Re-check after every push. A new commit moves the head, and the head is what the absence attaches to. | . An agent holding a standing merge authorisation must not read zero checks as nothing-red: could-not-determine is never rendered as clean, at the merge decision as everywhere else. | One branch. Develop on the assigned claude/* branch; moving work to a different branch needs explicit permission. | NEVER DELETE A FEATURE OR branches/ BRANCH without explicit assent from the user or the repository owner. Not after a merge, not as cleanup, not to quiet a tool that complains about it, and never by passing --delete-branch or its API equivalent. A merged branch is still the record of how the work was done, the base a revert or a follow-up is cut from, and the ref a staging deploy is served under. Deleting it is irreversible from the agent’s side and buys nothing the owner asked for. The same rule is in prepare-merge-auto.md Phase 4 and the anti-patterns, because an agent following either skill must meet it. If you change one copy, change the other. When a tool or hook complains about a branch, fix the tool — for example a reachability check in a stop hook — never delete the branch. | .

f6c912c66081.title: Processes that run this skill
f6c912c66081.content: | process | step(s) that name it | . | Actor and role administration | Branch, gates, PR and review (calls a sub-process) | . | CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance | Phase 6: Implement (feature branch + PR) | . | Code change and review | Prepare the merge, and watch it through (calls a sub-process) | . | Merge the base branch in | Merge the base in, without committing; Regenerate, asking every CI gate; Resolve by hand, then regenerate | . | A refused merge-train member | Fix the PR, report on the PR | . | A merge train | Merge each member onto the base (calls a sub-process) | . | Adopting an upstream version bump | Move the pin and open the PR | . | Merge and publish a content change | Merge, on explicit confirmation | . | Content Change and Review | Merge and publish (calls a sub-process) | . | Guideline Updates | Merge the re-pin with its decided revisions | .

b2916bb93c01.title: Prepare-merge
b2916bb93c01.content: Generated from cat-harness/sdlc/skills/sdlc-core/prepare-merge.md — do not edit here. ✎ Edit this page’s source .

27debbbeba9d.title: Process state — the task you are in, inside the process you are running
27debbbeba9d.content: An agent working a BPMN process holds nested state: a task, inside a process instance, under a role that owns a swimlane. Losing track of the outer level while still acting on the inner one looks like ordinary work and produces changes nobody authorised.

9c49f7afb4ec.title: The three levels, and what each one answers
9c49f7afb4ec.content: | level | answers | where it lives | . | process instance | which run of which process is this? | beans/workflows/ (state graph on the branch store, cat/cat-harness/beans) | . | swimlane / role | am I the actor who may do this? | the lane on the activity; checked by the executor (task-authorization) | . | task | which step am I on, and is it enabled? | workflow_next | . workflow_next reports what is enabled now, which lane owns it, and which skill implements it. workflow_complete refuses a step that is not enabled. Those two are the ground truth; your memory of where you were is not. Name yourself when you complete a step. Pass actor as a declared actor id, not a free-text name: workflow_complete checks that actor against the lane’s role and the ODRL policies before recording anything, refuses a role mismatch or a deny, and writes the verdict into the history. An actor you type is recorded as asserted, not authenticated. Say so rather than presenting it as identity. workflow_gate takes the same actor and target, so ask it before doing the work (task-authorization). The history is checked again afterwards. bun run cat prov:qaqc turns every instance’s history into a W3C PROV-O log and re-runs the same check on each step; claude or a login in actor, rather than a declared actor id, shows up there as undeclared-actor. It is advisory: the findings are listed on the /prov-qaqc/ page, and CI fails only when that page is stale (task-authorization §”The after-check”).

b3f609d97307.title: Say which process you are in — every turn
b3f609d97307.content: Claiming a work item says what you are working on. This says where in the process you are working, which is the question a reader cannot answer from an id. Name the process, the lane and the task, and say when you switch: . Process: crdm-requirements, Agent lane · Phase 6 — implement. Completed A_Implement; next is A_Summary. The engine’s “what is enabled now” call (workflow_next) reports the enabled step, the lane that owns it, and the skill that implements it. Say which permission you are acting under. Entering a task in a lane means performing it as that lane’s role, and that needs an ODRL rule that permits it there (permits() in schemas/content/odrl.ts: the actor, the action, and the process, task and role as scope). If the answer is unknown or deny, you are out of process for that task: route it to a lane whose actor holds the permission, or stop and ask. The engine enforces this before the task at the deterministic end of the spectrum; at the agentic end nothing stops you, and the QA/QC report over the PROV-O record finds it afterwards (agentic-harness.html#bpmn-execution). Switching processes is the case that matters. Moving between processes changes who is accountable for the next step and which gates apply, and a reader who does not know you switched will assume the old lane’s rules still hold. Naming it is not the same as recording it (advisory) . A turn that is in a process has an INSTANCE under the declared workflow-state graph. Naming the process in prose is the report; the recorded instance in the state graph on the branch store is the evidence. Without recorded instances, a reviewer sweeping a window of merged work cannot classify a single session by lane. workflow_start creates it, workflow_next and workflow_complete advance it, and the state lives on the branch store precisely so a sibling session reads the same position — workflow-state.md §”Where running instances live”. Opening or claiming a work item for a process step means starting or resuming its workflow instance: . | Claiming or starting work in a process (code-change-review, merge-train, crdm-requirements, etc.): start an instance with workflow_start passing bean: "<id>" (CLI: bun run cat workflow:start --process <process> --subject <subject> --bean <id>), or resume the running instance that already names that work item. workflow_start writes the process:<Process_Id> tag and Workflow: backlink onto the work item so the visualiser can place the work item on its current BPMN step. | Advancing through tasks: call workflow_complete (bun run cat workflow:complete --id <instance> --task <node> --actor <actor>) as each step finishes so the token moves with the work. | Closing the work item: complete the final step so the workflow instance reaches status: "completed". If a work item is closed (completed or scrapped) while its workflow instance still sits running, run bun run cat workflow:instances --sweep to close stale instances while preserving their history and PROV-O trail (cat-harness#988). | . The session-start sweep reads the branch store and reports “no instance recorded” as a FINDING, not as silence, when the directory holds none. A finding is not a failure — plenty of turns are legitimately outside any process — it is the prompt to say which. This rule is ADVISORY: nothing gates on it. Record the instance when the turn is in a process, but no check refuses a merge without one, and none should be added without a new ruling from the owner. It is labelled advisory because a rule called STRICT that nothing enforces teaches readers that the word is decoration, including where it is enforced. The gap is computed, never quoted, because a count written down goes stale with nothing to say so. bun run cat workflow:instances prints today’s count: instances recorded, instances started since the rule, first-parent merges in the same window, running instances whose work item is closed or missing from the store (staleInstances), in-progress work items carrying a process:<id> tag with no running instance (untrackedProcessBeans), and the CI workflows that read the graph. Merges are an upper bound on the instances owed, since a steward’s train, a docs-only fix or a revert may have none. The command reports the gap and exits 0 by default (--strict exits 1 on stale or untracked process work items; --sweep closes running instances whose work item is completed, scrapped, or missing); only a count it cannot make (store unmounted, shallow clone, an undatable instance) exits 2. Arriving without the sweep — a mid-session clone, a project thread . A session that clones a harness repository after it started has no route to this skill: . | the sweep above runs from .claude/hooks/session-start.sh, and a hook runs only when the repository is there at session start; | the workflow_* and skill_fetch tools come from the folio-assistant MCP server (.mcp.json), which starts with the session, so a mid-session clone has neither; | the repository’s CLAUDE.md reaches the agent only once the clone is registered. | . So, when you clone a harness repository after the session started: . | Register it if the platform offers that (Claude Code on the web: register_repo_root), so its CLAUDE.md and skills load. | Run the sweep by hand, from the checkout root: bash .claude/hooks/session-start.sh. It lays the mounts down and prints ## Running processes, the prompt this section depends on. | Name the process before the first edit. A code fix in a layer is sdlc/code-change-review; a repin is sdlc/upstream-version-adoption; a preview is sdlc/feature-staging. A delivery is delivery-summary plus the deep-link rule in staging-review. | With no workflow_* tools, say so. “Process X, not recorded: this session has no workflow engine” is the true third state. Never write it as recorded, and never leave it out. | . A coordinator that briefs a thread (a project’s coordinator session, a swarm lead, anything that spawns an agent) puts the process, or “none”, the governing skill and the repository in the brief. A spawned thread starts with nothing else that would tell it, and the coordinator’s own memory holds no process rules by design. When the brief is written during a live discussion with a person, it also names the discussion: who is talking with the person, how to reach them, the standing card rules, and any feedback channel in play (a review sheet’s id and tab, an issue). That is definitions.discussion of the hand-back-to-discussion input schema, and it is what lets the thread hand its cards, questions and results back instead of leaving them in its own channel.

45d72b42883a.title: How to tell you are out of process
45d72b42883a.content: You are outside the process if any of these is true, and each is cheap to check: . | workflow_complete refused a step you believed was next. The refusal is not an obstacle to route around — it is the detector working. | You are about to change a corpus file and cannot name the instance that authorised it. scripts/check-corpus-gate.ts refuses exactly this at the commit boundary; discovering it there is late. | workflow_next returns a step in a lane whose role you are not playing. | You cannot say which process instance you are in without looking it up — and looking it up returns nothing, or more than one candidate. | The work you are doing was not in the brief you opened the turn with. An unplanned detour is the most common way this happens, and the least likely to be noticed from inside it. | .

33a06ba0d22d.title: Recovering
33a06ba0d22d.content: When one of the five fires, stop making changes and recover in this order: . | Re-read the instance. work_plan_prime reports every instance’s position next to its work item. State is committed, so a sibling session’s progress is visible too. | Reconstruct from context what you were doing and which task it belongs to. You usually can: the branch name, the claimed work item, and the opening brief together pin it. | Say what you concluded, and confirm it with the user before resuming: . I completed the QA sweep but never completed Task_ReviewFindings, so the instance is still sitting before the editor decision. I believe I am in content-lifecycle instance cl-2f9, in the editor lane, at Gateway_EditorDecision. Confirm before I proceed? . This confirmation is not optional and not a formality. An agent that silently re-enters a process it inferred its way back into is asserting authorisation nobody gave it. The whole point of the swimlane guardrail is that the actor is assigned, not self-declared. The person owed the confirmation may give it in advance for a stated scope — see confirmation-waiver.md. | If you cannot reconstruct it, say so and stop. A wrong instance is worse than none: completing a step in the wrong run records an authorisation that did not happen. | .

a8544802556a.title: What you MOVED while you were out of process
a8544802556a.content: Steps 1–3 reconstruct where you were. They do not reconstruct what you changed position of, and for notes and stickies that is a separate problem with a sharper edge: . A move is not self-documenting. moveNote (schemas/ui/note-anchor.ts) returns the note with its new anchor and nothing about the old one. A note that has been moved cannot say where it was. So a sticky re-anchored during an off-process detour leaves no trace in the artefact. There is no field to read back, no diff that distinguishes “moved deliberately” from “moved by an agent that had lost the thread”, and — because a move keeps the id — nothing that even looks unusual. The only possible record is what was written to a work item at the time. Work items carry no anchor: a work item is not a thing pinned to a block, it is the record that a pinning changed. workflow/bean-link.ts has the note op that writes it. So, as part of recovery, before step 3’s confirmation: . | Name every note or sticky you re-anchored during the detour, with its anchor before and after. Read them off the work item’s note trail — not off the notes, which no longer know. | If the trail is silent and you moved things, say that. A gap is a finding. “I moved stickies and did not record where from” is recoverable by a person who remembers; “everything is fine” is not. | Do not move anything back on your own judgement. Re-anchoring to undo is another unlogged move, and it is a durable change made to cover one — see deletion-requires-confirmation.md, which is the same rule about a different verb. | . A note carries no movedFrom history. History kept in the artefact being moved is lost when the note is deleted, or moved by a tool that does not maintain the field. The work item is a separate record, which is what an audit trail has to be. Reading a bean back as the trail . A work item is a usable trail when a wrong claim is left in place, with the correction appended beside it rather than replacing it. Read back, the work item shows the premise, the disproof, and the re-scoped work in order, so an agent resuming can see that the original framing was abandoned and why, which is what it needs to avoid re-deriving the same mistake. A work item tidied to show only the correct conclusion reads as though the work had always been aimed there. That is why bean-coordination.md has unwanted work scrapped with its reasons rather than deleted: a record that shows only outcomes cannot distinguish a dead end somebody ruled out from one nobody tried.

50fd8c182a95.title: What not to do
50fd8c182a95.content: . | Do not start a fresh instance to escape a confusing one. Two instances for one piece of work is two answers to “was this authorised”, free to disagree. | Do not complete a step to “unstick” the process. Task_ReviewFindings, Gateway_EditorDecision, Task_Commit, Task_AuthorizeRelease and Task_PublishRelease are marked relaxable="false" precisely because they are the steps where skipping is most tempting and most costly. | Do not treat a refusal as a bug. workflow_complete refusing a step is the system telling you your model of where you are is wrong. | .

4de7e8a43be4.title: Relationship to the opening brief
4de7e8a43be4.content: The brief you open a turn with (turn-reporting.md) is what makes detector 5 usable: without a stated plan there is nothing for the current work to have diverged from. The two skills are one loop — brief the route, notice the divergence, confirm the recovery.

d38db0d3d9c8.title: Production vs exploratory vs numerology — the bright-line guide

69d3fe6e50d2.title: The rule
69d3fe6e50d2.content: A numerical near-match is not promoted to production before it has a derivation. A match found by a search at one parameter value is usually a coincidence, not structure. Escalate before promotion, not after review catches it.

929ff17b5c0e.title: Three categories of output
929ff17b5c0e.content: PRODUCTION . What it is — the project’s published predictions. Lives in the canonical compute pipeline; reported in dashboards; referenced as “the project predicts X”. (Identify the project’s production locations: the canonical *.py/scripts, the named published constants, the *-canonical/*-final witnesses, the “closed”-status migration backlog, the status dashboards, the calibration-anchor registry.) . Discipline. Production accepts ONLY: . | Proved theorems — algebraic identities or formally-proved statements. | Conjecture-conditional forms with explicit owner authorisation — a derived-from-foundations form adopted despite an open gap to data, when the owner authorizes the swap because the form is principled (no hidden input) even if not yet proved to match data. | Declared external inputs — the project’s fixed, enumerated calibration anchors. Quantities derived from these are derived, not calibrations. | . Disallowed in production. Any of: . | Empirical fits against measured data (a literal solved backwards from the target). | Rational-function / functional-form ansätze that hit the target by fitting. | High-precision integer-relation (PSLQ-style) matches against transcendental constants without a derivation explaining the match. | Higher-order correction terms fit to close the residual gap to data. | . EXPLORATORY . What it is — shape-probing, hypothesis generation work. May contain empirical fits, near-matches, ansatz tests, “what shape is this?” computations. Lives in probe_* / *_alt_* / *_refinement_* / spike_* scripts and dated audit docs. Discipline. Exploratory probes: . | MAY contain empirical fits as shape-hints. | MUST clearly label themselves exploratory in the docstring header. | MUST NOT be referenced as production (cross-reference is fine; a “project prediction” claim is not). | SHOULD propose derivations for any coefficient they find, citing the project’s derivation menu (below). | MUST classify their witness assertion so a numerical negative result doesn’t block CI — assert the refutation (assert(no_match), not assert(match)) so the expected-negative outcome reports as passing. | . CANONICAL INFRASTRUCTURE (distinct from production and exploratory) . Structural pipeline components that are valid and part of the derivation chain, but whose specific numerical output is not yet proved. The infrastructure is canonical; the specific coefficient is exploratory. A function that implements a valid pipeline step is canonical infrastructure; a function that returns a specific not-yet-derived value through that step is exploratory. Do not deprecate the infrastructure because the coefficient is unproved. NUMEROLOGY . Post-hoc fits to known constants (π, ζ-values, named transcendentals, catalogued geometric quantities, etc.) without any reason for that constant to appear. Numerology is a SUB-CATEGORY of empirical-fit that specifically anchors to a named constant. Discipline. Numerology findings: . | MUST be labeled “coincidence” or “post-hoc fit” in the audit doc. | MUST be checked against the locality criterion — does the form predict the right value across a neighbourhood of the parameter, or only at the single point? (See the locality gate below.) | MUST be tested against the derivation menu — does the constant appear in any derivation naturally? | SHOULD be retired explicitly if a falsification lands. | . Disallowed. Numerology MUST NEVER enter production.

342f32010936.title: The derivation menu
342f32010936.content: Maintain, per project, a menu of the legitimate structural drivers from which every production coefficient must be derivable (each entry: the driver, where it lives in the codebase/literature, and what it yields). Every production coefficient must come from ≥ 1 menu entry. When the menu is extended (the owner identifies a new driver), update this list.

c62ddbd246e6.title: Escalation rule — escalate off-menu coefficients to author
c62ddbd246e6.content: If a candidate coefficient cannot be derived from any menu entry, the agent MUST escalate to the author/owner via AskUserQuestion BEFORE adopting it in production. Exploratory shape-probing is permitted without escalation — but the moment a coefficient is proposed for production (a “closed” status, a dashboard refresh, a named published constant), escalation must happen. The escalation includes: the exact value at full precision; the candidate mechanism (if any); which menu entries the agent tried to map it to; and what closure would unlock. The owner may then identify a missing driver (extend the menu), authorise the coefficient as conjecture-conditional, or direct the agent to wait for a derivation.

5f342f98861e.title: Decision tree — where does my code go?
5f342f98861e.content: Does my code change any production location? (canonical scripts, named published constants, "closed" status, status dashboards, the calibration-anchor registry) ↓ YES → PRODUCTION. Every coefficient must come from the derivation menu. Off-menu → escalate. Use only: proved theorem | conjecture-conditional with owner authorisation | declared calibration anchor. If you can't satisfy this, make it a probe instead. ↓ NO → EXPLORATORY. Empirical fits / near-matches OK as documented finds. MUST label docstring exploratory. MUST NOT be referenced from production or "closed" status.

ef4cf3e7bf2f.title: Common antipatterns (recognize + avoid)
ef4cf3e7bf2f.content: . | “The literal is the project prediction.” A constant solved backwards from the target, labeled as if derived. Fix: rename truth-in-naming (*_FITTED_FROM_DATA), banner the discipline violation, then replace with a derived form. | “A near-match → it’s structural.” A search at a single parameter value finds coincidences. Apply the locality gate: sweep the parameter across a neighbourhood and plot the residual. A genuine structural identity gives a smooth residual (≈ flat); a coincidence gives a sharp zero-crossing that diverges rapidly away from the point. A candidate that fails the locality gate is coincidence-basin regardless of how close it is at the point. Run the gate; report the slope. | “We need this correction term to close the residual.” A correction fit to close a gap, with no derivation. Label exploratory, escalate, find a derivation OR get authorisation OR retire. | “The theorem is proved, so the project is done.” A proved identity adopted as the production form does not mean it matches data — frame the resulting accuracy honestly (the gap is the project’s honest accuracy under that adoption, not a match). | “Reading A vs Reading B agnosticism.” Two competing readings give different production predictions; punting forces the next agent to decide. Escalate to the author to pick one. | “Rebasing with witness drift — just push.” Re-run the self-emitting validators after a rebase so witness/script commit SHAs match; CI will fail otherwise. | .

eaebeaab43b3.title: Pre-promotion checklist (before adopting any candidate in production)
eaebeaab43b3.content: If you are about to modify a production script, add/change a published named constant, mark a backlog item “closed”, or update a status dashboard, run this BEFORE the commit: . | Categorize the candidate (production / exploratory / numerology). If the change touches no production location, it is exploratory — label the docstring and commit without further gate. | Locality gate — sweep the parameter neighbourhood; classify by residual slope (smooth → proceed; marginal → escalate; sharp → retire). Report the slope in the commit message. | Derivation-menu check — cite which menu entry the coefficient comes from. If none, escalate. | Locality on the FULL candidate — gate every correction term, not just the leading term (a common slip: the leading term passes, the subleading correction fails). | Naming discipline — production constants are named so the status is visible (*_CANONICAL/unsuffixed = proved; *_FITTED_FROM_DATA = empirical fit, never imported as a derived value; *_VALIDATION = external anchor; *_EXPLORATORY = shape-probe). Mislabeling is the most common cause of review threads. | Witness assertion — falsification probes assert the refutation so the witness reports passing on the expected-negative outcome. | Banner — every exploratory probe carries a header banner stating it is exploratory hypothesis generation and NOT for production without (locality gate + derivation-menu trace + owner authorisation if off-menu). The banner is what a post-hoc audit looks for. | . production change? → 1 yes → 2 locality smooth → 3 menu cite → 4 every term → 5 naming → 6 witness → 7 banner (any "no" → escalate) .

4148ee43148f.title: Tunable-knob fences
4148ee43148f.content: A syntactic complement to the categories above: a fence that labels the few legitimately tunable knobs — everything outside a fence is FIXED (derived, never tuned). Fence syntax in compute scripts: . # EVOLVE-VALUE-START kind=production knob=N rationale="truncation order; ..." N_TRUNCATION = 5 # EVOLVE-VALUE-END # EVOLVE-VALUE-START kind=exploratory knob=c rationale="near-match, NOT derived" C_NEAR_MATCH = -2.0 # EVOLVE-VALUE-END . Rules: varying a kind=exploratory knob in an exploratory script is fine; varying a kind=production knob is allowed only if the stated rationale still holds; tuning a value outside any fence is forbidden (it is derived); a new kind=production fenced knob off the derivation menu requires escalation; a witnessed (derived) value inside an exploratory fence is a contradiction (derived or tunable, never both). An audit greps kind=production to check each rationale against the menu, and kind=exploratory to confirm those values never reach a production script.

6d45844aa4fe.title: How to recognize what category an EXISTING script is in
6d45844aa4fe.content: Use the project’s naming conventions and docstring banners as the first-line signal: production scripts (canonical/*_final names, no fits), exploratory scripts (probe_* / *_alt_* / *_refinement_* / *_spike_*, fits OK), numerology (documented in audits as “coincidence”/”post-hoc fit”/FITTED_FROM_DATA). A file’s name and its docstring banner should agree; a mismatch is a review red flag.

68bc90028c56.title: Where this skill connects
68bc90028c56.content: . | The content type’s compute-authoring skill — sibling pre-work skill (precision and authoring patterns). This skill covers the discipline AFTER authoring (where does the result go?). | The content type’s compute audit — post-hoc audit; uses the 3-category classification here to flag empirical fits that ended up in production. | canonical-watcher — the integration watcher that catches hidden-input promotions; this skill is the rule it enforces. | prepare-merge — the standardized rebase / witness-drift pattern. | . The first two are shipped by the layer that defines a computational content type (for a paper folio, the science layer), which names this skill from its side.
