e3075198564e.title: Remote-mount a harness
e3075198564e.content: How a downstream folio gets the layers it is built on: . | no git submodules, ever; | no .deps/, because a dot directory collides with GitHub’s conventions and with this repository’s own dot-prefix guard; | a remote mount is a declared directory with a remote source, pinned to a full 40-character SHA; | the defaults live in the harness’s own declaration, so a downstream never restates the paths; | a downstream may override them by id, never by path; | mounts are resolved transitively across the dependency closure; | code arrives through the mounted code directories. | . |   | where | . | the process | mount-dependency.bpmn; the per-subgraph view is the remote and npm flows of mount-subgraph.bpmn | . | the schema | cat-harness/schemas/kg/remote-mount.ts, plus the remote, npm and hydrated members of SubgraphSource (schemas/kg/subgraph-source.ts); the per-pin index package is subgraphIndexPackage in schemas/kg/subgraph-manifest.ts | . | the tool | bun run cat mount:remote (--plan to resolve without writing), and bun run cat mount:remote:check (offline) | . | the entry point | bun run cat state:mount, which the session-start hook already runs | .

a7bb98a74fc0.title: Mount, subscribe or associate: choose first
a7bb98a74fc0.content: | you want | relation | what arrives | . | to build on a harness: run its scripts, import its schemas, read its skills as your own | remote mount (source.remote in index.config.json) | the harness’s declared directories and those of everything it needs, at one pin | . | to read another graph and hold chosen parts of it | subscription (subscriptions): the kg-subscription skill | a snapshot of its declaration, then parts you materialise one at a time through the five gates | . | to know of a harness and link to it | association (associatedHarnesses): the associate-harness skill | nothing | . | to retrieve or distribute as a package | npm distribution (kg-retrieve-npm, source.npm): the npm-kg-distribution skill | an npm .tgz tarball (unhydrated source or hydrated view) | . The test is whether your code imports theirs. If it does, mount. If you only read their content, subscribe: a subscription gates every part through copyright and purpose, and a mount does not, because the code it brings is the platform you are built on.

8315b9a34eb6.title: The two halves of the declaration
8315b9a34eb6.content: The harness side goes in the harness’s own <name>.json and is written once by the harness’s owner: . "mountDefaults": { "path": "cat-harness", "directories": ["schemas", "scripts", "skills"] } . What arrives is what the declaration NAMES: the declaration itself, the chosen directories, and the instance-scoped files in its assets (its README and AGENTS.md). A file the declaration does not name, such as a platform.ts beside it, never arrives. Code the mounted graphs import has to sit in a declared directory. Both fields are optional, and each absence has a meaning: . | path absent means the instance’s home path (livesAt.path, else its directory in its own repository). | directories absent means every declared directory whose content is in the checkout. A branch, family or remote source is somebody’s state, not part of the harness. | . The downstream side goes in the checkout’s root index.config.json, as the source.remote of the instance it brings in. Which instances a checkout instantiates, where each comes from, and the fallback for a folio with no index are index-config’s rule. This skill covers only what a remote source means once it is declared: . { "name": "<harness>", "source": { "remote": { "repository": "<owner>/<repo>", "ref": "<40-character sha>", "overrides": { "cat-harness": { "directories": ["schemas", "skills"] }, "bootstrap": { "skip": true } } } } } . The fields are a remoteMounts entry without its harness, because the instance’s name is the harness (RemoteSourceSchema in schemas/kg/index-config.ts). A folio with no index still reads remoteMounts on its declaration. Declaring a mount in both places is an error: readDeclaredMounts throws and names both files. bun run cat index-config:migrate --write moves the entries across. Every tool that writes mounts writes through writeDeclaredMounts, into index.config.json, and none writes remoteMounts. overrides is keyed by instance name, then by directory id: . | path moves an instance. | directories replaces its default list. An id may be one the instance declares in its <name>.json or from within one of those directories (a "subgraph": true entry of skills/skills.json, such as voices); both are resolved at the pin through instanceDirectories, the resolver every on-disk reader uses. A nested id mounts its own path alone. An id declared in neither place is refused, not dropped, and the refusal says where it looked. The same holds for the harness’s own mountDefaults.directories. An id may also be a concern name, a code from code-lists/concern-group.json such as sdlc. It expands to every kind-first member the instance declares, such as sdlc/processes/ and sdlc/skills/, read from each grouping kind’s own declaration file at the pin. Each member is locked as <directory id>/<code>. A code that none of the instance’s kinds declares is refused like any other unknown id. | After a review of hydrated metadata, `mount:remote –choose [:] --directories a,b --tools x,y` writes the choice into `overrides.` (the choice, never the state), so a fresh clone replays it. It ends the review: that instance mounts as files, so its `hydrated` is dropped. The pin and consent do not move. | skip leaves it unmounted, and the lock records it as an answer. | tools names Tools this instance declares, by id, and mounts each one runnable: its definition, its implementation and their import closure. The next section but one says what that brings. | hydrated: true (here, or on the entry for its harness) mounts each chosen directory as one file: its published index.hydrated.jsonld at the pin, a hydrated source. Read what is there, then choose what to mount as files. No declaration is laid down, and needs is not followed. Where that file comes from is the next section. With no directories, a hydrated mount offers every top-level in-checkout subgraph and ignores mountDefaults.directories on purpose: that list chooses which FILES a downstream gets, and a hydrated mount is the step before choosing. Each top-level file already carries its nested subgraphs inline (hasSubgraph), so a nested one is named only when you want it on its own. | .

40cfd60c5780.title: Hydrated: the index files are published per pin, in a package
40cfd60c5780.content: A pin’s subgraph index files (index.jsonld, index.hydrated.jsonld under <docs>/subgraph/<HARNESS>/) are published per pin in a package, and a hydrated mount fetches them through the Tool its source names (the hydrated source’s tool, which is remote-mount unless it says otherwise). | Not committed in each repository. The files are builtAtPublish: they are computed over the checkout’s other instances, so no commit can hold them current, and a committed copy turns every re-pin’s check red. | Not generated at mount time. The downstream would need the whole index, kg-export and the framing toolchain to read one file of metadata, which is the cost a hydrated mount exists to avoid, and two downstreams could frame two different files for one pin. | . What that means in practice: . |   |   | . | the package | <harness>-subgraph-index@0.0.0-pin.<sha>: the index files at their published paths, and subgraph-index.json (folio-subgraph-index/v1) giving each file’s sha256 and the repository, pin and harness | . | where | assets of the GitHub release subgraph-index-<sha> in the instance’s repository, with the tarball’s folio-binary-release/v1 record beside it. Every name is computed (subgraphIndexPackage in schemas/kg/subgraph-manifest.ts) | . | who publishes | the subgraph-index-package Tool, run on every push to main by the reusable workflow layer-publish-subgraph-index.yml (the tools layer); a harness opts in with one uses: line | . | what a mount checks | the pin’s git tree first (a commit that does carry the file still works); otherwise the package: the tarball against its record (size, sha256), the manifest against the repository, pin and harness asked for, each file against its sha256, then the same schema and subgraph-IRI check a tree file gets | . | the lock | a directory that came from the package records the tarball’s URL and sha256 and the file’s path in it (package), so mount:lock fetches the same bytes and refuses any others | . No release for the pin is missing, and the detail says the package was looked for. A package that fails a check is missing; one that could not be fetched is could-not-determine. Neither is ever an empty mount. The record travels with the tarball, so its digest proves the transfer, not the publisher: who may publish is the repository’s write access, the same trust the git tree at the pin already rests on.

93c65a8aeb92.title: Tools: choose by id, mount runnable
93c65a8aeb92.content: The workflow: load the Tools’ metadata, review it, then materialise a chosen set. The first step is a hydrated mount of the declaring instance’s tools directory. Its index.hydrated.jsonld holds every Tool whole, and each Tool is its own tools/<id>/ subgraph. The last step is tools on that instance’s override: . "overrides": { "cat-harness": { "tools": ["bean-query", "bpmn-checklist", "agent-memory"] } } . Three rules govern this step: . | A Tool brings both halves. Its definition is <tools dir>/<id>/<id>.ts in the instance that declares it, by the folder convention in schemas/tools/tool-folders.ts. Its implementation is what its invoke names: . | inProcess.module, found in the declarer or in an instance whose needs names it (resolveImplementingPath’s rule; two holders is refused); | the script a bun run cat <key> command resolves to through the instances’ checkoutScripts. | . A bare runtime command (gh, beans) or manual brings no code. Both halves arrive with their import closure. A definition without its code is not a Tool you can run, and code without the modules it imports does not load: either way the checkout is half-working. | One closure walker. The closure is bootstrap-tools’ importClosure (scripts/check-closure.ts). check:tools-closure and the staging cone use the same walk. Do not write a second walker: two of them give two answers to “what does this code load”. | Directory granularity. The mount brings every declared directory the closure touches, whole. It takes the most specific declared directory (a nested one such as skills/voices mounts alone) and never a single file, so the lock schema is unchanged. A closure file in no declared directory, and an import that resolves to nothing, are refused with the file named. Neither is ever dropped. | . With tools named anywhere in a mount entry, each instance of that entry mounts the directories the closure touches, plus any its override names in directories. It does not mount its default list. A whole instance stays whole. A Tool id the instance does not declare at the pin is refused at plan time. tools together with hydrated is refused, because metadata brings no code. What it costs. A Tool folder is not a declared directory: tools/ is, and most definitions import its lib.ts. So a definition arrives with the whole tools directory, which holds every Tool’s definition. The cost that matters falls on the implementation side, which brings the directories its closure touches (in the tools layer, typically scripts and src). Without tools, the tools layer mounts every in-checkout directory it declares. The end-to-end check is the remote-mount test “load tools metadata, choose three Tools, materialise them” in the tools layer.

4f6815bee620.title: Why the default path is the home path
4f6815bee620.content: At its home path, a mounted instance keeps its position relative to its siblings. Two things then follow with no extra machinery: . | instanceRootsIn scans one level deep, so it finds every mounted sibling and needs resolves exactly as it does in the monorepo. | A relative import such as ../../cat-harness/schemas/… finds the file it names. | . Moving an instance by override is allowed, and the overlay still finds it through the lock (mountedInstanceRoots, mountScopeFor). The override is then responsible for any import that climbs out of the moved instance.

a067a31e2af3.title: The closure
a067a31e2af3.content: . | The harness’s declaration is read from the pinned tree, not from this checkout. | Each needs name is looked for in the same tree. | If it is not there, the planner looks for a gitlink at that tree’s root. A submodule entry is itself a pin, so a need on bootstrap resolves to litlfred/bootstrap at the gitlink’s SHA. The downstream gets the bytes and never a submodule. | A need the downstream already holds as a local instance is local: it is supplied by the checkout and never mounted over. | A need found nowhere is missing. It is never dropped. | .

8e0cf2d535f8.title: The lock, and the three states
8e0cf2d535f8.content: index.lock.json sits beside the downstream’s index.config.json and is committed. It is generated by mount:remote and never hand-edited, which is why it is a separate file rather than part of the index. Readers also accept the legacy name <name>.mount-lock.json, and both present is an error. It records: . | the pins it was written for; | for each instance: the repository, the SHA, how the pin was found (declared / same-tree / gitlink), the declaration’s digest, each directory’s tree digest, and declared instance assets (such as package.json); | what was not mounted, and why. | . The mounted bytes are not committed. With an index, each mount path is ignored by a generated block in the root .gitignore, written from the index (check:index-ignores is the gate). A path that block does not cover is reported as missing, never patched locally, because a local exclude is invisible to every other clone. In a folio with no index, a path its rules do not ignore goes into the worktree’s info/exclude. Mount path and route collisions. A mount with no path override lands at <name>/ in the downstream root, beside the downstream’s own directories, and its site routes sit beside the site-wide ones. To prevent collisions on disk and in route space: . | Reserved names: RESERVED_ROOT_AND_ROUTE_NAMES in schemas/kg/remote-mount.ts declares the one authoritative list of reserved root directories and site route names: ["skills", "tools", "docs", "assets", "glossary", "api", "payload", "branches/", "beans", "todos", "fsh-guts", "uploads", "test", "build", "_site", "_docs", "_kg"]. | Mount path check: checkMountPathCollisions (run during planning in mount:remote and by bun run cat check:mount-collisions) rejects any remote mount whose effective path (path or <name>/) collides with: . | a directory the downstream declares in its own configuration; | a reserved root or site route name; | another mount’s path. When a collision occurs, the error states how to fix it: “set path” (on the instance’s overrides.<name>.path in index.config.json or source.remote.overrides). | . | Route rules: . | Canonical: every visualiser is reachable at <base>/<harness>/<visualizer>/. Every generated link uses that form unless an alias is declared. | Alias: <base>/<visualizer>/ exists only when a declaration opts in via alias: true or alias: "<alias>" in its Visualisation declaration (coverage.visualiser). The site build refuses an alias that collides with another alias, a harness route, or a reserved site route, and names both claimants. | The route rule itself is in schema-management §”Where a viewer publishes”. | . | . Every instance ends in exactly one state: . | state | means | exit | . | mounted | on disk, hashing to the lock | 0 | . | unverified-approver | mounted, on consent no mountApprovers list checked | 0, reported apart | . | missing | not on disk, edited since mounting, not in the tree, refused, or the lock is for other pins | 1 | . | could-not-determine | the fetch failed, a declaration or lock is unreadable, or an instance is reached at two pins | 2 | . Could-not-determine outranks missing, and missing outranks mounted. A fetch that failed is never an empty layer. Re-pinning: from a checkout mounted from the lock . A re-pin is mount:remote --seed <name>=<owner/repo>@<sha> (it writes the pin and its consent into index.config.json), then mount:remote (it lays the bytes down and rewrites the lock). Do it in a checkout whose mounts match the lock: a fresh one, or one replayed by .github/mount-from-lock.sh. A mount with local edits is left untouched by the next mount, at its old commit, while the lock’s top-level pin moves, so CI would keep testing the old layer. --seed refuses while a mount it moves has such edits, and mount:check reports an instance entry behind its pin as missing. After the re-pin, check that the moved instance’s sha in index.lock.json is the new pin.

65bf6557ad70.title: A changed lock re-renders the agent surface
65bf6557ad70.content: A mount is not done when the bytes are on disk. A newly pinned layer can bring new skills, renamed skills and new agent-memory entries, but an agent does not read the layer: it reads what is generated from it. | surface | generated by | from | . | .claude/commands/<name>.md | skill:commands | every user_invocable skill in the mounted kg graphs | . | .claude/agent-memory/<agent>/MEMORY.md, .agents/skills/, .agents/rules/ | agent-memory | the memory directories the mounted instances declare | . So when a mount:remote run changes the lock, it runs both generators from the checkout root before it exits, and a generator that fails fails the run. A re-pin commit then carries the new layers and the surface rendered from them. --no-agent-surface opts out; --check, --plan and --staging never run it, since they change no lock a commit would carry. The list lives in one place, AGENT_SURFACE_GENERATORS in cat-harness-tools/scripts/remote-mount.ts. A new generator of something an agent reads (a rule file, a settings hook) is added there, not to a checklist: a step a person has to remember is the step that gets skipped. The process step is Task_RenderAgentSurface in mount-dependency.bpmn, between writing the lock and checking against it.

1a78d1a8b476.title: Trust: what lets a mount proceed (H8)
1a78d1a8b476.content: A real mount needs a person’s consent for that pin (trust.consent); a --staging mount needs none. schemas/kg/mount-trust.ts has the rules. Four things to know: . | The lock records the basis for each instance: staging, or consent with who and when. mount:remote:check re-runs the trust check against the current declaration, so consent withdrawn later reads refused. | A gitlink needs consent of its own. An instance reached through a gitlink is another repository at another commit. Give its consent on overrides.<name>.trust, for the gitlink’s SHA. | Who may consent. Declare mountApprovers and a consent.by not on the list is refused. Without the list, mounts report unverified-approver: exit 0, but never shown as clean. A checkout whose mounts index.config.json lists declares the list there, as its top-level mountApprovers; declaring it on the instance declaration as well is an error. | A refused mount is not current. Its old bytes stay on disk (an agent does not delete them). The lock records them under unmounted as leftOnDisk, and the check reports them as not mounted. | . Standing consent: a site keeps itself on an upstream branch . Pins stay per site. A site may declare, on one instance’s trust.standing, that a named person consents to following a branch — {follows: "main", consentBy, consentAt, require?: "green"}. The repin tool (cat-harness-tools/scripts/repin-standing.ts, run by its standing-repin.yml workflow) then moves that pin to the branch’s newest (green) commit and writes trust.consent for the new pin, by that person and marked standing. The mount accepts it only while the same rule is still declared: withdraw or edit it and those pins ask again. A pin moved by hand still asks again, rule or not.

7676007b7d49.title: Publishing a remote-mounted downstream — provision gh-pages first
7676007b7d49.content: A mount brings layers into a checkout; it provisions nothing on the downstream’s remote. A downstream that publishes a site needs a gh-pages branch before GitHub Pages can be switched on, exactly as a new repository does. The step is Task_ProvisionGhPages (“Provision gh-pages”) in the getting-started process (getting-started §5), with the semantics of A_Provision in bootstrap-tools’ render-kg-to-github-pages.bpmn. Run bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pages-bootstrap.ts --provision (idempotent, never forced; without the flag it only reports unprovisioned and the exact command), then set Pages to “Deploy from a branch: gh-pages, / (root)”. A worked example is in repo-conversion §5.

1855fc8be67d.title: Never
1855fc8be67d.content: . | Never add a submodule to get a dependency, and never clone into .deps/. | Never pin a branch or an abbreviated SHA. The schema refuses both. | Never edit a mounted directory and expect a re-mount to keep the edit, or to throw it away. A re-mount leaves edited bytes untouched and reports them as missing. Move the edit upstream, or delete the directory and re-mount. | Never mount over tracked files, or over a directory that no lock says this mount made. Both are refused. | Never read missing or could-not-determine as “that layer has nothing in it”. A layer that is not mounted is absent from every overlay. | .

f9ff7cc344ea.title: Processes that run this skill
f9ff7cc344ea.content: | process | step(s) that name it | . | Remote-mount a dependency | Declare the mount: harness, repository, pin; Resolve the closure at the pin; Mount each instance at its declared path; Write the lock; Re-render the agent surface; Check disk against lock against declaration | . | Mount a declared subgraph | Mount the remote tree at its pin | . | Guideline Updates | Map the affected layers in order; Open the re-pin for the next ready layer | .

01db5964e81b.doc: Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN
01db5964e81b.title: Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN
01db5964e81b.content: Render the content of a Knowledge Graph, or a list of its Subgraphs, for publication to a CDN at a given publication root URL, independent of staging or release, and report the status of the push with a message. GitHub Pages is one Tool for this general step. Drawn as render-kg-to-cdn.bpmn.

22c43f7a4682.doc: Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN
22c43f7a4682.title: Inputs and output
22c43f7a4682.content: | input | what | . | Knowledge Graph | an instance root — or a tree the caller has already rendered and verified | . | Subgraphs | optional: declared directory ids; absent means the whole graph | . | publication root URL | where the rendering is served | . | CDN target | which Tool performs the push — a Tool that satisfies: ["render-kg-to-cdn"] | . | output | what | . | status | pushed, not-pushed, or could-not-determine — a check that could not look is never pushed | . | message | one line, postable as it stands: what is live (a commit), where, and the QA result | .

e7f45a594434.doc: Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN
e7f45a594434.title: Staging and release are the same step
e7f45a594434.content: A preview is this with a root under the release root; a release is this with the release root. What differs belongs to the caller: who may start it, what must be reviewed or verified first, what else lives on the same host and must survive the push. That is why feature-staging and docs-site-publish both call this process rather than restating it, and keep their own steps — the slug, the render log, restoring the open previews, the publication-manager alert — around the call.

3f6c94b6c5ba.doc: Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN
3f6c94b6c5ba.title: Name the Tool, not its steps
3f6c94b6c5ba.content: The general process has one call activity, bound by the Tool: the activity names this skill, the Tool for the chosen target satisfies it, and the Tool lists its own subprocesses — the diagram of its steps (skills-and-tools, bpmn-processes). The general skill never lists them. | target | Tool | its subprocess | its message | . | GitHub Pages | gh-pages | bootstrap-tools processes/render-kg-to-github-pages.bpmn | the commit merged onto gh-pages + the QA of what is staged and what is served | . A target may need provisioning before it accepts a push; the Tool’s subprocess owns that. For GitHub Pages a gh-pages branch has to exist before Pages can be switched on to serve it, so the gh-pages subprocess creates it first — the general step does not. Another CDN is another Tool with its own subprocess, and nothing here changes. A CDN in front of an origin is a layer, not a publication host (kg-to-portal): the publication root URL stays the origin’s canonical one even when a CDN serves it.

9d28973e1519.doc: Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN
9d28973e1519.title: What this is not
9d28973e1519.content: Not the verification of what a build produced — that is publish-verification, and it runs before a caller hands its tree over. Not the decision to release — content-publish and release-lifecycle. This step renders, pushes, and says whether the push landed.

6cd00566f6be.doc: Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN
6cd00566f6be.title: Processes that run this skill
6cd00566f6be.content: This skill has its own process: Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN. | process | step(s) that name it | . | Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN | Determine which CDN, the root URL and the Subgraphs; Render and push to GitHub Pages; Render and push with that CDN’s own Tool; Report the push: status and message | . | Publishing the docs site, and keeping the previews alive | Push to the CDN (full replace) (calls a sub-process) | . | Staging a feature branch preview, and taking it down | Push to the CDN under branches/ (calls a sub-process) | . | Draft, review and publish | Version, tag and publish | .

945fa28f955e.title: Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN

e83a4710f426.title: Render logging — the publish branch keeps its own history

fa658e373b6f.title: The question it exists to answer
fa658e373b6f.content: What happened to branches/<slug>, and why? . A preview can be cleaned up because its pull request closed, removed by a dispatch somebody confirmed, or deleted by an unrelated merge to main. Without a record on the publish branch itself, which one happened is not recoverable.

1625b597384f.title: Append-only, and never anything else
1625b597384f.content: A removal is a new entry, not the erasure of an old one. The pair — the rendered and the removed that follows it — IS the history. scripts/render-log.ts offers no verb that could lose an entry: no --remove, no --edit, no id to overwrite. The never-delete property is a shape of the tool, so a caller cannot be written wrongly. Emptying a log is a person’s decision, taken deliberately, with the confirmation every durable artefact here requires (deletion-requires-confirmation). No tool and no workflow does it.

d5494de853c7.title: The four events, and why retained earns its place
d5494de853c7.content: | event | what it records | . | rendered | published, or re-published over itself — so “when was this last built” needs no commit archaeology | . | removed | taken down. Requires a reason, refused without one | . | restored | carried across a full-replace deploy by restore-staging. Its own event, because “somebody pushed this branch” and “an unrelated merge nearly deleted it” are different facts | . | retained | a removal was considered and refused. Also requires a reason | . retained answers “why is this still up”: a preview still standing because a liveness signal fired leaves no trace otherwise.

6e7e8139239f.title: Where it lives, and why that is structural
6e7e8139239f.content: _render-log/<YYYY-MM-DD>.jsonl, at the root of the publish branch. Outside branches/, deliberately. The cleanup runs rm -rf "branches/$SLUG", and a branch named to collide with a directory under branches/ slugifies to exactly that name. A store outside branches/ is unreachable by that command whatever the slug says; a guard you have to remember is weaker than a location that cannot be reached. One file per UTC day, not one growing file and not one per entry. Six workflows publish to this branch; a read-modify-write of a single file loses whatever landed in between, and the tool appends a line rather than rewriting. One file per entry would make “what happened this week” a directory walk.

a7e733e38e92.title: It does NOT survive a deploy on its own — this is the part to get right
a7e733e38e92.content: docs-site.yml is a full replace: git rm -r --ignore-unmatch '*' over the whole branch, then copies _site in. It is the only one of this repository’s six gh-pages publishers without keep_files: true, and it is the one that fires on every push to main. So the log is carried across that deploy by restore-staging.ts, unconditionally — not gated on open pull requests the way previews are. A preview belongs to an open PR; a log entry about a closed one is exactly what nothing would carry, and exactly what a reader needs most. A log a deploy truncates is worse than no log, because a reader will believe its entries persisted. docs-site.yml runs restore-staging.ts from main, so a change to what the restore carries is not in force until it merges. --verify checks the carried prefixes as well as branches/, because a verifier blind to half of what the restore carried reports a clean run over the loss it exists to catch. A lost prefix is reported as not recoverable by re-running anything: a preview can be rebuilt from its workflow, and a record of what was already removed cannot. Only the prefixes the restore reported as carried are verified. A determined absent was never there to lose, and asserting on it would fail every deploy before the first entry is ever written. CARRIED_PREFIXES is where that is declared; it is a list, so another carried store is a new row, not a new code path. The carry runs before the preview check, so the log is carried even when there are no previews. A carry that could not be determined is not a warning. It collapses into the restore’s own unknown, exit 2, which fails the deploy step: continuing would run the full replace and delete the record. A determined absence — the branch is readable and has no log yet — is reported rather than omitted, because “there is no log yet” and “the carry never ran” look identical in a silent report and only the second is a defect.

934e597985f3.title: Who writes an entry
934e597985f3.content: Every path that can change branches/ writes one, and scripts/tests/workflow-yaml.test.ts asserts that by job rather than leaving it to be remembered: . | path | event | how it lands | . | feature-staging.yml → stage | rendered | the same commit as the deploy. The entry goes to the root _render-log/, never into _site, which would land it at branches/<slug>/_render-log/ — inside the directory a cleanup removes | . | feature-staging.yml → stage, preview cap | removed, one per rotated preview | the same commit as the deploy, written by staging-rotate.ts; the reason names the size budget, and the summary gives slug, age and size | . | feature-staging.yml → cleanup, confirmed | removed | the same commit as the removal | . | feature-staging.yml → cleanup, refused | retained | its own commit | . | feature-staging.yml → cleanup-dispatch | removed | the same commit as the removal | . | docs-site.yml → restore | carried, not written | restore-staging.ts | . The reason is the gate’s own, never a restatement of one branch of it. cleanup emits merged | labelled | closed-unmerged-and-unlabelled and the entry carries that value. A hardcoded reason would name the wrong rule for some of them, and a wrong reason reads as evidence. A removal and its record are one commit. A separate log push can fail on its own and leave a preview that vanished with nothing saying why. The rendered and retained entries are continue-on-error. A preview that deployed and whose entry did not is a gap in the record, not a failed deploy, and failing the job there would turn a logging problem into a lost review surface. The step goes red in the run, so the gap is visible. A removed entry has no such fallback and needs none: it cannot fail separately from the removal it describes.

579905ae0d36.title: Writing an entry
579905ae0d36.content: bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/render-log.ts --dir <gh-pages-checkout> \ --event rendered --kind staging-preview --path branches/<slug> --slug <slug> \ --summary "preview published" --branch "$BRANCH" --commit "$SHA" --run "$RUN_URL" . The tool writes into a directory and never pushes. The workflows that call it already hold a gh-pages checkout with their own retry and concurrency handling; a second pusher racing those is a new way to lose a deploy. One job knows how to push, this one knows what to write. Reading back: --read [--day YYYY-MM-DD]. It exits 1 when any line could not be read, and prints which — a short count must be visible as short, never passed off as complete. Same rule as ci-health: could-not-determine is never rendered as clean.

d78a143a1214.title: A path is checked by VALUE, never trusted by provenance
d78a143a1214.content: --path is refused unless it is / or a sequence of plain segments — no .., no leading /, no backslash. The staging slug sanitiser can emit .. (input .. gives output ..), and is safe only because git rejects every ref name containing it. That invariant holds for a slug taken from a ref and does not hold for one taken from a dispatch input — and cleanup-dispatch takes exactly that. So the check is on the value, not on where it came from.

cb6bf0f03cfe.title: It is a specialisation of folio-log/v1, not a rival

Three things differ, each deliberately: . |   | activity log | render log | . | subject | what an agent did | what was published | . | store | fsh-guts/logs/, in the repo | the publish branch | . | published | no | yes | . An agent’s audit trail is not published; a record of what is on the publish branch belongs where its subject’s absence can be seen.

cc28ca9bbbd8.title: Render order — flattening a dependency hierarchy, and the three stages
cc28ca9bbbd8.content: Two things live here: the general subprocess (flatten a hierarchy into one order) and the one pipeline this repository runs with it. A repeatable subprocess has one implementation — every caller that needs “run these in dependency order” uses this one, because separate copies become several topological sorts, subtly different and untested. |   |   | . | the rules + the flattener | cat-harness/schemas/kg/dependency-order.ts | . | the pipeline that uses it | cat-harness-tools/scripts/render-pipeline.ts | . | see the order without running it | bun run cat render:order | . | run it | bun run cat render | . | check an order someone WROTE, rather than compute one | checkDeclaredOrder in the same module | . Two questions, one module. flattenDependencies answers a pipeline’s question — give me an order that honours every needs. checkDeclaredOrder answers an authored list’s — does the order as written keep its promise, each item using only items above it and never itself. A glossary’s order is the second kind: it is part of what the author said, so it is checked and never recomputed (see the glossary ordering discipline, §”Ordered glossaries”).

f30b70ce82ea.title: The four rules, and each is a decision rather than a default
f30b70ce82ea.content: . | A node runs after everything it declares needs. Nothing else implies order — not position in the list, not the id. | Ties break on declaration order. Sorting ties alphabetically makes the flattened order churn when a node is renamed, turning a no-op rename into a pipeline diff nobody can read. | A cycle is reported, never broken. Breaking one picks a winner silently and the pipeline then runs in an order nobody chose. Every node in the cycle is named — naming one sends the reader to fix the wrong edge. | A missing dependency is reported, never dropped. needs: ["x"] with no x is a claim that failed. Running the node anyway reports a clean pass over a broken graph. | . Rules 3 and 4 share a consequence worth stating on its own: a broken graph yields NO order at all, not a partial one. A partial order over a broken graph is the thing that gets run.

876a08bc1416.title: fatal is per STEP, and it is required
876a08bc1416.content: Some steps must stop the build on failure (the current-state json/jsonld and the README) and the rest must not, so the runner cannot own one policy. The field is required rather than defaulted, for the same reason a graph typology must state holds: a default lets a step ship without anybody deciding, and the two policies are not interchangeable. A failure skips what NEEDED it, computed transitively from needs — not what merely follows it in the list. Two steps can be adjacent and unrelated, and skipping an unrelated one loses a rendering for no reason. A skipped step names the step that broke, not the nearest blocked neighbour. Three outcomes, and pending is the third . ran, failed, skipped — plus a step that is declared but not yet performable, which the report marks ◻ and never a tick — so a step that cannot yet do its job never reports success while doing something else. Naming the gap costs a line; finding it from a wrong artefact costs a release.

8b5841a2e3b6.title: The three stages
8b5841a2e3b6.content: | stage | renders | on failure | . | 1 | the CURRENT declared state as json/jsonld, then the README from it | fatal | . | 2 | the dynamic parts — viewers, visualisers, doc pages, diagrams | skip + log + QA | . | 3 | the DYNAMIC state, exported once stage 2 has contributed | fatal | . Two exports, not one. They are different documents. The first is what the declarations say now; the second is what the graph became after the renderers ran. Stage 1 is fatal because everything below is derived from it. A knowledge graph that does not render is not a degraded build, it is an unknown one, and a README generated from a half-read graph states a wrong fact in the file a reader opens first. Stage 2 is not, because a missing visualiser costs one rendering and nothing else. Bootstrap is the exception, and it is declared as one. It depends on nothing and nothing depends on it — that is what “as an exception” means here: bootstrap is read when no harness is installed, so it cannot wait on the graph and the graph must not wait on it. Same shape as its exemption from the visualiser criterion in check:subgraph-coverage, and a second criterion rather than a hole: it owes its own .json/.jsonld instead.

9a0b01cb07d2.title: What stage 3 writes: <harness>/state.jsonld
9a0b01cb07d2.content: The workflow pages are the dynamic-state visualiser. kg-dynamic publishes <site>/<harness>/state.jsonld (scripts/dynamic-state-export.ts in the tools layer), and each workflow instance page reads it when it loads. It is a different document from the stage-1 graph export, and a reader can tell them apart without the path: it is typed cat-harness:DynamicState, its $schema is cat-harness-dynamic-state/v1, and it holds only the running instances, the steps their tokens sit on, and their stuck states. A work item store that could not be read is named in unreadStores, so its instances read as unknown, never as none. Do not mint a published artefact name to close a gap the author left open; wait for the reader that names it.

e70e2fc3f6a1.title: This declares the order; docs-site.yml still publishes
e70e2fc3f6a1.content: render-pipeline.ts is not a second CI workflow. It holds the order and the policy in one readable, testable place and gives CI one thing to call. A pipeline order that exists only as the sequence of steps in a YAML file is an order nobody can test.

3c3e328c7d4c.title: Rendered impact — which rendered files a Change Set changes
3c3e328c7d4c.content: Skill id: rendered-impact · Package: sdlc-core . A Change Set’s PR is approved against what it does to the rendered site, not only against its source diff. A one-line FSH edit can re-render one page of 722 or all of them, and a reviewer cannot tell which from the diff. So every renderer answers one question, and the PR shows the answer.

725eca4aa119.title: Scope
725eca4aa119.content: . | Every renderer maps a list of changed input files to the list of changed rendered files, from its dependency cone. | The public-comment Change Set (changeset/1.0.0) is the Change Set for ANY folio change, and the rendered list is one of its fields. | The original stays in library/; a Change Set applies to the folio materialised in folio/, never to the library source. | .

b23c8dda2879.title: The contract: rendered-impact/v1
b23c8dda2879.content: Declared in cat-harness/schemas/ui/rendered-impact.ts. A renderer takes the changed input files and returns: . | field | says | . | files[] | each rendered file the change alters: path in the built site, change (changed, added, removed), role (content, data, index) and via, the chain that reached it | . | files[].anchors | for a page that assembles many units (a document page), the fragment ids the change alters; the review list links path#anchor | . | undetermined[] | each input the renderer could NOT place, with its reason, and scope: all when it can change any page | . | method | cone (predicted before a build) or build-diff (measured after one) | . Three rules, each one a refusal: . | Could-not-determine is never “no change”. An empty files with a non-empty undetermined is “not known”, and the PR says so in those words. A renderer that drops an input it cannot map is broken. | Index files are listed and marked, not dropped. The reviewer’s list (reviewList) leaves out role: index (search data, sitemaps, an artefact index) because review is of content, not indexes. The renderer marks the role; the reader filters. | A page whose bytes do not change can still change. An AST artefact page loads its resource in the browser, so the cone names the page AND its data file, and a build diff sees only the data file. That is unconfirmed, not a defect. | .

fd030bc6851a.title: Checking a prediction: the one comparison that matters
fd030bc6851a.content: comparePrediction(predicted, measured) sorts every file into three groups: . | missed: the build changed it, the cone did not predict it. A cone defect, never a pass. Report it on the PR and fix the renderer: the next Change Set relies on the same cone to tell the reviewer what to open. | confirmed: predicted and measured. | unconfirmed: predicted, not measured. Expected for content pages that load their data (rule 3). For anything else it means the cone is too wide: it is safe, but say so. | .

ab0ba9b60aac.title: The renderers today
ab0ba9b60aac.content: | renderer | maps | how | status | . | fhir-ig-pages | .fsh, .cql, input/pagecontent/*.md | fsh-cone forward cone → SUSHI’s fsh-index.json → AST artefact page + served JSON; a page → itself and every page that includes it | in the FHIR layer, documented with its AST tooling (skill_fetch ig-ast-delta) | . | document-site, public-comment-site, library-site | a block, a document/chapter/section manifest, media/*, the public-comment store, a file in a declared library entry or a folio review-anchors.json naming one (the entry’s Document view and doc.json; its structure.json also the library index) | loaded from the published changeset.json (each changed block’s label and file) and outline.json (the documents), never from source: a block lands on its document’s page, anchored at its label (anchors) — on a LAZY page (outline.json lazy) on its blocks/NNN.json chunk and index.hydrated.html instead, and a block added, removed, renamed or moved reshapes the shell and every chunk from its position on; a file no builder of the site reads is an input with no page: each builder in the folio’s build command exports siteReads (the folio; the comment store; every directory of a typology holding a kind it renders), and a file outside all of them, the submodules, .github/ and the root’s non-Markdown files reaches nothing — so beans/ reaches no page, while todos/, whose pages are rendered, still may. A step that exports no siteReads excludes nothing; never decide it from the instance’s declaration, which also declares what no builder reads | in the document layer, with the ChangeSet Tool | . | docs-site | any file | a file in the COMPOSED Jekyll tree (docsLayers, composedInstances) → its page (permalink, or .md → .html) or asset; an include → the pages that include it, transitively; _data → the pages and includes that read it; a layout, a THEME include (read from the installed theme; unreadable means every include) or an include nothing calls → any page; any page change → the search index; a file outside the tree → undetermined when the staging cone carries any directory, nothing when it reaches none | cat-harness-tools/scripts/docs-rendered-impact.ts | . | published-provenance | a mounted instance’s skill, process or schema (anything a generator renders) | the published root’s own record of what each page was generated from — the “Generated from <path>” note and data-src on the edit link — read back as source → pages; a new source has no page yet and an index names no source, so both stay for the QA diff | cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-changes.ts (predictByProvenance) | . Two builds of one commit differ in every page by a ?v=<build time> cache-buster, so diffBuiltSites blanks BUILD_STAMPS before hashing; without that, every page reads as missed. A renderer’s command line belongs to the layer that owns it; this layer names none above it.

acc29b770575.title: In the review process
acc29b770575.content: content-change-review.bpmn: . | Produce: the staging build writes rendered-impact.json beside the preview and puts the review list in the PR comment. Each entry links to the preview and to main’s copy of the page. | Read: at Compare main vs staging, the reviewer opens every file on the review list, not only the pages the author mentions. Use before-after-preview for the pairs, and visual-diff for figures. | Measure: the staging job diffs its build against main’s published site (measure-rendered-impact.ts, before the banner goes on) and writes rendered-measured.json: what changed, and what the prediction MISSED. Only when that site was built from the PR’s base does it count (status: known); otherwise main’s own changes would read as misses (not-base). No published main site, no file: “not measured”, never “nothing missed”. The review page shows it under the list, as the PR comment does: a run started by dispatch finds its PR from the branch, so the comment is not lost when no pull_request event started the run. | Show: every docs-site preview also carries branches/<slug>/changes/ (cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-changes.ts): the changed sources, with a re-pinned mount in index.lock.json expanded into the files its repository changed between the two pins (a re-pin handed to a renderer as one JSON line predicts nothing); the cone’s files and its undetermined inputs; and the build diffed against the site at the gh-pages root, its missed files listed as changed, not in the cone. That diff folds the preview’s base URL to the root’s, blanks BUILD_STAMPS and compares a page’s <main>, because a preview’s chrome differs on every page; a removed file is listed apart, by directory, since most are parts of the site the preview does not carry. The root records its build commit in build.json; a root not built from the PR’s base is said on the page, never read as this branch’s change. | Gate: review-coverage-gate.dmn reads three page counts beside the block counts, each with a status fact so an uncomputed count is never 0: . | unreviewedPages: review-list files nobody has reviewed at their current pin. A page is reviewed by a page: verdict, or block by block when every block anchored on it has a verdict; a data file goes with a reviewed page that shares its pin. | undeterminedInputs: inputs no renderer placed, until an input: verdict or waiver (with a reason) says somebody looked. | missedPages: measured but not predicted, until a page: verdict. | . A pin is the hash of the git blobs of the changed inputs on a file’s via (pinImpact), never the built bytes, which carry a per-build banner. An edit after review reopens exactly the pages it touched. The tag is in review-comments. | .

51c32087a372.title: Adding a renderer
51c32087a372.content: . | Map each input kind the renderer reads to the rendered files it writes, through the dependency information the renderer ALREADY has. Never re-derive a mapping the renderer’s own tool records (SUSHI’s fsh-index is the authority for FSH → resource). | Put every other input in undetermined, unless the renderer cannot read it at all: then it is an input with no file. Decide that from what the instance declares, never from a list of names here. | Test it against a real build with comparePrediction: 0 missed is the bar. | .

a946032d8887.title: /rendered-verification — look at it, then send the picture
a946032d8887.content: continual-progress holds that a human cannot assess a rendered artefact from a description of it. Neither can the agent that wrote it. A stylesheet is not a rendering, a generator’s output is not a page, and a green gate set is not a screenshot.

97a810b75cad.title: The rule
97a810b75cad.content: A change to a rendered surface is not done until you have looked at it in a browser and sent the author the picture. Not “ran the tests”. Not “checked the CSS”. Opened it, measured the computed result, and attached the image to the turn. Sending the screenshot is part of the rule, not a courtesy: an image lets the author disagree with you in one glance.

d34ccf4c821f.title: Why a green gate set does not cover this
d34ccf4c821f.content: Defect classes no test catches, because the source was right and the rendering was not: . | what happens | why the suite is green | . | a generator emits raw <h3>, kramdown assigns no ids, and every heading on a page shares one anchor | the generator’s own output looks right | . | two files hold their own copy of a shared size (a rail at 40px, a sidebar at 56px) | each file has a test asserting its own copy | . | a component renders with no colour | an invalid custom-property substitution fails silently — no parse error, no console warning, just the initial value | . | a region lays out below the viewport, rendered and unreachable | the markup is correct; a !important in the theme makes the flex column inert | .

1deceddc23e9.title: Measure the COMPUTED result, never the stylesheet
1deceddc23e9.content: getComputedStyle and getBoundingClientRect are the instruments. Reading the CSS tells you what was authored; only the browser tells you what won. Measure every time: . | display, flex, min-height on a region you believe is a flex child. A !important from a theme utility class silently makes every flex value below it inert. | scrollHeight against clientHeight. A region that “does not scroll” and a region whose content is ten times its height look identical in a screenshot of the top of it. | the resolved colour, not the declaration. A custom property holding a hue substituted into color-mix() yields rgba(0,0,0,0) and no error. | . Use a control. When you suspect a value is invalid, build the minimal element in the page and read it back, rather than reasoning from the spec: the probe is a measurement, and reasoning from the spec is a claim. const probe = document.createElement("div"); probe.style.cssText = "--h:268;background:color-mix(in oklab, var(--h) 28%, transparent)"; document.body.appendChild(probe); getComputedStyle(probe).backgroundColor; // rgba(0, 0, 0, 0) -> invalid .

e610a8c3e6ab.title: A before/after pair beats an after
e610a8c3e6ab.content: Build the base branch too and shoot the same element. Without it “the dividers have colour now” is unfalsifiable. git worktree add <dir> origin/main --detach is the cheap way; symlink node_modules and the docs vendor/.bundle into it rather than re-installing. When the pair goes to a reviewer rather than confirming the change to yourself, before-after-preview governs it: one build with one variable where possible, stable capture, a k of n count with its method, the status line, and where the preview sits in the review processes. It also covers papers, FHIR IGs and slide decks.

c7f0f9c22348.title: Running it here
c7f0f9c22348.content: Building the site is preview:site, whose header carries the two things that make a naive bundle exec jekyll fail in this repo. It is not what CI builds — CI uses the pinned remote_theme, this uses the gem — so read a theme-chrome question off the staging preview (next section), not off this. Liquid and kramdown are identical, and so is our own stylesheet. Two environment facts: . | Serve it under its baseurl. _config.yml pins baseurl: "/folio-assistant", so every stylesheet is requested at /folio-assistant/assets/…. Serving the build directory at / returns 200 for the HTML and 404 for every stylesheet — and an unstyled page renders, so the failure looks like a CSS bug rather than a 404. Symlink <serve>/folio-assistant -> <build> and serve the parent. | Pin the browser. Chromium is pre-installed but its build number will not match whatever playwright-core resolves to, and playwright install is not available. Launch with executablePath: "/opt/pw-browsers/chromium". | . Drive the control a reader would drive. page.click(".side-bar .site-title") (the avatar, which opens and closes the sidebar from 50rem up), not element.classList.add(…). A state you set by hand is a state you have not tested the way in to. And check that the state actually changed. Setting data-fa-scheme directly does not switch the scheme — the real toggle is jtd.setTheme(name). A test that silently does nothing reports the old state as the new one. Assert the switch landed (for example, the sidebar background changed) before reading anything off it. Know what that toggle does: setTheme swaps the theme’s first stylesheet, so while the new file is in flight the page has no ground but the browser’s white canvas, and it flashes white. A scheme check that only reads the SETTLED page cannot see it — hold the new sheet in flight with page.route and read the ground then, as first-paint-scheme.e2e.ts does. The rule itself lives in theme-artefacts §”The page ground: the first paint is DARK”.

d0a922960377.title: The REAL build is reachable — take it off gh-pages
d0a922960377.content: This environment’s proxy refuses litlfred.github.io, but feature-staging.yml deploys each preview into branches/<slug>/ on the gh-pages branch, and git reaches what HTTP cannot: . git fetch origin gh-pages S=claude-my-branch-slug # the deploy comment names it mkdir -p "/tmp/rv/folio-assistant/branches/$S" git archive "FETCH_HEAD:branches/$S" | tar -x -C "/tmp/rv/folio-assistant/branches/$S" cd /tmp/rv && nohup python3 -m http.server 8091 >/dev/null 2>&1 & # → http://127.0.0.1:8091/folio-assistant/branches/$S/<page>.html . That is the pinned remote_theme, the composed tree, the mounted instances and the post-Jekyll steps — the thing CI publishes. A whole preview is ~90 MB; git archive FETCH_HEAD:branches/$S page.html assets takes just what a page needs. Mount it at the branches/ path, not at the site root. A staged page requests /folio-assistant/branches/<slug>/assets/…, so serving the extract at /folio-assistant/ 404s every stylesheet.

85fa4510ba0f.title: Assert the CONDITIONS, or the check passes over nothing
85fa4510ba0f.content: An unstyled page still renders. It still answers elementFromPoint. It still returns PASS. A run mounted at the wrong path reports a pass over a page with zero stylesheets; what gives it away is the numbers beside the verdict, not the verdict. So every rendered check reports, beside its verdict: . | document.styleSheets.length — zero or one means the page is bare; | a count of responses with status >= 400, collected from page.on("response"); | the precondition the defect needs — the class, the state, the element count. If the bug only appears when fa-has-fullwidth is set, a run where it is unset has not tested anything. | . A check that cannot tell a styled page from a bare one is not a check: could-not-determine rendered as a pass. A COUNT over the built site needs its instrument validated first . Before trusting any “N of M pages have X”, run the instrument on a known positive AND a known negative, and on one positive of each way X can appear. Naive instruments give confident wrong numbers: an exact class match misses the theme’s own variant, a substring match counts the class name quoted in prose, a link count takes a stylesheet href as a way out. For navigated pages, the instrument that holds is <nav class="fa-nav" OR id="site-nav". For a site-wide count, the gh-pages route above scales. Use a --filter=blob:none --sparse clone of gh-pages, with sparse patterns for the files counted, and exclude branches/. All HTML is about 1.7 GB and takes minutes; one directory takes seconds.

c3fb13588a50.title: Visible is not usable — hit-test the control’s CENTRE
c3fb13588a50.content: A control can have the right size, the right colour and the right label, and still be un-clickable because something is painted over it — for example a wrapper that computes to height 0 because its only child is position: absolute, letting a flow sibling paint across the field. const b = el.getBoundingClientRect(); const hit = document.elementFromPoint( Math.round(b.x + b.width / 2), Math.round(b.y + b.height / 2)); const usable = hit && (hit === el || el.contains(hit) || hit.contains(el)); . Two ways this test lies: . | It resolves INSIDE the control. elementFromPoint returns the deepest element, often an <svg> or <span> within a button. hit === el alone reports a working control as covered — which is what the contains pair above is for. | It reports a preview-only overlay. The staging banner (a <div> with no class, z-index: 9999, a child of <body>) exists only on previews. Identify the coverer (document.elementsFromPoint(x, y).slice(0, 3)) before calling it a defect: what is on top decides whether it ships. | . Where the covered control is the ONLY route back to a state — the magnifier that reopens a collapsed search — being un-clickable means an action whose inverse is not reachable.

188d3f74b3a4.title: Two environment facts that cost cycles rather than correctness
188d3f74b3a4.content: . | Never pkill -f "http.server" from the shell running one. The pattern matches your own process group and kills the command issuing it — exit 144, no output, looks like the tool failed. Start each server on a fresh port in its own invocation instead. | Probe scripts must not be left in the repository root. check:undeclared-files fails the gate set on a stray probe.mjs. Playwright needs the script where playwright resolves, so write it to the repo root, run it, and delete it in the same command. | .

350f63010952.title: What to send
350f63010952.content: The frames that answer a question the author would otherwise have to ask: . | before and after of the same element, same viewport; | the surface in both colour schemes, if the change touches colour; | the state that is hard to describe — a region scrolled to its end, a menu open, an empty case. | . Caption them with what to look at, not with what they are. “The nav crushed to a 64px sliver, no home link” is a caption; “navbar screenshot” is a filename. SendUserFile is the mechanism; write into the working directory or the scratchpad, since a file the author cannot open is not a deliverable.

11dc4d459c69.title: Accessibility is measured here too
11dc4d459c69.content: Unique heading anchors and the 3:1 bar for meaningful non-text content are rendered facts: compute the contrast from the two resolved colours rather than from the tokens, because the token you authored and the colour that won are different questions.

c8eecda3bc19.title: Listen for pageerror, or a crash reads as a missing feature
c8eecda3bc19.content: A throw early in a page’s init() takes the rest of init() with it. The symptom is a feature that is simply not there — which looks exactly like a feature that did not mount — and a swallowed init is silent in a screenshot. So: attach the listener, and assert zero. page.on("pageerror", (e) => errors.push(e.stack || e.message)); . And check the base branch before you claim a crash is yours — or before you claim it is not. One run against a build of origin/main tells “something I just broke” from “a live defect nobody had reported”.

408cc9f52cfc.title: A STATIC read of a client-rendered page is not verification — in either direction
408cc9f52cfc.content: This skill stops a false red as well as a false green. Grepping a page’s committed HTML for content the page fetches at runtime proves nothing. The content is absent whether the page works or not. A library viewer, for example, carries DATA_HREF = "../../../assets/library/index.json", fetches it, and filters by instance. Its committed index.html never holds the entry names, so grepping it for them returns the same answer for a working page and a broken one. Loading it in Chromium settles it in one command. A false red files a bug against working code and sends the next agent to rewrite a correct generator, and because the report carries measurements it reads as thoroughly evidenced. If a page assembles any of its content after load, open it. The tell is cheap to check: a fetch, an XMLHttpRequest, a DATA_HREF, a <script> that writes into the DOM. Finding one means a static read cannot answer the question, and §"Running it here" above is how to answer it instead.

e5928114f6f6.title: What this does NOT replace
e5928114f6f6.content: The gate set. This is the layer above it: gates catch what is checkable from the source, and this catches what is only true once a browser has laid it out. A change that skips either is unverified.

3499543c103f.title: Processes that run this skill
