06b1d013a436.title: Adding a skill
06b1d013a436.content: One command, before you commit: . bun run cat skill:register . It generates everything derived from the skill and verifies each artefact landed. bun run cat skill:register:check is the same question without writing, and it is a gate — a skill that arrives undeclared fails CI. skill:register, singular. If you find skills:register in older text, it means this.

9b2e1d4843b9.title: What a skill file owes, and why you cannot see it
9b2e1d4843b9.content: Three things nothing derives for you, and none of them is in the file you just wrote: . | artefact | where | produced by | . | a skills entry | the package’s package-manifest.json | you — see below | . | a published reference page | the site’s reference/skill-instructions/<name> | skills:docs | . | a kg-qa sidecar | test/results/kg-qa/skills/<pkg>/<name>.kg-qa.json — the working copy | kg:audit | . The kg-qa sidecar is a derived QA result, and its record is not the committed file. The CI job qa-publish stores every run’s test/results/ on the orphan qa-reports branch under main/<sha>/ or pr/<n>/<sha>/. The file is also committed on main and kg:audit:check reads it, so skill:register writes it — but a judgement about your skill (an agent’s voice review, a pair attestation) does not go in it: that is test/attestations/kg-qa/…, on main, because no writer can regenerate it. Then a cascade: the schema reference, the glossary and its SKOS export, the auto-docs index and the detangle measurements all read something that just changed. The reason this needs a skill at all is that the feedback arrives somewhere else. CI judges the merge of each pull request’s head into the base, so an undeclared skill on main fails the gate set on every open pull request — and the author who sees the failure is whoever opens the next one.

e5f61c6f9d99.title: The manifest entry is yours, on purpose
e5f61c6f9d99.content: skill:register will not add it. Which package a file belongs to is your assertion, not a derivable fact, and a command that guessed it would register files somebody was still drafting. The command names the file and the remedy; you add the slug, sorted. Everything else it either performs (the derived artefacts, and stripping a retired key — see below) or reports and leaves alone. One exception to “commit what it writes”: skill:commands, one of its steps, writes .claude/commands/ in a composed checkout. That directory is a projection CI writes (harness-projections), so leave its changes unstaged and let the workflow commit them.

9d7f5d5c221c.title: A new folder is a named subgraph of its harness — declare it
9d7f5d5c221c.content: If what you are adding needs a new folder, decide first which of three kinds of folder it is. Each has exactly one way to be declared, and the place the folder sits decides which: . | A folder directly under the harness root (a new code area, a new graph): an entry in the harness’s own declaration (<harness>.json, e.g. cat-harness.json), under directories, with an id, the path, its graphTypologies and a one-line description. | A folder inside a folder the harness already declares: declared from within, in that directory’s own <dir>.json (as skills/skills.json declares voices). This is not a matter of taste: check:layout-norms fails a new top-level entry whose path lies inside another declared directory (the pairs it only lists are a baseline). Add subgraph: true when the new folder is a subgraph of the INSTANCE rather than a part of its parent’s graph (voices is the first kind, beans.json’s defs the second). | A folder that holds ONE node — one Tool, one voice: it is not declared. It sits inside the declared graph that owns the node and is found through that graph’s reader, as each voice folder is found by its voice.json. Never declare one Tool’s folder as a tools directory: discovery refuses a harness that declares two tools directories. The Tool’s folder is found by the loader (toolsFromFolders, in the tools layer), as each voice is by its voice.json. | . Both declared forms say what a folder holds the same way, by its graphTypologies: a from-within entry names its own kind (voices.json declares vendors as voice-vendors), it does not inherit its parent’s. One folder per Tool, always. A Tool is declared in tools/<id>/<id>.json ("$schema": "tool-definition/v1") inside the harness’s declared tools directory: the folder, the file stem and the Tool’s id are one string, and the folder also holds whatever is that Tool’s alone (its script, fixtures, tests). toolsFromFolders refuses a folder that breaks the convention. The tools/ directory is data only; the loader and shared helpers live in the tools layer. The JSON-LD of each Tool (<doc dir>/tools/<id>.jsonld, its own IRI) and the JSON Schema of each I/O type are written when the site is published, never committed. Why declaring is part of the process, not tidying: . | A folder nothing declares is a folder nothing reasons about. No check catches it for you: check:undeclared-files sweeps the repository root only, so a new undeclared folder inside a harness passes it. | Declared directories are what can be mounted and exported. A remote mount lays down declared directories only, so an undeclared code folder is missing downstream. A harness’s package exports are derived from its declared, shipped code directories (check:package-exports), so an undeclared one cannot be imported by package name either. A from-within id can be mounted on its own (remote-mount resolves it through instanceDirectories). | bun run cat harness:dirs then materialises every declared directory, so the folder exists in every checkout rather than only in yours. | .

45552d0f28d1.title: Why one pass is not enough
45552d0f28d1.content: skill:register runs each writer and then re-runs every :check on its own to assert the artefact landed. That second pass is the point: a writer can exit 0 over an artefact it failed to update, and only the :check form catches it. Do not re-derive the chain through bun run cat gates. bun test runs the detangle and kg-audit writers, so by the time those checks execute the artefacts are already repaired. A chain measured through gates comes out two steps short, and both omissions look correct. Do not recall the list from memory: recall goes wrong in both directions, naming steps that adding a skill does not stale and omitting ones it does. Each step in the command was measured red-then-green in isolation. Add one only with the same experiment, and put the measurement in the docblock. One pairing is worth knowing because it reads like a typo and is not: glossary:page is verified by check:glossary, which is that same script with --check. glossary:check is a different program over the SKOS projection. Do not “fix” the pairing to make every check end in :check.

9d73a24c0c94.title: Do not re-add roles:
9d73a24c0c94.content: roles: is retired front matter: nothing reads it, and the actor ids it named do not exist. Copying an adjacent skill’s front matter brings it back, so skill:register strips it and tells you it did — safe to perform automatically, since a retired key carries no author intent to guess at. A field saying who performs a skill must be declared in the schema before it is written.

8e4f0e18ac52.title: Removing or renaming a skill: two orphans, and they are yours
8e4f0e18ac52.content: skill:register reports these and does not fix them. That is deliberate, not an omission. | A manifest entry with no file. kg:audit calls this manifest-skill-exists at severity critical. Pruning it automatically would decide, on your behalf, that nothing referenced the name — and KNOWN_DANGLING in skill-manifest-coverage.test.ts is empty on purpose “so a future entry is added here consciously, with the reason, instead of the check being loosened”. | A derived artefact whose subject is gone. kg:audit reports SUBJECT GONE and refuses to delete it. That is deletion-requires-confirmation: an agent never removes a durable artefact on its own initiative. No amount of regenerating settles it, which is why the command reports the check as still red rather than looping. | .

36902bd3d6e3.title: What this does not decide
36902bd3d6e3.content: Whether a skill should exist, what it should say, or which package it belongs in. This is about the declarations a skill owes once you have decided to add it. For where a new thing goes at all, start at where-does-this-go.

cd9df1380d94.title: What this axis is, and what it deliberately is not
cd9df1380d94.content: A voice whose rules declare appliesTo: ["skill"] judges skill files. In agent-skills that is the shared base agent-skill-authoring and one override per vendor under skills/voices/vendors/ (vendors/vendors.json lists them), each extending the base. A voice counts only once the harness config activates it (voice.active in its index.config.json entry) — the same switch every other voice uses. The boundary: an agentic review, with no formal gate on rule content. “Best practice” drifts, and a vendor describing its own product is an assertion, not evidence. So: . | the criterion skill-voice-review-current (minor, gated by nothing) asks only whether a review exists for the skill and voice as they are now; | a rule you judge fail is recorded in the skill’s attestation file and printed — it is not a finding, and it must not be turned into one here. | .

cf9f7af57f8b.title: Reviewing one skill against one voice
cf9f7af57f8b.content: . | Print the rules you are judging, resolved through extends: . bun run cat voice:review -- --rules agent-skill-authoring-claude . A vendor voice lists its own rules and the base’s, because an inherited rule keeps the scope it was declared under. | Open each rule’s citation before judging it. Every rule carries the library entry, page and quote it was read from. Uphold a verdict from the source, never from the one-line title: the title is a summary, and the rule is what the quote says. | Judge the skill as the platform would load it — the front matter the router sees, the body, and the files the body points to. One verdict per rule: . | verdict | when | note | . | pass | the skill does what the rule asks | optional | . | fail | it does not | required — what is missing, where | . | n/a | the rule cannot apply to this skill (a scripts rule, and the skill has no scripts) | required — why not | . n/a is not a softer fail. If the rule could apply and the skill does not meet it, that is a fail with a note. | Record it — the writer refuses a set that misses a rule, judges one twice, or leaves a fail/n/a unexplained: . bun run cat voice:review -- --sidecar <instance>/test/results/kg-qa/<skill path>.json \ --voice agent-skill-authoring-claude --by agent --verdicts verdicts.json . verdicts.json is [{ "rule": "<id>", "result": "pass"|"fail"|"n/a", "note": "…" }]. The review pins the skill’s content hash and the hash of the voice’s skill rules, and replaces any earlier review of that skill against that voice. --sidecar names the subject, not where the review is written. A voice review is a judgement, so it is kept as voice_reviews in the skill’s attestation file, <instance>/test/attestations/kg-qa/<skill path>.attestations.json (qa-attestations/v1), on main — not in the derived kg-qa sidecar, whose record is on the qa-reports branch. Commit the attestation file. A store that cannot be read is UNKNOWN and the writer refuses rather than overwriting it. | Run bun run cat kg:audit so the sidecar’s criterion reads the new review from the store. | .

ed2868e3e75f.title: When the criterion reports stale
ed2868e3e75f.content: A review goes stale when the skill changes or the voice’s skill rules change. The earlier review is kept, not deleted — it is evidence of what was checked — and the finding stays until a new review replaces it. Re-review the whole voice rather than patching the one rule you suspect moved: a changed skill can break a rule nobody was looking at.

757793f3779a.title: Fixing what you found
757793f3779a.content: A fail verdict is information for whoever owns the skill. Editing the skill is a separate change with its own review. Do not edit a skill to make your own verdict pass in the same step: record the verdict first, change the skill, then review again — so the sidecar shows both states.

da27d20c5f06.title: Skills and Tools — the skill says what, the Tool says how
da27d20c5f06.content: A skill is a capability stated generically. A Tool content node is one concrete way to exercise it. One skill may be satisfied by several Tools; a Tool names the skills it satisfies through its satisfies field. This is the standard operating procedure for every skill in the harness, not a guideline for new ones. A skill that names GitHub, names the beans binary, or embeds a shell invocation has swallowed a Tool, and the swallowing is what makes a layer un-portable. Schema for the Tool node: schemas/tools/tool.ts in the tools layer; carrier convention (Zod authoritative, JSON-LD and JSON Schema generated) in directory-conventions §”What lives in the schemas graph”.

d039cf527689.title: The test, in one line
d039cf527689.content: Would this sentence still be true on a different forge, a different binary, a different machine? If yes it is skill. If no it is Tool. Applied: . | sentence | verdict | . | “Open a change proposal as soon as there is one commit to hang it on.” | skill — true anywhere | . | “gh pr create”, or the REST call it wraps | Tool — one forge, one transport | . | “Claim the item before you work, so a sibling session does not pick it up.” | skill | . | “beans update <id> --status in-progress” | Tool | . | “If the CLI is unavailable, the store is still writable by hand.” | skill — the fact is portable | . | “Edit the status: line in the front matter of beans/defs/<id>--*.md.” | Tool | . That last pair is the one people get wrong. Having a fallback is a property of the capability; performing the fallback is a mechanism. The skill must say a fallback exists and when to reach for it, because an agent that does not know one exists will stop. What it must not do is spell out the edit. When the mechanism is itself a procedure, it is the Tool’s subprocess (§”A Tool may describe its own subprocess”). The Tool node names the BPMN in subprocesses (process ids, checked by check:tools), conventionally under processes/tools/; the skill keeps the portable sentence. See bpmn-processes.

0c3d302cea56.title: Every bean skill has (at least) two Tools
0c3d302cea56.content: The work-plan skills are the worked example: . | Tool | when | . | beans CLI | normal case — installed via scripts/install-beans.sh | . | hand edit / scripts/beans-fallback.ts | CLI absent or cannot be installed here | . Both satisfy the same skills. Neither is the skill. A fresh container has no beans on PATH, so an agent that only knows the CLI reads the plan and touches nothing. The fallback is a second Tool with equal standing, and the skill must present it that way. An external project is a candidate Tool before it is anything else. When somebody asks whether another project could do a skill’s job — Beads for the work plan, say — that survey is research, not a proposal and not a skill edit: it files under <instance>/docs/research-and-analysis/ per placement, dated, with each project’s health measured rather than recalled (for example research-and-analysis/prior-art.md). Only if a candidate is adopted does it become a Tool node, with the selection its derived alternatives call for, below.

d991b2e9aef9.title: Substitutable Tools are derived, and each says how to choose
d991b2e9aef9.content: A pair like that is substitutable: same job, different mechanism, pick one. Nobody declares it. Two Tools are alternatives when they satisfy a common skill AND have the same I/O signature — the same input names, types and required flags, the same outputs, the same renders and maintains (deriveAlternatives in schemas/tools/tool.ts). A shared skill alone is not enough: most skills with several Tools have complementary ones, steps rather than choices, and their I/O is what tells them apart. So the discipline moves to the ports. Type and name a port for what it really takes and gives. A CSV reader and a workbook reader typed Text would derive as alternatives; DelimitedTextPath and WorkbookPath keep them apart. Two generators whose output is a bare pages would too; naming each output for what it writes does not. Each Tool with a derived alternative then carries selection — three fields, all required together (check-tools fails one without it): . | field | answers | . | when | the case this Tool is the right answer to | . | limits | where it stops, and which sibling picks up | . | cost | what having it available costs | . Do not skip limits: without it an agent reaches for the tool and discovers the boundary by failing. State it even when it is “none”, for the same reason install.none exists — so “no limits” is distinguishable from an unfinished record. cost is not install. install says how to obtain the tool; cost says what having it costs — CI minutes, a wheel needing a C toolchain, a network round trip. Two Tools can be equally easy to install and very differently expensive to keep. Not in description. It is projected verbatim as the MCP tool description and into the exported graph, and answers “what does this do”; comparative prose about cost does not belong there, because it would degrade the surface an agent reads when choosing among tools. Sharing a skill does NOT make two Tools alternatives . Most skills with several Tools have complementary ones: workflow-list, -start, -next, -gate and -complete are five steps of process-state, not five ways to perform it. Only Tools that also share an I/O signature are alternatives, and scripts/check-tools.ts checks that the relation is mutual, because a one-sided one means an agent arriving at the silent end never learns a choice exists. Keying substitutability on a shared skill alone would demand comparative prose where there is nothing to compare, and an author obliged to write it writes noise. The worked pair: stdlib vs extensions . ingest-stdlib and ingest-extended both satisfy library-ingestion, and the split falls where the dependency boundary actually is rather than on principle: . |   | ingest-stdlib | ingest-extended | . | install | nothing (install.none) | PyMuPDF, pypdf + Pillow, tesseract | . | covers | archives, CSV/spreadsheets, technical metadata, content routing | PDF outline, page text, OCR, images | . | runs in CI here | yes | no — CI installs ruff and nothing else | . Reading a zip’s central directory, sniffing magic bytes and parsing an xlsx’s XML are all in the Python standard library; rendering a PDF’s text layer is not and never will be. An agent picks by what the machine has, not by what the document is — and the stdlib arm refuses a PDF outright rather than half-ingesting one, so the choice is never made silently. This is also the shape to reach for whenever a capability has a heavyweight backend: two Tools, one skill, the dependency posture legible on each node, instead of a repository-wide yes/no that no reader of a skill can see.

9a38d231354c.title: The harness assumes no MCP — and knows how to emit one
9a38d231354c.content: agentic-harness must work with no MCP server running. Everything it needs is files in directories the instance declares: skills in the kg graph, Tool nodes beside them, the work plan in the beans graph. An agent with nothing but a filesystem and <name>.json can read all of it. MCP is acknowledged as a future transport, not assumed as the present one. Where a downstream instance runs a server, skill_list / skill_fetch / work_plan_prime are a convenience over the same files — and ToolDefinition accordingly declares invoke.mcp as one optional arm beside shell and container. A Tool whose only invocation is an MCP call is not usable by the harness that defines it. Editing a skill goes through skill_update, not a raw file write. Where the server runs, it is the write side of skill_fetch. It refuses unless every gate passes: . | the skill resolves as skill_fetch serves it; | the file is tracked in this repository, so not another layer’s skill and not a mounted copy; | the file is not generated; | a policy grants skill-update to the actor (no default policy does); | the file is unchanged since it was read; | the front matter parses and keeps the skill’s name; | every link the edit adds resolves. | . A gate that cannot decide refuses. The Tool writes the working tree, and the caller commits the change. That is a statement about dependency, not about ignorance. MCP is an output of this harness: mcp-projection is how an agent takes a Tool node describing a CLI and produces a working MCP service from it, mcp-assembly covers composing several into one namespace, and mcp-contract checks the result still matches its sources. The harness is the thing that knows the mapping; it just does not need the result in order to run. It is what makes the harness bootstrappable: the layer that defines what a Tool is cannot require a tool server to read its own definitions without arguing in a circle. It is also why sovereign-compute and air-gapped operation are reachable later without a second design — an instance with no server loses a transport, not a capability. So when this skill says “reach a Tool through the graph”, the floor is: read <name>.json, find the kg entry, open the directory. Anything richer is an optimisation an instance may offer.

132884ef06fd.title: GitHub is a Tool node, not a layer
132884ef06fd.content: The PR-choreography skills — prepare-merge-auto, pickup, watch, coordinate — assume a forge, but most of their text is portable: “pull request”, “PR”, “GitHub” as a noun. Only a few lines are concrete invocations. So forge-specificity is isolated at the Tool layer: the skills stay in the harness, stated generically, and Tool nodes carry the invocations — one per forge operation (table below). Adding another forge is more Tool nodes satisfying the same skills, not a repository or a fork. The forge operations, one Tool node each . One Tool node per forge operation, using the fields Tools already have. A skill names the operation in neutral words, and this table is where an operation meets its nodes. An agent picks the node for the forge the checkout’s remote is on; each pair is a derived alternative carrying selection (check:tools holds it). | operation (as a skill names it) | GitHub | GitLab | . | list change proposals | github-pr-list | gitlab-mr-list | . | read change proposal (body, comments, reviews) | github-pr-view | gitlab-mr-view | . | read change proposal (check runs) | github-pr-checks | — | . | list changed files | github-pr-files | gitlab-mr-files | . | comment on change proposal | github-pr-comment | gitlab-mr-comment | . | request review | github-pr-request-review | gitlab-mr-request-review | . | resolve review thread | github-pr-resolve-thread | gitlab-mr-resolve-thread | . | list branches | github-branches | gitlab-branches | . A dash is a known gap. Two GitLab nodes run a script rather than glab directly: glab mr diff has no --name-only, so gitlab-mr-files reads the paths out of the raw diff; and glab mr update --reviewer NAME replaces the reviewers, so gitlab-mr-request-review passes +NAME, which adds one. Its names are GitLabUsernames, since GitLab usernames do not fit Login. Branches alone are also listable with git ls-remote --heads origin, which needs no forge. Subscribing to a change proposal’s activity is not a forge operation. It is the session platform’s (in a Claude Code remote session, its PR-activity subscription), so no forge Tool node offers it, and a skill says so rather than naming a forge for it. A Tool may describe its own subprocess . When one mechanism takes several steps, they belong to the Tool, not to the general skill: the Tool lists subprocesses (process ids, each the stem of a .bpmn the checkout declares), and a general diagram’s call activity is bound by it. General skills name the Tool, never its steps. Example: render-kg-to-cdn is the general step (render a Knowledge Graph for a CDN at a publication root URL; output a status and a message), and gh-pages is one Tool for it whose subprocess is bootstrap-tools’ render-kg-to-github-pages.bpmn — declared below the harness, so the reference points down. Vocabulary — name the concept, not the vendor’s word for it . GitHub calls it a pull request; GitLab calls it a merge request; Gerrit calls it a change. A skill that says “pull request” has picked one vendor’s noun, which is a milder form of the same defect. Prefer the neutral term on first use and the local term thereafter, rather than scrubbing every occurrence — a skill written entirely in invented vocabulary is unreadable, and unreadable is worse than mildly GitHub-flavoured. The rule is that an agent must never have to resolve a vendor noun to act: it is fine for a skill to say “pull request (PR)” once and use PR after it; it is not fine for the only statement of what to do to be gh pr create.

b94d2f0b59df.title: Writing or editing a skill — the checklist
b94d2f0b59df.content: . | Grep your own draft for vendor names, binaries, endpoints, file paths under a tool’s control, and flag characters. Each hit is a Tool that has not been declared. | State the capability first, in a sentence that survives the mechanism being replaced. 2b. If an input reaches a command line, give it a type that cannot be a payload — and put free prose on stdin. See untrusted-input; check:tools fails CI on a violation. | Say a mechanism exists and where to find it — never inline it. A Tool is reached the same way a skill is: resolve the kg graph from the instance’s declaration and read from the directory it names. Not a remembered path, and — see below — not necessarily a tool call. | Say when each Tool applies if there is more than one, because choosing between them is judgement and judgement is skill. | Name what happens when no Tool is available. Three states, as everywhere here: the Tool worked, the Tool is absent and here is the fallback, and we could not tell — which is never rendered as success. | .

e3c9a3e337f1.title: The Tool schema, and the remaining debt
e3c9a3e337f1.content: schemas/tools/tool.ts (in the tools layer) defines a Tool, tools/ holds the nodes, and bun run cat check:tools fails when a satisfies names a skill that does not exist. ToolInput.repeated marks a list input (rather than a list type per scalar type, which would multiply the shared $defs and break the identity property the shared vocabulary exists for). invoke.inProcess names a TypeScript function for a Tool with no shell equivalent; it is runnable by the harness directly, and is the projection source rather than something to proxy, so the refusal of an mcp-only Tool does not reach it. Many skills still carry their invocations inline. Most of the remainder is fine — a great many skills are pure judgement (interaction-modality, one-voice-style-guide) and have no mechanism to name. check:tools reports the coverage count rather than failing on it, for exactly that reason. What it cannot tell you, and what needs a human eye, is which of the uncovered skills describe an action — those are the ones whose mechanism is still swallowed. A satisfies edge is checkable against the skill’s own contract . satisfies is the one part of a Tool node a schema cannot check, and it was being written on judgement alone. bun run cat check:tools compares a Tool’s io against the input contract of every skill it claims — the contract the skill names in its own front matter (input:), never one found by directory name. Two rules: every required property of the contract must appear as an input on the Tool, and where a Tool input and a contract property share a name, their JSON types must agree (an integer port may serve a number property). If either fails, the Tool cannot exercise the skill and the edge is false. What is compared, and what is not. A skill’s contract is free-form JSON Schema; a Tool’s io is named ports referencing shared $defs IRIs, so they meet only at names and at the JSON type each port’s vocabulary type projects to. The type rule is weak — nearly every contract property here is a bare {"type": "string"} — but not vacuous: it catches an array contract served by a string port, which the name rule passes. A mismatch that is “only” a naming difference — path against targetPath — is a finding, not a false positive to suppress. Two names for one input, across a skill and the Tool claiming to implement it, means an agent reading the contract cannot call the Tool. Three states, as everywhere. No contract (the common case, not a defect) is undefined; a contract requiring nothing is [] and passes; a contract that is declared but missing or unparseable is reported and fails, never counted as agreement. An external https:// contract is not fetched by this offline check. For example, a Tool that validates a .po against its .pot does not satisfy content-validate, whose contract requires targetPath: validating translations is not validating a folio’s content. Which uncovered skills actually need one — bun run cat tools:coverage . The count alone does not say which. A grep for shell blocks over-reports, because a skill may legitimately QUOTE a command while stating its capability generically. The corpus carries a better signal — BPMN task type. A process step is a serviceTask (runs without a person) or a userTask (performed by one), and the diagrams already say which. Triaged on that, plus an I/O contract under schemas/skills/, the tiers are A (automation evidence), B (userTask-only), C (ambiguous) and D (nothing), and only C needs a human read. Run it for the numbers; do not quote them from prose: a count in prose is a claim that nothing re-checks, and it drifts unnoticed. Many skills are both: two activities name interaction-modality, a serviceTask that reads the preferences file — a mechanism — and a userTask about how to frame a question — judgement. The question is not “is this skill a Tool?” but “which PART of it is.” . A skill with both halves is not mis-modelled. Migrating it is a split: the mechanical half becomes a Tool, the judgement half stays as prose. Expecting a clean move makes the migration look bigger than it is. So when you write or edit a skill: follow the checklist above and reference a Tool. When you read one that inlines gh pr create or beans update, that is the debt, not the pattern — do not propagate it. Authoring a Tool node: tools/<id>/<id>.json, one folder per Tool, a "$schema": "tool-definition/v1" document validated against the Tool schema; the loader lives in the tools layer. io ports reference the shared vocabulary in schemas/tools/tool-types.ts by its type name ("$type") — never a free-form string, because a reference nothing checks is eventually wrong. For the end-to-end guide on authoring, implementing, packaging, and registering concrete tools across separated repositories, see tool-authoring. For runtime conventions, test preloading, and TypeScript configuration, see bun-use.

c1a2a7906d07.title: Covered is not reachable — see its own skill
c1a2a7906d07.content: A skill can be satisfied by the neighbours of its mechanism while the mechanism itself is reachable from nothing, and check:tools reports it as covered and is right to. That discipline, the two questions it keeps apart, what to do when you meet one, and the two reasons not to write maintains: covered-is-not-reachable.

d94a52529b35.title: smart-base Toolchain
d94a52529b35.content: Skill id: smart-base-tools · Package: authoring-who-smart-guidelines . Run WHO’s DAK toolchain from a smart-base checkout. Load it; never vendor it. smart-base/tools/ holds Tool nodes: declarations of what each upstream capability consumes, produces and satisfies, so a BPMN activity can bind it. A Tool node duplicates no code. The Python stays in WorldHealthOrganization/smart-base, which the DAK repositories’ GitHub Actions run in place; a copy here would be a second, drifting toolchain. Declare here, execute upstream, until the execution moves as one migration with a cutover (toolchain-ownership). strip_library_binaries.py and strip_library_content.py are not declared here: they are not DAK-shaped and belong to fhir-harness (smart-stack-layering).

67f35ee95696.title: Before you start
67f35ee95696.content: export SMART_BASE_HOME=/path/to/smart-base # default: /opt/smart-base python3 smart-base/scripts/smart-base-transform.py --check . --check exits non-zero and names what is missing. Without a checkout the skill degrades to skip — it does not report a clean run over a toolchain it never had.

6d99db758665.title: Transforms
6d99db758665.content: Both render an authored source artefact into a published representation (the extractors go the other way). # BPMN → FHIR Shorthand python3 smart-base/scripts/smart-base-transform.py bpmn2fsh <file.bpmn|dir> -o OUTDIR # DMN → HTML python3 smart-base/scripts/smart-base-transform.py dmn2html <file.dmn|dir> -o OUTDIR . Omit -o for a dry run that reports counts and writes nothing.

b8b8b52bc575.title: Two things to expect
b8b8b52bc575.content: bpmn2fhirfsh.xsl emits many files per input. Its output is an envelope, <files><file name="…">…</file>…</files>, and each entry is a separate artefact at the path the transform names. Measured on smart-dak-immz: 8 business processes → 313 files, one process alone accounting for 157. Paths collide across inputs. Those 313 land at only 201 distinct paths, because shared actors and near-duplicate processes name the same outputs. The runner counts and names every collision on stderr instead of overwriting silently. Decide for each whether it is a duplicate input to remove or two processes that legitimately contribute the same actor.

ce07427e0776.title: What else is in there
ce07427e0776.content: smart-base carries ~54 Python scripts: extractors (dd_extractor, dt_extractor, req_extractor, extractpr), generators (generate_jsonld_vocabularies, generate_*_schemas, dmn_questionnaire_generator), a translation subsystem, and IG build/CI orchestration. The two transforms above are wrapped, and extract_dak.py (which runs dd_extractor, req_extractor and dt_extractor) is declared as the Tool extract-dak. The IG build and CI scripts want no skill: GitHub Actions is their caller.

48c74ee0ce2d.title: Adapting a DAK: use the toolchain the upstream used
48c74ee0ce2d.content: An adaptation changes the upstream’s components, so it produces them the way the upstream produced them. Before writing any converter, generator, checker or test runner, find that way, in this order, and record it in the stage-3 or stage-5 dependency row of smart-guideline-end-to-end (toolchain): . | The tools graph. bun run cat check:tools from the instance root lists every Tool the mounted layers declare (smart-base, fhir-harness, folio-assistant-core, cat-harness), with the skills each satisfies. | The upstream repository’s own toolchain. Read the dependency’s repository, not only its published IG. For the WHO immunizations DAK (https://github.com/litlfred/smart-immunizations), what it uses: . | component | upstream source | how it is produced | . | decision-support logic | input/decision-logic/IMMZ DAK_decision-support logic.xlsx, DAK template | the repository’s own tools/node/processDTInput.js, processDTOutput.js, processDTCheck.js (node-xlsx → CQL, FSH); extract-dak (dt_extractor, → DMN) reads the same layout | . | scheduling logic | the schedule tabs of that spreadsheet | tools/node/processDTSchedule.js <xlsx> <sheet> … | . | core data elements, indicators | input/L2/IMMZ DAK_core data dictionary.xlsx, IMMZ DAK_indicators.xlsx | tools/node/processDAK.js -f <xlsx>, processIND.js; extract-dak (dd_extractor) where the layout is input/dictionary/ | . | requirements | DAK requirements template (input/system-requirements/, empty in this repository) | extract-dak (req_extractor) | . | CQL libraries (compile and refresh) | input/cql/*.cql | cqf tooling-cli -RefreshIG (_refresh.sh); the IG Publisher compiles CQL in the build | . | test cases | input/tests/plandefinition/<Library>/*.yaml | tools/node/makeExample.js into FHIR test bundles | . | L1 recommendations transcribed verbatim | *.l1.yaml (measles) | litlfred/test tools/build_l1.py | . | L1 authored from pictures (posters, slides) | *.l1.yaml with image: / from: | the smart-base Tool l1-transcription-verbatim | . | WHO’s method. The WHO IG Starter Kit (smart.who.int/ig-starter-kit: l2_dak_authoring, l3_decisiontables, l3_cql, l3_testing) and its DAK templates (decision-support, scheduling, requirements, data dictionary, indicators). Jurisdiction training material where there is some, e.g. litlfred/uganda-sg-training for Uganda. | . Only when all three come back empty is something new written, and then as a Tool node under tool-authoring, with the search recorded in the dependency row (toolchain: none, and where it looked). Never write a script into the adaptation repository without a Tool node. Step 2 is not optional: upstream converters, CQL refresh scripts and test formats are usually not declared Tools, so the graph search alone misses them. There is no PDF renderer in smart-base. Its only PDF dependency is pdfplumber, used to read PDFs when extracting personas.

18ee839cc4ef.title: What the generic authoring skills need to know here
18ee839cc4ef.content: The platform’s bpmn-authoring, dmn-authoring and translation-manager are generic and name no DAK. What a DAK adds to each: . | BPMN is a source artefact. bpmn2fsh turns an authored business process into FHIR Shorthand, so names and ids chosen in the diagram appear in the generated FSH. Author it knowing it will be transformed. A changed diagram also changes its picture and its translation templates: re-render it (smart-base/scripts/render-processes.ts) and run bun run cat regen (prepare-merge), which re-extracts the .pot files translate-bpmn:check gates on. | DMN is a source artefact. dmn2html renders decision tables for human review, and dmn_questionnaire_generator derives questionnaires from them; the caveats are §”Two things to expect” above. | Translation. smart-base defines the formal actor SGAuthoring.Persona.Translator, with the skill requirements SGAuthoring.Skills.TranslateContent and SGAuthoring.Skills.ReviewTranslations. The translation subsystem is invoked from a smart-base checkout, never copied. | .

71f74d262d50.title: smart-guideline-create
71f74d262d50.content: Skill id: smart-guideline-create · Package: authoring-who-smart-guidelines Specialises fhir-ig-create . A new SMART guideline is created either in a new repository or inside the folio of an existing harnessed repository. Run fhir-ig-create and change only what is below. Its facts, decision table, question and default (in-repo, a staged sub-KG) all hold. This skill adds what is WHO’s, which the FHIR layer must not know (check:fhir-harness-exclusions).

4049f4945f5a.title: What changes
4049f4945f5a.content: 1. A fourth fact: which level is being started . A SMART guideline is L1 narrative, an L2 DAK, or an L3 IG (smart-stack-layering), and they are not a chain. Ask it as one more numbered question, only when the request did not say: . What are you starting with? . | The FHIR IG (L3) (recommended). The level the pipeline builds today. | The DAK (L2): the ten components. Its document kind is still being built, so this starts as plain authoring. | An L1 narrative document from the smart-base library. | Tell me more. | . Default if you do not answer: 1. An L1 or DAK start is a document kind inside smart-base, authored with l2-dak-authoring or as an L1 document, not a new instance. Only the IG (option 1) goes through the routes below. 2. The declaration needs the IG-publication layer, not fhir-harness . Where fhir-ig-create writes needs: ["fhir-harness"], a SMART guideline needs the layer every ingested guideline already needs: copy the needs of an existing staged guideline’s declaration rather than typing a name. That layer brings smart-base, and through it the WHO template’s theme and chrome. Never copy a theme or a chrome.json into the new instance: chrome is keyed to the template, not to one guideline. 3. The layout is the same in every repository . Every guideline repository instantiates smart-base the same way. | at the repository root | under smart-base/ | . | the IG source as WHO publishes it (sushi-config.yaml, input/), unchanged | this guideline’s data: its declaration, artefact index, menu, generated pages, QA results | . | index.config.json, whose smart-base entry carries the instance’s config inline (there is no smart-base.config.json) |   | . So while the guideline is staged in place (route in-repo), its directory is already that smart-base/ data directory, under whatever path livesAt names. When it leaves, the directory becomes smart-base/ in the new repository, so nothing may key on the directory name: identity comes from the declaration’s name. Check every new generator for this before it ships. 4. A new repository is a litlfred fork first . litlfred/smart-* forks are the staging ground before any WHO repository. In route new-repo, and in sub-kg-lifecycle’s stage 8, the planned repository is litlfred/<name>, a fork of the WHO repository when one exists. Moving to a WorldHealthOrganization/* repository is a later, separate owner decision, never part of this skill. The question before creating is the same one, with the same default (“not yet”). 5. Pages are generated with the WHO labels passed in . The page generator is fhir-harness’s and knows nothing of WHO; the WHO names are configuration. Model the new instance’s <name>:pages script on smart-base:pages in smart-base/package.json: --publish-note, --sidecar-label "DAK API", --label and --chrome-owner smart-base. 6. A new repository carries its entry point and its platform mount . An empty repository gives an agent no skills, no process and nothing saying the work is staged L1 → L2 → L3 (smart-guideline-end-to-end, The order is a rule). So route new-repo writes these before any guideline content, copied from an existing guideline repository (https://github.com/litlfred/smart-immunizations), never typed: . | file | what it does | . | AGENTS.md, declared in <name>.json as the asset agent-instructions (role agent-instructions), with README.md as instance-readme | names smart-guideline-end-to-end as the entry point for any authoring or adaptation work, and nothing else. CLAUDE.md is the pointer stub init-folio writes (@AGENTS.md; in an index checkout whose root declares no instance, bun run cat index:render writes it); never put guidance in it (placement, The agent-file stub) | . | .claude/settings.json + .claude/mount-platform.sh | the SessionStart hook that mounts the platform, so the skills and processes are on disk in every session | . | index.config.json | the mount of smart-base (and through it the platform), as in every guideline repository (§3) | . | its site, its checks, its .gitignore mount block, and an IG’s site templates | what sub-kg-lifecycle stage 10 (its site, its checks, .gitignore) and fhir-ig-create new-repo step 5 list, copied from the guideline repository named above | . | <name>.json | the instance declaration: its assets (above), library/ as library, and one l1-extraction entry per extraction directory as each is created (recommendation-extraction, Declare every output directory) — an undeclared one fails folio-assistant’s check:l1-complete and with it the staging build | . An existing repository that lacks any of these gets them copied first, in their own commit.

dca5fefcc9fb.title: What does not change
dca5fefcc9fb.content: The import seam (<name>/platform.ts), the separation guard, seed:ready, the two owner confirmations and the fresh-clone check are all sub-kg-lifecycle’s, and apply to a SMART guideline unchanged.

f511e75ccbb5.title: Anti-patterns
f511e75ccbb5.content: . | A per-guideline harness. smart-base is the harness; a guideline is an instance of it (smart-stack-layering §”Two consequences”). | Creating under WorldHealthOrganization/ first. The forks are the staging ground (§4). | Copying the WHO theme into the guideline to make a page look right. It arrives by needs. | Writing L3 into a bare repository: FSH or CQL with no declared entry point, no mount and no library/ (§6). | Extraction output the declaration does not name. An l1-extraction/ directory, or a scenario directory beside the library entries, missing from <name>.json passes every check in the guideline repository and fails folio-assistant’s QA working copy once the index mounts it (§6). | A hand-written CLAUDE.md. It is read by one vendor’s agent and checked by nothing. Declare AGENTS.md and keep CLAUDE.md the generated stub (§6). | .

554a763a5d08.title: smart-guideline-end-to-end
554a763a5d08.content: Skill id: smart-guideline-end-to-end · Package: authoring-who-smart-guidelines · Process: smart-guideline-end-to-end.bpmn . This skill holds the order of the stages, the hand-off between them and the adjudication rule. What a stage does is in its own skill; if a stage needs something its skill does not say, fix that skill, not this one. Every record uses an existing schema (What it reuses).

6e55d650b3ff.title: Input and output
6e55d650b3ff.content: The contract is input.schema.json and output.schema.json. | In: the request, verbatim; the useCase when stage 0 is already done; the guideline’s feature branch. | Out: every stage’s artefact under the name the stage table gives it (useCase, l1Sources, l1Kg, l2Dependencies, l2Assets, l3Dependencies, ig, applicationBrief, wireframes, application), and one adjudications entry per stage with its QaReview and outcome. The guideline is done only when no outcome is pending. | .

8dd3e674fbdb.title: The rule that shapes everything: adjudication is QA, not a gate
8dd3e674fbdb.content: Every stage ends in a fork: the agent goes on to the next stage while a person adjudicates the last one. stage n (agent) ──┬──► stage n+1 (agent) keeps going └──► adjudicate stage n (human) runs beside it . | Every stage is adjudicated, and the guideline is not done until every adjudication is recorded. Not waiting is not skipping. | An asset built on unadjudicated input says so. Each derived KG node names its inputs in wasDerivedFrom (hash-pinned; smart-base/kg/src/graph.ts); the edge’s open properties carry adjudication: pending until the input’s review closes. | A rejection reopens the stage, and the flag spreads downstream. A request-changes or reject decision files a bean against the stage. Every asset derived from the rejected item gets adjudication: rejected-upstream on that edge and is re-derived when the stage is redone, not deleted ahead of time: the re-derivation may come out the same. | The agent never adjudicates. It may prepare the review material; the verdict is recorded by the person in the role the stage table names. | .

afb649dd2230.title: The order is a rule: L1, then L2, then L3
afb649dd2230.content: QA-not-a-gate is about verdicts. It never licenses skipping a stage. | Each stage’s output exists before the next stage starts. Stage 2 writes the L1 extraction for every source of the use case; stage 4 writes the L2 assets; only then does stage 6 write FSH, CQL or any other L3 file. Source documents (a schedule poster, a slide deck) are stage-2 input, never direct input to L3. | Sign-off is requested before the next stage starts. Each asset’s review item (Process_Review) is opened, staged and handed to its adjudicating role. The verdict is not awaited, but an asset whose review was never requested has not finished its stage. | Every L3 asset names the L2 asset it implements, and every L2 asset the L1 node it rests on, in wasDerivedFrom with the edge’s adjudication state. An L3 asset with no L2 upstream is a finding, even with a green build and passing tests. | A request that skips stages is still this process. “Adapt X to using these documents" is stages 0–6. If the request names no L1/L2 work, the agent does it anyway and says so. | . A new repository carries a pointer to this skill and a platform mount (smart-guideline-create §6). In l2-dak-authoring.bpmn the Clinically accurate? decision runs beside assembly: a parallel fork after the authoring join starts clinical validation and assembly together. changes needed sends the work round again, re-assembling the DAK; validated ends in its own event.

2ac0f52c15bc.title: The stages
2ac0f52c15bc.content: Each stage’s Out is the next stage’s In, under the same name and definition in each standalone contract. The two stages run by other layers’ skills are called through the mapping in their row. | # | stage | skill | In | Out | adjudicated by | . | 0 | Describe the use case | guideline-use-case | the request | useCase | (the requester is the source) | . | 1 | Identify L1 guidelines and recommendations | dak-l1-library | useCase | l1Sources: each candidate in-library / in-kg / not-yet, included or not, and why | Clinical SME | . | 2 | Ingest into an L1 KG the sources not yet in one | recommendation-extraction (after bun run cat ingest and dak-l1-library’s generic-document layer for a source not in library/) | l1Sources | l1Kg: per source, library/<bib>/l1-extraction/, coverage, every WARNING | l1-extraction-reviewer (exclusions, coverage), Clinical SME (recommendations) | . | 3 | Choose L2 dependencies (WHO / jurisdiction DAKs) | l2-dependency-choice, with smart-base-tools §Adapting a DAK for how each candidate produces each component | l1Kg | l2Dependencies: one decision row per candidate DAK, and per component the toolchain stage 4 will use | Programme manager + Business analyst | . | 4 | Create or adapt the L2 DAK assets | l2-dak-authoring, once per component, with the stage-3 toolchain (smart-base-tools), in the steps of l2-dak-authoring.bpmn, each an edit-then-review call into l2-component-edit-review.bpmn; pre/post-processing by dak-preprocessing / dak-postprocessing as smart-base’s overlay on fhir-harness’s AST cache refresh | dakComponent, sourceGuideline, l1Kg, l2Dependencies | artifacts of every pass, which are l2Assets | per asset, see Per-asset review | . | 5 | Choose L3 dependencies (WHO / jurisdiction IGs) | l3-dependency-choice, indexing with ig-artifact-ingestion, with smart-base-tools §Adapting a DAK for how each candidate builds and tests its CQL and examples | l1Kg, l2Assets, l2Dependencies | l3Dependencies, and per artefact type the toolchain stage 6 will use, and the IG indexes | FHIR modeller + Terminologist | . | 6 | Produce the L3 assets, only once Gateway_L3Ready says yes on l3-readiness (the order rule) | fhir-harness l3-fhir-authoring with l2-dak-authoring and the stage-5 toolchain, in dak-l3-ig.bpmn, up to a clean IG build | per artifact: artifactType, sourceModel = an l2Assets path; the adjudicated l3Dependencies rows become sushi-config.yaml dependencies | fshFiles, sushiResult, generatedResources, read as ig with its igRoot | per asset, see Per-asset review | . | 7 | L4: describe the consuming application | l4-application-brief | useCase, l2Assets, ig | applicationBrief, and the wireframeRequest | (the requester is the source) | . | 8a | L4: wireframe the application | cat-harness wireframe-design-review, design use | wireframeRequest, unchanged | the candidates and the choice, read as wireframes | Business analyst + Clinical SME, with the requester choosing | . | 8b | L4: build the consuming application | l4-application-build | applicationBrief, ig, wireframes | application, with its conformance and scenario tests | Business analyst + Clinical SME (does it do what the L2 says?), FHIR modeller (does it conform to L3?) | . Between stages 5 and 6, Task_L3Ready runs l3-readiness (in: l1Kg, l2Assets, the reviews requested and the L3 artefacts about to be written; out: ready and the findings), and Gateway_L3Ready decides on it. No goes back to stage 4. Publication of the IG (the end of dak-l3-ig.bpmn) is not on the path to stage 8: an application can be built against an unpublished IG. Every adjudication calls cat-harness’s generic review, Process_Review (processes/content/review-task.bpmn), which runs the review that fits the change and accepts or sends back; disagreement goes to Process_Adjudication. Staging: every review looks at a staged preview . Each stage commits to the guideline’s feature branch, which feature-staging (Process_FeatureStaging) stages on the site its section Which site names: a guideline in its own repository on that repository’s Pages, smart-base itself by a staging re-pin on folio-assistant’s site. An IG repository’s site needs its AST cache seeded first (fhir-ig-create, new-repo step 5). The IG Publisher’s branches/ preview (ghbuild.yml, /deploy) is never the preview for this content. A review item links to the staged page through staging-review, which returns before (main) and after (staging) URL pairs. A new guideline with no repository yet is staged inside the current one first (in-repo, a staged sub-KG, the smart-guideline-create default).

e5a3c6cfa551.title: Per-asset review
e5a3c6cfa551.content: Every asset a stage creates or changes gets its own review item; one reused unchanged gets none. The review item shows the asset on the staged preview the way its reviewer reads it, not as source. At L2 it is a run of l2-component-edit-review.bpmn, whose skill gives each row’s checker, renderer and reviewer: . | level | asset | review shows | . | L1 | recommendation / remark / practice | the node beside the printed sentence and page | . | L2 | persona, user scenario | the card: role, goal, setting | . | L2 | business process (BPMN) | the rendered diagram (render:bpmn / dak-swimlanes) | . | L2 | decision table (DMN) | the table (dmn2html), with the L1 recommendation each rule cites, and its test cases | . | L2 | core data elements | data-dictionary rows (dak-data-dictionary) and their term diff (dak-data-dictionary-diff), and the chosen wireframe of each form that captures them (see Forms are designed as wireframes) | . | L2 | indicators, requirements | the indicator definition / requirement list, each with the persona and process it serves | . | L3 | Questionnaire | the L2 wireframe it was derived from, beside the Questionnaire’s field ↔ item correspondence; this checks fidelity to the design, not the design again | . | L3 | profile, logical model | the IG Publisher’s differential view | . | L3 | CQL / PlanDefinition | the logic beside the DMN rule it implements, and its test cases passing or failing | . | L3 | terminology | the expansion, and the mapping to ICD-11 / SNOMED CT / LOINC | . | app | screen / flow | the chosen wireframe beside the running screen, walked through the L2 scenario it serves | . Forms are designed as wireframes at L2 . A data-entry form is designed once, at L2, and the L3 Questionnaire is derived from that design. | Stage 4: design. For each business-process activity where a persona records data, the agent runs wireframe-design-review in its design use, with intent from the L2 assets: the persona (who), the activity and its user scenario (what they do), and the core data elements it captures (what it shows). That gives two or more candidates, each with a web and a mobile layout, using real content: data-element labels, value sets and the DMN rules that show or hide a field. Each field carries the id of its core data element in a data-element attribute. The agent goes on with its recommended candidate; the review and the choice (Process_Adjudication, Process_OptionsAnalysis) are that form’s stage-4 adjudication. | Stage 6: derive. The Questionnaire follows the chosen wireframe: one item per field, in its order and grouping, each item’s definition pointing at the logical-model element of the same core data element, and enableWhen taken from the same DMN rules. | Stage 6 review: fidelity. fhir-harness’s skill fhir-questionnaire-wireframe (Process_QuestionnaireWireframeReview) runs on each built Questionnaire with the chosen wireframe. Its check, check-wireframe-questionnaire, pairs the wireframe’s data-element attributes with the items’ definitions (or code[].code), per data-layout; a field with no item, an item with no field, or a different order is a finding: . bun run fhir-harness/scripts/check-wireframe-questionnaire.ts <wireframe.html> <Questionnaire.json> . | . If the chosen wireframe changes later, the Questionnaire derived from it is flagged rejected-upstream. A change request on either side (✍ suggest or the questionnaire-change issue form) says which side was edited, and the other is brought back in line (fhir-questionnaire-wireframe, step 7). An adaptation is reviewed as a diff. When the asset came from a stage-3 or stage-5 dependency with decision: adapt, the review item shows before (the upstream asset at its pinned version) and after side by side, with the change highlighted and the L1 node that justifies it. At L3 the diff is fhir-harness’s ig-ast-delta (element-level, per resource); at L2 and for anything rendered, before-after-preview with a DiffRenderer (cat-harness-tools/schemas/ui/diff-renderers.ts). A changed asset with no L1 justification is a finding: the KG must say whether an adaptation is local evidence or local policy. The record of a review item is a cat-harness QaReview (qa-review/v1, cat-harness-tools/schemas/sdlc/qa-review.ts): subject is the asset, and each verdict is a Decision whose role is the adjudicator’s role id: . | outcome | meaning here | . | approve | the asset stands | . | request-changes | reopen the stage for this asset. If the reviewer wrote the fix themselves, it goes in an AuditNote and the agent applies it as given | . | reject | the asset is wrong at the root (wrong source, wrong dependency). Reopen the stage that chose it | . At L1, recommendation-extraction keeps its review: {by, at} fields on the mapping; the QaReview records the stage’s review beside them.

24f59f228710.title: New guideline or adaptation: one process
24f59f228710.content: An adaptation is this process with stages 3 and 5 returning adapt decisions, so stages 4 and 6 show diffs. A new guideline is the case where those stages return only reuse, extend or nothing.

c96f26f765b1.title: What it reuses
c96f26f765b1.content: | need | reused from | . | each stage | the stage skills in the table | . | adjudication | cat-harness Process_Review, then Process_Adjudication on disagreement | . | review record and verdict | cat-harness qa-review/v1: QaReview, Decision (approve · request-changes · reject), AuditNote | . | who adjudicates | role ids clinical-sme, programme-manager, business-analyst, fhir-modeller, terminologist, reviewer, and smart-base’s l1-extraction-reviewer | . | staged preview, before/after links | feature-staging, staging-review | . | diffs | ig-ast-delta (L3); before-after-preview with a DiffRenderer (L2, rendered pages); smart-base’s dak-data-dictionary-diff.ts (data-dictionary terms) | . | form and app design | wireframe-design-review, design use; fhir-harness fhir-questionnaire-wireframe and check-wireframe-questionnaire for stage-6 fidelity | . | dependency row | DependsOnRecord, DependsOnGap and KG evidence, plus decision, reason and toolchain (l2-dependency-choice) | . | component tooling | the tools graph (bun run cat check:tools), the upstream repository’s own scripts, WHO’s DAK toolchain (smart-base-tools) | . | provenance flag | KG wasDerivedFrom edge properties, with the values pending and rejected-upstream | .

51cecc7499c3.title: What this does not change

Run it before stage 4 if the guideline has no home yet. | The persona-swimlane lifecycle (planning, QC, translation, publication) on the IG’s Authoring Process page. This process says what goes into its phases 2a and 2b, and what comes before and after them. | .

365515f8e2d1.title: smart-launch
365515f8e2d1.content: Skill id: smart-launch · Package: fhir-client · Instance: fhir-harness .

8c12ef44e3b1.title: Provenance — read this first
8c12ef44e3b1.content: |   |   | . | Library | @topologyhealth/smarterfhir 0.4.3 (package.json) | . | Source | https://github.com/TopologyHealth/SMARTerFHIR | . | Pinned commit | 506463af4bd82848f414649dac608d578c8aae44 (2025-12-02) | . | License | Apache-2.0 — LICENSE, package.json and the README agree | . | Built on | fhirclient ^2.5.2 (a peer dependency) — SMARTerFHIR wraps its FHIR.oauth2.authorize and FHIR.oauth2.ready | . Every name below is from src/ at that commit; each section cites its file. Upstream ships no skill files, so this skill is authored here. If the pinned commit moves, re-read the source before trusting any signature here. Where the source leaves a behaviour to fhirclient, this skill says so rather than describing fhirclient from memory.

f51a10931453.title: The public surface
f51a10931453.content: src/index.ts exports exactly: BaseClient, ClientFactory, EMR, LAUNCH, SmartLaunchHandler, ClientUtils. The vendor client classes are not exported; you get one from ClientFactory. | LAUNCH (src/Client/ClientFactory.ts): EMR, STANDALONE, BACKEND. | EMR (src/Launcher/SmartLaunchHandler.ts): CERNER = "cerner", EPIC = "epic", SMART = "smart", ECW = "ecw", ATHENA = "platform.athena", ATHENAPRACTICE = "fhirapi.athena", MEDITECH = "meditech", NONE = "none". | new SmartLaunchHandler(clientID: string, clientSecret?: string, scope?: string | string[]) | authorizeEMR(launchType: LAUNCH = LAUNCH.EMR, redirectPath?: string, emrType?: EMR): Promise<void> | new ClientFactory().createEMRClient(launchType: LAUNCH.EMR | LAUNCH.STANDALONE): Promise<BaseClient> | .

3f629a4a644c.title: Steps
3f629a4a644c.content: The launch is two pages: a launch page that sends the browser to the authorisation server, and a redirect page that turns the returned code into a client. | Launch page. Construct a SmartLaunchHandler with your registered client id, and call authorizeEMR. | EHR launch: authorizeEMR(LAUNCH.EMR, redirectPath). | Standalone launch: authorizeEMR(LAUNCH.STANDALONE, redirectPath, emrType). | . | What authorizeEMR does (executeWebLaunch, then the private launchEMR): . | reads iss from window.location.search, and throws if it is absent — for both launch types; | infers the EHR vendor from the iss URL unless you pass emrType, and throws "EMR type cannot be inferred from the ISS" when neither yields one; | builds the scope string (below), calls FHIR.oauth2.authorize with noRedirect: true, then sets self.location.href to the returned URL. | . | Redirect page. Call new ClientFactory().createEMRClient(launchType). It calls FHIR.oauth2.ready() and wraps the result in the vendor client chosen by ClientUtils.getEMRType(client); EMR.NONE throws "Unsupported provider for EMR Client creation". | . import { SmartLaunchHandler, ClientFactory, LAUNCH, EMR } from "@topologyhealth/smarterfhir"; // launch page — the URL must carry ?iss=<FHIR base> (and, for EHR launch, the EHR's launch param) const handler = new SmartLaunchHandler("my-client-id"); // no secret in a browser app await handler.authorizeEMR(LAUNCH.EMR, "/redirect"); // browser navigates away // redirect page const client = await new ClientFactory().createEMRClient(LAUNCH.EMR); client.getEMRType(); // e.g. EMR.EPIC client.getR4Endpoint(); // URL of the FHIR server the token is for .

22e4048a8837.title: Scopes
22e4048a8837.content: Built in launchEMR / generatePreconfiguredScopes (src/Launcher/SmartLaunchHandler.ts): . | Always prefixed with openid fhirUser, then de-duplicated and space-joined. | A scope passed to the constructor replaces the vendor defaults (a string is split on spaces), but openid fhirUser is still prepended. It does not add launch for you — include it yourself for an EHR launch. | Otherwise, the vendor defaults: | . | EMR | EHR launch (LAUNCH.EMR) | standalone (LAUNCH.STANDALONE) | . | EPIC, SMART, default | launch online_access | launch/practitioner online_access | . | CERNER | the Epic set plus the per-resource user/<Resource>.read and .write scopes named in src/Launcher/Config.ts (cerner.scopes, mapped through scopes.json) | same, with launch/practitioner | . | ECW | launch user/Patient.read user/Encounter.read user/Practitioner.read | launch/patient + the same reads | . | ATHENA | profile offline_access launch user/Patient.read | launch/patient in place of launch | . | ATHENAPRACTICE | launch profile offline_access user/Patient.read | the same without launch | . | MEDITECH | launch/patient patient/*.read | the same | . Scope strings for single resources are produced by FhirScopePermissions.get (src/Launcher/Scopes.ts), which renders <actor>/<Resource>.<action> with SMART v1 .read/.write suffixes only. Note that FhirScopePermissions is not exported from the package root.

28a5fbb7b08a.title: Redirect handling
28a5fbb7b08a.content: From executeWebLaunch: . | an absolute redirectPath is used as-is (it may be another domain); | a relative one is joined to window.location.origin, adding a leading / if missing; | no redirectPath means the redirect URI is the bare origin. | . Register exactly that computed URI with the EHR. PKCE: pkceMode: 'ifSupported' for every vendor except ECW, which gets pkceMode: 'unsafeV1' and completeInTarget: true (getEMRSpecificAuthorizeParams).

8930947b74a4.title: Where the token lands
8930947b74a4.content: SMARTerFHIR does not store a token itself. The code exchange and the token live in the fhirclient Client that FHIR.oauth2.ready() returns; SMARTerFHIR keeps that object as client.fhirClientDefault and reads fhirClientDefault.state.serverUrl from it. Where fhirclient persists its state between the two pages, and how it refreshes, is fhirclient’s behaviour and is not covered by this source — check fhirclient’s own documentation rather than assuming. For a server-side app that already holds a token response, createEMRClientBackend(req, res, serverConfig) builds the client from a FhirClientConfig — { serverUrl, tokenUri, tokenResponse, clientId } (src/types.ts) — using fhirclient’s Node entry point. It performs no authorisation.

96ebe649d785.title: What the library does NOT do
96ebe649d785.content: . | No backend-services launch. authorizeEMR(LAUNCH.BACKEND) throws "Direct Backend Authorization not supported yet."; no JWT client-assertion flow exists in src/. | No SMART v2 scopes (.rs, .cruds) — FhirScopePermissions emits only .read/.write. | No endpoint discovery of its own. ClientUtils.getEndpointsForEmr is @deprecated and always throws; the vendor is inferred from the iss URL text, not from .well-known/smart-configuration or a CapabilityStatement (the README says “metadata/capabilities”; the code does a substring match). | No token storage or refresh logic — both are fhirclient’s. | Browser only for the launch half: executeWebLaunch reads window and writes self.location. | .

4d1555784053.title: Pitfalls
4d1555784053.content: . | Standalone still needs ?iss= (step 2). Put the FHIR base URL in the link that opens the page. | Vendor inference is a substring match (ClientUtils.getEMRType): the EMR values are tried longest-first against the whole iss string. A sandbox or proxy URL that does not contain epic, cerner, smart, … is EMR.NONE; one that contains two of them picks the longer. Pass emrType when the host is not self-describing — and note createEMRClient re-infers from serverUrl with no override, so an un-inferable server fails there too. | clientSecret in a browser is public. The constructor forwards it to FHIR.oauth2.authorize; in a SPA that ships it to every user. Pass undefined for public clients. | The authorise promise does not reject on a bad URL. If authorize does not return a string, launchEMR only console.errors "Failed to build authorize URL" and resolves — check that navigation actually happened. | Athena Practice’s response_mode=query appears never to be appended. addSearchParams iterates Object.keys(new URLSearchParams(...)), which yields no keys for a URLSearchParams. This is a reading of the source, not a runtime observation; verify against the vendor before relying on either behaviour. | .

86eeafb427f9.title: The stack
86eeafb427f9.content: folio-assistant-core └── fhir-harness bare FHIR IG pipeline — no WHO anything └── smart-base WHO SMART harness rules + data models; instantiates smart.who.int.base │ ├─ L1 document kind — semi-fixed, computed from smart-base's library (+ PICO, Cochrane …) │ └─ DAK document kind — fixed: the ten components └── smart-ig L3 — the FHIR IG publication a DAK feeds . There is no smart-guidelines layer. L1 and DAK are document kinds, not layers: things an author produces with the smart-base harness, with no code, tools or processes of their own. An IG is a layer, because it is published through the IG Publisher; every ingested IG (smart-trust, smart-immunizations) needs: smart-ig. L1, DAK and the IG are not a chain. An L1 document with no DAK behind it is real, and so is an IG with no L1; an IG does not depend on a narrative corpus it never reads.

1e10c59d79b7.title: The question that settles placement
1e10c59d79b7.content: Ask in this order; the first match wins: . 1. Would a non-WHO FHIR IG need this? → fhir-harness. 2. Would every WHO SMART asset need it, L1, L2 and L3 alike? → smart-base. 3. Is it about publishing one guideline’s FHIR IG? → smart-ig. 4. Otherwise → smart-base, as part of the L1 or DAK document kind it serves. Question 1 is yes only if you can name one non-WHO IG that would want the thing.

be302ced5ea3.title: No layer between smart-base and its kinds
be302ced5ea3.content: smart-base is the home of WHO SMART policy and also instantiates its own IG. Do not re-introduce a smart-guidelines layer under another name: a smart-common, a smart-core, a shared/ skills package that only the WHO kinds import. A rule that L1, DAK and the IG all need is smart-base’s. A “layer” that holds no code of its own is a kind.

9ead470ae241.title: What each layer may hold, and what it may not
9ead470ae241.content: | layer | holds | must NOT hold | . | fhir-harness | SUSHI, IG Publisher invocation, Jekyll assembly, publication to a pages branch, the artefact-index reconstruction | any WHO term, the DAK declaration (index.config.json contentTypes.dak), any DAK pre/post step, any smart.who.int canonical | . | smart-base | the SMART harness rules, the DAK logical model, the schema of the contentTypes.dak index section, WHO voices and methodologies, the smart.who.int.base IG — and the two document kinds: L1 (narrative assets, figure narratives, the corpus a DTH is written from) and DAK (the ten components, DMN/BPMN authoring, the DAK-shaped pre-processing) | subject matter for any one guideline; FHIR resources in an L1 document; FHIR profiles or publication in a DAK | . | smart-ig | L3 — FSH, profiles, terminology binding, the IG build for one guideline | L1 narrative; DAK authoring | .

83bd9db75ff9.title: Two consequences
83bd9db75ff9.content: 1. There is no per-IG harness. smart-trust and smart-immunizations are instances of smart-ig, not harnesses: they add no new functionality. 2. fhir-harness may not import the WHO package. A dependency on authoring-who-smart-guidelines would stop a non-WHO IG from instantiating it while still passing every gate. The upper layer may know the stack; the lower layer may not. This skill lives in the WHO package and describes fhir-harness, which is that direction.

97e82d631829.title: smart-base becomes a conventional IG
97e82d631829.content: WorldHealthOrganization/smart-base does two jobs: it is an IG (smart.who.int.base, FHIR 4.0.1, its own profiles and logical models), and it hosts the toolchain every downstream SMART IG runs — ghbuild.yml is a reusable workflow, and a downstream build curls its scripts from smart-base’s main at build time. The second job is to end, because: . | A downstream IG’s build depends on a branch it does not control, so it can change without its repository changing. | The IG and the toolchain version together. A fix to one is a release of the other. | The tooling is invisible to the harness. Scripts in input/ are not Tool nodes, so no process can bind them and no audit can reach them. | . The migration is smart-base/tools/: Tool nodes now, execution later. Declaring is not vendoring — see smart-base-tools. This is work in litlfred/* only; nothing at WorldHealthOrganization/* changes, and the DAK declaration in index.config.json is ours until upstream adopts it.

abd74a2e97dc.title: The falsification test
abd74a2e97dc.content: Every step of the existing WHO build assigns to exactly one layer. The build is the DAK pre- and post-processing around one Publisher run, plus the deploy, in WorldHealthOrganization/smart-base’s .github/workflows/ghbuild.yml (the do_dak input gates the pre and post phases). If a step cannot be placed, or two layers both claim it, the split is wrong and this skill changes. Do not resolve a conflict by adding a layer; report it. The per-step assignment is in dak-preprocessing and dak-postprocessing. Current result: all 26 steps place (6 pre-processing, 1 Publisher run, 9 post-processing, 10 deploy), none needs a new layer and none has two owners. Three are placed against their labels: . | step | labelled | placed | . | strip_library_binaries.py | DAK Postprocessing | fhir-harness | . | strip_library_content.py | DAK Postprocessing | fhir-harness | . | comment on PR — deployment completed | (deploy) | cat-harness | . The deploy phase is entirely generic — see ig-build-pipeline §”The deploy phase”. Re-run the test when a step is added upstream.

f722f1c2241b.title: Where an instance says which layer it is
f722f1c2241b.content: In its declaration’s needs, and nowhere else: needs: ["smart-ig"] is a published WHO SMART IG, needs: ["smart-base"] a WHO SMART instance that publishes no IG, needs: ["fhir-harness"] a non-WHO IG. Which document kinds an instance authors (L1, DAK) is a property of its content. There is no layer field. Conventions for the declaration: directory-conventions.
