8ef255dea84b.title: Session Task Manager (beans)
8ef255dea84b.content: Disambiguation: . | beans (todo-manager, this file) = the agent’s session work-plan. Managed entirely via the beans CLI issue tracker (data stored in beans/). | sidecars (*.qa.json and *.witness.json files) = content state tracking. Work items and sidecars are NOT synonymous! Do NOT convert bulk QA queue items into work items. They are completely separate workflow systems. | todo-review = triage of content feedback stored under feedback/<paper>/ and surfaced via the MCP /todos dashboard. That is paper-content scope, not session scope. | . Instead of an in-memory list or markdown checklists, we manage session work and cross-agent coordination using the beans CLI issue tracker. A work item is a memory record with more structure (owner, 2026-11-03, ruling Q17; the schemas are memory-record-core and bean/1.0.0 in cat-harness-tools schemas/kg/memory-record.ts and schemas/sdlc/bean-graph.ts). It carries what every kept memory carries (an id, a title, tags, when it was made and changed) and adds a status, a type, a priority, a parent and what it blocks. So the memory Tools work on it as on any memory record: memory_note and memory_checkpoint add a dated entry, memory_recall reads them back, and the work-plan store adds what only a work item needs (get, list, create, claiming). The glossary defines the term: Work item, narrower than Memory record. The program and its files keep the name beans; in prose, say work item. This skill holds the work item mechanics: installing the CLI, the STRICT check before beans create, the fallback when the CLI is absent, the status vocabulary, and the coordination rules below. Report formats are elsewhere: . | opening-brief.md — what you say before starting a work item or a topic. | turn-reporting.md — what you say during and after each turn, including the STRICT “next”-line rule. | .

6919e28173b2.title: Installing beans (fresh sandbox / cloud container)
6919e28173b2.content: beans is the hmans/beans Go binary — a flat-file issue tracker storing issues as markdown under beans/. Cloud sandboxes do not ship it, so reinstall on demand (Go ships in the sandbox): . cat-harness-tools/scripts/install-beans.sh # idempotent; installs into a PATH dir # equivalently, the one-liner it runs: GOBIN="$HOME/.local/bin" go install github.com/hmans/beans@latest . Note: the npm package named beans is an unrelated abandoned tool — do not npm install beans. Verify with beans list && beans check.

55f44ee504ac.title: What the session-start sweep emits, and why in that order
55f44ee504ac.content: A session-start hook runs the sweep where a hook runs at all. It installs the CLI when it is genuinely missing — bounded and quiet, falling through to the degraded reader rather than failing the hook — and prepends the install directory when the binary is already there, so a second session does not reinstall. If the sweep still reports the CLI missing, it could not be installed there. The sweep installs rather than recommends, because an instruction somebody has to act on is weaker than the act itself. The order is not arbitrary: . | Interaction preferences — first, because they change the form of every question that follows. A question asked before them may have to be asked again. | Work-plan priming and the open list. | The roadmap. A flat list of a hundred ids in creation order is data, not a plan; the milestone/epic structure is what lets an end-of-turn report say what is next and why. | The commands the person can run themselves, the interactive browser first. An agent cannot drive a TUI on somebody’s behalf, so the only useful thing to do with one is print it where they will see it — with a copy-pasteable line whose path and branch are computed, never written in. | Default-branch delta, sibling branch activity, CI health. | . Heavy triage of new commits belongs in a background subagent, not the foreground. The sweep’s job is to tell you what changed, not to spend your first minutes reading it.

d33632cf6759.title: Core Directives for Sessions
d33632cf6759.content: . | A session is a LOG, never an epic or a milestone. Do not create a Session: … work item. What one sitting did is recorded in two places that already exist and are already read: the PR body (## Intent / ## Session results, session-intent) and a work item note on each work item you worked — bun run cat beans:note <id> --title "…", written to the declared notes directory of beans/beans.json and keyed by branch, so it is one file per session per work item by construction (bean-coordination §”Adding to a bean”). See §”A session is a log, not a parent” below for why. | Every todo is a work item, parented by SUBJECT. Each task, probe or action item is a work item (--type task) under the epic whose subject it is — §”WHICH parent” — not under anything representing the session. beans create "<Task Title>" --type task --parent <subject-epic-id> | No manual .md checklists: Never use session-beans.md or raw Markdown - [ ] checklists to track global tasks. Always use the beans CLI to prevent namespace pollution and maintain the official project tracking. | Check before you create: beans create is not idempotent. Run the existence check below before every beans create — no exceptions. | Brief before you work: claiming a work item records which item is taken; the opening brief records what it is taken for. Write it before the first tool call, in the chat. See §”Opening brief” below. | Write work items to the work-plan store, never into a code PR: create, claim, note and status changes go to the store through its Tool. The store’s operations are in work-plan-store; how the Tool in use performs them (today the git state branch, work-plan-store-git-branch) is on that Tool’s page. Do not commit work item files to code PR branches on main. | .

567f2e2cfebd.title: Where beans live
567f2e2cfebd.content: The work plan is a data store with a contract, work-plan-store, and this skill uses it only through that contract’s operations (get, list, create, update, note, history, positions). Which Tool backs it is the deployment’s choice Today every checkout uses the git state branch; how to mount it, which commands perform each operation and how changes are pushed are on its page, work-plan-store-git-branch. | Never bundle work items in code PR commits. Code PRs touch code and documentation; work item changes go to the store, which keeps the work plan current for every session without merge conflicts or spurious CI runs. | .

6bfa2ca2596d.title: Check before you create — beans create is not idempotent (STRICT)
6bfa2ca2596d.content: beans create mints a fresh random ID on every call and dedupes on nothing. Re-running a work-plan step is therefore not a no-op — it creates a second work item. Before every beans create, check whether the work item exists: . T="Prove Foo.bar" beans list --json --search "title:\"$T\"" | python3 -c ' import json, sys t = sys.argv[1] m = [b for b in json.load(sys.stdin) if b["title"] == t] print(f"{len(m)} exact match(es)") [print(" ", b["id"], b["status"]) for b in m]' "$T" . | ≥ 1 match → do not create. Claim the existing work item instead, with bun run cat beans:claim <id> — which reads the shared store first, refuses a work item a sibling holds or one already closed, and records a holder note so the next session’s check can see you. Not beans update <id> --status in-progress. It writes no holder note, so the claim is invisible to beans:claim’s own already-claimed check. Read the outcome — three of them are refusals, and held-unknown means it could not tell a live sibling from an abandoned claim: bean-coordination.md §”bun run cat beans:claim <id> — how it behaves”. | 0 matches → run the semantic check before creating: . bun run cat lsi:near "$T" # add --body "<first paragraph>" when you have one . The exact-title check above catches the same WORDS; this catches the same work in other words. It folds the title into an LSI index of every work item (all statuses — a completed one is often the answer) and prints the nearest five plus the closest epic. Read every hit marked ← (cosine ≥ 0.7) before creating. If one is the same work, claim or reopen it rather than create; if it is related, create and say so in the body. The score proposes; whether a hit IS the same work is your call (method lsi, refusal 3). | A work item ABOUT ONE OBJECT is keyed on the object, not the title. When the work targets a single named thing (a Lean declaration, a block label, a file), titles drift: “Prove Foo.bar”, “PROVE(lean): Foo.bar”, “close sorry in Foo.bar”. Neither check above is guaranteed to pair them, and generator re-runs are the usual source of such duplicates. So write the key into the work item as a line of its own, Target: lean:Foo.bar (or block:<label>, file:<path>), and before creating search the WHOLE store for that line, archive included, because a completed work item is often the answer: . grep -rlF "Target: lean:Foo.bar" beans/defs/ # the archive is beans/defs/archive/ . A hit is the same work: claim it, reopen it with a note, or link to it. A generator that files work items MUST write the key and run this check, since a re-run is exactly the case the title checks miss. | Still new → beans create "$T" --type task, under the epic lsi:near printed if it fits (§”WHICH parent — the criterion nobody wrote down” below). | . --search is a fuzzy Bleve query, so the exact-title comparison inside the pipe is load-bearing — do not drop it and trust --search alone. Why this is STRICT. Because create is unconditional, an agent that re-runs a work-plan step in a loop mints thousands of duplicates: the sweep and the backlog then read mostly noise, duplicates can collide with real work item ids, and corpus searches over beans/ are inflated. An unguarded create is what the rule prevents. It is platform-level so every folio inherits it.

b7f8444609d5.title: Check before you UPDATE — --body-file REPLACES the body (STRICT)
b7f8444609d5.content: beans create is not idempotent; beans update is not additive. They are different failures and both cost a durable artefact, so they sit together. A work item’s body is an append-only record of who found what, when. Every note in it is dated and signed, and later notes cite earlier ones. Replace the body and you have deleted findings that other work items, commits and issues point at. beans update offers four ways to write one, and only one of them appends: . | flag | what it does | . | --body-append <text> | --body-append - | appends. - reads stdin | . | --body-file <path> | REPLACES the whole body with the file | . | --body <text> | --body - | REPLACES | . | --body-replace-old/-new | replaces one substring; leaves the rest | . --body-file replaces with exit 0, no warning, no diff, no prompt: nothing in the output distinguishes it from an append. For a long, multi-paragraph note, use --body-append -: . beans update <id> --status completed --body-append - <<'NOTE' _2026-09-22T06:51:22Z_ — what you found, and how you know it. NOTE . Do not reach for --body-file because the note is long. (beans create rejects --body-file - with a heredoc, so the two subcommands also disagree about that flag.) . The timestamp prefix is an authored convention, not a CLI feature — no flag adds it. Write it yourself or the note joins the previous paragraph undated. Recovery, if it has already happened. The store is committed, which is the whole reason this is survivable: git show HEAD:<bean-file> returns the body as of the last commit, and the lost notes can be reassembled with the new front matter. Recover from git, not from your own scrollback — a transcript is a copy you made, and the repository is the artefact. Then say plainly what was lost and restored; a silent repair leaves the next reader unable to tell a reconstruction from an original.

6a9f7f2bd69a.title: WHICH parent — the criterion nobody wrote down
6a9f7f2bd69a.content: A work item’s parent is the epic whose SUBJECT it is, not the epic you happen to be working in. Nothing catches a wrong parent. check-bean-parents tests exactly two things: that an open work item HAS a parent, and that the parent NAMES A WORK ITEM THAT EXISTS. A work item filed under the wrong epic satisfies both, so it is textually clean, the guard is green, and it is only findable by a person reading the roadmap. The check cannot distinguish a right parent from a wrong one, so the criterion has to live here or nowhere. How to choose . | beans list and read the EPICS first — there are many, each with a thematic scope in its title. Do this BEFORE beans create, at the same time as §”Check before you create”; both are questions about where a work item belongs, and both are cheaper before the file exists. | Ask what the work item is ABOUT, not what you were doing when you wrote it. A visualiser whose blocker is an unrecorded ingest relation is an ingest work item. A sticky’s art is a rendering work item. The topic that makes the work hard is usually the right epic. | When two epics both fit, pick the one whose OTHER children you would want read alongside it, and say in the body why the other was not chosen — a parent is a claim about where somebody should go looking. | . A session is a log, not a parent . Do not create a Session: … epic or milestone. It turns the roadmap’s top level into a diary, and: . | An epic is a claim about where to look for a SUBJECT. A session epic points at one sitting, which ended; nobody looks there for the work, so its children are lost to the next agent filing by subject. | It defeats the guards. check-bean-parents passes a task parented to a session epic, because the parent exists and is an epic. The wrong parent is textually clean. | Its status lies. A session epic stays in-progress after its session ends, so it is a stale claim from birth, and the quiet-claim findings fill with logs. | . Where the log goes instead — each already declared, already read: . | what the session wants to keep | where | . | what it intended and what it got done | the PR body, ## Intent / ## Session results (session-intent) | . | what it found about a work item | a note: bun run cat beans:note <id> → beans/notes/<bean>--<date>--<branch>.md | . | a survey of a commit window it read | beans/surveys/ (session-survey) — only if it surveyed one | . | a handover to whoever comes next | a note on the work item being handed over, plus handover-report | . A handover is the same case. A Handoff: … or Handover: … work item typed epic or milestone is a session log with a different title. bun run cat health reports it — the bean-store check’s bean-session-log-roots finding names every OPEN work item whose title starts Session, Handoff or Handover and whose type is epic or milestone. Report-only: the remedy is a person’s (or a reviewed work-plan-restructure plan’s) — re-parent the children by subject, move the narrative into a note, then set the log to completed or scrapped with a pointer. Never beans delete it: other work items, commits and PRs cite its id.

94b27700c764.title: A GOAL is a milestone bean, and an epic joins one by parenting to it
94b27700c764.content: A “goal-scoped” queue needs the goal to exist as an object, or every review re-derives the classification from scratch. A goal is a milestone work item, in the owner’s own words, and the epics serving it are parented to it. beans create "<the goal, verbatim>" --type milestone # after the existence check above beans update <epic-id> --parent <milestone-id> . Three properties make this the cheap answer rather than a new mechanism: . | The type exists and check-bean-parents permits an epic under a milestone. | beans roadmap groups by parent:, so the goals become the roadmap’s top level the moment the epics are parented — which is what a roadmap was always for. | “Prioritise against the goals” becomes a query: walk down from the milestone. An item under no goal is then visible as such, which is itself the finding a review wants. | . Verbatim, and this is not a style note. A goal is the owner’s sentence, and a tidied paraphrase is a different claim that nobody agreed to — the same rule confirmation-waiver applies to a waiver’s quote, and for the same reason: the reader auditing the classification has only that string to check it against. If you do not have the owner’s words, you do not have the goal — record the paraphrase as a paraphrase, say so, and ask. This does not conflict with filing by subject (§”WHICH parent”). A milestone sits ABOVE the epics; a work item is still parented to the epic whose subject it is, and the epic is parented to the goal it serves. Two levels, one criterion at each.

372f5988af9b.title: A WORK PLAN is an epic or milestone that names the process it runs
372f5988af9b.content: Owner, 2026-11-05: “At the beginning of a large process (like creating a new collaborative document, or adding software features,) there should / may be a work plan. Not every process needs a work plan. Docs/proposals/ once approved become workplans”, and on the card, “Epic is the plan”. So a work plan is not a new kind of file. It is the epic (or milestone) that already groups the work, with two tags saying what it runs and where it came from: . beans update <epic-id> --tag process:<bpmn:process id> # what it instantiates; repeat for several beans update <epic-id> --tag proposal:<repo-relative path> # the approved proposal it was made from beans list --tag process:<bpmn:process id> # every plan that runs that process . | Tags, not front-matter fields. The beans CLI drops every front-matter key it does not know on its next write (measured 2026-11-05), and keeps tags. | A process: tag is what makes it a plan. A proposal: tag alone does not: a proposal with no process to run is not a plan yet. A plan filed as a feature or a story is reported, not refused (the work-plan schema in the tools layer reports it). | Start the process under the plan: workflow_start with plan: <epic-id> (bun run cat workflow:start <process> <subject> --plan <epic-id>). The instance names its plan, as it names its work item; the plan does not list its instances, because where the work is lives in the instances. | Not every process needs one. A small process tracked by one work item runs with no plan, exactly as before. | The work items under the plan are its work: parented to the epic, as always. A work item is a memory record with more structure; a work plan is a work item that says which process it runs. | . The work-plan page marks each plan in its tree with its process, its proposal and how many instances are running under it. Approving a proposal seeds its plan . When the owner approves a proposal (owner, 2026-11-05, card “Proposal seeds plan”), one command writes both ends, so neither is kept by hand: . bun run cat proposal:approve <path/to/proposal.md> --process <bpmn:process id> [--process …] \ [--plan <epic or milestone id>] [--parent <goal id>] [--dry-run] . | With no --plan it creates an epic titled as the proposal. With --plan it tags that epic or milestone instead; a feature or a story is refused. | The plan gets the process: and proposal: tags. The proposal’s front matter gets status: approved, approvedOn: <date> and plan: <id>. | At least one --process is required, unless --plan already names one: a plan is defined by what it runs. | Approve only on the owner’s word. The command records an approval; it does not decide one. Run it with --dry-run first and show the owner what it will write. | bun run cat proposal:approve --check <proposals dir> checks the two ends against each other and reports rather than fails: an approved proposal with no plan, a plan id that is no work item, a plan that names no process, or a plan whose proposal: tag names another file. | .

313c481b5365.title: After you create — parent it, and re-run the guard before you push
313c481b5365.content: check-bean-parents fails on an open work item with no parent, because such a work item lands in the roadmap’s Miscellaneous section where nobody looks for it. Two ways past it: . | A multi-flag beans update can apply only some of its flags and still report success (-s in-progress --parent <epic> can set the status and leave the parent unset). After setting several properties at once, read the front matter back — grep -n "^status:\|^parent:\|^priority:" beans/defs/<file>.md — rather than trusting the “Updated …” line. | A work item created after your last test run is an unguarded work item. | . So: beans create and the --parent that follows it are one action, and touching the work item store invalidates your last test run. Re-run at least bun test cat-harness-tools/scripts/tests/check-bean-parents.test.ts before pushing. A green suite is green for the tree you ran it against. A new bean also owes readme:subgraphs — and this is the most-missed step . beans/README.md is GENERATED and carries per-subdirectory counts, so creating or archiving a work item makes it stale. Nothing in the beans CLI regenerates it, and the gate that catches it is named for the generic case rather than for work items: . Repository gates (hard) · step 65: "Every declared directory's README is current" . That is readme:subgraphs:check. Run its writer before you push: . bun run cat readme:subgraphs # updates beans/README.md; push state via branch-store bun run cat readme:subgraphs:check # must exit 0 bun cat-harness-tools/scripts/branch-store.ts push --id beans # or: bun run cat state:push . The check’s name gives no hint that adding a work item dirtied it, so a session that reads only the name looks at directories and never at the work item it just created. Read the failing STEP, and remember that beans/ is a declared directory like any other. The same shape applies one door along: editing a skill owes bun run cat skill:register, which skill-registration carries in full. Both are instances of one rule — a declared artefact has generated neighbours, and the CLI that writes the artefact does not write them.

15c5be5a06a8.title: When the beans CLI is not there — you are still not read-only
15c5be5a06a8.content: scripts/beans-fallback.ts writes the same store in the same layout: same files, same front matter, same id shape, read from .beans.yml. The CLI reads everything it writes once installed. There is no import step and no second store. bun run cat beans:fallback list --status todo bun run cat beans:fallback show <id> bun run cat beans:fallback claim <id> bun run cat beans:fallback create "<title>" --status in-progress bun run cat beans:fallback note <id> "<what you found>" . A read-only fallback would let a session see its plan but not claim it, so it would do its work unclaimed. Its create refuses an exact duplicate title and names the work item to claim instead; the CLI’s create does not. --force exists for a genuinely intended duplicate and has to be typed.

84a663437a5d.title: Check before you WORK — a checkbox is a claim, not a measurement (STRICT)
84a663437a5d.content: beans create is not idempotent, and §”Check before you create” above is the guard. This is its twin at the other end: a work item’s stated state is a claim somebody wrote down once, and the code has moved since. Re-measure a work item’s open items against the code before you act on them. The cost of skipping this is not wasted effort; it is acting on a stale claim. The two failures this prevents, and they are different . 1. Doing work that exists. Siblings finish items without ticking the box. 2. Undoing a decision that was recorded elsewhere. An open item can read like a gap when the absence is deliberate and explained in a comment in the file the work item is about. Doing the obvious thing then re-introduces the defect the decision avoids. The decision is in the file, not the work item. What “re-measure” means, concretely . | Run the thing — the audit or check that measures the item. | Read the body, not just the boxes. | Date it. git log -S on the symbol or the file against the work item’s created_at separates fixed since from wrong when written. | Read the file the work item is about, for a comment saying why it is the way it is. That is where a deliberate absence lives. | . And a bean you re-measure, you record . Leave what you found in the work item, with the commits and the times — a stale checkbox you silently worked around is one the next agent meets unchanged. Tick what is done and name who did it; withdraw a done-when you no longer believe, with reasons, rather than leaving it unmet. Where the work item and the code disagree, the code is what is true and the work item is what is wrong — the same rule AGENTS.md states for a skill against that file. This is the work-plan half. The cross-session half is bean-coordination §”Claims are global via the branch store”.

31481a565d67.title: Working with Beans
31481a565d67.content: 1. Finding Tasks & Graph Analytics (beans:query / bean_query) Use beans list for simple listing, or bun run beans:query (and the bean_query MCP tool) for fast in-memory SPARQL 1.1 analytics over the work item store (loads ~1,000 work items into an Oxigraph store in ~70 ms): . | bun run beans:query --named safe_drain_candidates: leaves with >= 2 open siblings under their parent container (safe against check:bean-rollup) | bun run beans:query --named actionable_leaves: open/todo leaf work items with zero open blockers, ready for an agent to claim immediately | bun run beans:query --named critical_path_blockers: blockers ranked by how many open work items they directly hold up | bun run beans:query --named epic_burndown: per-epic child status breakdown (total, open, completed, scrapped, and completion percentage) | bun run beans:query --named rollup_invariant_violations: completed containers with open children, or in-progress containers with 0 open children | bun run beans:query --named stale_claims: in-progress work items whose updated_at timestamp is older than 7 days | bun run beans:query --named unparented_open_tasks: open non-epic work items that have no epic or milestone parent | bun run beans:query --named circular_blockers: circular blocking deadlocks | bun run beans:query --named high_fanout_epics: epics with high fanout (>= 15 direct children) that may need decomposition | Arbitrary SPARQL: bun run beans:query --sparql "SELECT ?id ?title WHERE { ?b bean:id ?id ; bean:title ?title }" | Export RDF graph: bun run beans:query --export-nq beans.nq | . 2. Setting Dependencies You can map out sequence blockers using: beans update <id> --blocked-by <blocker-id> beans update <id> --blocking <blocked-id> . 3. Updating Status & Adding Comments . | When starting work: bun run cat beans:claim <id> — a claim goes through the claim tool, never through beans update, so it is visible to the next session’s check | When completed: beans update <id> --status completed | To add notes or discussion: beans update <id> --body-append "Your note", or --body-append - with a heredoc when it runs to paragraphs. Never --body-file — it replaces the whole body, silently, exit 0: §”Check before you UPDATE”. | . 4. A work item that delivers a requirement copies its success criteria When a work item is part of a work plan — it delivers one or more req: statements (or a plan’s REQ-### / FR-###) — it names them in its body and its ## Done when is copied from their success criteria, one checkbox per criterion, with the criterion’s key. Closing the work item is then judging those criteria. The work item ids are also listed in the requirement set’s workPlan — a set at planned with none is refused by check:requirements. The rule and an example are in the content layer’s requirement-definition skill (skill_fetch requirement-definition) §”The work plan is beans”.

ef35a6f5908f.title: Archiving — two dispositions, and they answer different questions
ef35a6f5908f.content: beans archive moves every completed or scrapped work item out of the working set. It moves, never deletes: an archived work item is still resolvable by id, which is what makes it a disposal an agent may perform at all (deletion-requires-confirmation). There are two ways it can be driven, they are not alternatives, and a process author needs to know which one they are reaching for. |   | a per-activity op | a periodic sweep | . | what it is | a step inside one process — a fourth <cat-harness.processes:bean op> beside claim, note, resolve | a scheduled run over the whole store | . | the question it answers | is this item’s work over? | is the store still readable? | . | what decides | the process reaching a step that means completion | a uniform, process-independent criterion — completed or scrapped | . | what the archive then records | why — “archived because the release shipped” | when — “archived in the sweep of that date” | . | what it cannot do | reach a work item no process resolved | know that this release is what terminated this item | . Why neither replaces the other . The op cannot cover the store. A work item resolved by a process with no archive step, by hand, or by a sibling session, is never reached; coverage would depend on every path having been drawn, and paths are added faster than they are wired. The sweep cannot carry authority. It knows only status. It cannot say that a requirement was archived because the stakeholder signed off, which is the fact an audit of the CRDM close would want — and crdm-close.bpmn is precisely where that authority exists. So the honest shape is: the sweep is the floor, the op is the exception. The sweep guarantees the store stays readable whatever anyone forgot; an op is worth adding only where a process’s completion is itself the reason, and recording that reason is worth the extra edge on the diagram. Where this sits against resolve — two layers, not two spellings . resolve is the process saying “I am done with this item.” Archiving is the store saying “this is no longer in the working set.” They are different layers and they are allowed to be far apart in time — which is why resolve must never imply an archive, and why the sweep is still needed. The per-activity op: a step carrying <cat-harness.processes:bean op="archive"/> moves the instance’s work item into beans/defs/archive/, with a line saying which process closed it. It does so only once the process has finished and the work item is completed or scrapped; otherwise it leaves the work item in place with a note saying why, because check:bean-archive allows only terminal work items in the archive. Where the bean ops live — OPEN and CLOSE, called by every process . The claim, resolve and archive ops live in two called processes, and nowhere else, so no process can open a work item it never closes: . |   | process | what it does | ops it carries | . | OPEN | Process_BeanOpen (sdlc/processes/bean-open.bpmn) | check before you create, create, whose work item, claim — or leave it alone | claim | . | CLOSE | Process_BeanClose (sdlc/processes/bean-close.bpmn) | outcome: complete, or scrap with reasons, then one shared archive step; or record the blocker and hand back | resolve, archive (and a note for the blocker) | . Process_BeanLifecycle is OPEN → work → CLOSE, calling both. Process_BeanDrain (sdlc/processes/bean-drain.bpmn) is the same over a queue: build the queue grouped by owner, then for each work item OPEN → work → CLOSE, and refill when a drainer’s list runs dry. A work item OPEN finds is someone else’s is marked skip on the queue, not worked. How a process uses them. Call Process_BeanOpen where the work item becomes the process’s own — usually its first step — and follow it with a gateway (claimed / not yours): the engine hands a called process the caller’s work item but not its end event, so the caller reads which end OPEN reached, and not yours stops at an end of its own without touching the work item. Call Process_BeanClose straight before each end the process reaches after OPEN. Straight before matters: resolve counts the process as finished when nothing but archive steps is left (onlyArchiveLeft), and a CLOSE followed by more work turns its resolve into a note. note ops stay where the work happens. A called phase does not open or close again. A process only ever called by another (the CRDM phases under crdm-requirements.bpmn) runs on its caller’s work item, so the caller opens and closes it. A process that is both run on its own and called (code-change-review, upstream-version-adoption, editing-hci-validation) keeps its own pair: nested, OPEN’s claim is idempotent and CLOSE notes instead of closing while the outer process still has work. The check. check:bean-calls (also run inside check:workflow-refs, which CI gates) fails on a claim, resolve or archive op outside OPEN and CLOSE, on a process that calls one of them without the other, and on an entry process that names a work item by ref without calling both. A process whose only marks are note (or a bare <cat-harness.processes:bean/>) and that nothing calls is reported, not failed: it writes on whatever work item its instance was started with and never decides that work item’s fate. The sweep is still beans archive, run deliberately — the floor under every process that never reached CLOSE. Note the CLI prints .beans/archive/ but honours path: from .beans.yml; here that means beans/defs/archive/.

cf0a58ec8456.title: Status Display Format
cf0a58ec8456.content: When the user asks “status” or “show beans”, run beans list and display the work items this session touched under their subject epics — the epic is the heading because it is where the work lives; the session is a filter, not a node: . ## Beans this session touched (branch <branch-name>) - [abcd] PROCESS: how an agent decides what it is doing (epic) - [task-124] Task A (completed) - [task-125] Task B (in-progress) - [efgh] QA: verdicts, sidecars and the audited review record (epic) - [task-126] Task C (todo) .

1c5521b842a1.title: Coordination discipline
1c5521b842a1.content: . | Claim before you work, with bun run cat beans:claim <id>, so sibling sessions working the same goal do not duplicate the effort. Full rule: bean-coordination.md §”Claims are global via the branch store”. Brief it in the same turn you claim it — opening-brief.md. The claim tells a sibling the item is taken; the brief tells them, and the author, what it is being taken for. | One source of truth per concern. Do not fork a work item into a parallel todos/*.json queue; link to the queue from the work item instead. | Move wiring and script together. When relocating a hook-backed script, move its hook reference in the same change — a script without its wiring, or a hook reference without its script, leaves a dangling reference. | Close on landing. 7118d6746cf8.title: Where the feedback came FROM — this skill starts mid-air without it
7118d6746cf8.content: Materialized content (held by reference or materialized from elsewhere) is read-only; a reviewer cannot annotate it in place. The first step of review is copy-out-materialized (diagram: processes/library/copy-out-materialized.bpmn): the reviewer copies the materialized sub-graph into their own folio/, carrying provenance.local back to the original, annotates the copy, and those annotations arrive here. While triaging: . | Feedback is on the COPY, not on the original. Resolving an item edits the copy. The original still hashes to its recorded digest, and check:materialized-fixity fails if somebody annotated held content in place. | provenance.local makes a resolved item traceable to the thing it was about; without it the copy is indistinguishable from original work one rename later. | .

b3fee7d4cab5.title: Role

Each file exports an array of FeedbackItem (extends TodoItem with author/authorEmail): . import type { FeedbackItem } from "../../schemas/types"; export default [ { "id": "todo-mn159z53", "summary": "short description of the issue", "comment": "longer description of the issue", "status": "open", "priority": "medium", "origin": "human", "assignee": "editor-agent", "createdAt": "2026-03-22T02:35:33.543Z" } ] satisfies FeedbackItem[]; .

6d75708fe078.title: Session Start: Todo Workflow
6d75708fe078.content: When the editor skill enters the session start protocol and open feedback exists, follow this flow: . Step 0 — Offer the todo workflow . Present a brief overview and ask: . You have N open feedback items (X critical, Y high, Z medium). Would you like to work on feedback today? . Options: . | Yes, let’s review feedback → proceed to Step 1 | No, I have something else in mind → exit to normal triage | . Step 1 — Overview and scope selection . Show a quick summary grouped by chapter: . ## Feedback Overview | Chapter | Open | Critical/High | Sample |---------|------|---------------|--------| Ch 1: Introduction | 12 | 3 | "this does not need to hold in general" | Ch 4: Methods | 4 | 1 | "missing cross-ref to prior section" | Ch 11: Results | 6 | 0 | "clarify the derivation" | . Then ask: . Where would you like to start? . Options (dynamically generated): . | High priority first — all critical + high items across paper | **Ch N: ** — one option per chapter that has feedback | Show all — flat list sorted by priority | . Step 2 — Present the selected feedback . Show the filtered items as a table: . ## Open Feedback — Ch 1 (12 items) | # | Priority | Block | Summary |---|----------|-------|---------| 1 | high | initial-conditions | this does not need to hold in general | 2 | high | main-point | need a supporting statement for the claim | 3 | medium | core-definition | clarify notation convention | ... | . Ask: Which item(s) would you like to address? (pick by number or “all”) . Step 3 — Review and address each item . For each selected feedback item: . | Show the feedback — full comment, author, date, priority | Read the block — load content/<paper>/<chapter>/<rootName>.md and .ts manifest for context | Propose a fix — suggest specific edits to the .md content | Ask for approval — show the proposed changes and ask: Does this address the feedback? (yes / revise / skip) . | Apply if approved — edit the file, mark todo as in_progress | Iterate if “revise” — ask what to change, re-propose | . Step 4 — After each item, offer next steps . After completing (or skipping) an item: . Done with “this does not need to hold in general”. What next? . Options (context-aware): . | Next item on this block (if more exist) | Next item in this section/chapter | Back to overview — re-show the chapter summary | Done for now — exit todo workflow | . Step 5 — Wrap up . When the author says “done” or all items in scope are addressed: . Session feedback summary: . | Reviewed: 5 items | Addressed: 3 (edits applied) | Skipped: 2 | Remaining open: 9 | . The addressed items are marked in_progress. You can resolve them from the viewer feedback panel when you’re satisfied with the changes.

2f33f08ad65d.title: Resolving Feedback
2f33f08ad65d.content: Only the human author may resolve or remove a FeedbackItem. Agents must never set status to resolved or wontfix, and must never delete items. Agents may set status to in_progress after making edits. Resolution happens in the viewer’s feedback panel (click the status badge on any feedback item).

79f3e4f4a76f.title: Tool Authoring — from capability to concrete mechanism
79f3e4f4a76f.content: Skill id: tool-authoring · Package: folio-core Companion: skills-and-tools . A skill states a capability generically. A Tool node in the Knowledge Graph carries the concrete specification, and the tools repository contains the executable implementation. When authoring or modifying tools in the separated architecture: . | The Skill (skills/) defines what an agent or user accomplishes, free from vendor or CLI specifics. | The Tool Node (cat-harness/tools/) declares the tool in the Knowledge Graph with its I/O contracts, capability bindings (satisfies), and execution metadata. | The Concrete Implementation lives in the dedicated tools repository (the tools layer or <name>-tools/), maintaining its own standalone dependencies, build scripts, ambient type definitions, and test suites. | .

dcf1794ddcf4.title: 1. Repository Boundary & Layout
dcf1794ddcf4.content: The platform splits content/schemas from tool implementations: . | layer | repository | role & contents | . | Graph & Schemas | litlfred/cat-harness | Declarative Tool nodes in tools/ (JSON data, validated against the Tool schema), and skill contracts. | . | Tool Execution | the tools layer’s repository | The Tool schema (schemas/tools/tool.ts, tool-types.ts) and the Tool loader, executable TypeScript implementations in src/tools/, MCP server in src/server.ts, ambient moddle/type definitions in types/, standalone package.json (@litlfred/<tools-layer>), tsconfig.json, and bunfig.toml. | . This split guarantees that a content-only consumer or reader does not drag along heavy runtime dependencies, SDKs, or compiler toolchains.

36987891704c.title: 2. Step-by-Step Tool Authoring Lifecycle
36987891704c.content: Step 1: Identify or Author the Skill Contract . Before writing code, identify the generic capability the tool satisfies: . | Find the skill in skills/ (e.g., sdlc/skills/sdlc-core/package-release.md). | If the skill accepts inputs, verify or define its input: JSON Schema contract in the skill’s front matter or under schemas/skills/. | . Step 2: Implement the Handler in the tools layer . Create a dedicated module under cat-harness-tools/src/tools/<tool-name>.ts: . | Use Zod for input validation: Define explicit input schemas with descriptions. | Support three-state returns: . | success: action completed with verified outcome. | failure: action failed with actionable error message. | undetermined: prerequisites or state could not be inspected — never report “clean” or “success” when an audit or check was skipped. | . | Keep handlers deterministic and pure where possible: Isolate file system writes or network calls behind explicit arguments or testable adapters. | . Example handler: . import { z } from "zod"; export const PackTarballInputSchema = z.object({ instanceRoot: z.string().describe("Root directory of the instance to pack"), outDir: z.string().optional().describe("Output directory for the .tgz tarball"), }); export type PackTarballInput = z.infer<typeof PackTarballInputSchema>; export async function packTarball(input: PackTarballInput) { // Implementation... } . Step 3: Register with the MCP Server . In cat-harness-tools/src/tools/ or cat-harness-tools/src/server.ts: . | Export a registrar function: register<ToolName>Tools(server: McpServer). | Register the tool with server.tool(name, description, schema, handler). | Re-export the tool from the tools layer’s src/index.ts if it is part of the public programmatic API. | . Step 4: Declare the Tool Node in the Knowledge Graph . In tools/<id>/<id>.json, one folder per Tool (Step 4b): a "$schema": "tool-definition/v1" document whose tool object carries . | id (the same string as the folder and the file stem), title and description; | satisfies: ["<skill-id>"], linking it to the skill; | io.inputs / io.outputs, each port naming a shared vocabulary type from schemas/tools/tool-types.ts as "schema": { "$type": "<Type>" }, with required and, for a command-line input, arg; | invoke: shell (a command), inProcess ({ "module": "<path>" }), or mcp ({ "tool": "<name>" }) — never mcp alone; | install, and selection when the Tool has a derived alternative. | . Example: . { "$schema": "tool-definition/v1", "tool": { "id": "pack-tarball", "title": "Pack Knowledge Graph into npm tarball", "description": "Runs `bun pm pack` to build a deterministic .tgz tarball.", "satisfies": ["npm-kg-distribution", "package-release"], "install": { "none": true }, "invoke": { "shell": "bun cat-harness-tools/scripts/pack-tarball.ts" }, "io": { "inputs": [ { "name": "instanceRoot", "schema": { "$type": "RepoPath" }, "required": true, "arg": { "positional": 0 } } ], "outputs": [ { "name": "tarballPath", "schema": { "$type": "Text" } }, { "name": "sha256", "schema": { "$type": "Text" } } ] } } } . Step 4b: A new folder is a named subgraph of its harness — declare it . If what you are adding needs a new folder, decide first which of three kinds of folder it is. Each has exactly one way to be declared, and the place the folder sits decides which: . | A folder directly under the harness root (a new code area, a new graph): an entry in the harness’s own declaration (<harness>.json, e.g. cat-harness.json), under directories, with an id, the path, its graphTypologies and a one-line description. | A folder inside a folder the harness already declares: declared from within, in that directory’s own <dir>.json (as skills/skills.json declares voices). This is not a matter of taste: check:layout-norms fails a new top-level entry whose path lies inside another declared directory. Add subgraph: true when the new folder is a subgraph of the INSTANCE rather than a part of its parent’s graph (voices is the first kind, beans.json’s defs the second). | A folder that holds ONE node — one Tool, one voice: it is not declared. It sits inside the declared graph that owns the node and is found through that graph’s reader, as each voice folder is found by its voice.json. Never declare one Tool’s folder as a tools directory: discovery refuses a harness that declares two tools directories. The Tool’s folder is found by the loader (toolsFromFolders, in the tools layer), as each voice is by its voice.json. | . Both declared forms say what a folder holds the same way, by its graphTypologies: a from-within entry names its own kind (voices.json declares vendors as voice-vendors), it does not inherit its parent’s. One folder per Tool, always. A Tool is declared in tools/<id>/<id>.json inside the harness’s declared tools directory: the folder, the file stem and the Tool’s id are one string, and the folder also holds whatever is that Tool’s alone (its script, fixtures, tests). toolsFromFolders refuses a folder that breaks the convention. The tools/ directory is data only; the loader and shared helpers live in the tools layer. The JSON-LD of each Tool (<base>/tools/<id>.jsonld, its own IRI) and the JSON Schema of each I/O type are written when the site is published, never committed. Why declaring is part of the process, not tidying: . | A folder nothing declares is a folder nothing reasons about. No check catches it for you: check:undeclared-files sweeps the repository root only, so a new undeclared folder inside a harness passes it. | Declared directories are what can be mounted and exported. A remote mount lays down declared directories only, so an undeclared code folder is missing downstream. A harness’s package exports are derived from its declared, shipped code directories (check:package-exports), so an undeclared one cannot be imported by package name either. A from-within id cannot yet be mounted on its own: remote-mount reads top-level entries only. | bun run cat harness:dirs then materialises every declared directory, so the folder exists in every checkout rather than only in yours. | . Step 5: Test the Tool . Author fast unit tests in the tools layer’s test/ or whole-checkout integration tests in the tools layer’s test/coordinator/: . | Test valid arguments and expected outputs. | Test invalid inputs and error handling. | Verify with bun test <tools-layer>/test/<tool>.test.ts or bun test <tools-layer>/test/coordinator/<test>.test.ts. | . Step 6: Validate Reachability and Skill Coverage . Run verification gates: . bun run cat check:tools # verifies satisfies edges match existing skills & types agree bun run cat tools:coverage # checks automated coverage across skills .

Never place tools-specific ambient types in content-only subgraphs. | Bundled Dependencies: Tools declare their runtime dependencies in the tools layer’s package.json. Subgraphs that only import schemas or markdown docs must not list tool runtime dependencies in their manifests. | Packaging: The tools package is packaged and published using bun pm pack as @litlfred/<tools-layer>. | .

6519b813e1fa.title: toolchain-ownership
6519b813e1fa.content: Skill id: toolchain-ownership · Package: authoring-who-smart-guidelines . How the WHO SMART toolchain moves out of an IG and into the harness without becoming a fork nobody can merge back. The goal is a WorldHealthOrganization/smart-base that is a conventional IG with no tooling.

071b4482fcc5.title: The gate
071b4482fcc5.content: A script moves only when a Tool node, a skill and a process step that binds them all exist for it. All three, before any Python relocates. The Tool node says what it consumes and produces; the skill says how and when a person or agent performs it; the process step is what hands it out. A Tool with no process step is unreachable: a script moved into that state leaves a place where a workflow runs it every build and arrives where nothing runs it. The gate does not limit declaring. Declaring runs ahead: smart-base/tools/ carries Tool nodes for scripts that still execute upstream, which is the intended state for now — declare here, execute upstream, until the execution moves too.

c768dea2297e.title: Declaring is not vendoring
c768dea2297e.content: smart-base-tools’s rule load it; never vendor it stands: a copy of the Python would be a second, drifting toolchain. A Tool node is a declaration and duplicates no implementation. When code does move, it is a cutover, not a copy: afterwards exactly one repository runs that script. If both do, a fork has happened, not a move.

59f0cb9b8a78.title: Where ownership lives
59f0cb9b8a78.content: The smart-base/ harness instance in litlfred/smart-base, whose smart-base/tools/ holds the Tool nodes. It is not a separate fork of the WHO IG. Nothing at WorldHealthOrganization/* changes. This is work in litlfred/*, which is also why the DAK declaration in index.config.json (contentTypes.dak) is ours until upstream adopts it. WorldHealthOrganization/smart-base is read-only from here and stays the executing home until the gate is satisfied per script. A moved script arrives in a directory that is not a FHIR IG: ghbuild.yml cannot run it and there is no input/scripts/ for it. So a move is a rewrite to the harness’s own invocation surface, which is the Skill I/O work below.

7f343780b76d.title: What “adhere to Skill I/O requirements” means
7f343780b76d.content: A rewritten script must be describable by its Tool node without hedging: . | Declared inputs and outputs, each with a type from the shared vocabulary — not “it reads the repository and writes some files”. | A determined empty is distinguishable from a failure. The upstream scripts report files_expected against files_missing, which separates “this DAK has no DMN” from “the DMN directory was not found”. Keep it. | Exit status means something. Several upstream steps warn and continue when their script is absent, so a missing capability reads as a clean run. The ci-health rule — could not check is never green — is the most common thing to fix while rewriting. | No hidden fetch. Upstream scripts curl themselves from smart-base main at build time. A rewritten script does not fetch itself. | .

05d69f523d68.title: Rewrite in this order
05d69f523d68.content: . | Declare the Tool node against the script as it is today, not as it should become. | Write the skill, which shows whether the capability is one thing or several (update_sushi_config.py is four jobs in one script). | Bind it in a process, in the lane whose role performs it. | Then rewrite and move, with a cutover. | . Steps 1–3 are reversible and cheap. Step 4 is neither.

640df8ea5c3d.title: What is already declared
640df8ea5c3d.content: smart-base/tools/ declares the upstream DAK scripts beside the harness’s own tools; count the directory rather than trusting a number. The two Library strippers (strip-library-binaries, strip-library-content) are declared in fhir-harness/tools/, because they are not DAK-shaped; see smart-stack-layering.

3a1464dbf284.title: Translation manager
3a1464dbf284.content: Skill id: translation-manager · Package: folio-core . Manage the translation lifecycle for folio content. This skill covers the full round trip from source content to translated content, including extraction, translation, injection, quality assurance, sign-off, and automatic badge rendering.

9e15d4249d18.title: Reference
9e15d4249d18.content: The authoritative documentation is docs/guides/translation-support.md. Read it before using this skill. This file is the operational checklist, not the architecture.

62c9327c771e.title: The two-axis model
62c9327c771e.content: A content node varies along two axes: . | Format — .md (Markdown), .lean (Lean 4), .tex (LaTeX), .bpmn, .dmn, etc. | Language — BCP 47 locale tags (en, fr, es, ar, zh, ru). | . The format axis is handled by companions. The language axis is handled by the PO/POT pipeline with TranslationNode manifests in translations/<locale>/.

b97b91e913db.title: TranslationNode — .po/.pot files as KG nodes
b97b91e913db.content: Each .po/.pot pair is wrapped by a .ts manifest that makes it a first-class node in the knowledge graph: . import type { TranslationNode } from "../../schemas/translation"; const node: TranslationNode = { label: "trans:fr/index", locale: "fr", sourceFile: "docs/index.md", potFile: "translations/fr/index.pot", poFile: "translations/fr/index.po", status: { locale: "fr", official: false, generatedBy: "agent" }, coverage: { translated: 37, total: 37, pct: 100 }, }; export default node; . The manifest carries the status, coverage, and QA results inline — no separate status.json or .qa.json files.

f8e78a9f5a03.title: PO source resolution (fallback behavior)
f8e78a9f5a03.content: Content blocks can declare explicit PO sources via poSources[] on BlockBase. When not declared, the pipeline resolves by convention: . | Block-level: translations/<locale>/<block-stem>.po | Chapter-level: translations/<locale>/<chapter-slug>.po | Folio-level: translations/<locale>/global.po | Dependency walk: walk <name>.config.json dependencies depth-first | . When poSources is declared, only the listed files are consulted (no fallback). Later entries override earlier for the same msgid.

296976250f08.title: What is translatable
296976250f08.content: | Content | Translatable? | Notes | . | Block titles | ✅ | From .ts manifests | . | Prose bodies (.md) | ✅ | Segmented by paragraph | . | Chapter/section titles | ✅ | From chapter.ts / section.ts | . | Kind headings | ✅ | “Definition”, “Theorem”, etc. → locale catalogue | . | LaTeX math | ❌ | Universal notation | . | Block labels | ❌ | Structural identifiers | . | Code blocks | ❌ | Programming language content | . | Lean companions | ❌ | Formal mathematics | . | FHIR resources | ⚠️ | Use FHIR’s own designation system, not gettext | .

a70f283e9cd2.title: The exported GRAPH per locale
a70f283e9cd2.content: The graph a machine consumes is translated per locale, not only the rendered page: bun run cat kg:locale writes it (kg:locale:bootstrap for the nested instance, kg:locale:check in the gate set). Four rules; an implementation breaks the first by default. 1. The core graph must not reference its translations. No hasTranslation, no availableLocales, no translationOf, no per-locale @id, no locale key in the @context. The obvious implementation hangs a pointer off each node; that grows the core by an edge per locale per node and makes bootstrap’s graph reference artefacts it does not own and cannot validate. The arrow runs one way — a per-locale document references the core, never the reverse — and the core is complete with no translation existing. The same relation board-diagram-interchange states for a board and its folio. localeDocumentsUnreferenced checks it rather than trusting it. 2. A translated node keeps its @id. A translation is not a new term. Locale-suffixed IRIs are ruled out by that, not chosen against. 3. The language tag rides the VALUE, never the document. A blanket "@language": "fr" would assert French over every string that fell through — and fall-through is the normal case, because parsePo takes only non-empty msgstr and skips fuzzy entries. A translated value is {"@value": …, "@language": …}; a fall-through stays a plain string under the document’s declared sourceLanguage. Fall-through is then visible in the data rather than inferable from a coverage number. 4. A catalogue is scoped to the asset it was extracted from. Merging every .po under a locale lets a docs page’s "yes" → "oui" translate every BPMN gateway branch label — output that looks right while no diagram catalogue exists, so it can only be caught by provenance, not by reading the output. So a .po is read only when its stem names an asset the graph projects. A residual is accepted and named: a msgid from diagram A applies to an identical string on a node from diagram B — not a new assumption, since kg-export already dedupes lane-derived Role nodes by lane name across every diagram. What the gate is not. kg:locale:check says nothing about how much is translated. Where a diagram template has no .po in a locale, the exporter writes nothing and reports the locale saying so. A locale with nothing to say is reported, never a missing file a reader cannot tell from a broken build; --all-locales emits a source-language copy per locale for the other reading.

132f01a80971.title: Workflow
132f01a80971.content: 1. Extract (POT generation) . bun run pipeline/pot-extract.ts [--chapter <dir>] [--block <label>] . Or use the translation_extract MCP tool. Produces .pot files at the configured granularity. 2. Translate . Options, in order of preference: . | Existing .po from SMART Base — if the DAK already has translations from Weblate/Crowdin, use them. | FHIR/translation-utils — the po-translate CLI for batch machine translation via DeepL/Google Translate. Tags results # fuzzy. | Agent translation — LLM translation of .pot → .po. Also tagged unofficial. | Human translation — the gold standard. | . 3. Inject (PO → translated Markdown) . bun run pipeline/po-inject.ts --locale <locale> [--chapter <dir>] . Or use the translation_inject MCP tool. Reads .po files and produces translated .md in docs/<locale>/ for docs pages, or in the content directory for content blocks. 4. Create TranslationNode manifest . After injection, create or update the .ts manifest: . # The pipeline does this automatically, or create manually: translations/<locale>/<stem>.ts . The manifest carries status, coverage, and round-trip QA results inline. Validate with TranslationNodeSchema from schemas/content/translation.ts. 5. Round-trip QA . After injection, run round-trip translation QA: . bun run pipeline/translation-qa.ts --locale <locale> . Or use the translation_validate MCP tool for coverage and staleness. Semantic verification is per block and lives in the sidecar, not in a node-level summary field: TranslationNode.roundTripQA was removed with the numbers it held. See §”Per-block translation QA” below, and route drift to a human reviewer. 6. Sign-off . A human reviewer signs off at the desired level: . bun run pipeline/translation-signoff.ts --locale <locale> --level <block|section|chapter|folio> [--path <content-path>] . Or use the translation_signoff MCP tool. Updates the TranslationNode manifest with sign-off metadata and source hash. 7. Staleness watch . On every content change, the pipeline checks whether any official translation’s sourceHash no longer matches the source .md. Stale translations are flagged in the viewer and in translation_status output.

de6384d4b342.title: Per-block translation QA, and the agentic round trip
de6384d4b342.content: Two sweeps, two subjects, and confusing them is how a site reports a translation nobody measured. | translation-qa-sweep.ts measures the docs site: how much of each page exists in each language. It writes docs/_data/translation-qa.json and feeds the badge under a page title. | translation-block-qa.ts measures a block, one sidecar per (block, locale): <stem>.<locale>.translation-qa.json, in the block-qa/v1 entry shape, which is what the per-block TR icon opens. | . bun run cat translation:block-qa # write the sidecars bun run cat translation:block-qa:check # fail if any is stale . What a script may claim, and what it may not . Three criteria are deterministic and carry a script witness: translation-coverage, translation-terms-preserved (acronyms, numbers and URLs that must survive translation and did not — the class a fluent mistranslation passes) and translation-not-echo (a “translation” identical to its source; a warn, because that is right for a proper noun and wrong for a sentence). translation-semantic-roundtrip is written with no entry. A round trip asks whether the MEANING survived, and that needs a translator that has not seen the original. The only back-translation available to a script here is the PO’s own msgid→msgstr map read backwards, which returns the source exactly, always: a perfect similarity score measuring the lookup table. Do not fill this criterion mechanically. A green tick nobody should trust is worse than a gap that says it is a gap — a reader who sees the tick stops asking. This was not hypothetical. translations/fr/index.ts carried roundTripQA: { fail: 21, total: 36, method: "jaccard-word-overlap" }, and its own description explained those failures away as expected “with limited vocabulary back-translator” — a measurement whose author has to explain it away is about the instrument, not the translation. The generator’s back-translation map held 6 entries for 36 strings: every string nobody had back-translated scored 0 similarity and was counted as drift, so fail: 21 was a count of absences. A second script back-translated by applying a 40-pair word-substitution table to the French and wrote the result as a block-qa/v1 sidecar with an agent reviewer. All of it is removed — the numbers, the roundTripQA field, the page badge that displayed them, and both scripts. The agentic round trip — an INSTANCE of untainted verification . The discipline is generic and lives in untainted-verification: the two parties, why neither may see what would let it shortcut, the TOOLS_USED declaration that is recorded rather than assumed, which party rules, how both are written as witnesses, the model / model_source rule, and the two traps — a sweep replaces only entries whose reviewer is itself, and a verdict is hashed to what it was about. Read that first. This section is only what translation adds. The round trip was where that discipline was first written down, and generalising it turned up a defect in the generalisation: the spine’s UntaintedDispatch was typed over CompanionRole, and po is deliberately not one — a PO is a companion of a (block, locale) pair, not of a block. So the founding case could not be expressed in the type taken from it. The abstraction was widened rather than the case bent; untaintedPartitionDefects now takes its artefact universe as a parameter. The declaration . ROUNDTRIP_DISPATCH in pipeline/translation-block-qa.ts: . | party | sees | never sees | . | back-translator | po — the target text, and nothing else | md, ts | . | adjudicator | md — the original, plus the back-translation | po | . Disjoint, which is the whole rule in one line. Shown the source, a back-translator writes the source back and the check passes vacuously — measuring the lookup table rather than the translation. That is not a warning here any more: untaintedPartitionDefects reports it, and a test asserts it. What counts as drift, and what does not . Both halves, always. Told only what to look for, an adjudicator returns a style review and every translation fails. Synonyms, articles and re-ordering are not drift. A claim added, dropped, weakened, strengthened or reversed is; so is a term of art swapped for something that means a different thing, and a named entity or quantifier moved. This is the part that does not generalise — the spine requires a drift statement and checks only that one exists, because “states what is not drift as well as what is” is a reading, and a gate pretending to measure it would be the defect the whole mechanism exists to stop. Recording it . bun run pipeline/translation-roundtrip.ts --payload <file.json> . Where it lands: translation-block-qa writes translation-semantic-roundtrip: [] on every run, and before mergeCriteria an unrelated re-run deleted a round trip a pair of agents had produced — silently, with nothing in the output to say so. That incident is why the spine carries the replace-only-your-own rule. Staleness is per locale here: the entries hash the .md, the .ts and the .po, so editing the source stales every locale’s round trip and editing one translation stales only that locale’s. The instrument, not the translation . translations/fr/index.ts carried roundTripQA: { fail: 21, total: 36, method: "jaccard-word-overlap" }, and its own description explained those failures away as expected “with limited vocabulary back-translator”. The generator’s back-translation map held 6 entries for 36 strings: every string nobody had back-translated scored 0 similarity and was counted as drift, so fail: 21 was a count of absences. A second script back-translated by applying a 40-pair word-substitution table to the French and wrote the result as a block-qa/v1 sidecar with an agent reviewer. All of it is removed — the numbers, the roundTripQA field, the page badge that displayed them, and both scripts. A measurement whose author has to explain it away is about the instrument, not the subject.

12c38aa14c1d.title: Automatic badge rendering
12c38aa14c1d.content: Translation badges are automatically rendered on every docs page by docs-ui.js. There is no need to manually add badge includes or front matter. How it works . | head_custom.html publishes a <script type="application/json" id="fa-translation-meta"> block on every page, reading from page front matter | docs-ui.js reads that block and auto-injects into the page title: . | 🌐 Language coverage badge — 0/5 languages (grey), 1/5 (amber), 5/5 (green) | ⚠️ Unverified warning — auto-injected when translation_status: unverified | . | . Front matter for the translation pipeline to stamp . The translation pipeline stamps this front matter on generated pages: . # Source pages (English): lang: en available_locales: ["en", "fr"] # every locale the page can be read in # Translated pages: lang: fr translation_status: unverified # or "official" translation_source: index.md # source file available_locales: ["en", "fr"] . The terminology glossary — translations/<locale>/glossary.po . translation-terms-preserved can see that a source term is absent from a translation. It cannot see whether that is a correct localisation or a silent loss: WHO missing from a French sentence is either OMS or a dropped term, and guessing either way is worse than saying so. The glossary is how a folio tells it which. | entry | meaning | when the term is absent | . | msgstr "OMS" | the expected form, pinned | fail — the glossary said what it should be | . | msgstr "FHIR" (identity) | must survive verbatim | fail | . | #, localised | rendered in the target language, form NOT pinned | pass | . | no entry | unknown | warn | . #, localised exists so a glossary needs no translated content. Pinning a form means authoring target-language material; the flag says the one thing the checker needs — this term gets localised, I am not pinning how — and it is reviewable by someone who reads only English. Pin a form when you want the stricter check. It is a reading rule and cannot become a mute button, which is the property to preserve if you touch it. localised only converts a would-be finding about that term into a pass: it never reaches strict tokens (a URL or a number consults no glossary — nothing localises a 3), it cannot act on a term it does not name, an entry with neither a form nor the flag is unfinished rather than permission, and each locale’s file is read alone, so marking a term in French says nothing about Arabic. Every one of those is a test in translation-block-qa.test.ts. The file is hand-authored and has no POT — schemas/content/translation.ts declares that slot, and TranslationNode.potFile is optional for exactly this. Work item he0e. available_locales includes the SOURCE language, and that is not a formality. It is the list a reader’s language bar and coverage badge are computed from — “which languages can I read this page in” — and the page is certainly readable in the one it was written in. It is not the list of translations that exist, which is what availableLocales() in pipeline/po-resolve.ts returns by resolving translations/<locale>/<stem>.po; that lookup can never name the source language, because there is no translations/en/ and there never will be. Use localesAvailableFor() in pipeline/translation-index.ts to go from one to the other. Both halves of the corpus — generated and hand-authored translated pages — must stamp the same meaning, or a badge reads a numerator larger than its denominator. Do not stamp qa_translation_* keys: stamped from a node-level round trip, they publish every string nobody back-translated as semantic drift. Per-block QA is the record: the TR icon beside each block opens <stem>.<locale>.translation-qa.json, where a verdict names the witness that reached it. docs-ui.js injects the unverified-translation warning itself, from the page’s own front matter. There is no include to add: buildLanguageBar renders the six UN languages and greys out the ones not yet translated. Do not add a translation-warning.html, language-selector.html or qa-translation-badge.html include.

21ecfe0c2e4b.title: The navbar filters by locale
21ecfe0c2e4b.content: Translated pages are labelled as translated content in the graph and are not shown in the navbar unless their locale is selected; with no translation, the navbar falls back to the source language. Three rules, and each is enforced somewhere different because each can break somewhere different. 1. A page is a translation because the PAGE says so . Three fields in its own front matter, and nothing else anywhere: . lang: fr # this page is French nav_exclude: true # keep it OUT of the static nav translation_source: index.md # which page it expresses . pipeline/translation-index.ts walks the site and reads those. A page with no lang is the instance’s source language — absent means the default, not unknown. Never match a directory name against a list of language subtags. A layout coincidence is not a contract, and it is wrong in both directions: a folio with a no/ chapter (Norwegian, or the English word) is silently hidden from its own navbar, and a pt-BR/ or translated-fr/ directory is silently shown as source. Neither announces itself — the navbar simply has the wrong entries in it. Put the French page at accueil-fr.md beside its source and it is indexed correctly; put an English page in a folder called fr/ and it is left alone. There is deliberately no translated-content graph typology. A declaration per locale subtree restates what every page already says and grows as O(locales × subtrees). What is translatable is a node’s content (Markdown, BPMN, …), not its schema: translatability is a property of a format within a content type. Each instance that owns a content type declares, under contentTranslations in its own <instance>.json, which formats have an extract/inject pair, and schemas/library/translation-tools.ts collects them — Markdown, LaTeX, PlantUML, SVG, ArchiMate, Excel, BPMN, FSH, FHIR JSON — and isTranslatable(contentType, extension) is the predicate. The index asks it rather than inventing a second answer, so a .json beside a page is data and never a language. translations/ is declared, as translation-sources. That one earns a kind: a .po catalogue is not content in any language, so no file inside it can declare one. There is no nav_order on a translated page. It stands where its source stands, because it replaces that item rather than joining the list. A nav_order beside a nav_exclude is two facts that contradict each other, and the check refuses it. 2. nav_exclude is the half that JavaScript cannot do . just-the-docs builds the navbar at build time, from front matter, on a static site serving the same HTML to every reader. It cannot know which locale anybody chose, so a translated page left in the nav is in it for everybody. A script can swap a nav item; it cannot un-render one without a flash of the wrong nav first. So the translations leave the static nav entirely, and a reader with no JavaScript gets the source-language navbar — the correct degraded answer rather than an arbitrary one. 3. The swap, and the fallback that is not a code path . pipeline/translation-index.ts writes docs/_data/translations.json; _includes/head_custom.html publishes it into every page as #fa-translation-index; mountNavLocale in site-chrome/assets/js/docs-ui.js reads it. With a non-source locale selected, each nav item that has a page in that locale is rewritten in place — same position, same parent, translated title, translated href, and its own dir so an Arabic item inside an English column is not laid out backwards. Fallback is the absence of a rewrite. An item with no page in the selected locale is not touched, so it keeps its source-language title and link. There is deliberately no branch for it: a fallback implemented as its own code path is a code path that can be wrong, and this one cannot be. Which locale is “selected”, in precedence order: ?lang= on the URL, then the page’s own lang when the page is a translation, then the remembered fa-locale, then the source language. A locale the index has never heard of is not honoured — labelling the navbar tlh while every item is in English is a claim the page cannot support. Three states, and the third is why the index is published as null . | data-fa-nav-index | when | what the navbar does | . | ok | the index parsed and holds pages | filter it | . | empty | it parsed and holds none | nothing to swap; every item is source language | . | unknown | no island, unparseable, or index: null because the data file was absent at build time | left exactly as built | . empty and unknown produce the same navbar and are not the same answer: one is “this folio has no translations”, the other is “this build could not tell”. A build that could not determine the translation set must never render as a folio that has none — so translation:index exits 2 rather than writing a partial index over a complete one, and the deploy fails rather than publishing it. Adding a locale . | Write the pages, each carrying lang, nav_exclude: true and translation_source. Where they sit is up to you — the convention here is <dir>/<locale>/<page>.md, and nothing depends on it. | bun run cat translation:index and commit docs/_data/translations.json. | . There is no third step and no declaration to remember. The thing that IS easy to forget is nav_exclude, which is why translation:index:check fails without it: a translated page left in the static nav is in it for every reader, whatever locale they chose, which is the bug this section records.
