aa9e7fa91d42.title: Adopting an upstream version bump
aa9e7fa91d42.content: An unpinned dependency is an unreviewed commit from a stranger, merged on every build. A pinned one is a commitment that somebody has to revisit. This skill is the second half: what happens between upstream cut a release and we are running it. It implements two diagrams, and the diagram is the source of truth for ordering: . | Diagram | What it is | . | upstream-pin-watch.bpmn | The watcher. Scheduled, mechanical, ends at either “every pin is current” or “one tracking issue says which is not”. | . | upstream-version-adoption.bpmn | The reusable subprocess, entered once per stale pin. Scope → impact → MVP → review → decide. | . The second is called, not copied: calledElement="Process_UpstreamAdoption". Any pinned upstream dependency enters it the same way, and a new tenant is a registry row plus a call activity — never a second diagram that says the same thing in different words.

af45d74a400d.title: The registry is the tenant list, and it does not hold the version
af45d74a400d.content: upstream/upstream-pins.json — in this harness’s declared upstream/ directory — declares each pinned dependency, with each pinnedIn resolved against the harness root: the upstream repo, the file the pin literal actually lives in, the pattern that reads it, what of ours binds to it, and the commands that constitute its MVP. It deliberately does not store the pinned version. The version lives in exactly one place — site-chrome/_config.yml for the theme — and the registry says how to read it from there. A registry that carried its own copy would be a second answer to “what are we running”, free to disagree with the build. bun run cat check:upstream-pins reads the literal out of the declared file; a pattern that matches nothing is reported as an error, not as “no pin”. binds and mvp are the reason the registry exists at all rather than the check simply grepping for version strings. They are what turn impact analysis and MVP from words in a box into a list somebody can work through.

ba5d75861eed.title: 1 — Watch
ba5d75861eed.content: bun run cat check:upstream-pins, weekly from .github/workflows/upstream-pins.yml and on demand. For each row: read the pinned ref out of its declared file, list the upstream tags that match tagPattern, and compare. Exit codes, and the middle one is the point: . | Exit | Meaning | What the workflow does | . | 0 | every pin is at the newest matching release | closes the tracking issue if one is open | . | 1 | at least one pin is behind | opens one issue labelled upstream-pin, or edits the existing one | . | 2 | could not determine — upstream unreachable, pattern did not match | leaves the issue untouched and fails the job | . Three rules it inherits from check-ci-health.ts, and they are not optional: . | “Could not check” is never rendered as current. An unreachable upstream is exit 2, not exit 0. A watchdog that goes blind must not read as good news. | One issue, edited in place. An edit does not notify, so a pin that stays stale for months stays one unread item rather than many. | The job fails on exit 2, which makes this workflow itself red on the default branch, which check:ci-health reports. The watchdog is watched. | .

b9b04a1d42fb.title: 2 — Impact analysis
b9b04a1d42fb.content: Scope the delta first, and scope it to what reaches our output. The upstream changelog is the claim; the diff is the evidence. For a Jekyll theme that means _sass, _includes, _layouts and assets — a change to upstream’s own docs, CI or tests cannot reach us: . git -C <upstream-clone> diff --stat <pinned>..<candidate> -- _sass _includes _layouts assets . Then ask what of ours binds to it, from the row’s binds list. This is the half that a changelog cannot tell you, because upstream does not know what you reached into. For the theme it is concrete and small: site-chrome/assets/js/docs-ui.js moves the theme’s own search markup into the action launcher, binding .search, #search-input and .search-label; site-chrome/assets/css/docs-ui.css overrides .side-bar, .site-header and .main-header; and three e2e specs assert the structure the theme emits. An upstream rename of any of those is not a build failure — it is a shipped feature that quietly stops working, which is the failure mode a pin exists to convert into a decision. Write the analysis down as the work item’s note before building anything. A candidate that touches nothing we bind to is a different conversation from one that renames a selector we depend on, and the reviewer needs to know which they are looking at before they look.

d96772cfa6b8.title: 3 — MVP
d96772cfa6b8.content: An MVP is a deployed build, not a description of one. Move the pin on a branch, let feature-staging.yml publish it under branches/<branch-slug>/, and run the row’s mvp commands. For the theme: . rm -rf _kg _site bun test # unit tests CI=1 bun run cat test:e2e # a11y, action tiles, sidebar panels, qa panel bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/site-links.ts --site ./_site # every navbar tile resolves in the BUILT site . site-links.ts checks the tiles against the real _site rather than against the attribute, which is what catches a tile that 404s. A red gate is evidence, not an exit. It does not end the process and it does not loop on its own — it goes to the reviewer with everything else, because “this version breaks us” is a finding the decider needs, not a reason to stop before they see it.

4aa46bec5a61.title: 4 — Review
4aa46bec5a61.content: Post the staging URL, the gate results and the impact analysis on the PR, then hand it over. The reviewer’s question is narrower than “is the new version good”: it is does anything in binds still hold, checked against the deployed page rather than against a screenshot. Findings the agent can fix — our overlay adapting to a renamed class, a test fixture updated to the markup the theme now emits — loop back into impact analysis on the same branch. Findings that are upstream’s behaviour rather than ours go to the decision as they are.

3561a7c2d8c7.title: 5 — Decide
3561a7c2d8c7.content: A person decides, and the diagram says so. PM_Decide is a bpmn:userTask in the publication manager’s lane, and that role admits person only, so activity-fulfilment-kind fails the moment somebody tries to make an agent the accepting party. It also carries <cat-harness.processes:policy relaxable="false"/>: no package may relax it. The lane is the publication manager’s rather than the editor’s because the pin is not a change to the corpus — it is a change to what the published artefact is built from, and that role is the one “accountable for what is live”. The gateway is not DMN-backed, and that is deliberate. Every other computed gateway in this repository reduces to arithmetic over tool output; this one weighs a rendering nobody can score against the cost of staying behind. A table here would look authoritative and would not be. Three outcomes: . | Adopt — move the pin, open the PR, and say in the body what the version range changed in rendered output. Record the evidence you used, not just the verdict. | Hold — record it as a block with an expiry and a revisit trigger (bean-blocking.md). A hold with no expiry cannot be told from abandoned work, and the next watcher run will re-raise the same pin with no memory of why it was left. | Decline — record the reasons on the work item and scrap it. A scrapped work item is what stops the next agent re-entering the same dead end; a deleted one leaves them unable to tell a decision from an accident. | . In every case the decision is written down before the process ends. The work item is resolved from the terminal step, so a run that stops at “we looked and said no” is as finished as one that moved the pin.

05095ebe5c4d.title: Adding a tenant
05095ebe5c4d.content: . | Pin the literal wherever the tool reads it, with a comment saying which process governs moving it. | Add a row to upstream-pins.json: repo, pinnedIn, pattern, tagPattern, binds, mvp. | Run bun run cat check:upstream-pins and confirm it reads your pin back. A pattern that does not match is exit 2 — “could not determine” — and the row is not watched until it does. | . No diagram changes. That is what reusable means here.

bceeeba13b89.title: How to pick the pinned version when you first pin something
bceeeba13b89.content: Pin what is running, not what is newest. Those are different changes, and doing both at once means neither is reviewable — a regression cannot be attributed to the pin or to the bump. Establish what is running by fingerprint, not by assumption. For the theme that meant finding a declaration in the deployed CSS on gh-pages (text-wrap: balance, in _sass/navigation.scss) that entered upstream after the newest release, which proved the live site was tracking the default branch rather than any tag. The newest release at or below that point is the pin, and the PR states the residual delta — one CSS declaration — rather than claiming there is none. If no fingerprint discriminates, say so and pin the newest release anyway; an unverified pin is still strictly better than an unpinned dependency, and “could not determine” written down is worth more than a confident guess.

8b5c3ccf09e3.title: Processes that run this skill
8b5c3ccf09e3.content: This skill has its own process: Adopting an upstream version bump. | process | step(s) that name it | . | A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories | 11 · Parent consumes, additively (calls a sub-process) | . | A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository | 10 · Re-point: livesAt, seam, mount or subscription | . | Watching a pinned upstream dependency | Read the pin registry upstream-pins.json; List upstream releases and compare to the pin; Close the tracking issue; Open or EDIT the one tracking issue; Pick up the stale pin; Adopt the version bump (calls a sub-process) | . | Adopting an upstream version bump | Scope the delta pinned → candidate; Impact analysis what of ours binds it; Record the hold or the decline | .

48575a3f74a6.title: The relation you are auditing
48575a3f74a6.content: uses[] is the editorial dependency relation: what must a reader have read to follow this block? It is authored content — a deliberate judgement about narrative order — and it is maintained by agents and humans, not generated. The same relation exists at term scale: a glossary term’s requires, and a schema term’s uses in bootstrap’s graph.schema.json, say what a reader must know before the definition. Same discipline — AUTHORED, never inferred, with a text matcher kept only as a guard that list and prose agree (see the glossary ordering discipline, §”Ordered glossaries”). It is not any machine-derived dependency graph. A content type with a formal layer also derives a formal relation, from what its proofs actually invoke, and the two relations answer different questions and diverge in both directions, correctly. The layer that ships such a content type holds that comparison and names this skill from its side (for a paper folio, the science layer).

3e747ab19203.title: interprets is the same relation under a second field name
3e747ab19203.content: uses[] is the curated list. interprets states the same reader-facing fact for a remark or example about one specific block, and the content graph counts both. Each editorial edge carries editorialField so a tool proposing an edit can still tell which field an author wrote: they are interchangeable to a reader and not to a writer, and collapsing them would make an automated edit rewrite the wrong field. Two caveats, both of which change what a number means: . | detangler-no-forward-ref builds its own uses-only adjacency and does not consume the shared graph, so forward-pointing interprets edges are outside what it counts. | The editorial graph is not acyclic. Counting both fields reveals genuine editorial cycles. Do not “fix” one without reading whether it is real. | . Do not quote a count from prose — run the check against the corpus in front of you. A number in a document is a claim; only a run is evidence. For impact questions — what breaks if this changes? — use the union, via the content graph’s accessors, which default to it.

c83878dda8ae.title: The prime directive
c83878dda8ae.content: Never populate uses[] from a machine-derived dependency graph. Copying derived dependencies in destroys the editorial signal and inflates every ordering metric computed from it (graph energy, forward refs, cone size, PageRank). Never “sync” the two. When reviewing, do not open a block’s formal or generated sibling to decide what belongs in uses[]. The question is about the reader.

d8f70e6c1a0c.title: Workflow
d8f70e6c1a0c.content: . | Read the .md as a reader. Cold. Do not read the .ts first — you want your own sense of what the block presumes before you see what the author declared. | List what the narrative actually leans on. Note every point where the prose: . | uses notation it does not introduce, | names an object (“the canonical $X$”) defined elsewhere, | argues against or refines a prior result, | presumes a construction the reader would otherwise have to reconstruct. | . | Now read uses[] in the .ts manifest and compare both ways. | Judge completeness. Anything from step 2 missing from uses[] that a reader would genuinely stumble over ⇒ fail (major). A reader who could carry on unbothered ⇒ at most warn. | Judge editorial fitness. For each listed entry, ask: would a reader be worse off having not read this first? . | Yes ⇒ fine. | No, and it looks like a derived artefact (an entry the prose never mentions, copied from a generated dependency list) ⇒ fail (major). This is the pollution case. | No, but it is defensible context ⇒ warn. | . | Write the sidecar entry under uses-editorial-completeness with reviewer.kind: "agent" (or "human"), citing file:line and a verbatim quote for every finding — the block-QA evidence contract. | .

895556d18579.title: Verdict rubric
895556d18579.content: | Verdict | When | . | pass | List reads as a deliberate editorial judgement; nothing a reader needs is missing; nothing present is dead weight. | . | warn | A marginal entry, or a missing dependency a reader could shrug off. | . | fail | A missing dependency a reader would stumble over, or an entry that is plainly a copied-in derived dependency. | .

bd57c40287d3.title: Forward references and foreshadows[]
bd57c40287d3.content: A uses[] entry pointing at a block that appears later in the chapter is a detangler-no-forward-ref finding. Sometimes that is right — the exposition really does defer — and foreshadows[] records it. foreshadows[] is independent of uses[], so a chapter overview can name results it previews without asserting a dependency that is not real. It covers two cases you must keep apart: . | case | in uses[]? | who records it | cost | . | Pure forward pointer — the prose names something coming later and does not depend on it | no | derived from the .md, not authored | zero by construction: it never enters the dependency graph | . | Deferred prerequisite — a real dependency the paper states later on purpose | yes | declared by the author, and only the author | exempt from ordering cost; still counted for cycles, cones and depth | . Do not hand-author the first case. deriveForeshadows reads the block’s own markdown links and backticked labels, keeps those that resolve to a real block sitting later in reading order and are not already in uses[], and loadChapterGraph re-derives on every load. Writing them into the manifest duplicates the prose into metadata, where it goes stale. The derivation never reads deferral language; it matches links and labels only (phrasing detection misreads e.g. “Below $n^*$”, a numeric comparison).

477b7e444c28.title: Declaring the second case
477b7e444c28.content: Only a deferred prerequisite needs your judgement: it exempts a real uses[] edge from the ordering metrics, hiding a genuine defect behind an authored claim that the disorder was intended, and nothing downstream re-opens it. The contract in BlockBase.foreshadows is strict — the prose must frame the reference as deferred (“we will need X, proved in chapter 9”). The bar is a first-person authorial hand-off that says the treatment happens elsewhere: “we establish this in X”, “we work this out separately”, “the derivation is recorded in X”. | Looks like a deferral | Actually | . | Bare cross-reference — “See [X] in Chapter 7” | ordering. Says nothing about direction. | . | Organizational pointer — “these tables are projections of this master table” | ordering. About structure, not sequence. | . | Block asserts the target’s conclusion as background, then reasons onward from it | ordering. Consuming a result is the opposite of deferring it. | . | Target listed under “## Rigorous results” / “## Consumers / downstream” | ordering — and check the direction; these often run target→source. | . | A forward-looking word (“below”, “later”, “we must show”) | ordering unless the sentence is about this target’s placement. “Below $n^*$” is a numeric comparison; “we must show” is usually about research, not chapter order. | . Two failure modes survive a verbatim quote, so check both before declaring: . | False locator. “the functor of the next subsection” where the target is 21 sections and ~300 blocks away. The prose defers; it does not defer this far, and the edge is a real defect. | Mis-aimed deferral. The quoted sentence hands off to a different block than the edge under review. A deferral pointed elsewhere cannot exempt this one. | . Both are about the declared case only. A derived pointer is aimed by the link itself, so it cannot be mis-aimed, and it carries no exemption to abuse. Two rules police the field: foreshadows-resolve (every target must exist) and foreshadows-not-self. The foreshadows-point-forward criterion catches a target the reader has already passed, which is either a prerequisite filed in the wrong field or an inert back-reference.

780375721c6a.title: A block’s uses[] may be carrying the whole family
780375721c6a.content: Never judge an entry from the block’s own .md alone. A block is the head of a family — X-proof, X-interpretation, X-tableN-data — and the dependency you are looking for is often in a child while the declaration sits on the parent. | Table children. Pointer-style blocks (“See Table 3”) keep their substance in tbl:…-data. A name-and-notation search of the parent’s .md reports an absence that is not real. | Proof children. A proof cites what the statement assumes. The parent’s prose may never name a target its proof child cites by label; if the proof declares no uses[] of its own, the parent’s entry is the sole record of the dependency, and deleting it as “unsupported by the prose” erases the edge entirely. | . So before removing an entry, check whether any child leans on the target, and whether that child declares anything itself. An entry that looks like dead weight on the parent may be the family’s only declaration. Searching for the target’s words also misses a lean on the target’s object — a source writing “the canonical $\tilde w_\lambda$” depends on whatever defines the undeformed $w_\lambda$, whether or not it ever says so.

978f27c0c632.title: Sibling parity is evidence only until a bulk edit touched the family
978f27c0c632.content: “All the siblings declare nothing, so declaring it here would be the anomaly” is evidence only if no bulk operation has run over the family: a bulk edit (for example a transitive-prune pass) produces parity by construction, so parity cannot distinguish a shared convention from shared damage. Before resting on it, check the family’s history, not just the block’s: . git log --oneline -- <chapter>/<sibling>.ts # for two or three siblings . A convention shows up as blocks that were authored empty. Damage shows up as one commit emptying all of them on the same day. If the emptiness has a single commit behind it, parity tells you nothing about intent. The same caution applies to any evidence drawn from what “the corpus does”: a corpus that has been swept is a record of the sweep as much as of the authors.

68f561dc5f6b.title: One reading is not the standard
68f561dc5f6b.content: A single careful pass is not enough: on re-review, destructive uses[] verdicts and foreshadow declarations are overturned often, and keyword search over the .md alone misses real dependencies. Use two readers who cannot see each other’s verdicts for anything that edits the graph, and treat agreement as the signal. Where they disagree, or where either is unsure, leave the edge alone: a wrongly deleted editorial edge silently corrupts every ordering metric computed from the graph. A retarget carries both burdens. It asserts this edge is wrong and that one is right, so it needs evidence for each half separately. When only the second half holds, it is an addition, not a swap.

33eb594369fd.title: Reading the mechanical findings first
33eb594369fd.content: Run the script half before adjudicating — it is cheap and it changes what you should look at: . bun run pipeline/qa-checkers-uses.ts # via qa-sweep --axis uses . | Mechanical finding | What it means for your review | . | uses-editorial-hygiene fail — unresolvable label | A dangling reference. Fix the label or add the missing block before judging completeness; the graph is wrong until you do. | . | uses-editorial-hygiene warn — transitive redundancy | Tidiness only. The graph is correct, just not minimal. Do not let it distract from the completeness question. | . A content type with a formal layer adds its own advisory finding here; the layer that ships it says how to read it.

e04fd8fb4c82.title: Interaction with other skills
e04fd8fb4c82.content: | Skill | Interaction | . | content-graph | Owns the graph the mechanical checks read | . | prepare-merge | Runs the uses axis as part of the content gates | . A content type’s own skills that consume or extend this relation are named by the layer that ships the type, which links down to this skill.

b99fe9908cba.title: uses[] Editorial Review
b99fe9908cba.content: Generated from cat-harness/skills/authoring/authoring-core/uses-editorial-review.md — do not edit here. ✎ Edit this page’s source .

3547372f77bf.title: uses[] against the formal graph
3547372f77bf.content: The harness skill uses-editorial-review audits uses[], the editorial relation: what a reader must have read first. It says that a content type with a formal layer derives a second relation, and that the layer shipping the content type holds the comparison. This is that comparison for a paper folio, whose formal layer is Lean.

819cdadc02c9.title: Two relations, diverging correctly
819cdadc02c9.content: uses[] is not the formal dependency graph. What a proof actually invokes is machine-derived from lean.ref (see cat-harness-tools/pipeline/content-graph.ts). The two relations are different questions and they diverge in both directions, correctly: . | Situation | Formal edge | Editorial edge | Correct? | . | Proof calls a simp lemma / typeclass instance | yes | no | yes — nobody reads about it | . | Theorem motivated by an example it never cites | no | yes | yes — the reader needs the motivation | . | Definition the statement is phrased in terms of | yes | yes | yes | . | Library lemma pasted into uses[] from Lean | yes | yes | no — pollution, see below | .

13f75dc53179.title: Never populate uses[] from the Lean graph
13f75dc53179.content: The harness rule is general: never populate uses[] from a machine-derived graph. For a paper folio that graph is the Lean dependency graph. When you review, do not open the Lean file to decide what belongs in uses[]; the question is about the reader, not the proof term. A simp lemma, an instance, or a library lemma the prose never mentions that appears in uses[] is the pollution case, and it fails (major).

f49caae218de.title: The advisory finding uses-formal-coverage
f49caae218de.content: | Mechanical finding | What it means for your review | . | uses-formal-coverage warn — formal-only targets | Advisory. A list of blocks the proof leans on that the narrative never introduces. Read each one and ask whether the narrative owes the reader an introduction. Most will not — that is the expected answer. Never bulk-apply these to uses[]. | . uses-formal-coverage returns n/a when the Lean Atlas cache is absent; an empty formal edge set means the data was unavailable, not that the block is clean. When an exposition gap is real . If uses-formal-coverage surfaces a formal dependency and, reading the narrative, you agree a reader is left stranded — the fix is usually prose, not a uses[] entry: introduce the object, or cite the result inline. Add to uses[] only when the reader genuinely must go read that other block first. Record the reasoning in the sidecar notes either way, so the next reviewer does not re-litigate it.

9b3567e78de0.title: Skills here that consume the editorial relation
9b3567e78de0.content: | Skill | Interaction | . | detangler-integration-watcher | Consumes the editorial relation for ordering metrics — a polluted uses[] corrupts its output | . | proof-gap-audit | An exposition gap here often coincides with an inter-proof gap there | . | proof-simplifier | Extracts shared lemmas; new blocks need uses[] entries authored, not derived | .

5cbc800f2594.title: uses[] against the formal graph
5cbc800f2594.content: Generated from folio-assistant-sci/skills/content/folio-paper-adapter/uses-formal-comparison.md — do not edit here. ✎ Edit this page’s source .

0d07b5ed0993.title: Overview
0d07b5ed0993.content: This skill checks a key structural invariant of the paper: every result block of a designated class must trace back to a designated anchor definition through the uses[] dependency DAG. The anchor is typically the bridge definition between the project’s foundational layer and its downstream predictions. A result block that does not connect to the anchor is either: . | Missing dependency declarations in its uses[] array, or | Genuinely independent of the anchor (rare — flag for review). | . Configure two things per project: the anchor label (the definition every claim must reach) and the result class (which block kinds / tags are required to connect).

1c3f80e128cb.title: Scope
1c3f80e128cb.content: The verification covers the configured result class, for example: . | Block kinds checked | Where to look | . | proposition, conjecture | the results chapters | . | remark with a configured observational tag | all chapters | . | definition with a configured tag | wherever introduced | .

4ab2a1818670.title: Algorithm
4ab2a1818670.content: Step 1: Collect result blocks . Scan all .ts manifest files under the paper directory for blocks matching the configured class — provable blocks in the results chapters, or any block whose tags include a configured tag. Step 2: Trace each block’s dependency chain . For each result block, do a breadth-first traversal of uses[], resolving labels to .ts files and reading their uses[] in turn. Stop when: . | the anchor label is found → CONNECTED; | a leaf (empty uses[] or already-visited node) is reached without finding the anchor → continue to the next branch; | all branches exhausted → GAP. | . Set a maximum traversal depth a couple hops beyond the deepest known chain. Step 3: Classify results . | Status | Meaning | Action | . | CONNECTED | traces to the anchor | none | . | GAP | no path found | add a missing uses[] entry or flag for review | . | ISOLATED | empty uses[] on a result block | add dependencies | . Step 4: Report . Output a table: . | Block label | Kind | Status | Shortest path | Action needed | . For GAPs, suggest which intermediate block should be added to uses[] to restore connectivity. Common fix patterns: a result about external/measured data → add the anchor directly; a result about a derived quantity → add the relevant intermediate definition; a conjecture about structure → check whether a known foundational definition provides the link.

acf0618a547f.title: Known dependency chains
acf0618a547f.content: Maintain, per project, a table of the verified paths from key result blocks to the anchor (direct 1-hop connections and the longer indirect chains). This serves as the regression baseline: a path that was CONNECTED and becomes a GAP signals a dropped uses[] edge. Record the anchor’s own upstream chain to the foundational axioms too, so the anchor itself is grounded.

709637d1d62c.title: Tabulated-data connectivity
709637d1d62c.content: Data tables (formula tables, periodic/summary tables) are result blocks too — they tabulate predicted quantities derived through the anchor. Every such table must trace to the anchor. Record the known table blocks and their connection paths in the same baseline table.

ea68d24f9c48.title: Checklist
ea68d24f9c48.content: . | All provable blocks of the result class trace to the anchor | All blocks carrying a configured result tag trace to the anchor | No result block has an empty uses[] array | The report table is complete with a shortest path for each block | GAPs have suggested fixes with specific uses[] entries to add | .

10983bce8a06.title: Visual diff — see a figure change
10983bce8a06.content: Skill id: visual-diff · Package: sdlc-core . For a figure, a diagram, a table, an equation or a simulator, the change a reviewer must judge is how the block LOOKS. The Markdown or SVG diff of a recoloured bar chart is noise. So the staging job pictures each such block on both sides, and the review page shows the pictures. For a before/after of anything the staging job does not picture (page chrome, scroll behaviour, a PDF page, an IG page, a slide), and for the rules every reviewer-facing pair follows, see before-after-preview.

8322a8c6ec6f.title: Design rules
8322a8c6ec6f.content: . | A Skill and a Tool, built into the processes. The steps live in the folio-block-screenshots Tool and in this skill. The staging workflow and the review process CALL them; nobody copies them. | No new dependency. The pictures are taken with Playwright, which the platform already uses, and the comparison runs in Chromium’s own canvas, so nothing new needs a licence. | One key or one click; never a drag. The page offers four views as radio buttons, not a slider. | .

d27455393041.title: What the reviewer sees
d27455393041.content: On the review page, a visual block opens on “Pictures, before and after”. It shows: . | a sentence stating how much changed: “12.3% of the block’s pixels changed”, or “No pixel changed beyond anti-aliasing”, or “Only one side could be pictured”; | four views, each one click (or an arrow key): | . | view | shows | . | Changed pixels | the after picture faded to grey, with every changed pixel marked in magenta | . | Before | the block on the published site | . | After | the block on this preview | . | Both | before and after side by side | . When a build published no pictures, the block opens side by side (the live pages in frames) instead, because the page takes the first view that can run and lists the block’s kind.

52f3a98f1a44.title: What the percentage means, and must NOT be read as
52f3a98f1a44.content: | it is | it is not | . | the share of the block’s pixels, in the larger of the two pictures, that differ by more than a small tolerance (24 of 255 per channel, to absorb anti-aliasing) | whether the change is right. A one-pixel line through a chart can be the whole point | . | counted over the larger picture, so a block that grew counts the new area as changed | a measure of text change: a reworded caption moves many pixels | . | of the light theme only | a check of dark mode | . Zero means nothing changed that the eye would see. A block the ChangeSet lists as changed with 0% is still worth a look at its markup: the change may be in alt text, a label or a link.

4bb71b1f56c8.title: When a picture is missing
4bb71b1f56c8.content: A missing picture is said, never drawn blank: . | message | means | what to do | . | “Not on main: this block is new.” | an added block has no before | nothing: there is nothing to compare | . | “Its page is not in the published site” | the before side has no page for the block’s document | the document is new, or main was never published. A folio publishes main when its staging caller lists push to main; the build log warns when _main-site.json is absent | . | “Its anchor is not on the … page” | the page exists, but has no <a id="<label>"> for the block | the block was renamed without renamedFrom, or the build dropped it. Check the id-stable QA criterion | .

ad29be79dee9.title: How a picture is taken
ad29be79dee9.content: The site build writes an empty <a id="<label>"> before each labelled block. There is no element that wraps the block. So a block’s picture is the region from its anchor down to the next anchor, as wide as the anchor’s container. A page with anchors out of order pictures the wrong region, so if a picture looks wrong, check the anchors first.

07a9bc8f5d00.title: The Tool
07a9bc8f5d00.content: # how many blocks would be pictured (no browser needed) bun run <platform>/cat-harness-tools/scripts/block-screenshots.ts --changeset _site/changeset.json --count # picture and compare bun run <platform>/cat-harness-tools/scripts/block-screenshots.ts \ --changeset _site/changeset.json --base pages --head _site --out _site . It writes visual-diff.json (folio-visual-diff/v1) and visual/*.png next to the site. The review page reads ../visual-diff.json.

131c75d242bf.title: Where it runs in the processes
131c75d242bf.content: . | folio-staging.yml, step “Picture changed figures, diagrams and tables”. It runs after the step “Choose the before side”, which picks: . | main’s site, at the publish branch’s root, published by the same workflow’s publish-main job on every push to main; | for a stacked PR, its base branch’s preview, branches/<base-slug>/, so the pictures and the ChangeSet compare with the same branch. When the base has no preview, main’s site is used and the banner, the review page and the PR comment all say so. | . It installs Chromium only when --count is above zero. | publish-main (same workflow) deletes only files its own manifest, _main-site.json, lists. branches/, _render-log/ and anything a person put at the root are never touched, and the first publish removes nothing. | content-change-review.bpmn, task Compare main vs staging. The reviewer’s comparison names this skill beside staging-review, so a reviewer handed that task is told the pictures exist. | .

aa29d20a4a91.title: Tests
aa29d20a4a91.content: . | cat-harness-tools/scripts/tests/block-screenshots.test.ts: the pixel compare, the tolerance, a size change, block selection, and page paths (including .. being refused). | the tools layer’s test/block-screenshots.e2e.ts: the whole Tool in Chromium. It covers a recoloured block, an unchanged block, a new block, and a missing anchor. | the tools layer’s test/review-visual.e2e.ts: the renderer, keyboard only. | .

4f50321fbd8f.content: | process | step(s) that name it | . | Committee review of a content change | Compare main vs staging | . | L2 component edit and review | Review the staged component (calls a sub-process) | . | SMART Guideline end to end | Review each L2 asset (before / after if adapted) (calls a sub-process) | .

a2225249da11.title: Visualizer loading — the page is layout, the graph is fetched

54150fa9be13.title: The rule
54150fa9be13.content: A generated page for a complex visualizer holds three things: . | Identity: the title, description and front matter that navigation, search and a link preview read. | Layout: headings, tabs and links, arranged by a template (liquid-templates). | A pointer: the KG file the content comes from, resolved by the generator. | . The content (a sidecar file, a node’s properties at length, a table derived from the graph) is fetched by the browser from the committed KG artefact. It is never copied into the page. Each copy is a second answer, free to drift from the first, and copied into a thousand pages it is most of the site’s bytes. kg-viewer is an instance of the pattern: one page that fetches its sibling graph document and computes back-links at load.

9ee96e3f28a8.title: What stays server-side
9ee96e3f28a8.content: Moving content client-side has costs: a reader without JavaScript loses it, a search index loses it, and so does the first paint. So these stay in the page: . | What navigation and search need: title, description, headings, and the link labels a reader scans for. | The way to reach the data without JavaScript: a link to the raw file, under <noscript> if nowhere else. A view that renders nothing without scripts must still say where its content is. | Anything short and unique to the page. A one-line value is not bloat, and fetching it costs a request to save a few bytes. | . Move a block when it is large or repeated and already a KG file. A block that would need a new file published just to be fetched is a design question for the owner, not a default.

1bd3df347389.title: Where the data is served from — served: true
1bd3df347389.content: The fetched file is the KG’s own, published verbatim. A directory declares served: true in its instance’s <instance>.json, and mount-instance-docs copies its bytes to /<instance>/<path> after Jekyll: no Liquid, no layout, no index page. Pages under the instance’s composed docs then reach it with a relative path. Never copy the file into docs/ beside the page instead — a gate flags it as an unknown file family in a docs directory. A generator whose data is not served writes no page that would fetch it, and says why.

f77822ee5426.title: How to fetch
f77822ee5426.content: . | Relative to the page’s own location, never via a configured base URL, so the same bytes work in production and in a staging preview (kg-viewer §”The page is generated, not committed”). | One shared loader per visualizer kind, published once and referenced by every page, never inlined in each page. | No dependencies: no CDN or framework. Same reason as kg-viewer: the data is this repository’s, and a third party in its trust boundary is at odds with that. | Three states on the page: loading, loaded, and could not load, which names the file and the error. A failed fetch that leaves a blank or a permanent “Loading…” is the silent-gap defect in another form. | .

ffa4aca87714.title: Stay equivalent to the render you replace
ffa4aca87714.content: When the page replaces another renderer’s page (for example the IG Publisher’s, which every phase must render equivalent to), compute the display the same way that renderer does, and then check it. For example, a page that shows a file as JSON.stringify(parsed, null, 2) differs from the file’s own bytes whenever the file has integer-like keys, which JavaScript orders first; showing the raw bytes would look right and be wrong.

0e3b151afb33.title: Printing and PDFs
0e3b151afb33.content: A browser prints the page as it is at that moment, so fetched content prints once it has loaded and not before: a PDF taken at domcontentloaded holds “Loading…”. | Every loader signals completion. Each counts itself in and out of window.__kgLoads, and the last one to finish sets <html data-kg-loaded>, on success or failure. A failed fetch still ends the wait, and its message is what prints. | Anything that prints or renders a PDF waits for that attribute, never for a fixed delay. That includes a Playwright page.pdf(), a PDF build step and a screenshot test. A page with no loader never sets it, so a tool that waits must first check whether the page loads one of the loader scripts. | A reader pressing Ctrl+P gets the page as loaded. The loaders are fast, but a print from a cold cache can still catch “Loading…”. That is a visible, honest state, not a blank. | .

2edbbbfbf578.title: Verify in a browser, not in the HTML
2edbbbfbf578.content: A static check cannot see fetched content: the built HTML holds only “Loading…”. Verification therefore means loading each page in a browser (Playwright, with the pre-installed Chromium) and comparing what it displays against the reference, as rendered-verification requires of any rendered artefact.

7c918ba6e4c2.title: Finding what to move
7c918ba6e4c2.content: A QA review over a built site: . | The mechanical half measures per-page bytes, blocks repeated across pages, and blocks matching a committed KG file, and writes a QA sidecar. | The agentic half judges each candidate against §”What stays server-side”. | . Repetition is a measurement, but whether a block may leave the page is a judgement.

232d5e9fe5fa.title: Do not
232d5e9fe5fa.content: . | Bake a KG file’s text into a page “for now”. That copy is what the next person will have to find and remove. | Move navigation or search terms client-side to save bytes. The saving is small and the loss is the page being findable. | Add a framework to fetch a JSON file. fetch and textContent are the whole loader. | .

2cf42ceecfb9.title: Vocabulary authority — one fact, one home, N renderings

e9616cc530d5.title: The rule
e9616cc530d5.content: A fact has ONE authoritative vocabulary. Every other vocabulary that carries it is a RENDERING, reached by a declared mapping with stated equivalence — never a second copy of the fact. | the fact | authoritative | why not the others | . | what a term MEANS | SKOS | the only candidate here whose subject IS a meaning | . | a resource’s metadata | Dublin Core | a document has a title; a concept has a preferred label. Different subjects | . | a clinical code’s operational semantics | FHIR CodeSystem / ValueSet / ConceptMap | versioning, designations with a use, expansion-as-release. SKOS has none of these | . | a release of any of the above | DCAT (held, not built) | it is not a term model at all; it describes a published dataset | . ┌──────────────────────────────┐ AUTHORITATIVE ──▶ │ skos:Concept = the MEANING │ └───────────────┬──────────────┘ skos:exactMatch / closeMatch / broadMatch / relatedMatch │ │ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ FHIR Code- Dublin Core schema.org TBX DCAT System (resource DefinedTerm termbase (release of (clinical metadata, (SEO / (CAT-tool any of these operations) bib records) discovery) exchange) as a dataset) . SKOS is the hub because its mapping properties exist for exactly this, and because it is the only one of the five whose subject is a meaning rather than an artefact, a record, or a distribution.

1c980bc2cebe.title: Pros and cons, as ruled
1c980bc2cebe.content: The reasons are measured against this corpus, not read off the specs. SKOS — adopted, authoritative for meaning . |   |   | . | Pro | Native JSON-LD. Multilingual labels first-class. notation is the code — TermGloss’s prefixed names. Mapping properties with stated equivalence. Carries the vocabulary terms and swimlane roles here | . | Con | No versioning model at all. No designation use. No post-coordination. Mapping properties carry no provenance | . The con is why convergence STOPS at SKOS. The failure this exists to prevent: reading “one glossary mechanism” as “one terminology mechanism” and binding an ICD-11 code to a skos:Concept with a notation and no version. That graph validates, publishes, and is wrong the next release. Dublin Core — kept, authoritative for resources . |   |   | . | Pro | ISO 15836. Qualified, repeatable and language-tagged as IRIS actually uses it — the content core’s schemas/dublin-core.ts is shaped by one measured record that does all three | . | Con | Two predicates overlap SKOS (below) | . schema.org — kept at 3 predicates; never a source of truth . |   |   | . | Pro | Search engines consume it. Native JSON-LD | . | Con | A publishing vocabulary, not a terminology one. DefinedTerm has name + description and stops: no versioning, no designation concept at all, no mapping semantics, no deprecation-with-successor | . It has no definitions to speak of. Used for 3 predicates (softwareVersion, codeRepository, text). Measuring usage: a naive grep for schema.org mostly matches json-schema.org (JSON Schema’s $schema keyword) and the schema:viz npm script. Never cite that count. TBX — not closed, and still not adopted . ISO 30042:2019 is published both as an ISO standard and as a free open industry standard; dialects and schemas are public. So “closed” is false and the ruling does not rest on it. |   |   | . | Pro | Genuinely open. Purpose-built for multilingual term entries | . | Con | Its niche is CAT-tool termbase interchange. This repo translates through gettext .po, not a termbase. XML-only | . Legitimate as an export if translators ever ask for a termbase. Rejected outright . SKOS-XL — it reifies labels to fix part of the designation gap and nothing else; the gap it does not fix is the one that matters. OWL — overkill: prose definitions, no reasoner in the pipeline. DCAT — held, for the render of whatever is landed on.

543834e5b59b.title: DC ↔ SKOS: the overlap, and what stops the drift
543834e5b59b.content: | pair | relation | . | dcterms:title ↔ skos:prefLabel | real overlap | . | dcterms:description ↔ skos:definition | real overlap | . | dcterms:subject → skos:Concept | not overlap — the designed JOIN. DC points at a concept | . | dcterms:hasPart, dcterms:source | no SKOS equivalent | . DC describes a RESOURCE. SKOS describes a CONCEPT. One object, one type, one naming predicate. They collide only where a node is genuinely both — such as the glossary document, which is a file and a skos:ConceptScheme, carrying both skos:prefLabel and dcterms:title. Two predicates for one fact, with nothing declaring which is authoritative, drift apart. The node is a concept scheme, so skos:prefLabel is the source and dcterms:title is the derived copy for resource-metadata consumers.

8619902d946e.title: Guidance for schema and data modelling
8619902d946e.content: . | Model in an open standard. Not a proprietary or house schema that happens to be convenient. | Proprietary input is mapped, not adopted. A mapping is a declared artefact with stated equivalence — not a rename in a loader. | Normalise FIRST. The first step of any mapping exercise is data normalisation. Mapping un-normalised data encodes the source’s accidents into the target and they are invisible afterwards. | The exercise runs as a defined process, not as a one-off script. | .

ded913b30f43.title: Where the pins live
ded913b30f43.content: cat-harness/external-schemas/ — one record per specification, pinning the edition and carrying the operative terms derived from the corpus, never hand-listed. bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/external-schemas.ts --check. A vocabulary can be used in more than one syntax (a BPMN file, a JSON-LD @context); a usage check that reads only one reports the other as absent.

79750e24c444.title: Vocabulary authority
79750e24c444.content: Generated from cat-harness/skills/kg/kg-core/vocabulary-authority.md — do not edit here. ✎ Edit this page’s source .

ad11fe0a6506.title: Read the voices before the first sentence, not after the first review
ad11fe0a6506.content: A voice is an editorial register — spelling, punctuation, terminology, how a normative statement is phrased. Get it right while drafting; correcting it afterwards means rewriting prose somebody has already reviewed. bun run cat check:voices # what this instance ships, and how many rules each carries . The active set is in the instance’s config, its index.config.json entry: . { "voices": { "active": ["milnor"] } } . An empty or absent list means no voice, and that is a real answer. The platform’s own documentation activates none. Do not add one because a voice exists.

1bd8ce2e7c8d.title: What to load, and what to do with it
1bd8ce2e7c8d.content: Each voice’s rules carry three things you need while writing: . | terminology — preferred/deprecated pairs. Apply these as you type; a terminology change ripples into every sentence built around the old word. | patterns — what the mechanical check will look for, i.e. which constructions will be questioned. | judgementOnly: true — no lexical check can decide it, so nobody will catch it for you. These are the rules to hold in mind rather than fix on a later pass. | .

00dab5fe8a8b.title: The rules most often broken by drafting on instinct
00dab5fe8a8b.content: The rules worth knowing in advance are the ones where instinct is wrong. For example, under the science layer’s milnor voice, “clearly” is fine in a mathematical block when it routes the reader away from a routine verification; do not write around it to appease the checker. This skill restates no voice’s rules: each rule belongs to the instance that derived it, with the publication, page and verbatim quote it was read from, and a copy here would lose that citation — and the uncited copy is the one a reader meets first and nothing can check. To learn which of your voices’ rules are counterintuitive, open the voices.

61f629532f31.title: When two active voices disagree
61f629532f31.content: Rules are unioned, not merged, and both stand. If honouring one would break the other, that is a finding for the author and not something to resolve silently in the prose — say which two rules and which voices, and let the editor decide. A silent choice hides a genuine conflict between two documents the folio has adopted.

ab52658dfd1a.title: Do not
ab52658dfd1a.content: . | Do not apply a voice the folio has not activated. An unasked-for register produces confident findings against prose never written to it. | Do not treat a voice as a substitute for the base house voice. Voices overlay one-voice-style-guide.md; they do not replace it. | Do not add a rule to a voice while drafting. A voice rule needs a citation that resolves (check:voices enforces it) — a rule you inferred from the prose you are writing is circular. | .

ae7cdb5a99f2.title: Voice authoring guidance
ae7cdb5a99f2.content: Generated from cat-harness/skills/authoring/authoring-core/voice-authoring-guidance.md — do not edit here. ✎ Edit this page’s source .

4c7fc08fc04b.title: The axis you are adjudicating
4c7fc08fc04b.content: Six criteria in pipeline/qa-criteria-registry.ts describe one house voice: . | criterion | what it matches | severity | . | voice-status-leak | status markers and derivation-status speech in body prose | critical | . | voice-scholarly-default | second-person address, lecturer-cadence openers, paper-past-tense narration | major | . | voice-author-notes-pollution | status banners, PR/commit refs, agent names, ISO dates | major | . | voice-emoji-content | emoji as content outside tables | major | . | voice-first-person-work | first-person work tone — “we’ll add”, “let me”, “needs more work” | major | . | voice-editorializing | “surprisingly”, “it is worth noting that”, “rather than merely …” | minor | . They are heuristics over phrase lists. A match is a question, not a verdict; a reviewer entry on the same sidecar confirms or overrules it.

2e885e7169a7.title: The scoping question comes first, and it is usually the answer
2e885e7169a7.content: Every criterion above was written for a paper: a scholarly artefact in third person, where a status marker really is a leak of the work tracker into the published text. A criterion without profiles scoping also runs over documentation, whose register addresses the reader: “you need bun, latexmk and Lean” is a correct sentence in a prerequisites page and a voice-scholarly-default match. Ask which is true before touching the prose: . | The register is wrong for this genre. Fix the passage. | The criterion does not belong in this genre. Add profiles: ["paper"] to it in the registry. One edit clears the finding for every document folio and records why. | The criterion belongs and this block is an exception. Record a reviewer entry on the sidecar saying why. It leads the criterion, so the block reads pass with the reasoning attached, and nothing is silently rewritten. | . Many instances of one criterion across many guide pages is evidence about the criterion’s scope, not about the authors.

7a265c155bbb.title: What the criterion cannot know
7a265c155bbb.content: The checkers match text. They do not know what the page is about. Typical false positives: . | voice-status-leak on a page that is a deliberate inventory of gaps (**Not yet implemented:** is its subject, not a leak). | voice-status-leak on prose about a work-plan lane: prose about a to-do store contains the words of a to-do store. | voice-emoji-content inside a transcript of an agent session, quoted as data. | . Each is a criterion reading a quotation as an assertion, and the reviewer entry says so in those words.

ffe3209fd9ec.title: Adjudicating one finding
ffe3209fd9ec.content: . | Open the block, not just the evidence line. The sidecar quotes one line; the register is a property of the passage around it. | Name the genre. Paper, guide, reference, transcript. That decides which of the three outcomes applies before you read another word. | Record the outcome where the next reader will find it — a prose edit, a registry edit with profiles, or a reviewer entry. A finding left open comes back on the next sweep. | Re-run the sweep — bun run pipeline/qa-sweep.ts --root docs/source — so the sidecar, the icon and the panel agree with what you decided. | .

635899013f47.title: Where the open findings are
635899013f47.content: Tracked in the work plan, one item per criterion, each carrying its blocks with file, line and the matched text: . beans list | grep "Voice axis" . The evidence itself lives in <block>.qa.json beside each block, and is published per block on the docs site: the QA icon opens the criterion, and the criterion opens the witness that ruled on it — which checker, at which script_hash, and whether the verdict still matches the file on disk.

1f68be504ccb.title: Do not
1f68be504ccb.content: . | Do not edit prose to silence a criterion you believe is out of scope. That hides the scoping defect and costs the next folio the same argument. | Do not mass-apply one finding’s resolution across its siblings without reading them; one criterion can fire for different causes. | Do not treat critical as “fix first”. Severity ranks the criterion’s authors’ concern, not the confidence of this match. | Do not delete a finding from a sidecar. The sweep rewrites its own entries; a hand-removed one comes back with no record that anyone looked. | .

ac09325c7ff4.content: | process | step(s) that name it | . | Narrative review | Adjudicate the voice findings (calls a sub-process) | .

54bc6757f6e5.title: Voice editorial review
54bc6757f6e5.content: Generated from cat-harness/skills/authoring/authoring-core/voice-editorial-review.md — do not edit here. ✎ Edit this page’s source .

70ace6ffd2b5.title: What you are reviewing, and against what
70ace6ffd2b5.content: One block, against the rules of the voices the folio has activated — not every voice it ships. The instance’s config (its index.config.json entry) holds the list; an empty list means there is nothing for this skill to do and that is a pass, not a gap. bun run cat check:voices # the voices, their rule counts, and that every citation resolves .

0d1a9f789467.title: The rule’s citation is the argument, so open it
0d1a9f789467.content: Every voice rule carries a source that resolves to a real file — a library/<doc>/sections/<section>.md for a rule read from an ingested document, or a path for a house standard. It also carries the quote the rule was read from. Open the citation before upholding a finding. | A reviewer who has read the source can say why the rule applies to this block. | The rule may be wrong. A rule derived from a document can misread it. If the quote does not support the rule, the rule is the defect and the work item goes against the voice, not against the block. | .

2e939233053f.title: Three outcomes, as with the house voice axis
2e939233053f.content: Identical to voice-editorial-review: . | The finding stands — the register is wrong for this block. Fix the prose. | The rule does not apply to this content — record it, and consider whether the rule needs appliesTo scoping on the voice. One scoping edit beats many per-block overrules. | The rule applies and this block is an exception — a reviewer entry on the sidecar saying why. It leads the criterion, so the block reads pass with the reasoning attached and nothing is silently rewritten. | .

a81044ea636d.title: A mechanical match is a question
a81044ea636d.content: A pattern is a regex over text; it does not know what the block is about. Examples of non-defects it matches: . | voice-scholarly-default on documentation pages whose register is correctly second-person. | voice-editorializing on merely inside a comparative, where the contrast is the block’s claim. | voice-editorializing on clearly used as proof economy. | . Verify before upholding, and when a rule fires repeatedly across a corpus on the same non-defect, that is evidence about the RULE.

50841bf0ffc6.title: Recording the verdict
50841bf0ffc6.content: Voice findings go on the block’s QA sidecar like any other, through the same writer, so the icon and the published witness agree with what you decided: . bun run pipeline/qa-merge-findings.ts --file findings.json . insertAdjudication places your entry ahead of the script entry, because list[0] is a criterion’s effective verdict. The script’s entry is kept beneath yours, because the disagreement between a checker and a reviewer is information.

dc6c0f1715a0.title: Do not
dc6c0f1715a0.content: . | Do not uphold a finding you have not traced to its quote. A rule that misreads its source is the failure this design exists to prevent. | Do not review against a voice the folio has not activated. | Do not delete a script finding from a sidecar. The sweep rewrites its own entries; a hand-removed one returns with no record that anyone looked. | Do not resolve a conflict between two active voices in the prose. Both rules stand: name them and let the editor decide. | .

c0ef40f271db.title: /watch — background watcher with integration check
c0ef40f271db.content: A unified watcher that handles branches (poll git ls-remote) and change proposals — pull requests, PRs — (subscribe to their activity through the session platform; subscribing is not a forge operation). On every event, walk the §3 integration checklist and either act, defer, or flag the user.

87e6b1e1eb2c.title: Invocation
87e6b1e1eb2c.content: The user’s request maps to one of three modes; pick the right one without asking: . | user phrase | mode | how | . | “watch main” / “watch upstream” / no target | branch:main | poll origin/main every 5 min | . | “watch PR 516” / “watch the PR” / “watch this PR” | pr:N | subscribe to its activity — the session platform’s subscription (event-driven) | . | “watch branch foo/bar” / “watch claude/x-y” | branch:foo/bar | poll origin/foo/bar every 5 min | . | “watch foo/bar PR 42” | pr:42 + maybe branch | subscribe + poll | . If ambiguous, default to branch:main.

00ffa003782e.title: 1.  Stash the baseline
00ffa003782e.content: Before arming anything, record the current state so the §3 review compares cleanly: . # Explicit refspec, ALWAYS. `git fetch origin <BRANCH>` writes FETCH_HEAD and # refreshes refs/remotes/origin/<BRANCH> only when the clone's configured # refspec covers it — and exits 0 either way. A baseline read from a tracking # ref that was never updated is not a baseline. git fetch origin "+refs/heads/<BRANCH>:refs/remotes/origin/<BRANCH>" 2>/dev/null # Sanitize branch name for use in a file path: replace `/` with `_` # (e.g. `feature/foo` → `feature_foo`). Without this, branches with # slashes silently land in non-existent directory trees. SAFE_BRANCH=$(printf '%s' "<BRANCH>" | tr '/' '_') git rev-parse "origin/<BRANCH>" > "/tmp/_watch_baseline_${SAFE_BRANCH}.sha" . For PR mode, instead capture the latest PR head SHA: read PR N with the read change proposal forge-operation Tool and stash its head commit SHA.

601f170318ab.title: 2.  Arm the watcher
601f170318ab.content: Branch mode — Monitor with poll loop . Use the Monitor tool, persistent: true, 5-minute poll: . Monitor: description: "origin/<BRANCH> new commits" persistent: true command: | BRANCH="<BRANCH>" last=$(git ls-remote origin "$BRANCH" | cut -f1) while true; do cur=$(git ls-remote origin "$BRANCH" 2>/dev/null | cut -f1) if [ -n "$cur" ] && [ "$cur" != "$last" ]; then git fetch origin "$BRANCH" 2>/dev/null # one line per new commit, oldest first git log --reverse --oneline "$last..$cur" | head -20 last=$cur fi sleep 300 done . Each new commit becomes one notification line. PR mode — activity subscription . Subscribe to the PR’s activity through the session platform (in a Claude Code remote session, its PR-activity subscription). This is not a forge operation, so no forge Tool node offers it. Already event-driven — no polling needed. The harness delivers <github-webhook-activity> events for comments, CI status, reviews, and merges. See the existing PR-subscription guidance in the system prompt for handling.

74025cf2f1d8.title: 3.  Per-event integration checklist
74025cf2f1d8.content: For every notification (branch commit or PR event), run through these four questions in order — stop at the first “no” or “no action”: . Q1 — Should we integrate? . | Is the change on a file we touch in this branch? Quick check: git diff --name-only HEAD <NEW_SHA> -- $(git diff --name-only $(git merge-base HEAD origin/main)..HEAD). | If yes and the change is small, rebase / pull now. | If yes but large, defer until the immediate task ships and add a TODO. | If no overlap, skip Q2/Q3/Q4 and acknowledge with a one-liner. | . Q2 — Does it conflict? . | Try a dry rebase in a fresh worktree. Use mktemp -d so the path is unique (avoids collisions with previous failed runs and with parallel /watch invocations) and clean up unconditionally via trap: . PROBE=$(mktemp -d /tmp/rebase-probe.XXXXXX) trap 'git worktree remove --force "$PROBE" 2>/dev/null; rm -rf "$PROBE"' EXIT git worktree add "$PROBE" HEAD >/dev/null ( cd "$PROBE" && git rebase "origin/<BRANCH>" ) status=$? # trap fires on EXIT . | Conflicts (status != 0) → first attempt auto-resolve for the recurring drift-conflict pattern (see §2a below); only flag the user if auto-resolve fails or the conflict is non-trivial (overlapping logic edits, schema rewrites, etc.). | . §2a — Auto-resolve drift-conflict pattern (CI-regenerated artifacts) . Some artifacts (*.witness.json sidecars, generated caches, derived reference files) are routinely regenerated by the CI validate job and frequently conflict on rebase against fast-moving main. These conflicts are always the same shape: our branch’s committed artifact was regenerated against an older main; main now has a fresher version. Resolution is mechanical: regenerate against current main and recommit. The recipe (run on the real branch, not the probe worktree): . # When `git rebase origin/<BRANCH>` halts with a regenerated artifact # in the conflict list, do NOT hand-merge the JSON. Instead: # 1. If the conflicting commit was a pure regen of these generated # artifacts (no other changes), skip it — main already has the regen: git diff --name-only --cached | grep -qE '\.witness\.json$' && \ ! git diff --name-only --cached | grep -vE '\.witness\.json$' && \ git rebase --skip # 2. Otherwise, abort the rebase, regenerate the artifacts # on the rebased branch, then re-rebase. This produces a clean # apply because the regenerated artifact now matches main. git rebase --abort git rebase origin/<BRANCH> # re-rebase, skipping bad commits as above # regenerate the affected artifacts via the project's generator(s), e.g. bun run cat regen git add <regenerated-artifact-paths> git commit -m "Regen generated artifacts post-rebase against latest main" git push --force-with-lease . Only flag the user if: . | The conflict is in a source file (.py, .lean, .ts, .md) — those are real semantic conflicts that need human judgment. | The conflict is in a generated artifact whose regenerated content differs substantively from a simple drift (e.g. a numerical value changed, not just a timestamp/hash) — that means a CI-run generator on main produced different output, which deserves a closer look before blindly accepting. | The auto-resolve recipe itself fails (regen script errors out, push rejected for non-fast-forward reasons, etc.). | . For generated artifacts specifically: if upstream regenerated files our branch also touched, prefer rebase-and-regenerate over hand-merging. Drift is structural; merging is fragile. Q3 — Can we reuse? . Apply four reuse questions: . | Definitions / lemmas / helpers / witnesses — does the new commit add something our branch is duplicating, paraphrasing, or reinventing? Replace with uses[] / a citation and delete the local stand-in. | Proofs — does a new lemma or tactic discharge a hypothesis, collapse a chain, or close a gap? Apply via the project’s proof-simplification / build-fix skills. | Exposition — does our .md re-derive what main now defines upstream? Replace with a forward-reference; route through the project’s accuracy / readability skills. | Computation — does a new script or witness supersede a hand-rolled loop or stale witness in our branch? Swap in and regenerate the artifact. (See §2a for the routine drift-conflict pattern.) . | When the upstream commit adds or modifies a prop: / thm: / lem: / cor: block (or its sibling formalization), delegate to the project’s compute-integration watcher to check whether the new claim is wired into the production compute chain. Capture the verdict here and feed it into Q4. | . | . Q3a — Did upstream land a new skill file? . For each main-refresh, check whether a skill directory the instance declares in its kg graph (skill_list names them) gained a new file between this branch’s prior baseline and the new origin/main: . git diff --name-only --diff-filter=A "$LAST_BASE..origin/main" -- <skill-dirs> . For each new skill file: . | Read its frontmatter — extract name, roles, description, and any inherits field. | Match against branch scope — does the skill’s description overlap with what this branch is doing? Heuristics: . | skill description mentions a file kind / domain / pattern that appears in this branch’s git diff origin/main..HEAD --name-only, OR | skill is a new integration-watcher child (inherits: local/integration-watcher) and your branch is itself an integration-watcher PR, OR | skill is a content-block QA skill (e.g. one-voice-*, proof-*, compute-*) and your branch touches .md / .ts / .lean content blocks. | . | Surface to the user via AskUserQuestion with the standard 3-chip pattern: . New skill <name> landed on main: . <one-line description from frontmatter> . This branch’s scope overlaps because <one-line match rationale + file paths>. 1) Adopt now — invoke the skill on the relevant subset of this branch’s diff before continuing. 2) Defer to follow-up branch — record the decision and note for the next branch; don’t change this branch. 3) Not relevant — record so the watcher doesn’t re-prompt on future main-refreshes. | Record the decision as a note on the watcher’s work item (or in chat for the bare /watch flow) so subsequent main-refreshes don’t re-prompt for the same skill. | . This rule applies to skill files only. Skills landing on sibling PRs that haven’t merged yet do NOT trigger this check — only main commits count, mirroring the §2 “watch origin/main” scope. Q4 — Report or act? . | Acted (made the change): one-line summary + the new commit SHA. | Will act after current task: add a TODO with what + why. | Skipped: one-line reason (“no overlap”, “blocked on $TASK”). | .

3e0873940e69.title: 4.  Stop the watcher
3e0873940e69.content: Stop when the branch ships (PR merged, or you switch branches): . | Branch mode: call TaskStop on the Monitor task ID. | PR mode: the harness auto-unsubscribes when the PR merges/closes; otherwise unsubscribe through the session platform. | .

3cbefce7c6b7.title: 5.  Common upstream patterns (heuristics)
3cbefce7c6b7.content: . | Artifact drift: upstream regenerated generated artifacts (*.witness.json, caches) while we also modified them → rebase-and-regenerate, never hand-merge. | Toolchain version bumps: a dependency/toolchain hash changed → check our branch’s toolchain pin aligns before continuing a build. | Schema or generator changes: run bun run cat regen before continuing. | Routine review-cycle commits (Gemini/Copilot fixes on unrelated PRs): almost always Q1 = no overlap = skip with one-liner. | .

c7076535ab68.title: 5b.  Monitor-timeout recovery (MANDATORY when re-arming)
c7076535ab68.content: Background Monitors time out ([Monitor timed out — re-arm if needed]). Do not just re-arm and continue — between the last event and the timeout, main may have moved substantially. Mandatory steps on timeout-recovery: . # Compare the stashed baseline against the WATCHED BRANCH's actual head. # # This fetched `main` and then measured `origin/<BRANCH>` — a different ref # from the one it refreshed. The recovery step that exists to catch what was # missed while the watcher was down therefore compared the baseline against a # tracking ref nothing had updated, found them equal, and reported 0 missed # every time. Fetch the ref you are about to read, with an explicit refspec so # the tracking ref is actually written. git fetch origin "+refs/heads/<BRANCH>:refs/remotes/origin/<BRANCH>" 2>/dev/null SAFE=$(echo "<BRANCH>" | tr '/' '_') LAST=$(cat /tmp/_watch_baseline_${SAFE}.sha 2>/dev/null || echo "") CUR=$(git rev-parse origin/<BRANCH>) if [ "$LAST" != "$CUR" ]; then MISSED=$(git log --oneline "$LAST..$CUR" 2>/dev/null | wc -l) echo "MISSED $MISSED commits while watcher was down" git log --oneline "$LAST..$CUR" | head -10 # Update baseline AFTER reporting git rev-parse origin/<BRANCH> > /tmp/_watch_baseline_${SAFE}.sha fi . If MISSED >= 5 OR any missed commit touches a file in your branch’s diff, run the §3 integration checklist on the missed range BEFORE arming a fresh monitor. This catches main moving many commits ahead during a long focused session while the watcher is timed out.

1ce9aa5938fc.title: 6.  Output style
1ce9aa5938fc.content: Follow interaction-modality: . | One sentence per commit / event by default | Numbered choices when integration is non-obvious | Run small fixes proactively; flag big ones | .

b4a4481271a0.title: Where a proposal goes — docs/proposals/
b4a4481271a0.content: A design proposal is a document in docs/proposals/<slug>.md, with kind: proposal and a row in docs/proposals/index.md. Its assets go beside it, in docs/proposals/<slug>/ (wireframe candidates in docs/proposals/<slug>/wireframes/). It is committed on the feature branch, so the branch’s staging preview publishes it with the rest of the change. A proposal is kept and addressable because the decision it produced is cited later, and a citation needs a stable path.

e4517a017b0a.title: What a proposal is, and what it is not
e4517a017b0a.content: A proposal is the argument about what to build: the needs, the options, what each costs, and what was agreed. It is not reader documentation, so a page for a reader never depends on it: . | a reader-facing page states the rule and its reason, and does not link into docs/proposals/ for either; | the rule that came out of a proposal goes in the skill it governs, in a paragraph, because that is where an agent looks it up; | who decided it and when goes in that skill’s provenance log (<skill>.prov.jsonld), not in its narrative. | .

1361fe0570e3.title: Where each thing goes
1361fe0570e3.content: | what | where | . | a design proposal, an options analysis, an impact assessment | docs/proposals/<slug>.md | . | the discussion while it is open | a comment on the issue it is for | . | a harness feature’s agreed requirements, once the feature ships | docs/requirements/<slug>.md, by git mv from docs/proposals/ (crdm-requirements-workflow) | . | the rule a decision established | the skill it governs | . | who decided, when, and under which issue | the skill’s provenance log | . | structured content worth keeping but not publishing | fsh-guts/ — see fsh-guts | . | what a reader of the folio needs | docs/, outside proposals/ | .

4636a6e241a5.title: Where does this go? — the question, then the skill that answers it
4636a6e241a5.content: Skill id: where-does-this-go · Package: folio-core . This skill answers nothing. It is a switchboard: you arrive knowing you have something to put somewhere, and it tells you which of this repository’s filing rules you are actually standing in front of. The rule itself lives in its skill: every row below is a question and a pointer, never a summary of the answer, because a summary would be free to disagree with its skill.

391d90fed2a8.title: Why a router at all
391d90fed2a8.content: Each specialised answer is well argued in isolation, but an agent who has not realised they are, say, choosing a graph kind files by resemblance to the last thing they filed. An agent who does not know a rule exists cannot look it up; this table puts the rules side by side.

fdf26da50cca.title: The ten questions
fdf26da50cca.content: Read down the middle column until one matches what you are actually deciding. If two match, you have two decisions, not one — take them in the order below, because the earlier rows decide the object and the later ones decide its placement. | # | the question you are actually asking | who answers it | . | 1 | Is this a work item, a sign-off, or a code review? | issue-working §”What an issue is for, against its neighbours” | . | 2 | Is this feature work that needs a GitHub issue first? | crdm-detect §”Issue association” | . | 3 | What TYPE of work item is it, and under which parent? | todo-manager, and check:bean-parents enforces it | . | 4 | Does a work item for this already exist? | todo-manager §”Check before you create” | . | 5 | May I claim it — is a sibling already on it? | bean-coordination §”Claims are global via the branch store” | . | 6 | Which directory, and what KIND of graph does it hold? | content-context-and-state-graphs and directory-conventions | . | 7 | Is this an adapter, a profile, or a visualiser? | content-profiles | . | 8 | Does this belong in AGENTS.md or in a skill? | AGENTS.md §”What is specific to THIS layer” — always the skill | . | 9 | Is this a skill, or an agent’s memory? | agent-memory | . | 10 | Am I adding a new INSTANCE (a harness) or a new graph TYPOLOGY — and what does it owe, and how does it relate to the instances it sits beside? | instance-kinds first (most new things are not a new kind; the cat- / folio-assistant- / who- prefixes), then harness-requirements (the five obligations, and a node’s .json / .jsonld / .schema.json IRIs), associate-harness (needs vs associatedHarnesses) and instance-publication (ids and release IRIs, and which graph is published where, under which IRI, with which schema, and what is stripped) | . The count in the heading is a claim about the table beneath it: when a row is added, update it.

c7b566061ae2.title: Two rows that are easy to confuse, and the discriminator for each
c7b566061ae2.content: Rows 1 and 3. “Bean or issue?” and “what type of bean?” feel like one question and are not. The first asks what KIND OF OBJECT this is — a work item is the work plan, an issue is where a human signs off, a PR is where code is reviewed. The second only arises once row 1 has answered “bean”. Rows 6 and 7. Both sound like “what is this thing?”. Row 6 is about a DIRECTORY and its graph; row 7 is about a CONTENT TYPE and its vocabulary. The discriminator: row 6 asks what does a running process do with this — produce it, read it, or write it as it goes; row 7 asks whose vocabulary is this word from, and may this folio use it. A directory has no vocabulary and a block kind has no holds.

0da3b3f1b1fc.title: When no row matches
0da3b3f1b1fc.content: That is a finding, not a licence to improvise. Say so — in the turn, to the person — and propose where it would go if a new row existed. If the same unmatched question recurs, it has earned a row, and the route to adding one is surprise-to-corpus: the recurrence is the evidence, and the person decides.

8cbf1e9e270a.title: What this skill is NOT
8cbf1e9e270a.content: It is not a decision procedure you run every turn: a router consulted for every obvious filing gets skipped, taking the non-obvious cases with it. Reach for it when you notice yourself about to guess — the same trigger opening-brief uses.
